title: How Casper Failed & Why DTC Startups Lose Money
note: Rise-and-fall explainer on D2C economics: hype, unicorn, failed IPO, then the unit-economics diagnosis, closing on the irony of retail and the refused Target offer.
sections: The D2C model and investor hype
The numbers: losses and ad spend
Slow growth and slow mattress cycle
lines: through 2014 to 2018 Casper was everywhere on the internet flooding advertisements to every trending podcast website and YouTube video.
need a mattress by Casper?
not comfortable buying a mattress online that you've never seen or touched before?
no problem buy your Casper mattress today sleep on it and if you're not happy at any time return it for a full refund within your first 100 100 days.
no questions asked.

With a radically generous return policy and aggressive multi-million dollar advertising budgets, Casper quickly rose to fame as the flashiest and fastest growing online consumer brand hot out of Silicon Valley.
Venture capitalists fueled Casper's rise, as they were all really eager to showcase Casper as another shining example of technological innovation and business transformation.
Casper, Warby Parker, Dollar Shave Club were all pioneers of a new type of business model that venture capitalists were rarely obsessed with called direct-to-consumer.
Direct-to-consumer.
Direct-to-consumer.
Direct-to-consumer.
Direct-to-consumer.
To go direct-to-consumer.
The direct-to-consumer movement.
That direct-to-consumer.
Le D2C direct-to-consumer.
They're able to get those prices because it's direct-to-consumer.
That's right.
The D2C business model is simple.
One, you make a quality consumer product.
It can be something as simple as a pair of glasses, a razor, or in Casper's case, a mattress.
Two, you cut out the middleman retailer.
Three, you brand your product with sans serif font, pastel colors, and other hipster designs.
Four, you package that all onto a cool online website, and you sell your product direct to consumers at a low price.
On paper, the advantages of this D2C model look pretty strong.
Traditional consumer brands operate in a wholesale model, and so the only way that traditional consumer brands make money is by getting their products into retailers and selling in bulk quantities.

Since all these consumer brands are fighting with each other to get their products into the shelves of Target, Costco, Kroger's, Whole Foods, Sam's Clubs, Safeway, and there are only so many shelves to go around, these consumer brands end up designing their products to appeal, impress, and satisfy the retailers rather than actually solving the end consumer's need.

And so by By removing the retailer from the equation, D2C businesses in theory can design and offer products to consumers that are higher quality and cheaper than the kind of stuff they'd have to buy off the shelves of a target.

A D2C company can then promote its products very cheaply and efficiently through social media and sell them exclusively to customers over the internet, removing the need for real estate and storefronts.

Eager to ride on Silicon Valley's hottest trends, venture capitalists all over the world poured their money into D2C companies, all eagerly chasing this vision as this would redefine e-commerce as we know it.
Venture capitalists have poured over $3 billion to date into D2C companies.
Casper was the shining crown jewel and poster child for this business model, attracting $340 million in investment over five years.
The hype for Casper and the D2C business model got so big that even celebrities like Ashton Kutcher, Leonardo DiCaprio, Maroon 5, and 50 Cent all joined in as investors.

Even big retailers like Target couldn't ignore Casper's rise, and those executives became so smitten with the idea that acquiring Casper would inject freshness, quirkiness, and millennial appeal into its antiquated retail stores, which is something that Target has long since been obsessed with.
If we go back in time, you think about that Target guest, that Target shopper as the suburban housewife.
Now she's pulling up in the van with a couple of kids and they're certainly coming to our source today, but we're appealing much more to that millennial family.
Target offered to acquire Casper for $900 million, but quickly found that Casper's founders were not willing to settle for a purchase of anything lower than a billion dollars.
That shut everybody up.
Unable to match that price tag, Target settled for just being a pre-IPO investor.
And in just a few short years, Casper had become a true Silicon Valley unicorn with a pre-IPO valuation in 2019 of $1.1 billion.
Fast forward one year to 2020, where Casper was now making its long-awaited IPO debut on the public stock market.
But instead of the glamour and champagne, Casper's entry into the public markets was widely criticized as a desperate, downright embarrassing disaster.
The company ended up slashing its lofty billion-dollar valuation by 50% to $500 million in a last-ditch attempt to make the company palatable to public investors.

Since its IPO, Casper's struggles have continued, dropping another $100 million in its valuation, the stock price has dropped by 40% to date, they've shuttered down their European business, they've lost their COO and their CFO, and they've ended up laying off 21% of their workforce.
Casper's investors, including all the celebrities that had joined in at that billion dollar price tag before the IPO, have all ended up losing their money.
It's been an epic collapse for Casper, the one-time unicorn, darling of Silicon Valley, and the D2C business poster child.
A startup that no one could seemingly get enough of has now quickly become taboo in venture capital circles.
So what happened to Casper?
The answer lies in numbers.
As a private company, Casper had been able to spin the numbers to its unicorn status, but as soon as Casper went public, its true financial performance was laid out for everyone to see.
Casper had lost money in every year of its existence.
In 2017, negative 73 million, 2018 negative 92 million, 2019 negative 93 million, and 2020 negative 90 million.
Losing money is nothing new to Silicon Valley and tech startups these days.

To be honest, Wall Street has clearly shown an appetite in the past few years, and especially under COVID, to look past companies that were putting in losses and put hope in future growth, like at Tesla, AMD, Datadog, and Atlassian.
But in Casper's case, the reality is that it's not a tech company.
Casper sells mattresses at the end of the day, not software or hardware.
The average Casper mattress sells for about $700.
After paying off the supplier and the delivery costs to get it from their warehouse to your door, Casper makes about $377 from each mattress sold.
When you do that math, it actually gives Casper a very sexy and appealing 50% gross margin.
So what's the rub?
The catch is that Casper dumps all the money that it makes into advertising.
In 2017, Casper spent 91% of its gross profit on advertising.
In 2018, 80% of its gross profit on advertising.
2019, This means that every $1 Casper makes off of each mattress sale, $0.60 to $0.73 of that $1 is going back into Facebook, Spotify, or Instagram for ad.
That means that every company expense like salaries, R &D, warehouse, rent, delivery, website, design, customer support, all of those expenses have to come out of the company's pocket.
Advertising is ultimately meant to grow, not to sustain a business.
The nuance here is that online advertising itself has also dramatically evolved since Casper's founding in 2014.
In 2014 and 2015, when Casper was just getting off the ground, internet advertising and influencer marketing online was extremely affordable.
Running Facebook ads was a very easy, inexpensive, and effective way to target consumers, much cheaper than any billboard or television advertising ever was.
But as more companies have flocked to Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and other popular platforms to target consumers online, advertising has gotten saturated, competitive, and expensive.
It's no longer just Casper who's able to dominate the airways with $340 million of a war chest.

It's Casper and thousands of other D2C startups and big consumer brands like Unilever and Procter & Gamble all throwing in millions of dollars every year, targeting the same consumers, trying to hit the same demographics, and ultimately driving up advertising costs for everyone else.
In 2019 alone, it was reported that the cost per click for Facebook rose by nearly 93%.

To break this down into simple math, that means for every $1 a company used to put in to promote a Facebook advertisement, they would now need to put in at least $2 just to get the same result as before.

The saturation and explosion of online advertising costs have popped the bubble not just for Casper, but also for the hundreds and thousands of other D2C startups that had all been fundamentally dependent on these unsustainable business models that were reliant on cheap online advertising and an endless IV drip of venture capital.
But with the death of Brandless and the struggles of Honest Company, Everlane, and Dollar Shave Club, a lot of venture capitalists have begun to see their losses in D2C startups.
Casper currently spends $275 to $300 to acquire a new customer.

With the increasing competition from other mattress startups that have followed and copied Casper's identical business model, who are now aggressively competing for their same customers using the same online channels, Casper really has no choice but to keep throwing money into their advertising pit to stay competitive with their new competitors and to maintain their baseline growth.
So with this in mind, Casper's business model basically boils down to 1.

buy a mattress from China for $400, two, sell a mattress for $700, three, make $300 from that transaction, and then lose 20% of all the mattresses you sell every year thanks to your excessively generous 100-day return policy.

And then after that, you take your $300 in gross profit and you spend it on advertising, you spend another $300 on your administrative expenses, and you'll end up losing $200 for every mattress that you sell.
Now, Casper's massive advertising budget and strategy would be forgivable if all that spend was leading to a comparably large multiplier in revenue growth.
But between 2017 and 2018, Casper only grew its revenue by 43%.
From 2018 to 2019, that growth had fell down to 23%.
Between 2019 and 2020, growth under COVID was a measly 18%.

And that means that without even a one-to-one correlation between advertising dollar and revenue growth dollar, it's hard to imagine what light at the end of the tunnel is for Casper to reach profitability.
On top of that, the mattress industry reports that the average American only changes their mattress every nine to ten years.
So Casper's first customers came in 2015, and that was when the company had been pricing its product at the cheapest and had been advertising at the most aggressive levels.

With a 10-year-long deal cycle and product life for a mattress, it means that as an investor, you would have to wait until 2025 just to understand Casper's true consumer retention rate and standing in the mattress industry.
But more importantly, it sheds light into the possibility that growth for the mattress industry is maybe just that slow and constrained.
No amount of advertising is going to change the underlying market reality and consumer behavior.
The fastest growing sales channel for Casper today is currently, wait for it, retail.
Retail sales for Casper have grown 74% year over year and now accounts for 20% of the company's overall revenue.
In comparison, its traditional direct-to-consumer sales revenue has only grown by 20% in the same period of time.
Casper's retail sales aren't just beating their online sales when it comes to growth.
The average order for Casper is 15% higher in retail than it is online.
In the company's early days, the Casper founders were very prideful about never needing to open stores to grow their business.
how you'll sleep just seem very perverse to us.
50% off, always signs.
There's commission salespeople.
It's like worse than buying a used car.
You know, we're totally different from the ground up.
The shopping experience is completely different.
We only sell our product through our website, casper.com.
You can take your time, read about the product and how we developed it.
The customer experience is completely different from anything else and it's not confusing.
We designed it to be simple, straightforward, authentic and transparent with what we build and how we build it.
Well, it's just the ironic wall that Casper has run into here is that online growth is limited.
There are only so many people you can hit online before your endless spam of Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and podcasts just become exhausting and ineffective.
So brick and mortar, the very thing that Casper was invented to disrupt has now become that very slim bastion of light that the company's executives are hoping will save their business.
Casper isn't the only DTC brand doing this 180 of embracing the very thing it was trying to disrupt.
Everlane and Away, two other formerly hot DTC companies, have now found themselves opening stores and begging to get on the shelves of big retailers to try and grow their businesses.

Everybody loves to say you don't spend money on online, but the way it works now with Facebook and Instagram and how much it costs to acquire a customer, and then you have to ship it all, you end up, what online-only company is really profitable?
basically none of them.
That's the dirty secret.
With retail, when we move to customer first, we get to figure out which channel is right and do the right thing for the customer and be profitable.
Most recently, Casper shut down its European business to quote, focus on the American market.
But the numbers are pretty painful in that by all measures, the American market is barely growing and only becoming more competitive.
Casper's future as a company just looks very bleak and painful.
If you couldn't crack Europe, it's hard to imagine being able to crack any other major geographic market.
Turning down that $900 million offer from Target before the IPO just because it wasn't a billion dollars looks very regrettable by the day.

With investor sentiment at an all-time low, geographic expansion out of the equation, and the bursting of the D2C hype bubble, Casper, the once-untouchable Silicon Valley unicorn seems now destined to become forgotten in a sea of worthless penny stocks on the New York Stock Exchange.

title: How McDonalds Evolved from Boomers to Zoomers
note: Turnaround explainer: 2015 crisis, new CEO, then tests of what actually drove growth (franchising, delivery, celebrity meals).
sections: Worst year, CEO out, Easterbrook in
Rick and Morty and celebrity meals
Identity crisis resolved, number one again
lines: The year is 2015 and the burger wars are heating up.
For the very first time in history, McDonald's was no longer the undisputed king of fast food.
New competitors like Shake Shack and Five Guys were surging, beating the once-untouchable Golden Arches with the unique promise of quality over quantity.

In 2015, McDonald's had just continued the fan-favorite snack wraps, removed hot mustard from their McNugget lineup, and axed the bacon habanero ranch, bacon and cheese, and the deluxe quarter pounder with cheese from the menu.

To freshen things up, McDonald's rolled out a series of new items that same year in an effort to freshen up their old-school image, appeal to the modern health-conscious consumers, and to try to better compete with these upscale burger joints.
McDonald's newest product in 2015 was Create Your Taste, which was a program that let people build their own fancy $12 burgers with gourmet toppings like guacamole, mushrooms, and brioche buns.
McDonald's also added three more fancy sandwiches to the menu permanently, the Bacon Clubhouse, the Premium Crispy Chicken Clubhouse, and the Premium Grilled Chicken Bacon Clubhouse.
Even the dollar menu got its own fancy new addition in the jalapeno double.
Beyond the short-lived viral buzz of these new items, consumers were not about to start going to McDonald's for fancy burgers.
These new items were not only out of character for the Golden Arches, but also clear representation of the identity crisis that was happening at McDonald's leadership in the mid-2010.
A touchscreen kiosk, some fancy fry baskets, and some new burgers were not about to change that.

So McDonald's combined these new menu items with this massive multi million dollar marketing campaign led by MythBusters Grant Imahara where he went around to McDonald's factories to prove that McNuggets were not actually pink slime and the beef was made of real beef.

But even though Grant's documentary style ads were successful in their reach on social media, their engagement, they were informative and fun and entertaining to watch, it was also a very rare showing of transparency by McDonald's, consumers still weren't convinced.

With the rapid growth and popularity of fast casual dining, spearheaded by giants like Chipotle where you could get a more quality wholesome meal for just a few dollars more than what you'd pay for fast food, old legacy fast food companies like McDonald's were finding themselves in this fight or flight or sink or swim mode.
It's just a healthier option.
I feel like McDonald's is very just greasy, a bad reputation.
The ingredients are better.
There's more, there's like more selection on the menu.
I feel as though the meat's better, just everything in general is kind of more high quality as opposed to McDonald's.
Customers always vote with their wallets.
In 2015, McDonald's experienced the worst business performance in the company's 80-year history.
Now, when something bad happens in corporate America, heads will roll.
And so in this case, the McDonald's CEO retired shortly after, but basically what happened was the board asked him to either step down quietly or endure the public embarrassment of being fired.
And so the worst part for McDonald's is that that decline that they experienced in 2015, it was global in all markets, Europe, Asia, and the West, not just in the United States.

Steve Easterbrook, who was a longtime brand director and Brit known for leading McDonald's UK business, who had been with McDonald's since 1993, was appointed as the new CEO and tasked with turning around McDonald's in mid-2015.
Now, the business model of McDonald's is well known.
McDonald's is the largest owner of real estate on planet Earth with more property than even the Catholic Church.

And so here's the thing that most people don't realize is that everything that a McDonald's franchise owner sells, from the burger wrappers that you wrap your McDoubles in, to the fries, the burger buns, the napkins, even the stove that cooks the hamburger patties, the fryers that make the fries, the heating lamps that keep the fries warm, even the salt shakers and ice cream machine.
These are all items that franchise owners have to exclusively buy from McDonald's corporate.

So McDonald's, by being in control of the land, is able to milk the franchise operators for not only the rent but also making these franchise operators pay for everything that they need to operate mcdonald's from the food to the equipment and down to the cups.
since mcdonald's is a middleman there are really two customers they have to satisfy.
on one end the first obvious customer they have to satisfy is the actual end consumer who buys and eats mcdonald's.
the second is the franchise operator.
this is the person that actually runs the mcdonald's on day-to-day.
so they're the person who's in charge of hiring the staff cooking the food cleaning the store and paying the fees royalties and rent to McDonald's corporate.
So during the great decline of 2015, franchise operators were fed up with McDonald's.
They felt like the company at a corporate level was out of touch.
They were introducing all these expensive new items, fancy and healthy burgers that weren't selling and they were running ads that were really failing to bring consumers back in.

You know, those nice modern touchscreen kiosks that McDonald's pushed out for the Create Your Taste program, those ones where you could tap and customize your burger perfectly like a giant iPhone screen, those machines alone cost franchise operators $125,000 to install in their stores.

Now, six years later, since Steve took helm in 2021, Steve is no longer actually the CEO of McDonald's, having been fired for having an inappropriate relationship with an employee, which ironically violates the same code of conduct that he approved and mandated all other McDonald's employees to adhere to.

But despite the scandal, Easterbrook is still widely heralded as a progressive CEO who aggressively made the right moves to modernize McDonald's, and has been largely and fairly credited with turning around the company.
On his first day as CEO when he was appointed in 2015, Easterbrook didn't hold back on how poorly McDonald's had performed to date.
We can no longer afford to carry legacy structures, legacy commitments, or legacy attitudes.
That is why I'm changing the structure.
Our new structure will be simpler and more concentrated around the reality of where our operating income comes from.
In his five years as CEO, some of Easterbrook's biggest wins were rolling out all-day breakfast, removing artificial preservatives from McNuggets and McDonald's hamburgers.
running the first celebrity partnership meal in fast food with Rick and Morty.
pushing out a new dollar menu.
heavily investing in mobile first with the McDonald's app, embracing fast food delivery ahead of any other large fast food company.
running the well-received McDonald's worldwide campaign, and then cutting the fancy $12 cut Create Your Taste program.
But Easterbrook's track record at McDonald's was not without some failures.
He certainly pushed out a lot of items that really failed to stick on the McDonald's menu.

Things like mozzarella sticks, muffins, kale salad, donut sticks, buttermilk crispy chicken tenders, a signature crafted recipe, pico guacamole signature crafted sandwich, sweet barbecue bacon sandwich, maple bacon Dijon sandwich, and the spicy McNuggets.

Easterbrook's new vision for McDonald's was heavily influenced by modern tech companies, and he sought to incorporate as much of Silicon Valley's disruption and innovation mindset into the company on his first day.

Technology was at the forefront of Easterbrook's new vision and he was ready to spend big on mobile apps, touchscreens, anything that could remove the manual labor from the equation of serving customers.
And we were to say who would guess in five years time that the largest taxi company in the world does not own a single car and does not employ a single driver?
You're the kind of shaking your head and think they've had too much of a liquid lunch.
Or that the largest department store in the world doesn't have a single storefront.
Or that the largest provider of overnight accommodation does not own a single hotel, doesn't own a single room, doesn't actually own a single bed.
That's Airbnb.
Or that the largest provider or show up of films does not own a single movie theater or cinema doesn't have a single screen Netflix.

and the reason I say this is it's not because technology is disrupting the world which clearly it is but why is it relevant to a business like ours which is these were really traditional industries getting disrupted.
this wasn't the creation of new industries it was technology disrupting it.
you know the the bricks and mortar of the hotel industry, the bricks and mortar of department stores, the tradition of the taxi companies.

So in amongst that somewhere was, I thought, a warning signal that we are in a very traditional business and you might as well expect it to get disrupted and there's a really good chance that technology will be part of the disrupting mechanism.
So the attitude was, do you wait to get disrupted or do you try and become the disruptor within the industry and lead that and anticipate it and move before you get caught.
So that's part of some of the mental approach that we've taken to what we have ahead of us.

One of the largest moves Easterbrook made as a CEO was at the corporate level, where he first reorganized a 300,000 person company globally from separate geographic regions and into four clear market stages.
There were now four markets for all of McDonald's to focus on when it came to doing work and setting the strategy on a day-to-day basis.
The first market was the US, the second was international lead markets, which were mature global markets that have similar economic and competitive dynamics like France, Germany, UK.
The third was high growth markets, markets with high growth potential like China, Italy, Russia, and Korea, and the remainder being foundational markets.

Easterbook also refocused the company to prioritize franchising and to aggressively and continue continue removing itself from the burger business and is strictly into the real estate business by setting a new target of having franchised 90% of all McDonald's stores by 2018.
With the reorg and the executive restructuring, McDonald's estimated that under this new Easterbrook regime, it would save about $300 million annually.
And so under the six years of Easterbrook's reign at McDonald's, the company has enjoyed a really major turnaround.
When you think of McDonald's today, you can see that the company is really finding its form with hit celebrity partnerships from Travis Scott to BTS and to Mariah Carey.
There's no more salads, gourmet sandwiches, or fancy burgers.
And investors have certainly noticed and supported this turnaround with a stock up 110% over five years.
Now, while the stock is up and the sentiment is positive, it's interesting to note that McDonald's overall income is actually in decline.
It's been declining for the past six years, even if we remove 2020, which was really the COVID year.
But McDonald's net profit margin has actually been going up in the same time period from 18% to 25%.
When you're operating at the scale of McDonald's, when you're dealing with numbers in the billions, a 7% increase in profit margin is actually really massive.
And so with the shift towards a more financially conservative business model, McDonald's is intentionally running and operating less and less restaurants directly.
Whereas under prior CEOs, McDonald's corporate always held on to operating the most highest potential stores and locations to make sure the company would be able to capture all the growth themselves.

You know, under Easterbook, McDonald's became a company that was more than happy to hand off things to franchise operators and were basically okay with giving up the earnings upside in exchange for a smaller but more stable and consistent cash flow of royalties and rent.

So given that McDonald's has been operating fewer and fewer restaurants over the years, the company's revenue over the past few years have been transforming with more and more revenue coming from franchise royalties than anything else.
If the franchise operators are selling lots of Big Macs, McMuffins, cheeseburgers, McGriddles, then it's a win-win for everyone.
Both the operators who make more money and take home more money themselves, and then for Mickey D's as they get the same cut of a bigger pie.

So when we look at franchise sale, which really is the dollar amount of food, drinks, and desserts that are purchased at franchise McDonald's stores worldwide, which again, we know that's 90% of McDonald's stores.

So that means basically if you're going down the street, you pass 10 McDonald's, you know, nine out of those 10 and McDonald's are going to be run by some individual franchise operator rather than McDonald's corporate, we see that things are actually really doing well year over year.
But hold on, let's do the math to see if franchise sales itself is a misleading metric.

So if McDonald's is franchising more and more of its restaurants every year, then that could potentially skew this data as obviously the more franchise restaurants there are, the more everything will sell.
So it makes sense the total annual franchise sales will be up year over year, no matter what happens.
What we really want to look at is the average annual sales of each franchise restaurant.
This number will give us insight into how the average McDonald's store is performing.
When we run that math we can see that the annual revenue or earnings of each franchise McDonald's is actually growing really well.

So it means that even though there are more franchise stores, you know more McDonald's that you can spend at, more dilution, each store is actually still selling more and more food and drink every year.

If we look deeper at years 2016 and 2017, which is when All Day Breakfast was launched, you know despite the consumer hype and popularity we can see that All Day Breakfast was actually pretty overrated from an earnings perspective.

Letting consumers buy McMuffins and McGriddles and hash browns late at night certainly helped improve the company's image and its connection with millennials, but it didn't really noticeably drive up sales.

The real leap in earnings comes in 2018 and 2019, and when we dig deeper into those years we can see that some of those biggest growth drivers was the launch of the new dollar menu, a hit limited time offering in the McDonald's worldwide campaign, and extending delivery to DoorDash and Grubhub, and not just an Uber Eats.
So under Easterbrook, delivery was a strategic channel that he had always hugely prioritized and invested in for many years.
While other fast food giants like Burger King, Taco Bell, and even Chipotle were really slow to embrace delivery, Easterbrook sought to make delivery a first-class experience on McDonald's.
He knew that the convenience factor of delivery and the form factor of McDonald's foods like nuggets and burgers would hold up really well to the rigors of delivery.
All McDonald's food had long since been designed to be transportable, packageable, sturdy enough to survive a bumpy car ride, reheatable, and even eaten lukewarm.
Perhaps Easterbrook deep down knew that there was really nothing that could save McDonald's dining and store experience except having delivery where people could eat McDonald's outside of the store.

By 2017, McDonald's was already the global leader in fast food delivery thanks to Easterbrook's early investments, and they were offering delivery in over 20% of their restaurants and had plans to roll out to even more locations.
Over 60% of McDonald's orders actually occur in the evening and late night across the world.
And so in their pilot run, consumers are spending 1.5 to 2 times the amount of money than they would spend on an in-store order.
And to Easterbrook's credit, McDonald's really helped evangelize and mainstream food delivery for consumers, being one of the first and only large fast food companies to openly promote free delivery.
Two years later in 2019, from 2017, delivery had already grown to a $3 billion business for McDonald's and was accounting for 14% of its revenue that same year.
Delivery was now available in over 50% of McDonald's stores worldwide.

Fast forward another two years to 2021, delivery alone was now a $13 billion business, accounting for roughly 40% of McDonald's overall revenue, and delivery was now an option available in 70% of all McDonald's worldwide.
Delivery certainly makes it more convenient to get McDonald's, but what is really pulling people back into the golden arches if the food underlying really hasn't changed?
That answer lies in Rick and Morty.

The popularity, excitement, and surge of millennial demand that came from the partnership with Rick and Morty was a real phenomenon that had pushed McDonald's even temporarily to the forefront of the internet.
While the Cetron sauce really failed to stick on and the promotion was relatively short-lived, McDonald's knew that there was something promising about this partnership.

And other fast food giants, upon seeing the Rick and Morty sensation, tried to capitalize on the trend by also partnering with Rick and Morty that same year, but the reality was none of their events and marketing campaigns ever really reached the popularity of the Cetron sauce.
Rather than introduce new permanent items to appeal to all customers like salad and premium sandwiches for the picky high-end consumer, McDonald's instead under Easterbrook chose to focus.
They chose to streamline its menu to a core set of bestsellers, McNuggets, Filet-O-Fishes, Big Macs, Quarter Pounders, McFlurs, and so forth.
Things that weren't healthy but represented the company and was a core item in every order at the Golden Arches.
Easterbrook knew that the days of habitual McDonald's consumption were over.
This was a social phenomenon that even legacy CPG companies like Pepsi and Coke were learning the hard way as well.
The days of people drinking three Cokes a day or chomping on McDonald's every lunch were over.

So rather than trying to convince people of the impossible tasks that McDonald's was suddenly healthy and good for you, McDonald's embraced the fact that consumers were simply not going to be regulars, and no amount of advertising or ingredient changing was going to change that fact.

And so with a lower standard, McDonald's shifted their marketing focus from trying to convince consumers to eat at McDonald's as many times a week as possible to simply doing everything they can to make sure that average customer still gets in the door and eats McDonald's once in a while.

To do that, McDonald's built off on the Rick and Morty success in 2017, spending the next few years experimenting, researching, and then eventually launching a proper celebrity meal campaign that continues on this day with hits like Travis Scott, BTS, S.A.W.E.D.E.S., and even Mariah Carey.

These celebrity meals are LTOs or limited time offerings that only last for a certain period of time so that consumers, just like how they were optimized during the Rick and Morty phase, to get that viral urgency to get in and order McDonald's before the event ends, even if these meals themselves are made up of the same burgers, fries, and sauces that you could get anytime on the menu without these events.
These limited time celebrity meals are not only successful in bringing in consumers and generating social media hype but they're also great profit drivers for mcdonald's.

compared to before where mcdonald's would have to spend months researching testing new permanent items and then spend even longer rolling it out to franchise operators training them how to make these new items sourcing entirely new ingredients.
all these celebrity meals are are really just a repackaging and rebranding of existing food items that are already on the mcdonald's menu.

but to make sure that these events feel special they aren't just hacks these celebrity meals often have something special and unique like let's say a new sauce, new packaging, or maybe limited time merchandise like a t-shirt to go with the meal.

For a big fast food giant like McDonald's to ask their suppliers to make a one-time limited amount of let's say a new sauce, a t-shirt, or even a burger wrapper is something that is cheap and easy for the company.
Compare this to for instance the kale salad that McDonald's rolled out back in 2015.

To support the kale salad McDonald's had to go out there, find new suppliers, interview farms, and rework their entire supply chain, storage, and transportation just to get in raw kale every day that's fresh enough to use in a salad.

And because kale salad was at the time a permanent part of the menu, McDonald's had no idea how many kale salads would sell, but because it's a consistent part of the menu, you just have to keep bringing fresh kale even if that kale is going rotten and it's not selling.

These limited time celebrity meals like the Travis Scott meal or the BTS meal are these low-risk, high-upside partnerships that sell as a function of the star power of the celebrity rather than a function of the food itself.

So running the celebrity limited time meals every quarter really helps McDonald's freshen its image so that even if the company isn't rolling out 4 or 5 new items every year, the menu doesn't feel stagnant and stale to the average consumer.

The Travis Scott and J Balvin Celebrity Meals broke records in the US when they first launched, and that in turn gave McDonald's the confidence to take the celebrity meal concept and campaign global where they were able to partner with an even bigger celebrity in BTS and the company.
Many hit record breaking levels of McNuggets sales, mobile app downloads, and social media engagement.
All of this came from Rick and Morty.

Other fast food companies like Popeyes have copied McDonald's celebrity meals in recent months but the reality is none of those meals have had the staying power or virality that have come close to McDonald's success.

And so many companies in multiple industries, not just McDonald's and fast food, find themselves in this identity crisis of being caught between the iconic legacy reputation that brought them previous success and the newer millennial market that is now no longer as easy to sell as it used to be.

It's thanks to food delivery, all day breakfast, and Rick and Morty that McDonald's has actually completely transformed as a company, returning this year to the throne as the number one fast food giant in 2021.

title: The Extraordinary King of Luxury Fashion
note: Industry comparison explainer that builds through Gucci, YSL and Moncler to a withheld reveal of Hermes, then explains its scarcity model.
sections: Luxury fashion as Game of Thrones
lines: To outsiders, luxury fashion, or high fashion, is a curious industry where consumers seem to irrationally shell out hundreds or thousands of dollars for simple sneakers, handbags, wallets, hats, or t-shirts.
But take a step inside and you'll find the world of high fashion is really more like Game of Thrones, with Italian, English, and French houses all duking it out to be the king.
For the houses that do get to sit on the throne, they don't last for very long.
Luxury brands like Versace, Tony Birch, and Coach once dominated in the 2000s.
But fast forward to the 2020s, and today's top players are totally different.
They're Gucci, Louis Vuitton, and YSL.

And competition today has also heated up with surging smaller brands like Moncler, whose puffer jackets have taken over TikTok, and Balenciaga, whose sneakers have become a crowd-cult favorite, along with Louis Vuitton's timeless red-bottom stilettos.
The world of high fashion appears fragmented with so many different brands, but in reality, it's an industry run by oligopolies.
Gucci, YSL, Louis Vuitton, and Balenciaga are not independent brands anymore.
They've all been acquired by conglomerates and converted into subsidiaries.
Let's say you go out and you buy a pair of Alexander McQueen $600 sneakers, then pick up a $4,000 Gucci bomber jacket to go with your new $2,500 YSL handbag.
In this example, even though you've bought three items from three different brands, your money is actually going to the exact same company.
The biggest conglomerate in the industry is LVMH, who owns Dior, Fendi, Givenchy, Marc Jacobs, and Louis Vuitton.
The second biggest conglomerate in the industry is Kering, who owns Balenciaga, Bottega Veneta, Gucci, Alexander McQueen, and YSL.
LVMH is a clear leader, with annual earnings of 54 billion euros, over four times the amount of Kering's annual revenue.
While Kering seems like in a far-off second place, as their annual revenue is only 13 billion euros, Kering is challenging the throne in a different way.
Kering's portfolio is spearheaded by blue-chip fashion brands like Gucci, YSL, and Balenciaga.
These three brands alone today enjoy exceptional popularity amongst millennials.
When people are trying to flex or thinking about flexing, they're usually thinking of the red and green Gucci flip-flops, the silver-laced YSL purses, or Balenciaga sneakers.
If you look at the operating strategy of Gucci or Louis Vuitton, you'll find that these brands operate very similarly.

They go for a scale by branding, licensing, and selling as many products as possible from watches, perfumes, flip-flops, sneakers, hats, belts, eyeglasses, children's clothing, skateboards, furniture, and even play cards.
They add their colorways and patterns and design on it and mark it up to hundreds or thousands of dollars.
In addition, these brands spend hundreds of millions of euros every year on celebrity endorsements, sponsorships, advertising, and product placement.

They boast white glove high-end stores that make consumers feel special when they walk in, and they also sell wholesale to department stores and operate outlets to sell discounted items to those consumers that want the status and brand but don't want to pay the full price.
When it comes to business results, Gucci leads the way.

Their aggressive advertising, successful branding, and almost blitzkrieg strategy has enabled them to grow like a rocket ship, earning from 4.3 billion euros to a record 9.6 billion euros in just three years.
That's a growth of over 35% or 2 billion euros every year.
Even in a down year with the pandemic, the company grows 7.4 billion euros in 2020.
Gucci operates nearly 500 stores worldwide.
With the most physical store of any high fashion brand, Gucci's strong offline presence and massive product mix make retail its strongest arm.
Over 85% of Gucci's sales come from retail in the past five years.
And to maintain the brand's popularity with millennials, Gucci spends a reported 12% of its revenue or 1.2 billion euros every year on advertising across social media, print, and television.
And this approach is paying off for Gucci as over 50% of their customers today are 35 years old or younger.
Now, Gucci takes a fast-paced and aggressive approach when it comes to R &D.

Whether you're the conservative connoisseur who wants only those traditional timeless looks that have never changed for decades, or you're the modern shopper who's on a budget and you want the brand, but you also want it styled in a contemporary way that you would actually wear and get use out of, you know, there's something for you at Gucci, no matter what kind of person you are.

Gucci frequently rotates and updates its products and marketing to capitalize on trends, And Gucci reportedly rotates half of its product mix on an annual basis, maintaining 50% of its bestsellers to be available to be purchased at any time, but then releasing new or refreshed products as their other 50%.
This strategy has really paid off, with new products accounting for 30% of Gucci's total business every year.
With an eye-opening 40% operating margin, Gucci is clearly at the top of the game.
If we look at other examples, let's take a look at YSL.
YSL is a French brand, best known for its black leather bags and wallets that retail in the $1,000 to $2,000 range.
It's also really well known for its iconic silver emblem that it brands onto all of its items.
Unlike Gucci though, YSL is a traditionalist company.
They price themselves at the mid-range and they operate very conservatively and carefully.
It's very rare for YSL to make changes to their core product mix outside of a few seasonal additions.
And so while YSL does do wholesale to department stores, the company doesn't operate outlet malls or participate in licensing at the same scale as Gucci.
For instance, there are only 200 YSL stores worldwide.
And as a result, YSL has grown really slowly, from 1.5 billion euros to just 2.1 billion euros in three years.
That's a growth rate of 12%, or 200 million euros every year.

While the company has tried to win over millennials by appointing K-pop star Rose as its newest brand ambassador, YSL still has a difficult time balancing its tradition with the fast modernization that millennials are looking for.
And YSL's operating margin today stands at around 25%.
If we look at the smaller surging players like Moncler, we see that the apples just don't fall too far from the tree in this industry.
Moncler is best known for its shiny $1,000 puffer down jackets, and the company has grown its revenue at a similar pace of around an additional 200 million euros every year.
Moncler has grown from 1.2 billion euros to 1.6 billion euros in the span of two years.
But it also has an identical footprint to YSL, as they only have roughly 250 stores worldwide.
And as a newer independent brand that isn't backed by a conglomerate, Montclair also has a much smaller war chest and they only spend about 6% of its revenue on marketing every year.
Montclair's operating margin is also pretty consistent with YSL's, hovering at around 27 and 28%.
Now, what if I told you that there was a high fashion brand that's more lucrative and more successful than Gucci, YSL, and Montclair?
A fashion brand whose products are so in demand that they're never available, never sold online, or even displayed publicly in their stores.

A brand who sells its products to a carefully curated list of only its highest spending customers, takes no pre-orders, has no waiting lists, refuses to expand inventory or scale its production in a way where everyone can buy those items.
A brand whose products are so elite and elusive that they actually appreciate thousands of dollars over time and can be resold for profit.
A brand that never allows returns, refunds, or exchanges after purchase.
And a brand who has remained independent, manufactures its products entirely by hand, spends the least amount of money on marketing, and yet still grosses very close to what Gucci makes every year.
That brand is Hermes, and they are the current king in high fashion.
Hermes operates their business with a playbook that no other brand can even come close to emulating.
Hermes has quietly grown, going from 5.5 billion euros to 6.8 billion euros in just three years.
Their growth rate has doubled in the same time frame, going from 7% to 15% year over year.
Hermes has a moderately sized retail footprint with 300 stores worldwide.
But if Gucci has tripled the growth rate and higher revenue, what makes Hermes the king?
Hermes to this day remains independent, and the company has been free of the M &A and Game of Thrones that has dominated the industry in the past decades.
Hermes is best known for its leather handbags.
The company takes what it calls an independent craftsman model to manufacturing.
80% of all Hermes products to this day are manufactured by hand exclusively in France, where the company owns and operates 44 factories.
In today's day and age, businesses ruthlessly focus on improving speed, technology, efficiency, scale, and automation.
It's all about lowering costs, increasing production, selling faster, and involving as few humans as possible.
You generally want to take the complexity of manufacturing, break it down into single steps, avoid single points of failure, and follow the assembly line production.
The funny thing is Hermes doesn't do any of these things.
Each Hermes bag to this day is handmade by a single craftsman in France from beginning to end.
Before a craftsman can begin working on a bag, a craftsman has to be formally trained for years at a vocational school.
They must have graduated from one of Hermes' in-house tanning schools and undergo 18 months of direct mentorship from a master trainer.
The concept of an assembly line simply doesn't exist at Hermes.
Each handbag is cut from hides and entirely hand-stitched with needle and thread by the same individual craftsman from beginning to end.
Depending on the intricacy of the design, a single craftsman can take anywhere between 25 to 48 work hours to create a single Hermes bag.
A craftsman makes at most 2 to 4 Hermes bags every week.
So instead of asking its craftsman to just simply work faster or introducing machinery to reduce the manual labor, Hermes takes the extraordinary viewpoint in today's society that less is more.
Hermes employs about 5,600 craftsmen across its 22 leather factories in France to make its leather bags.
This handmade craftsmanship naturally demands a high premium.
Hermes is the highest price of any high fashion brand, with their leather bags retailing from the tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars.
But here's the magic.
Hermes bags are not just simply expensive.
They're also elusive.
They're never shown online, never sold online, never available publicly in stores, never on display, and only available in private closed doors to an exclusive set of clientele.
If you want to buy or even see for yourself an Hermes Birkin, Kelly, or Constance handbag, no matter what style, size, color, or design, you have to earn that opportunity with Hermes.
Because supply is limited, handmade production is slow, and the quality is high, Hermes allocates there are few bags based on customer loyalty.
To buy a bag from Hermes, you need to have a relationship with your local store.
You have to be regular and show loyalty by regularly buying Hermes products that aren't those bags, whether those are their shoes, scarves, perfumes, jewelry, furniture, or watches.
At some point, once you've proven your loyalty to Hermes by showing that you've spent a high amount of money, you will be then offered that rare chance to purchase a bag.
A store will serendipitously notify you and then take you to a secret room in the back of the store where they'll present you with the bags that are available.
In these situations, you're presented with anywhere from one to three bags.
And the bag that you're presented with may not be the size, color, or style that you want.

While you can choose to decline the bag when you're offered this valuable opportunity, the reality is if you decline the bag, you run the risk of losing your loyalty points and being seen as unworthy.
And you might not be given the opportunity to buy a bag again.
So Hermes's sales system basically pressures you to buy the bag that's offered to you in private, it no matter the price, even if it's not the bag that you want.
This means that you have to spend thousands of dollars on buying Hermes products that you might not really want for the hope that you eventually get the opportunity to get the bag that you do want.
And so what you buy and how much you spend at Hermes will unofficially influence how fast you're given the opportunity to buy a bag.
This is a totally irrational way of selling, but it works for Hermes.

To be such an exclusive brand that you can get people to spend thousands of dollars endlessly buying things that they don't want in the hopes of one day being given the chance to buy the thing that they do want is totally unprecedented.
Hermes spends only 4% of its revenue on marketing and advertising, and the brand is on track to clear 7 billion euros in 2021.
If you look at Gucci, on the other hand, Gucci has to spend three times that amount of money on advertising and budget every year to sustain its popularity.
Given the constrained supply, slow production, and hot demand for Hermes, the company's bags carry value even post-purchase.

Since so many people are unwilling or unable to spend and become that loyal customer that Hermes requires, that demand naturally gets routed to the secondary market where Hermes handbags are constantly resold.
It's reported that Hermes bags appreciate on average 14.2%, which is a higher rate of return than the S &P 500 and gold.
This is why it's Hermes and not Gucci that sits on the throne today as the quiet king of high fashion.

While Hermes is nowhere as loud in its marketing as Gucci and its top line might not be as impressively high The reality is Hermes has a level of appeal and exclusivity that no other brand will ever be able to replicate.

title: Facebook's Collapse & The Metaverse Crusade
note: Opens on archive clips of apologies, diagnoses a stalling Facebook, then explains the Reels and metaverse strategies as responses to platform dependence.
sections: Next format: VR and the metaverse
lines: Facebook has long overplayed its cards as the global social media leader.
Over the past five years, Zuckerberg has taken a consistently nonchalant attitude in public towards issues like online privacy, misinformation, and political manipulation.
I know that we don't exactly have the strongest reputation on privacy right now, to put it lightly.
But I'm committed to doing this well.
We know that we did not do a good enough job protecting people's data.
I'm really sorry for that, and Mark's really sorry.

and there was this real turning point when when companies started trying to buy the company for a huge amount of money and you know I had to kind of get my friends together and we had to decide what was it that we really cared about and what was it that we wanted to do and you know we decided not to take those offers and right.
you know to me a lot of that decision was that what we wanted to do and what we wanted to spend.
you know a big part of our lives doing was just continuing to push and and and kind of build products that help people share information, build products that help people stay connected.
And that's really what we're spending our time doing.
And, you know, I think there's just been a lot of space between that early stuff and where we are now.
If I knew what I knew now then, then I hope I wouldn't have made those mistakes.
But I can't go back and change the past.
I can only do what we think is the right thing going forward.
So before we move off this privacy thing, and I thought that was a fascinating answer.
Okay, you wanna take off the hoodie?

I know you don't, what's with that?
There's a group of women in the audience that wish you would.
No, no.
Girls?
Whoa.
Even governments have noticed and attempted to hold Facebook accountable.
And while viral clips of Zuckerberg being roasted at congressional hearings are funny and seem damaging to the company's image, the reality is Facebook just doesn't give a shit.
Something that we call watch party, which lets you watch video and chat with your friends.
So, you know, let's say that your friend is testifying in Congress.
For example.
Facebook knows that at the very least, they'll get a tongue lashing on C-SPAN, and at most of a slap on the wrist fine from the SEC.
Then they'll go back to doing things as usual.
There's no threat from any government, not while politicians can barely understand how to use their iPhones or when to remove their credit card from the reader.
Facebook knows that no matter how much you might hate them, you're stuck with their products.
Whether you're scrolling through Instagram, chatting on Messenger, checking WhatsApp, browsing on Marketplace, Facebook plays a core part in people's lives online.
And if you're a business that's looking to reach consumers online, Facebook is still the holy grail.
You can put together an image and text and have an effective advertisement running in half a day to your target demographic with just a few bucks.
From an R &D perspective, Facebook has tried many things to deepen its moat.

The company has introduced new products like Facebook Gaming to compete with Twitch, Groups to compete with Reddit, Marketplace to compete with Craigslist, Messenger to compete with business landlines, Games to compete with Snapchat, and Shops to compete with Shopify.
Many of these bets just haven't worked.
Facebook Gaming is basically forgotten and has always been stuck as a distant third place when it comes to streaming, and that's even when Mixer was still alive.
Marketplace has solid traction, but it's also inevitably become this hotbed where thieves sell stolen goods, dropshippers run rampant, and escorts list their services.
Shops has improved, and games fail to get any traction even after Messenger tried to force that relevance onto its users.
And there's Oculus.
While VR has made strides, the overall ecosystem adoption and technology behind virtual reality still remains really young and niche.
Having a two-pound brick strapped to your face is still not exactly how most people would define fun.
Almost none of my friends post on Facebook anymore.
The dynamic is totally different now than compared to when I was in high school.
In high school, if you didn't post on Facebook, that was like social suicide.
These days, the only time someone really posts on Facebook is if they have some big life update or if they're raising money for a GoFundMe.
On the other hand, Instagram also feels like it's gotten worse.
Instagram feeds are packed with influencer spam, affiliate marketing, softcore porn, and advertisements.
And despite this, I've always personally remained very optimistic on Facebook's growth.
Even though its products feel stale and have lost a lot of social significance, Facebook is still an essential part of one's online identity.
But this year, everything seems to be changing.
Facebook's stock dropped by 26% in a single day, wiping out $230 billion in its valuation after its fourth quarter earning.
It seems like Facebook goes through a new crisis every month, where employees are now stepping out as whistleblowers, political pressures are growing.
But most damning of all in the fourth quarter announcement was that consumers are now spending significantly less time on Facebook.
For the first time ever, the company announced weaker ad impressions, fewer daily active users, and slowing spending from advertisers.
And while the world is still very much stuck in COVID, there's still enough signals to suggest that it's not just you and me.
Lots of other people are simply just getting tired of Facebook.
The golden era of seemingly endless growth is now over.
Facebook in a single month has gone through a complete rebranding and is now pounding the drum for a flashy new vision about metaverses, digital frontiers, and innovation.
These are all things that companies only really do when they feel like they have no other choice.
So what is Facebook's new strategy to combat the slowing growth?
And why exactly does Zuckerberg think the future growth lies in the metaverse?
Facebook's target audience is young adults between the ages of 18 and 29.
Now this audience is the early majority like me who grew up with Facebook and have been its most loyal customer base.
Zuckerberg recently admitted in the fourth quarter earnings call that in the past 10 years, Facebook has broadened so much in the name of growth that their focus has become diluted.
The company was so preoccupied with trying to serve everyone that they really stopped optimizing their products for young adults.
And now those same young adults are now active on TikTok, YouTube, Snapchat, basically everywhere but Facebook.
Facebook believes that the way to win back young adults is through short-form video.
Any video that's under 15 seconds or is shot vertically is what they consider a short-form video.
TikTok is clearly the leader in short-form video nowadays, and Facebook knows it has to do work to quickly catch up.
In some ways, this entire situation feels like Snapchat and Facebook back in 2017.
When Snapchat first came onto the scene, it was largely dismissed as a sexting app that was too tiny and silly to ever be a threat to Facebook.

But then teenagers began flocking to Snapchat and teenagers were a huge fan of the disappearing short-lived messaging, the geo filters, the face filters and the video sharing that Snapchat had to offer.
The biggest feature was probably Snapchat stories, which let you post photos and videos that disappeared after 24 hours and Snapchat stories became all the rage.
Advertisers began to notice the popularity of Snapchat and began moving their budget from Facebook to Snapchat.
Now Facebook reacted really aggressively at the time.
They copied Snapchat stories and added stories everywhere they could in Facebook, Messenger, WhatsApp, and Instagram.
Instagram stories became a massive success.
Just two months after its launch, it had 100 million daily active users.
By June of 2017, Instagram stories had hit 250 million daily active users and Snapchat only had 166 million daily active users.
Fast forward to today, Instagram stories are irreplaceable.
It's one of Facebook's most used and successful features of all times.
And Snapchat stories is still around as the first mover, but its usage is really nowhere near the popularity of Instagrams.
So Facebook knows that they have this proven muscle and playbook when it comes to copying the competition.
But TikTok's current momentum, their funding, their mainstream appeal, along with the content creators are really nothing like Snapchat.
If you really think about it conceptually, Snapchat and Instagram stories, those are all private, mostly private content that you produce for your friends and the people in your personal network.

But when you go to TikTok or even look at YouTube Shorts or other short-form videos that are really popular today, what you find is that it's mostly public content that you share and discuss with your friends.
Just like with Instagram Stories, Facebook's plan is to copy TikTok with a new product it's calling Reels.
And Reels is currently Facebook's fastest-growing content and its biggest engagement contributor.
For now, Facebook just wants Reels to focus on user adoption, so they intentionally show very few ads.

But once Reels picks up momentum and eyeball, Zuckerberg's plan is to monetize Reels in the same way as news feeds and stories, where advertisers are now going to be able to slip in their short form commercials into Reels, just like they do with Instagram stories.
And Zuckerberg is so bullish on short form videos that he believes that eventually Facebook will show more ads at a higher rate on Reels than on Instagram stories or news feeds.
And so Facebook believes it needs to get three things right for Reels to beat TikTok.
One, it needs tools that help content creators produce quality short-form videos.
Two, it needs algorithms that recommend engaging Reels to viewers to keep people watching.
And three, it needs programs that can help these content creators monetize their Reels.

With a more mature advertising network, Facebook believes that they can pay content creators on Reels much faster and in higher amounts than they would ever get on TikTok, which will naturally pull more creators to Reels and away from TikTok over time.
The format in which people communicate online has really evolved over the past 18 years of Facebook's existence.
When the internet first came about in the early 90s, people mostly communicated through text.
In the 2000s, smartphones became popular and phone cameras became mainstream.
Then photos then replaced text as the primary format for how people communicate.
Fast forward another two decades.
Now that mobile networks are super fast, we've gone from 3G to 4G to 5G, video is now the primary way in which people communicate online.
So while short-form video appears to be the next format for the immediate future, Facebook has its eyes set on trying to aggressively win the distant future.
Rather than waiting for Google or Apple to create the next format, Zuckerberg wants Facebook to own it entirely.
Zuck's big bet here is that virtual reality is going to be the format after video for which people communicate online.
Facebook has spared no expense in chasing this bet, And they've invested tens of billions of dollars in cash since 2014 on virtual reality.
And while VR tech has been around for decades, it's really only recently that Zuck has been able to put a name on his grand vision.
Metaverse.
To the Metaverse.
Metaverse.
Metaverse.
So before we dive into the VR technology and is it compelling or not, I think it's really useful to take a step back and understand why Zuckerberg is so obsessed with winning the next format.
Why is Zuckerberg such a shill for virtual reality?
Why is he so focused on winning the distant future when Facebook today isn't doing that great?
And Facebook today doesn't even do video well.
My theory is that Facebook is tired of being a services company.
Facebook today is really a software services company.
Instagram is a mobile app that's fundamentally an internet service.
Facebook is an internet service with a mobile client.
WhatsApp is a mobile app that's also basically an internet service.
Facebook ultimately has no control over the personal hardware devices and the operating systems, the browsers, and search engines that people use on those hardware devices to access its services.
To take a step back, what Facebook wants is your personal data.
Facebook wants to know you so well that it can predict the things that you want to buy before you even know them yourself.
And so then Facebook can give you advertisements for products that you will have a high likelihood of purchasing even though you didn't even know they existed.
The central problem that facebook has run into is that in order to achieve that level of truly personalized advertising you need an insane amount of personal data.
you need to know more than just someone's date of birth their city their ethnicity and their relationship status.
you need to know what that person likes what they don't like their taste their lifestyle their behavior their routine.
basically you need to know that person better than that person knows themselves.
The problem is the personal device manufacturers, the iPhones, the Androids, the MacBooks, the laptop companies.
The problem is all these personal device manufacturers, they don't like that.
Apple doesn't appreciate that Facebook is trying to collect more data on iPhone users than Apple is trying to collect themselves.
And Google doesn't appreciate it either that Facebook is always trying to get to a place where they know more about Android users than even Google would ever know themselves.
And so Apple and Google both believe that users are entitled to some degree of privacy.
But don't get me wrong here.
I don't believe for a second that Apple or Google are privacy white knights.
These are both still advertising companies.
Google is certainly more so than Apple.
Both of these companies, Google and Apple, admittedly hoard plenty of user data as well, but they have limits.

Apple and Google both believe in giving users just enough privacy that keeps those users comfortable coming back to using the Google search engine, watching videos on YouTube, and buying new iPhones and Androids.
If Apple users found out that Facebook was just selling their data wholesale, that would have a pretty dramatic impact on market of people who would want to buy iPhones.
And so Apple and Google here are watching their own backyard first.
They're first making sure that their own bottom line is taken care of before they could let someone else like Facebook have a seat at the table.
But Facebook is the total opposite of Google and Apple.
They don't have anything to lose because Facebook doesn't have any personal hardware devices.
So Facebook's the opposite.
They would rather have no privacy at all.
And the personal data that Facebook is aggressively looking to collect on each individual, truthfully, goes beyond what most people would be comfortable with.

And because Facebook constantly refuses to respect the privacy agreements and actively has been caught investing in engineers to try to find ways around privacy policies, the personal device manufacturers like Google and Apple have begun drawing the boundary for Zuckerberg.
Tim Cook in particular decided he had enough and he gave Facebook the biggest middle finger with iOS 14.
With iOS 14, iPhone users can now in one finger tap permanently prevent Facebook or any other company from tracking their in-app activity.

So for users who choose to disable app tracking, Facebook can now no longer track those users properly, which then ruins their ad targeting accuracy, which ultimately leads to the wrong advertisements shown to the wrong audience.
For example, lipstick ads that are meant to target young women might end up showing up in older men's news feeds.
Unpersonalized ads are kind of like the bane for Facebook.
They're trying to move away from those shitty billboards that you see on the highway that are asking for things that you don't really want, that are promoting services that you don't really need.
When you drive on the highway and you see all those crappy billboards from all those cheap, scammy lawyers, you just tune them out.
You don't actually pay attention to it.
In Facebook's world, that means fewer clicks, which leads to lower ROI and inevitably lower ad spend.

Advertisers are going to spend less money on Facebook if they know that their money is not giving them the results that they want, if their ads are ultimately getting shown to the wrong people, and that's less money in Facebook's pocket.
So iOS 14 has done massive damage to Facebook's operation.

The company is currently undertaking this massive multi-year effort to rebuild its advertising infrastructure, and they're reworking their targeting and optimization systems to be able to function with less data.
To suddenly go from having this exact, precise, accurate personal data to now suddenly having to rely on this imprecise, this aggregated, this anonymized data is a massive change for Facebook.
The accuracy and effectiveness of Facebook's advertisements dramatically decreased with the company reporting a $10 billion decrease in profit just due to iOS 14 changes alone.
This is why Zuckerberg is pushing so hard for the metaverse.
It's this virtual reality world that would run on hardware and software that Facebook entirely owns.
Facebook is too smart to try and compete with Google and Apple to create the next search engine or the next iPhone or the next web browser.
The smartphone is just a personal device that Facebook knows it'll never be able to win.
Pretend that you're Zuckerberg.
You're this lizard man.
You look around at all the personal devices that people used to take to see where you can maybe compete.
It's actually kind of depressing.
you look and you look at the OS.
you look at gaming consoles oops You know Microsoft Sony Nintendo dominate that space.
you look at search you look at video.
you look at web browsing.
That's owned by YouTube.
you look at smart watches headphones laptops That's owned by Apple.
So when you start looking at the personal devices that people have today, you don't really have a place to compete.
So then you start looking at the personal devices that people don't have today, but might one day have in the future.
So virtual reality fits that bill perfectly for Facebook.
It's this personal hardware device that maybe one day people in the future will eventually use like smartphones.
No one knows if that's true.
But objectively, for Facebook, that's a better bet than trying to compete for scraps with entrenched winners for personal hardware devices that they'll never be able to win in the immediate future.
Facebook wants to own its own hardware, software, and ecosystem.
Zuckerberg doesn't want his future of Facebook to be another app in someone else's app store.
He wants to be the app store.
And so by owning its own hardware and software, Facebook can have its own ecosystem.
Facebook can control its own app store.
Facebook can have this fully controlled environment where they set their own rules and policies around privacy and content.
No more iOS 14.
No more having to play nice with Apple or Google or Microsoft.
Facebook will be able to call its own shots and collect as much data as it wants from its users that are on their hardware and software.
No one would ever be able to stop them.
And so Zuckerberg's bet here is that virtual reality will succeed video and mobile internet.
This metaverse, in his mind, will unlock this large ecosystem where people buy and sell digital goods that exist only in their virtual worlds.
But first, before you get to the end state, you have to first populate this metaverse with real people.
And Facebook is doing that with Oculus.
So every year they're proactively doing their best to release cheaper, newer, lighter, slimmer headsets to try to make virtual reality accessible for everyone.
but facebook knows that the public is still a long ways off.
not everyone is really sold on the technology.
the company continues to spend millions of dollars every year running these glorious marketing campaigns hosting free oculus booths to try to evangelize virtual reality.

with the metaverse vision that's now been officially communicated to investors to the public to its users we should expect that facebook is only going to ramp up the evangelism around virtual reality even more in the coming years.
Facebook has also recently partnered with Luxottica to launch smart glasses as another way to achieve faster adoption.
Virtual reality is the foundational hardware piece that Facebook is trying to win.
It wants to get its VR headsets in the hands of as many people as possible.
And if virtual reality is too much of a leap for the broad public, then maybe it's AR hardware like those smart glasses.
Virtual reality or augmented reality doesn't matter.
As long as those hardware devices are owned by Facebook, it's a win for Zuckerberg.
Next comes the software that lives on top of this hardware.
Facebook is calling the operating system for the metaverse Horizon, which is this virtual world where people can come and live in.
In Horizon, you can choose what you wear and you can buy digital clothing that's made by developers.

And to lure people to get closer to the metaverse, Facebook is taking steps to integrate with brands who are bringing their brands to the metaverse and they're also integrating this vision with their current products.
Your 3D horizon avatar will also now be available in the 2D world of your Facebook, Instagram, and Messenger accounts.
So it's all linking.
As ridiculous as the metaverse sounds and as unlikable as Zuckerberg is as a public figure, the reality is the VR vision for Facebook is a true business play.
This isn't a case of Elon Musk where it's some tech billionaire that's too bored on Earth, dreaming of some dystopian future that they can control because they have more money than time.
Instead, Metaverse is actually really just a company that's trying to protect its advertising future from Google and Apple before it's all too late.

title: How Dollar Tree Conquered Low Income America
note: Explainer built around a counter-intuitive thesis (small beats big), compared with Walmart and Target on margins and expansion speed.
sections: Dollar Tree's conquest of low-income America
What Dollar Tree is: products and store count
Sales and margins versus Target and Walmart
lines: In the world of business, the rule of thumb is that bigger is better.
In American retail, companies embrace this saying like a truth.
The bigger the store you have, the more goods and services you can sell and the more money that you'll make.
If you think of some of the leading American retail companies like Walmart, Target, and Costco, their stores are built like cathedrals and they just keep getting bigger.
Retail, at its most abstract, is the heartbeat that fuels the domestic consumption, which in turn drives the whole American economy forward.
When in doubt, just keep printing.
But what happens when that consumption, spending, and money printing finally catches up?
I think we're starting to see some of that now.
15% inflation, the highest increase in prices since the 1980s, $8 a gallon for gas in some cities, shipping delays, supply chain problems, labor shortages, and so forth.
When I shipped a 40-foot container of goods from China to the West Coast three years ago during the Great Trade War, it cost around $2,500.
Well, $3,000 if you include the 25% tariff I had to pay to the Trump administration.
But nowadays, it costs $20,000 to ship that same container from China to the West Coast.

On top of that, we have a semiconductor shortage, where car manufacturers are cutting production, used car prices are hitting record levels, and buying a used car nowadays is just as expensive as buying a new car.
There's enough sticker shock just going to the grocery store these days and putting steak in your cart.
And prices just seem to be getting higher and higher.

Throw in the fact that the stock market is now crashing back to pre-COVID prices and many consumers, myself included, are now looking for discounts and deals in a world that no longer seems to offer any.

There is one Fortune 500 company that despite the supply chain issues, the labor shortages, this 15% inflation, and the rising gas costs that is so committed to giving you a discount that it puts the discount in their name.
That company is the Dollar Tree.
Dollar Tree doesn't rely on any of the traditional retail playbooks.
There's no flashy white lighting or minimalism decor, no modern sans-serif branding, and no marketing to millennials.
Instead, the Dollar Tree is focused on one mission, to become the retail monopoly of low-class America.
Dollar Tree's vicious conquest of low-income and rural America has been so successful that the company has found itself in political hot water.
Cities, small towns, and rural communities in New Orleans, Kansas City, and Alabama have all united together to ban Dollar Tree from opening more stores in their neighborhoods.
From the outside, the Dollar Tree is a fun, harmless store when you go to buy random, gimmicky, short-lived products for a buck.
But go inside, and the Dollar Tree is a ruthless business empire who knows that its best customers are low-income Americans.
The company will do everything it can to suffocate the competition and to be the only store physically available in low-income communities, small towns, and rural America.

So poor Americans keep buying Dollar Tree, no matter how flimsy or low-quality its products may be, because there's just no other store around that they can afford or is available in their neighborhood.
But let's take a step back and zoom out first to understand what Dollar Tree is as a company.
Dollar Tree operates exclusively in North America under two brands, Dollar Tree and Family Dollar.
When you walk into a Dollar Tree, the store is true to its name.
The price ceiling at Dollar Tree is strictly defined in every state that it operates, where everything is sold for at most $1.
Most things in a Dollar Tree sell for exactly $1, no matter what state you're in, but some things are certainly less.
But not even Dollar Tree can escape inflation and rising supply costs.
The company recently increased its price cap by 25 cents, much to intense backlash, so products now are priced at $1.25 and not just $1.
Still, this is the first time that the Dollar Tree has raised its prices in 35 years.
Dollar Tree stores on average are about 8,000 to 10,000 square feet, which is about the same size of a Trader Joe's or Apple store.
60% of products sold at Dollar Tree are purchased domestically, and 40% are imported from overseas.
The theory here is that everything is still manufactured overseas for cheap and in bulk, whether that's factories in China, Mexico, Taiwan, or India.
The only difference here is that Dollar Tree isn't the one working with the factories.
Dollar Tree greatly prefers doing business with domestic US-based distributors.
