The distributors are the people who directly interface and deal with the companies overseas, and in doing so, they help Dollar Tree reduce their supply chain complexity, and they minimize any optics that the company would suffer from being overly dependent on exports.

If you can't even get custom t-shirts in America these days printed for less than $10- $15 a shirt, you can be sure that there's no factory in the US that's manufacturing keychains, toys, and toothpicks for less than a dollar.
Birthday cards, sticky notes, and other paper products, sure, you can find that in America for really cheap, but not everything else.
The Dollar Tree sells three main types of products.
The first type is consumable merchandise, which is everyday goods like candy, food, health and beauty, household supplies, and chemicals.
Consumable merchandise used to be the best-selling product type and historically has made up nearly 50% of Dollar Tree's annual revenue.
The second product category is Variety Merchandise, which the company defines as toys, houseware, gifts, stationery, party goods, greeting cards, clothes, or blankets.
Variety Merchandise is currently the best-selling product at Dollar Tree and makes up 49% of their annual revenue.
The third product type is Seasonal Goods, which are Valentine's Day, Easter, Halloween, and Christmas merchandise.
Seasonal Goods have been the weakest contributor to Dollar Tree's top line, making up only 5-6% of the company's annual gross revenue for the past three years.
There are about 8,000 Dollar Tree stores across the United States and Canada.
Texas, Florida, and California are the states with the most Dollar Tree locations with over 600 Dollar Tree stores in each of those states.
To put into perspective just how widespread the Dollar Tree is, there are almost as many Dollar Tree stores as there are Walgreens in the United States alone.
Here's another way to visualize it.
For every two Starbucks or McDonald's that exists, there is one Dollar Tree.
Or for every Chipotle that you pass, there are three Dollar Trees that exist.
For every Trader Joe's that you see, there are also $15 Tree stores.
There are seven times as many Dollar Tree stores as there are Kroger or public supermarkets.
Dollar Tree stores, by design, are meant to feel small and efficient.
The goal is to make consumers feel like they can pop into the Dollar Tree, buy something quickly, and get out without feeling overwhelmed.
This is the complete opposite of the traditional retail playbook.
A typical Walmart or Target clocks in about 150,000 square feet, which is about 15 times the size of a Dollar Tree.
When you walk into a Walmart, a Target, a Costco, a Kroger's, what's happening is that those stores actually want you to get lost.

They design their stores like mazes, where they put milk and other essentials all the way in the back, so that you have to walk through the store and you get distracted by all the displays and promotions.
you go through these colorful, never-ending aisles of brands and merchandise, all in a way so that you end up buying more than what you intended to.
In the future, when you're running up and down aisles and you're having trouble finding something at Target or Walmart, know that this frustrating shopping experience is actually intentional.
Dollar Tree's goal is to make it easy for consumers in comparison to shop and encourage fast repeat trips for small items.
The other core aspect to the Dollar Tree's shopping experience is the treasure hunt.
When you go to a Target, a Walmart, or Kroger's, or a local bodega or supermarket, all these stores are optimized to be risk-averse.
They optimize for consistency, availability, and predictability.

Retailers know that consumers are looking for things like Gillette razors, Sara Lee cake mixes, Ben & Jerry's ice cream, Oscar Mayer hot dogs, products, Charmin toilet paper, and other essentials from reputable brands.
The brands and products that you see at these large retailers generally don't change.
If a new product is introduced, these stores will only roll it out very slowly in small quantities to test their demand.
Retailers, even if it's the local bodega or supermarket, will never risk their valuable shelf space to carry new products or brands unless the demand is clear and obvious.
This is fundamentally why it's so hard for new CPG or consumer packaged goods companies to get their products on the shelves of retailers.
But Dollar Tree once again is the opposite.
They optimize for unpredictability and serendipity.
Their products are constantly changing, which means that shoppers can find something new at Dollar Tree on each trip.

This treasure hunt experience adds FOMO, freshness, and urgency in a way where shoppers are incentivized to buy the products that stand out to them as soon as they see them, as there's no guarantee that they'll be stocked again in the future.
Dollar Tree stores, generally speaking, are also disorganized, bare bones, and pretty messy.

Shoppers are encouraged to be proactive in finding the best deal or rare products by tearing open the boxes, moving inventory, and digging around piles and messy aisles, all in the name of getting the most value out of their buck.
This treasure hunt shopping experience is the quote-unquote charm of the Dollar Tree that keeps consumers hooked.
This is just the first brand, Dollar Tree.
Now let's get into the second brand Family Dollar.
Family Dollar is a complimentary store to Dollar Tree and it positions itself as the neighborhood discount store.
Products at Family Dollar stores sell for at most $10 with most products on sale for less.
Interestingly enough, Family Dollar stores are smaller than Dollar Tree stores.
Family Dollar stores range about 6,000 to 8,000 square feet.
And whereas most products at Dollar Tree are not branded, Family Dollar offers leading brands and private label products.
Family Dollar offers a wide variety with four main product types.
The first is again consumable merchandise, which is food, beverages, tobacco, health and beauty, household chemicals, paper products, hardware supplies, diapers, batteries, and pet food.
The second category is home products, so things like houseware, home decor, giftware, comforters, sheets, and towels.
The third category is apparel and accessories, so things like clothing, fashion, and even shoes are carried at Family Dollar.
And the last is electronics and seasonal merchandise for Valentine's Day, Easter, Halloween, and Christmas.
Consumables are Family Dollar's best-selling products, and they make up over 75% of its sales for the past three years.
Seasonal merchandise and electronics, on the other hand, make up only 9%.
Apparel accounts for 6%, and home products make up only 8% of Family Dollar's annual net sales.
There are about 8,000 family dollar stores in the US.
Texas, Florida, and Ohio are the states with the most family dollar stores.
Even though both Dollar Tree and Family Dollar target low-income Americans, the two brands are designed to be strategic complements to one another.
To prevent sales cannibalism, Dollar Tree operates more in the suburbs, whereas Family Dollar operates in the rural and low-income urban communities.
Total annual sales for Dollar Tree in 2021 was $26 billion across 16,000 stores.
Compared to other retail heavyweights, Dollar Tree's overall top-line revenue and earning potential doesn't seem all that great.
In comparison, Target grosses around $90 billion every year with less than 2,000 stores.
The average Target store makes $49 to $50 million per year.
Walmart U.S.
on the other hand grosses $370 billion with less than 5,000 stores nationwide, and the average Walmart store makes about $78 million.
Both Target and Walmart are also much farther ahead than Dollar Tree when it comes to technology, online ordering, and delivery.
But like most things in life, the devil is in the details.
The average Dollar Tree store grosses $1.7 million a year.
So what Dollar Tree lacks in size and scale, it does make up for in margin.
The company's annual gross margin hovers at 30%, with a cogs of 70%.
That means that for every product that Dollar Tree sells for $1, the product cost is $0.70 and the company pockets $0.30 as gross profit.
If you were to repeat the same exercise with Target and Walmart, the numbers are actually fairly interesting.
Despite having much larger stores, greater inventory diversity, a much bigger brand, a broader customer base, and a higher sales volume, Walmart's annual gross margin is only 24% with a COGS of 76%.
Target's gross margin on the other hand is similar.
It's remained steady at 28% with a COGS of 72%.
But here's where we can go more into exploring the big retailers.
Target and Walmart are both extremely successful and massive retailers that are known as anchor tenants.
If you're a landlord, getting Target or Walmart into your shopping center as an anchor tenant can single-handedly turn your shopping mall from failing to thriving.
You generally want to give them a very generous, cheap multi-year lease because of how much they bring to the table.

On the other hand, if you're a CPG company and you want to get your products on the shelf of a Walmart or Target, you know that's going to unlock massive reach, brand credibility, and consistent revenue.

Because of how much Target and Walmart have to offer, suppliers, both in real estate and in products, are more than happy to give them massive discounts in exchange for steady cash flow and customer reach.
But even though there is this dynamic, Target and Walmart just can't get their product costs as low as Dollar Tree.
Two to six percent difference in cogs might not seem like much, but in the world of retail where margins are tight and every penny matters, a single percentage point in any direction is significant.
The other aspect to compare here is an expansion.
Target and Walmart and other big retailers are like mammoths.
Each store is massive and clock in at hundreds and thousands of square feet in order to be able to carry every product that someone would want throughout their life.
Because of how big these retailers stores are, it makes their expansion inherently difficult.

When Walmart and Target and Costco are thinking about a place to go to, they have to find a space that's not only big enough for them to operate in, but they'll also need all the surrounding to support it.
They need the parking spaces, the parking lots, and proximity to major highways for their trucks to easily access and unload cargo to.
On top of that, these large retailers need large towns or urban areas with high population density that have enough sufficient daily consumer demand to make that one store profitable.
Because the cost of expansion is so expensive, these big retailers move really slowly and carefully when it comes to opening new locations.
Target has only opened 58 new stores in the past three years, or 19 new locations on average every year.
Walmart on the other hand in the past three years has actually decreased the number of stores it has opened.
it's closed down 27 stores in the US in the past three years and hasn't dared to open another one.
in comparison the Dollar Tree over the same three years has opened 700 new stores in the US alone.
the hair and the tortoise is a tale as old as time about how being faster more nimble and lean doesn't necessarily beat the slow and steady.
this same moral has been applied religiously in the world of retail along with the rule of thumb that bigger is better.

title: Why Airbnb Fails to Disrupt the Hotel Industry
note: Industry explainer that sets up the Airbnb-as-disruptor narrative, then reverses it by showing hotels already run the same asset-light platform model.
sections: Why hotels aren't scared: they are platforms too
lines: From a distance, hotels seem like a simple business.
As a guest, you pay a nightly rate for a room of your choice.
The better the location, the more that you pay every night.
The more upscale the hotel is, the nicer your stay will be with better service and amenities, like business centers, gyms, fire pits, pools, and jacuzzis.
During your stay, you can pay more for add-ons like breakfast, shoe shining, room service, or even laundry.
After you check out your charge for everything, the hotel cleans up the room and rents it out to the next guest.
Rinse and repeat.
Hotels have high fixed and variable costs.
Let's say you run the luxury JW Marriott in downtown Los Angeles.
That's 21 floors, 900 rooms, complete with a full service spa, fitness center, outdoor pool, meeting room, rooftop bar, and valet.
Let's say the hotel is now in low season and only 30% of the rooms are occupied.
But the rooms still have to be cleaned, hallways still have to be vacuumed, the lobby has to be kept tidy, and counters have to be wiped.
Housekeeping still has to be on hand to deliver toothpaste, towels, and laundry upon request.
The bartender still has to be ready to take orders and pour drinks, even if no one's at the rooftop.
The same goes for the valet, the spa masseuse, the front desk, the pool guys, the doormen, and the security guards.
The nicer the hotel, the more amenities that are offered, but the higher the direct operating cost becomes with the additional labor, materials, and overhead.
Hotels operate on economies of scale and economies of scope.
Their objective is to achieve consistent volume and keep new guests flowing in after the prior guests' checkout.
This is why hotels aggressively slash prices in the low season and then hike the room prices as high as possible during the high season.
Low season is between November and March.
That's the end of the school year, when businesses tend to slow down, everyone winds down to Christmas, people travel back home to their families, and winters generally reach their coldest levels.
Few people will want to take a vacation during wind chills, ice storms, or heavy snows on the east coast.

High season, in comparison, is between May and August, so think of Miami during the summer, where everyone wants to go spend time on a beach, when the weather is at its nicest, when students break from school, and families go on vacation.
If we go back to that JW Marriott in downtown LA, all those additional amenities like the spa, the pool, the bar, and the valet are all tools to increase the average guest bill.

Even though these amenities and the overall hotel is a seasonal business, they'll go through their slow periods in the low season where they might end up operating in the red, the loss is generally made up during the high season.

Selling drinks, food, pedicures, valet, along with the optionality of pools and gyms and meeting rooms are all levers for a hotel to increase its revenue and customer lifetime value while slowly increasing the room price.
If you set too high of a room price, people will just book another comparable on an aggregator like Priceline, Expedia, or Trivago.
If you set too low of a room price, the rooms will sell out quickly, but the hotel still has plenty of ways to make money off the guests once they check in.
But not every hotel is a 5-star luxury building, and not everyone is willing to spend hundreds of dollars every night.
Luxury hotel rooms account for less than 2% of all available hotel rooms in the United States.
The hotel industry categorizes hotels under four main types.
Economy, mid-scale, upscale, and luxury.
The type of hotel you go to dictates how much you should expect to pay per night, the quality and breadth of service you should expect to receive, and the amenities that are available on site.
If we look at the leading hotels today, there are really five main players.
These five corporations own entire portfolios of recognizable hotels and brands that span across all these different hotel types.
Let's start with the most well-known player in Hilton.
Hilton's luxury brands are the prestigious Waldorf Astoria, Alexar, and Conrad hotels, which are all located in landmark destinations like Dubai, Turkey, Rome, and New York City.
But as legendary and prestigious as these luxury brands are, these hotels account for less than 5% of the total hotel rooms in Hilton's portfolio.
Hilton's moneymakers are in its upscale and midscale brands.
The Hilton is the company's flagship hotel that provides everything from event spaces to restaurants and bars in their lobbies.
Doubletree is famous for its warm chocolate chip cookies that it serves guests upon check-in, is also another well-known upscale Hilton hotel that's mainly targeted towards business travelers.
Garden Inn and Embassy Suites are other examples of leading upscale Hilton hotels.
In the mid-scale category, Hilton owns the respected Hampton Inn, which also attracts leisure travelers with its complimentary hot breakfast and waffles.
Hotels make money as a function of how many rooms they have, and Hilton in 2021 grossed $6 billion with a little over 1 million rooms worldwide.
Before the pandemic, Hilton was earning $8-9 billion consistently every year.
But despite their first mover advantage and fame, Hilton is only good enough to take second place when it comes to revenue and total rooms available.
First place goes to Marriott.
Marriott has the highest market cap and grosses nearly three times as much revenue as Hilton.
Marriott's luxury brands include the Ritz Carlton, St.
Regis, JW Marriott, and the W.
Its other upscale concepts include the Sheraton, Westin, and Marriott hotels.
What's really unique about the Marriott portfolio is that they have the mature, mid-scale market share that Hilton lacks.
Marriott owns trusted brands in the mid-scale category like Courtyard, Fairfield, Aloft, and Residence Inn.
Marriott grossed $14 billion dollars in 2021 across 1.5 million rooms and was the undisputed industry leader with the most revenue and rooms available worldwide.
Before COVID, Marriott was grossing $20 billion a year.
If Marriott is in first place and Hilton is in second, then third place goes to Intercontinental Hotel Group.
Intercontinental Hotel Group, or IHG for short, is based in Europe, but their portfolio contains plenty of recognizable American brands.
IHG's luxury portfolio is spearheaded by the Regent and Sixth Sense, which are located in places like the Maldives, Fiji, and Portugal.
IHG owns Crowne Plaza, as well as Holiday Inn, and the company grossed $2.9 billion in 2021 across 900,000 hotel rooms.
Before the pandemic, IHG's annual revenue was around $4-5 billion every year.
Hyatt Hyatt's portfolio boasts top-end luxury brands such as Grand Hyatt, Park Hyatt, and Destination.
For the upscale market, Hyatt owns Hyatt Regency, Hyatt Place, Hyatt House, and Hyatt Hotel.
Hyatt grossed $3 billion in 2021, which puts the company on par with IHG, but is also half of what Hilton makes every year.
Hyatt caters more towards business travelers, and the company's results in that regard are really impressive.
Hyatt has less than 300,000 hotel rooms worldwide, which is a third of IHG, a third of Hilton, and a fifth of Marriott's scale.
But to generate $3 billion off of so few rooms speak to how successful Hyatt has been in cornering the upscale business travel market.
Before the COVID pandemic, Hyatt grossed $4-5 billion every year.
In 5th place is Wyndham.
While all these other players are duking it out over the high-end market, Wyndham is the quiet player that chooses to sit at an entirely different poker table.
They specialize in mid-scale and economy hotels.
Super 8, Travel Lodge, Microtel, and Days Inn are all well-known budget hotels in Windham's portfolio and targeted for value-oriented travelers.
For economy hotels, free coffee and high-speed internet are the extent of the amenities.
These economy hotels are simple, affordable, functional, and widespread.
Windham also owns reputable mid-scale hotels such as La Quinta, Ramada, and Baymont.
In 2021, Windham grossed $1.5 billion across 800,000 rooms, And before the pandemic, their gross revenue was clocking in at around $1.5 to $2 billion every year.
Then came a little startup called Airbnb.
As this tech company began to pick up momentum and funding in the early 2010s, a narrative began to take shape.
Why stay in a hotel room when you can instead rent an Airbnb condo or home?
Here's the kitchen.
It's all newly remodeled, all new appliances, farmhouse sinks.
One reason for Airbnb's surging popularity is the chance to rent a whole house for the price of a hotel room.
It is not just a game changer, it's a huge game changer.
The numbers are staggering.
Imagine this, 25 million people booking rooms through Airbnb.
And they're not just rooms.
You can book everything from a Winnebago to, they've got 600 castles on their list.
So the variety and the diversity is great.
It's changing the name because you've got $13 billion in market valuation of just Airbnb alone.
That surpasses already the market valuation of companies like Intercontinental Hotels.
Airbnb is fundamentally changing the hotel industry.
Airbnb's gross bookings last year were $240 million, according to PrivCo.
That's approaching Marriott's $1 billion, Starwood's $2 billion, Hyatt at $2 billion, and Hilton at $4 billion.
That's a big deal.
And Airbnb's growth is at the expense of hotels.
A Boston University study found that for every 1% increase in Airbnb's business, the rest of the hotel industry falls by five basis points.
And think about it.
Airbnb's growth is unconstrained by limits of real estate or capital.
Even to this day, hotel executives can't get through interviews without being asked about Airbnb.
But what's interesting is that their collective response and position has been measured and consistent over the years.
Well, I think the disruptor that people think of first for the hotel space is Airbnb.
But I would talk about two others as well.
One would be online travel agents, which have been in place now for 10 to 15 years, Expedia, Priceline, Rakuten, Ctrip in China, a number of different players.
And then the Googles and Amazons and Apples of the world, who have these extraordinary technology platforms, the ability to monetize them in ways which are pretty profound.
They all pose threats to us.
They are different kinds of threats.
I think Airbnb, because it's the newest, captures the most attention.
But in some respects is maybe the least threatening.
And I don't mean to suggest that they're not a disruptor and they're not relevant.
They are a big player and I think they're here for a long time.

But But they are increasingly getting to a place where they are selling dedicated units on their site as opposed to the guest room in somebody's occupied home, which is where it started as classic shared economy.
That classic shared economy is a different experience than a hotel room.
Some people are going to be drawn to that because it's local and it seems individual, it doesn't seem institutional in any respect.
and you can understand that.
But when it's a dedicated unit, then it's simply a question of, all right, what's the location?
What's the price?
What's the product look like?
How well is it cared for?
That's the competition we've been having for decades.
And I think in many respects that competition, while worthy and threatening, is not a wholly different kind of competition than we've had in the past.
Is Airbnb a threat to the established hotel industry?
I would not position them as a threat.
There are players within our market, even though they're not really direct players because they only offer an online platform.
We are offering accommodation.
They don't.
They just list companies in their database to be able to offer accommodation.
So I would not really call them a threat at this point, but they are a growing player that we need to be looking at in detail in terms of how are they playing and is within the rules of the game.
I do not think it's a real competitor to us.
So if you think about what we do, it's something different than what they do.
And I think we coexist with them quite well.

We deliver a high-quality, consistent product with the amenities wrapped in service with all the technology, loyalty, and people pay us generally a big premium for that because they want that level of consistent, high-quality experience.
What they do is something different.
What they're doing is, by definition, can't have the consistency and the quality and the products and the amenities that are tailor-fit because it's just something different.
But it doesn't mean it's bad.
It just means it's satisfying a different kind of trip occasion.
So if you look at the numbers, even pre-COVID, we were coexisting quite well.
We were at the peak levels of performance at a time where they were growing leaps and bounds.
And we weren't really seeing significant competitive threat as a result.
Cost is the biggest barrier to scale in the hotel industry.
It takes on average two to three years to build a new hotel.
The upfront cost for design, permits, and construction can range from $30 million to $130 million, depending on location and category.
These estimates don't even include the cost of the land.
Since these numbers are publicly shared by nearly every hotel giant, it's no secret how cost prohibitive and expensive it is to grow your market share in the hotel industry.
Airbnb's innovation is on the supply side.
Anyone around the world can list and monetize their room, apartment, or house with just a few steps on Airbnb's website.
The company's business value is to serve as a trusted platform between travelers and hosts.
Discovery, communication, and transactions between both parties all occur on Airbnb.
Hosts set their own prices for their own listings, they provide service, and they accept travelers in whatever way that they see fit.
As a middleman, Airbnb charges service fees to both guests and hosts as a percentage of their total reservation cost.
Airbnb's advantage is that as a platform, the company doesn't own, lease, manage, or maintain any physical real estate.
Hosts can add or remove their listings at any time.
For example, if a host isn't seeing the business they want on Airbnb, they can simply choose to remove their listing at no additional cost.
There's an opportunity cost, but there's no marginal cost.
Airbnb is ultimately monetizing housing that already exists.
So, it's not a question of demand or supply, it's just whether or not that housing supply exists on Airbnb.
Hotels, on the other hand, are the exact opposite.
Demand has to be validated first in order for the housing supply to exist.

If the destination is not popular enough to fill the hotel rooms, if the local labor pool is not robust enough, if the land is not available or too expensive to purchase, then the hotel will simply not exist.
While there are no limits to how many listings there can be on Airbnb, there are hard ceilings on how many hotels can exist based on zoning ordinance.
Airbnb is an asset-light, fee-based platform business in an industry that notoriously demands significant capital upfront and capital expenditures.
This platform advantage has enabled Airbnb to outperform hotels at scale.
Airbnb had 6 million active listings in 2021.
If we combine Marriott and Hilton for the sake of comparison and we add these two industry leaders together, we get a total of 2.5 million rooms.
That's not even half of Airbnb's listings.
Even if we add up all the properties and hotel rooms of the five major players that we've covered earlier, Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, and Wyndham, they still don't come close to Airbnb's scale.
Between 2020 and 2021, Marriott added 30,000 rooms, Hyatt and Hilton each added 50,000 rooms, Wyndham added 20,000 hotel rooms, and IHG actually shrunk.
They closed down 6,000 rooms.
In the same exact time frame, time, Airbnb added 400,000 listings to their platform.
Airbnb's scale fuels its top-line revenue.
Airbnb's gross revenue in 2021 was $5.9 billion, which beats Hyatt, Wyndham, and IHG by a large margin and puts the tech companies slightly ahead of Hilton when it comes to annual earnings.
So why are hotel executives more scared of Airbnb?
Are Hilton, Marriott, and Hyatt executives pretending not to care publicly, but secretly freaking out in their boardrooms?
are these hotel giants too stubborn to evolve?

The secret is that Hilton, Marriott, Hyatt, Wyndham, IHG, and every hotel giant in the industry, they're actually all asset-light platform businesses who make most of their money on fees just like Airbnb.

So while the media and analysts will spin stories about how the hotel industry is dying and about to be disrupted, the reality is that Hilton, Marriott, Hyatt, every big hotel company has been operating exactly like Airbnb long before the startup even existed.
Disruption can't happen if the new firm and the old incumbents are all operating in the same way.

Most people think of the hotel industry as this deeply traditional, slow-moving business where companies buy the land, hire the staff, build the hotel from the foundations up, and run it themselves until it pays off.

And that's true when you look at the roots of the hotel industry, where legendary founders like Conrad Hilton, John Marriott, and Hyatt Robert Van Den own, manage, and build every single hotel under their names starting from the 1920s to the 1950s.
This traditional owner-operated, asset-heavy business model does have some upsides.
If the hotel performs well, then the owner directly benefits from all the income generated.
If the owner also owns the underlying land, they also benefit from the real estate appreciation, which is often a higher return than running the hotel itself.
The challenge with this traditional owner-operated business model is the capital requirements, slow growth, high operating risk, and low cash-on-cash return.
Even though the owners can pocket all the income generated under this business model, they also bear all the operating expense and risk of running that hotel.
It can take a hotel decades to break even with its initial investment.
Even though the assets like the land and the building carry high book value, hotels are typically cash-starved and desperately need cash flow to offset their daily high operating expenses.

Unless the company is backed by credible lenders who can provide significant financial safety nets or cash infusions, it really only takes one underperforming hotel under this asset-heavy, owner-operated business model to pull a company towards bankruptcy.
You can see how fragile the traditional owner-operated hotel business model is by looking at Hyatt, Hilton, and Marriott's business performance before and after COVID.
In this dataset, we just look at the few hotels that these corporations still own and operate themselves.
Before COVID, Hyatt and Marriott had clearly achieved economies of scale and were enjoying healthy 20% and above gross margins on its hotels.
Hilton wasn't performing as well as Hyatt or Marriott, but they were still in the green with 7% positive margin on the hotels that it was operating.

After COVID, a lot of these hotel giants still haven't recovered their economies of scale, They've struggled to maintain consistent guest volume, and the gross margins for the hotels that they directly operate have taken significant hits.
Marriott's gross margin for the hotels that it operates dropped to 8%, and Hilton went all the way to negative 14%.
When you're in this owner-operated model, reducing variable costs is one of the few levers you have available to reduce your burn rate.

But cutting employee hours, eliminating non-essential staff, shutting down amenities, reducing services, lowering these variable costs are simply not enough to maintain your margins when you're already faced with such high fixed costs under this traditional owner-operated model.
The critical misconception that many people have today is that Airbnb is the company who pioneered this platform business model in the hotel industry.
But in reality, the hotel giants have already been operating as platforms for many decades long before Airbnb even existed.
The platform business model is not some new novel idea.
Instead, it's an established and well-proven monetization path that has enabled the hotel industry to scale to its current heights today.
They're able to achieve faster returns, unlock faster growth, with less capital and operating risk.
Just like McDonald's or Subway, Hyatt, Hilton, and Marriott, and really every other major hotel, they all engage in franchising.
Under the franchise model, you shoulder the initial startup costs and take on the responsibility for operating the hotel and hiring the staff.

In return, you get to brand the hotel as a Hyatt, Hilton, or Marriott, and you tap into an active customer base, write off the brand's prestige, integrate into the company's tech infrastructure and supply chain, and take part in a robust loyalty program like Honors or Bonvoy.
And, ultimately, if you're a franchisee, you never have to worry about advertising or marketing or whether or not people know about your hotel.
If you were a new hotel owner and you were to forge your own independent brand, it would likely be a long and painful journey.
You would be buried deep in a sea of other independent hotel brands on aggregators like Hotels.com, Trivago, and Priceline.

And since two-thirds of hotel bookings worldwide are for business purposes, there's little chance a business traveler would take the risk staying at an unknown hotel over the consistency, reliability, and reputation of a Hyatt, Hilton, or Marriott.
To play out the franchisee example, in exchange for being able to brand your hotel as a Hilton, you kick up 2-6% of your gross booking revenue to Hilton.
You also pay a percentage of your gross food and beverage sales along with a monthly program fee up to Hilton.
The only upside here is that if you own the land yourself as the franchisee, you still get to keep all this real estate appreciation for yourself.
If you're a hands-off owner that doesn't want to take on operations, you can enter into a separate fee-based management arrangement where the hotel giant comes in and manages your hotel for you.
It will still be branded as a Hilton, Hyatt, Marriott, whatever hotel you want, but the hotel giant will essentially operate the hotel.
They'll hire, train, and manage all your employees on your behalf.
In return, the hotel giant will take a percentage of your gross revenue as a management fee.
They'll take another percentage as a bonus fee, along with a fixed monthly fee.
While you would still be legally recognized as the owner, you would not be responsible or involved day-to-day in any aspect of running the hotel.
The catch here with this fee-based management model is that you still have to reimburse Marriott, Hilton, IHG, or whoever for all the operating expenses that they incur running your hotel for you.
And that's interestingly enough why cost reimbursement is the biggest contributor to every hotel giant's gross revenue.
The traditional owner-operated model is really a relic of the past these days.
The hotel portion is an incredible model.
Think about it, Jim.
500 million, half a billion dollars of royalty fee income alone every year.

So consistent and it flows through at 90% margin generating 450 million dollars of royalty fee income before you get to the management and all the other ways that we could drive this business from from a growth standpoint.

Given our asset light business model and the actions we took during the pandemic to further streamline our operations, we expect permanent margin improvement versus prior peak levels in the range of 400 to 600 basis points over the next few years.
Our fourth quarter results reflect the clear resilience of travel, our strong focus on cost containment, and the benefits of our asset-light business model.
Gross fee revenues reached $831 million in the fourth quarter.
Hilton today owns and operates less than 2% of its hotel rooms.
Hyatt owns and operates 5% of its hotel rooms.
And Windham actually owns none of its hotel rooms.
They just recently sold off their last two hotels in their fourth quarter of 2021.
For Hilton, they make three times as much money from franchise fees than they do from gross bookings at the hotels that they do operate.
Marriott makes twice as much money from franchise fees than they do from hotels that they own and operate.

Windem, on the other hand, is an example of a company that has embraced the platform business model with 95% of its hotel rooms under franchise ownership and the remaining 5% under fee-based management.
The narrative around Airbnb's disruption and platform business model is intriguing, but it's not the groundbreaking phenomenon as the media and academics would pose it to be.
The entire hotel industry had been undergoing this transition from asset-heavy operators to asset-light, fee-based platforms for decades long before Airbnb existed.
In particular, Hilton, IHG, Wyndham, and Marriott have been very aggressive in selling off their hotels and lands to anyone who would buy them every year for the past 20 years.
It's really worth noting here that the platform business model in itself is not a silver bullet.
While Airbnb continues to outperform the hotel industry in terms of scale and listings, things, the challenge the tech company is facing today is the realization that quantity is not quality.

Safety issues, service inconsistency, guest volatility, intrusive hosts, privacy concerns, and excessive policies have resulted in Airbnb travelers feeling more like burdens than guests to their hosts these days.
On the flip side, regulation has also caught up.

With mandatory city fees, licensing, and permit costs now factored into each booking, Airbnb can no longer use the tagline that they're cheaper or more unique than a hotel when they're already being taxed like one.
And since affordability was a major driving force behind the company's early popularity, it's an open question mark as to how Airbnb will navigate these choppy waters ahead.
When the playing ground becomes level and price becomes equal across hotels and Airbnbs, service will inevitably become a competitive advantage.

The reliability, predictability, and consistency in guest experience is really where hotels have continued to edge out Airbnb across business and leisure travel for the past several decades, and why the industry as a whole doesn't think of Airbnb as a threat.

title: La Croix's Succession of Coca-Cola & Pepsi
note: Industry shift story: soda declines, a successor question is posed, La Croix rises, then limits and rival responses. Several long interview clips are embedded.
sections: Big Soda's denial and disastrous interview
Coke and Pepsi revenue vs reality
lines: In the early 2000s, soda was named public enemy number one in the war against obesity.
In the three decades since 1975, obesity rates worldwide had tripled, the number of people with diabetes had quadrupled, and the number of obese children and adolescents had increased tenfold.
By 2007, nearly 40% of Americans were obese.
One in every five calories was from a liquid.
Sugary drinks were the largest contributor of calories in the average American diet.
By 2008, these patterns were clearly spreading beyond the United States.
Mexico had the highest soda consumption per person in the world at 135 liters, which means one person in Mexico every year drinks 68 of those big, party-sized bottles by themselves.
Future studies would place Argentina and Chile above Mexico as countries with even higher soda consumption per capita.
Coke and Pepsi, the two soda titans, put aside their rivalries and went on the attack united as a collective entity known as Big Soda.
Big Soda claimed that it was unfair to single them out when there were other contributors to poor health, like candy, fast food, and lack of exercise.

Big Soda spent millions of dollars funding scientists and lobbyists to influence research and policy, pushing assertions that it was a lack of exercise and not soda for the biggest contributor to obesity.
Big Soda even went on to claim that there was quote-unquote near-zero association between sugary drinks and BMI.
Most of the focus in the popular media and in the scientific press is, oh, they're eating too much, eating too much, eating too much, blaming fast food, blaming sugary drinks, and so on.
And there's really virtually no compelling evidence that that, in fact, is a cause.
What consumers need to know about soft drinks and blood sugar is that soft drinks do no more to blood sugar than any other food or beverage.
And Dr.
Whelan, how about the soft drinks?
What's your take on those?
Well, the claim that soft drinks are a cause of obesity really has no factual basis.
Well, people get heart disease and diabetes from obesity, but that doesn't mean that...
Which is caused, they're saying in part, by the sodas, right?
Well, it's caused by eating too much and not burning off those calories.
So I think it's important to stick to facts, not mislead consumers, and not imply that soft drinks contribute to diabetes or heart disease disease or any other disease in any unique way.
They really don't.
But the independent science was too strong, and the global health crisis was getting simply too severe to be ignored.
People just weren't buying what Big Soda had to say.
Well, James Quincy is the president of Coca-Cola Europe.
What good does Coca-Cola do you physically?
I think Coca-Cola, as the introduction said, does have some sugar in it.
It is energy.
Is it an absolute necessity?
No, it's not.
Millions of people enjoy it as part of their diet across the UK.
It does have some sugar in it, you say.
It does.
Why don't you say specifically how much sugar there is in this can, for example?
I think if you find, if you turn...
On the side, you say 30, you have a percentage on there, don't you?
Yes, right here on the front, it quite clearly calls out the amount of sugar in this can of Coke.
What does it say?
35 grams, which is six teaspoons of sugar, which is, you know, about the same amount of calories as a cappuccino or half a croissant.
So there is calories.
And actually, what we're doing is to say, look, the information is here.
We want to actually float and make sure people don't know.
Do you imagine people know if they go to the cinema, and this is a small one, and there are big ones here too, you go to the cinema and you get a jug of coke like this.
Do you think people have any idea how much sugar's in it?
And maybe they don't, and I think one of the things we need to do...
Do you know what it is?
Look at this.
23 sachets of sugar in that single container, the equivalent thereof.
That is a staggering amount of sugar, isn't it?
That is why we're very focused as one of the things we're doing on getting the information out there.
We're not trying to hide the information behind what's in a Coca-Cola classic.
But you're all trying to hide it.
But there's zero sugar in a Coke Zero.
Well, clearly it's called a Coke Zero, but a Coke Classic, look at this one here.
There's 44 packets of sugar in this one.

Indeed there are, and I think what we're saying is, look, we want to make sure that people have the information available to them so that they can make the choices, and if they don't want the big one, then fine, and that clearly is not one that's going to be for everyone.
We want to make sure the information is available.
We want to make sure there's more availability of more choices, whether it's smaller packages as you had in your intro.
Yeah, but whether it's 23 in something this size or 44 in something this size, each of which is to be consumed in one single sitting of a cinema, this is staggering, isn't it?
Look, I think we do need to recognize that things need to change, that the bigger cups need to come down.
I don't think that we are talking that the world can't change and the world doesn't need to move on.
I think what it comes back to is we recognize that we need to play our part in helping to fix this very important issue of obesity.
It's something that's come about from us taking in too many calories and not burning them off with activity, many things over many decades, and we're taking actions.
We are promoting the information, By the way, the gentleman who gave this disastrous interview is now the CEO of Coca-Cola.
Since this interview went viral back in 2013, Coca-Cola has intentionally conducted very few public interviews.
Any interview nowadays that involves Coca-Cola is a scripted and paid arrangement where the reporter asks softball questions that the company has already prepared the answers for.
Eating too much sugar is objectively unhealthy, and soda was the worst offender.
as a beverage with no nutritional value, it's priced very affordably, easily consumed, it's deceivingly light and refreshing, and it's also highly concentrated in sugar.
After much failed lobbying, Coke and Pepsi eventually gave in, and they admitted causation, not just correlation, between soda consumption and poor health.
Policymakers have attempted to crack down on soda consumption in the past decade.
Select countries and US cities have added a special tax for sodas and other sugary beverages.
The theory behind that is that by artificially increasing the cost of soda through a special tax, consumers would naturally decrease the quantity they consume.
In lower income countries like Chile and India, the soda tax starts at 18% and goes as high as 40%.
American municipalities have also banned soft drink sales in schools, and governments worldwide have continued to push for even more aggressive measures.
Singapore has outright banned advertising of soda and other sugary drinks, while Mexico has to restrict when soda drink commercials can be aired on their television.
While Big Soda has been unsuccessful in influencing science and research, they've been really effective at shutting down any anti-soda legislation in America at the state and federal level.
Any measures against soda like taxes or bans in the United States these days mostly only exist at the city or county level.
Despite Big Soda's successful lobbying, soda consumption has substantially declined in the past two decades.
Consumers worldwide have become more conscious about the things that they eat, what they drink, and the consequences of those choices on their health.
By 2015, sales of soda in the United States had dropped 25%.
According to the CDC, soda consumption amongst teenagers, who are a critical target audience for big soda, had dropped by 24%.
By 2017, soda consumption had plummeted to a 30-year low.
The average American went from drinking 50 gallons of soda every year to 37.5 gallons in nearly two decades, which was a 30% decline in consumption.
Fruit juice, including the iconic orange juice which was once regarded as a healthy essential of American breakfast, had also been in freefall.
By 2021, per capita consumption of juice in the United States had dropped 36%.

Coke Zero, Diet Coke, Diet Pepsi, Pepsi Zero, Sprite Zero, and Diet Mountain Dew are all examples of low-calorie, no-sugar offerings that the Coca-Cola Company and PepsiCo have aggressively marketed towards health-conscious consumers.
Despite this, consumers are still skeptical with concerns over the artificial sweeteners that were used heavily in these quote-unquote healthier sodas.
When we look at the top line of PepsiCo and Coca-Cola from 2011 to 2021, Coca-Cola's annual revenue has actually dropped by 20% from $48 billion to $33 billion.
PepsiCo on the other hand is surprisingly bucking the trend with an unexpectedly upward going from $66 billion to $79 billion every year.
But PepsiCo's top-line revenue is misleading.
While Coca-Cola is a beverage company that sells only drinks, PepsiCo has a diversified portfolio of drinks and convenience food brands.
Doritos, Cheetos, Fritos, Lay's, Ruffles, Tostito, Captain Crunch, Quaker Oats, Chewy Granola Bars, and Rose Gold Pretzels are all examples of food brands that are owned by PepsiCo.
These best-selling snacks pad PepsiCo's top-line revenue and help compensate for declining soda sales.
Snacks make up 55%, and drinks make up the other 45% of PepsiCo's annual revenue.
If we adjust PepsiCo's total revenue to just their beverage sale, the real story emerges.
Pepsi's revenue isn't a straight drop like it is for Coca-Cola, but their drink revenue has clearly stagnated.
Coca-Cola's sales on average have gone down 1% every year for the past 10 years.
Pepsi's sales, on the other hand, have remained in line with US inflation at positive 2% every year for the past 10 years.
2016 was a groundbreaking year where for the first time in American history, people were drinking more water than soda.
But the future looked bleat for the beverage industry.
You could get water from the tap for free, or you could spend a little bit more to buy bottled water.
You could pay a bit more for branded water like Fiji, Smart Water, or Evian, but very few consumers care deeply enough about water quality to consistently pay for that premium.
Even when soda consumption was declining, these high-end water brands that had been around for decades weren't able to capture any additional market share.
Coconut water and tea were emerging, but appealed to only a few select audiences.

If soda wasn't selling anymore, juice was out of fashion, bottled water was now commoditized, and premium water was really never able to outgrow its niche, the beverage industry was faced with a big question.
Who would be the successor to Big soda.
What drink could directly replace soda, and what company could take over Coke and Pepsi's multi-billion dollar market share?
In 2016, the same year where Americans drank more water than soda, a small beverage company that had been under the radar since 1991 suddenly exploded in mainstream popularity and record sales.
The chosen one had seemingly arrived, boasting growth rates, unit volume, revenue, virality, consumer excitement that the beverage industry hadn't seen in decades.
To avoid sugary soft drinks, some make La Croix their all-time favorite drink.
Sparkling water, La Croix.
La Croix, I have flavored sparkling water.
La Croix, all the way.
What's the fucking deal with La Croix, am I right?
Mmm, La Croix.
Fizzy, cold, refreshing, and incredibly addicting.
It starts with just one can a day, and then before you know it, this happens.
It's one of the most popular fizzy drinks in the country.
Yeah, nothing's going to stop me from drinking my La Croix.
There's not a single office you can go to now without finding one of these.
Everyone here drinks them.
I drink four to six a day.
Our favorite new drink is La Croix flavored sparkling water.
This is the grapefruit.
Again, my personal favorite.
Zero calories, zero sugar, zero artificial flavoring.
Just a really great way to make sure you're meeting your water needs, but also a lot more fun than just plain water.
LaCroix, a fruit-flavored sparkling water brand owned by National Beverage Corporation, was suddenly the hottest beverage in town.
A fizzy seltzer that was once laughed at as a Midwest mom's occasional indulgence, seemingly overnight became the primary drink of choice for millennials.
Without sugar, sodium, artificial sweeteners, or ingredients, LaCroix ticked off all the boxes from a nutritional perspective.
National Beverage Corporation, the owner behind LaCroix, knew that in order to win over millennials, they needed authenticity.

Rather than blasting mainstream television with high-production advertisements like what was traditionally done with Coke and Pepsi, National Beverage Corporation opted to invest in social media marketing and packaging.
LaCroix consumers turned into organic champions, writing love-lesses about the drink in newspapers and flooding Instagram with their obsession.
The rainbow, colorful branding on its cans and retro look made LaCroix stand out physically at retail stores and quickly turned it into a fashionable status symbol.
Between 2016-2018, National Beverage Corporation's revenue exploded thanks to La Croix's popularity.
The company's top line grew at 10%, 16%, and 18% in each of those three years.
In the same time frame, Coca-Cola had its worst three-year run in company history with a combined negative 23% drop in annual sales.
Pepsi didn't fare much better with a combined 3% growth over those same three years.
Case volume is a key core performance metric for the beverage industry.
It's a measurement of how much drink volume has been sold for over a year, which then in turn serves as a lagging indicator for consumer demand.
The higher your case volume, the more product that you're selling, which means the more people are drinking.
Revenue is case volume times the average selling price.
What's annoying is that National Beverage Corporation disguises the true performance of La Croix by mixing in other drink brands into its financials.
When you look at National Beverage's breakdown, the company intentionally blends La Croix's sales and volume with its other brands like Clear Fruit, Rip It, Everfresh, and Mr.
Pure.
These are brands that I've never heard of and probably account for likely less than 1% of the company's overall revenue, but still, they do this.
PepsiCo and the Coca-Cola Company use the exact same tactic.
The Coca-Cola Company groups Fanta, Diet Coke, Coke Zero, Coke, Sprite, together into one group and reports on their combined sales and volume.
PepsiCo does the exact same.
They group Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Sierra Mist, Mug, Root Beer altogether, and then report on their combined case volume and sales.
This means that there's no way to really evaluate LaCroix independently and compare the seltzer one-to-one with Sprite, Coke, or Pepsi.
The same is true for analysis on the opposite end.
There's no way to know if Diet Coke or Coke Cherry sells better than normal Coke, if Sprite sells less than Mountain Dew, if Fanta is more popular than Sierra Mist, or how much Coke outsells Pepsi.
Only the company insiders know exactly how much each brand is selling.
While PepsiCo's beverage sales look stable from a dollar standpoint, the reality is that the consumer demand for its soda has been in the toilet for years.
Up until 2021, Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Mug Root Beer, and Sierra Mist combined had been regressing in volume for six consecutive years.
From 2015 to 2020, Pepsi was shipping and selling on average 3% less soda cases every year.
In two years, case volume had dipped as low as negative 5%.
If it weren't for Pepsi's non-soda sales from Brisk, Lipton, Muscle Milk, and Gatorade to help smooth this damage, Pepsi's beverage business would look far worse.
Instead of a straight decline as one might expect, the case volume growth for Coke, Diet Coke, Coke Zero, Fanta, and Sprite hasn't been positive or negative, it's just been non-existent.
Since 2015, case volume growth for the Coca-Cola company has been at 0%.
The volume growth, on the other hand, for La Croix and National Beverage is outstanding compared to Big Soda.
It's clear that LaCroix's popularity was no short-lived social media fad.
Since 2015, the company has enjoyed sustained 21% growth every year on average for the past six years.
In 2019, National Beverage surpassed $1 billion in sales for the first time in company history, and there are few signals that suggest LaCroix's reputation and growth is ending anytime soon.
The company has also kept its foot on the gas pedal, regularly launching new flavors to match seasons and to keep customers engaged.
As impressive as LaCroix's demand and National Beverage's growth has been, the reality is that the company still has a long way to go before it can truly rival Big Soda.
When you compare National Beverage and overall revenue or market cap, National Beverage is barely visible when you plot them with Coke and Pepsi.
LaCroix and flavored sparkling water for the most part still seems to be a North American phenomenon.
To reach the heights of Big Soda, National Beverage would need to scale its audience and operations beyond the United States.

But international expansion doesn't seem too likely with the nationalistic and old school vibes I get from their CEO, who writes some of the most entertaining shareholder letters in what appears to be 1996 Microsoft Word and Clipart.
His commentaries often come off more like rants, where the man has made it his personal mission to wage some religious holy war against Big Soda.
But to his credit, LaCroix really seems to be holding its ground.
Even with all these quirks, National Beverage Corporation does seem like a well-run, tightly managed ship with a clear vision and product.
As much as LaCroix's success has been fueled by its strong product-market fit and operational excellence, their rise has also been fueled by their first-mover advantage.
LaCroix as a brand had existed for more than 30 years, and for the longest time was the only seltzer in town.

Coca-Cola's leadership didn't seem to take LaCroix seriously, and appeared to dismiss its popularity as a millennial fad for years, believing that Diet Coke and Coke Zero would eventually win over the health-conscious consumers.
When I talked to you earlier, James, we talked about the resurgence in Diet Coke, and you mentioned that millennials were finding it.
How did that happen?
Yeah, Diet Coke in the U.S., it grew again.
It grew in revenue, grew in volume.
What's interesting is it's actually got more households coming into the franchise.
The brand indicator scores that we look at internally are getting better.

I think it's a combination of some marketing inviting reconsideration for a generation where perhaps not all of them are connected to Diet Coke with the flavor innovation, with the innovation in the sleek can, which is a more modern, more engaging package.
I think that combination executed by the bottlers has brought people in and they found something that they like in what is ultimately a great tasting beverage.

The company finally did respond to LaCroix in 2017 by extending its existing brands like Smartwater and Dasani to release seltzer variants, but neither really caught on and sparkling Smart Water and sparkling Dasani have been discontinued.
It was only until 2019 that Coca-Cola introduced AHA, its own flavored seltzer brand, and Topo Chico sparkling mineral water to American consumers.
PepsiCo responded faster than Coca-Cola by launching Bubly, their own flavored seltzer line, in 2018.
Bubly's playful packaging and branding are all a clear emulation of LaCroix.
If you can't beat them, join them.
From all accounts, Bubly seems to be gaining steam in the US market.
On my last several domestic business trips, they were the only seltzer that was available to order on United Airlines.
But first-mover advantage doesn't last forever, and LaCroix must be feeling the pressure.
There are new companies like Spindrift who have also ventured into the sparkling water market, who are all eager to carve off a slice of the pie for themselves.
Despite the strong fundamentals of the underlying company, Wall Street has turned mostly bearish on LaCroix.

National beverage corporations' unwillingness scale beyond the United States haven't really helped convince analysts who remain concerned that the company will devolve into a one-trick pony and that long-term, sparkling water might just be commoditized like bottled plain water.

Consumers may grow over time to not care so much about whether they're drinking Bubbly, Aha, Spindrift, or LaCroix, so long as it's a naturally flavored, not artificially sweetened, no-sugar sparkling water, the consumer will be happy.
Whether or not LaCroix and National Beverage Corporation become the true successor to Big soda will be up to its management, leadership, and time.
But there's no denying the historic impact that LaCroix has had in forcing Big Soda to rethink its strategy and accelerating the fall of soda in America.

title: Unfinished & Unstable: How SaaS Changed Video Games
note: Industry thesis explainer with three case studies (CD Projekt Red, Square Enix, Take-Two) building to a contrast winner and a lesson.
sections: How video games used to work
CD Projekt Red: Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk
lines: In 2011, legendary Silicon Valley investor Mark Andreessen published his most famous essay that software is eating the world.

His assertion was that despite the dotcom bubble in the 1990s, software would permeate all industries from agriculture to defense in the form of online services, and there would be a new wave of high-growth, high-margin, defensible software businesses.
Fast forward 10 years and Mark's thesis has held true.
The way software is developed, distributed, consumed, priced, and sold has radically transformed in the past decade.
Historically, software was self-hosted.
It was sold in stores, distributed in CDs, positioned as a lifetime one-and-done purchase, stored locally, and restricted to a single computer for offline use.
Stability was valued above all else, and updates were rare and risky.
Today it's the opposite.
it.
Modern software is consumed as an online service, generally in the form of web applications or mobile applications.
Digital distribution has become king.
For anything that can't be accessed through an internet browser or the app store, it can be downloaded directly.
License keys and activation codes are virtual, and software is now meant to be used on multiple devices.
Most of all, modern software is about rapid continuous improvement, where speed is the priority even at the expense of stability.
Updates are constant and new features are regularly introduced.
You can see software as a service in nearly every facet of modern life.
Look at Photoshop, a strictly licensed single device that was sold on CDs as a one-and-done purchase for $700 in the early 2000s.
Nowadays, you can only get Photoshop as a $9.99 monthly service through Adobe Creative Cloud.
Instead of building an iTunes library of $10 music albums and $30 movies, you can pay $9.99 a month for a service like Netflix or Spotify.
Software as a service has become equally popular with enterprises.
Salesforce, QuickBooks Online, Snowflake, Jira Cloud, and MongoDB are all leading B2B SaaS companies and products.
None of this is really news, though.
SaaS is a well-known phenomenon that's fueled by its unparalleled value creation and value capture.
When software is delivered as a service, consumers aren't locked into long-term commitments or risking hundreds of dollars up front.
You swipe a credit card for a few bucks, try out the service, and stop paying whenever you feel like you're not getting value.
For consumers, SaaS is affordable, convenient, and flexible.
For companies, SaaS allows them to monetize faster, ship code quickly, push updates after launch, and iterate.
Most important of all, SaaS is good business.
Facebook's gross margin hovers at 80%, Microsoft's at 70%, Google's gross margin is 60%, and Adobe's is at 90%.
Adobe makes more money today with its $9.99 a month Creative Cloud SaaS than they did selling $700 Photoshop licenses back in the 2000s.
When investors see margins like these, they can't resist jumping in.

This has led to the flywheel effect of venture capital, startups and IPOs that has been fueling tech for the past decade and funding software engineering jobs where 20-year-olds make six figures upon graduation.
But what most people are missing is that while software as a service has become more popular, the standards and quality of software itself have been declining.
Software as a service is so prevalent these days that the culture of startups and SaaS are basically intertwined.
The ship-fast, fail-fast attitude has meant that SaaS products nowadays often launch way before they're ready, with bugs and incomplete functionality.
Although companies tried to ride through the initial backlash with fast-follow improvements, they often don't live up to that promise.
SaaS products have also become ruthlessly monetized, meaning that companies will paywall anything they can to get users to spend more, even if that feature is essential to using the service.

As Mark and Dreesen predicted, industries all over have indeed embraced software as a service, but there is one particular industry that has taken advantage of the declining standards to deliver aggressively monetized, yet progressively worse, unfinished, buggy SaaS products for maximum profit year after year after year.
That is the gaming industry.
In the old days, people would line up at GameStop or Target to get their hands on the latest video games.
For $60, you get the game on a CD and a nice case.
You could spend some more and pre-order the game to get special goodies.
A few months later, you could drop $15-20 more for some downloadable content.
Back then, the purpose of DLC was to extend a game's lifespan.

After launch, if the game sells well, the studio goes back into R &D, players wait a few years, the sequel gets eventually announced at E3, pre-orders go live, players line up once again at GameStop, rinse and repeat.
Back then, consumers knew what they were getting for $60, an 8-40 hour single player campaign with maybe split screen co-op and multiplayer.
The traditional video game business model centered around this one-time $60 purchase.
Make a good game, build up a fan base, and the more sequels you release, the more money you'll make.
But video games are moonshots.
Making a good video game is hard.
A couple good video game also doesn't always sell.
To make a game, you invest millions of dollars every year for 2-5 years in continuous R &D.
If you get to launch, you'll need to spend millions more on marketing.
You do all this with no guarantee in the end that the video game you make will even sell.
In the early 2010s, if you exclude indie games, video game development budgets were anywhere from $5 million to $50 million.
If you include advertising and marketing, the total cost of producing a video game could be anywhere from $30 million to $300 million.
Like movies, the ROI for video games is completely unknown until it launches.
The only safe investments are the proven AAA franchises like Call of Duty, Grand Theft Auto, Halo, Mario, and Pokemon where customers drop money on sequels and DLC without hesitation.
Since the early 2000s, publishers like Activision, EA, Ubisoft, and Sega spend millions every year looking for the next blockbuster franchise.
To this day, Call of Duty, FIFA, Madden, Assassin's Creed, Yakuza, Need for Speed, NBA 2K are all franchises that pump out a sequel every year.
But AAA franchises don't always last.
The once best-selling Guitar Hero and Tony Hawk series ended up being milked to death by their publishers.
Sequels were launched so frequently that quality declined, players lost interest, and the IP became worthless.
Because of the Moonshot nature and the one-time monetization model, innovation was crucial to the gaming industry.
Just like venture capitalists looking for the next hot startup, video game publishers take a similar scattershot approach to find the next Call of Duty or Halo.

In the late 2000s, publishers were constantly bringing new IPs to market, funding up-and-coming studios, and encouraging creative freedom and risk-taking in hopes of fostering the next blockbuster game.
Video games back then were made under the Waterfall software development model.
Under Waterfall, you set a deadline years into the future, plan out all the R &D to support that deadline, and do design, art, programming, and testing in linear, sequential phases.
You assess regularly to see if things are still on track.
The objective for Waterfall is rigorous planning and slow, incremental, stable software development.
With Waterfall, it wasn't uncommon for games to get delayed, but the end product released was still stable and complete.
Modern video games are nothing like the offline single player centric video games of the past.
The most popular games today, Fortnite, Apex Legends, Warzone, Rust, PUBG, League of Legends, just to name a few, are all software as a service.
The gaming industry refers to SaaS games as live services.
Apex, Fortnite, Warzone, and League are all leading examples of free-to-play live services.
GTA Online, Escape from Tarkov, PUBG, and Red Dead Online are all examples of popular titles where you still have to pay up front to play.
DLC has become the primary monetization model for modern video games.
Microtransactions and loot boxes are present in so many video games to the point that not having them in a game is considered big news.
And unlike traditional video games which have fixed lifespans, modern live services are meant to last forever.
However, just like SaaS products and other industries, these games release a relentless stream of updates and content to keep players engaged and spending.

Compared to the past, where players would spend $10- $30 one time for maps and expansions, DLC nowadays is a never-ending spree of $10 season passes, $20 skins, and in-game cosmetics that can cost hundreds of dollars.
Even the latest Battlefront, Battlefield, and Halo games all operate like a SaaS.
At the same time, the quality of modern video games has declined.
Fallout 76, Cyberpunk, Anthem, No Man's Sky, Battlefield 2042, and Halo Infinite are all recent examples of just how far standards have dropped.
Launching buggy, unfinished SaaS games and then promising to fix it later is now standard industry practice.
Modern games are made with a mix of waterfall and agile software development models.

Under Agiles, development is broken down into two-week sprints to promote faster frequent delivery of software, breaking up deliverables into small bite-sized tasks, and promotes the flexibility to defer work into the future.
As long as something is being shipped, no matter how small, it's considered a win.
Almost every SaaS product in every industry these days is developed under Agile.
Under Waterfall and the traditional single-player video games of the past, it would have been a death sentence to knowingly ship an incomplete or buggy game.
Studios would much rather delay the launch than to launch a poor product.
But with today's games and digital distribution, delays are fairly rare.
Modern games launch even if the product is incomplete or unstable.
Under agile development and SaaS principles, this hasty output is permitted under the guise that improvements will come and everything will get better into the future.
SaaS has transformed not only how video games are developed and monetized, but also the surrounding ecosystem and industry.
The creativity, risk-taking, anticipation of E3, the stream of new titles every year, and the constant emergence of up-and-coming studios all feel like relics of the past.

Nowadays, fewer game studios are being funded, fewer IPs are coming to market, developers bypass E3 to talk directly with their consumers, publishers are putting themselves up for sale, and every game this generation seems to be a live-service multiplayer with microtransactions.
In this episode, we're going to look at three different gaming companies and see how their strategies and business models have evolved over time with software as a service.
First is CD Projekt Red, the Polish company behind the best-selling Witcher video game franchise.
While the industry has rotated to SaaS, multiplayer, and microtransactions, CD Projekt Red has actively resisted those trends.
They're a deeply traditional studio who focuses exclusively on single-player RPGs, they openly reject pumping out sequels for profit, and insist that they'll only launch games when they're ready.
CD Projekt Red's belief is that if you take the time and effort to make a great game, the quality will speak for itself, and the game will sell even years after launch.
No microtransactions needed.
CD Projekt Red's financials give us a real-world look at how successful but also how volatile the traditional video game business can In 2011, CD Projekt Red launched Witcher 2.
The game was a critical success, winning 50 awards and putting CD Projekt Red on the map as a promising young studio.
But video game sales only accounted for 30% of the company's revenue that year.
The company made most of its money back then as a distributor of movies in Poland.
After launching Witcher 2, CD Projekt Red went back into waterfall development for Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk.
Witcher 2 continued to sell after its launch but in declining amounts.
Video game sales dropped 50% from $10 million to $5 million one year after Witcher 2's console launch, but then rebounded 30% the year after.
CD Projekt Red's top line also declined over the next two years as the studio launched no new games and was heads down developing Witcher 3.
Between 2012 and 2014, Witcher 2 brought in a total of $23 million.
For a game that costs $10 million to make, that's a 130% return on investment with an annualized ROI of 13% over 3 years of R &D and 4 years of sales.
In 2015, CD Projekt Red released Witcher 3.
The game was a monster success at launch and is considered to be one of the best video games ever made.
In its first 6 weeks, 6 million copies of Witcher 3 had been sold.
In comparison, it took The Witcher 2 two years to sell 2.5 million copies.
CD Projekt Red had struck bold.
The company went from $30 million in 2014 to $177 million in 2015 with The Witcher 3, a 600% increase in revenue.
Witcher 3 sales accounted for 87% of CD Projekt Red's revenue that year.
Net income grew by 760%, going from $1 million in net income in 2014 to $76 million in 2015.
CD Projekt Red's profit margin went from 5% to over 40%.
The success of Witcher 3 elevated CD Projekt Red from a small, up-and-coming studio to one of Europe's most respected gaming powerhouses.
It cost $81 million to make Witcher 3.
Yet in its first year, Witcher 3 had already paid off its development costs with a 90% return on investment and an annualized ROI of 17% over 3.5 years of R &D and just 7 months of sales.
Witcher 3 continues to sell well to this day.
Its success validates CD Projekt Red's philosophy that good games, no matter how many years after launch, do indeed sell.
There has been a post-launch decline in revenue, but it's been a gradual descent.
Witcher 3 sales have dropped 30% every year after 2015.
But the legacy of Witcher 3 lives on as the title recently surpassed 50 million copies sold and has become one of the top 10 best selling video games of all time.
From Witcher 3's success, we can understand why publishers like Activision, EA, and Ubisoft are all hunting for the next blockbuster game.

You'll always miss more than you hit, but when you do hit, your revenue skyrockets by hundreds of millions of dollars, your profit exponentially increases, and your valuation goes up by several billion.
All it takes is just one game, and you can easily snowball that success into annual sequels to keep money flowing.
But that's not CD Projekt Red's approach.
However, just because you made one good game doesn't guarantee that your next game will be just as good.
CD Projekt Red snowballed the success of Witcher 3 into hype for its next game, Cyberpunk 2077.
Cyberpunk had been in development for 8 years and was considered one of the most anticipated games of all time.
The company promised a single player game, more immersive and dynamic than The Witcher 3, alongside a SaaS multiplayer with microtransactions.
Fast forward to Cyberpunk 2077's launch, and the game was nothing short of a disaster.
In response, CD Projekt Red basically turned Cyberpunk's single player into a live service, continually pushing out hotfixes, updates, patches, and new content to make the game playable.
Beyond the game-breaking bugs, refunds, public apology, broken promises, unfinished state, and the beta and switch marketing, Cyberpunk 2077 was still a commercial success.
CD Projekt Red's revenue quadrupled from $116 million in 2019 to $486 million in 2020 with the launch of Cyberpunk.
Net income increased six times from $40 million to $255 million in the same time frame.
Despite its disastrous launch and costing $300 million over 8 years of development, Cyberpunk 2077 still made out with a positive ROI in its debut.
But there have been consequences.
In 2021, CD Projekt Red's revenue and video game sales dropped over 60% just one year after Cyberpunk's launch.
This 60% drop is a much faster plunge than forecasted and has doubled the decline of Witcher 3's sales one year after a game's launch.
which consumer trust had clearly been lost.

After some soul searching, CD Projekt Red announced that they were cancelling Cyberpunk's live service multiplayer game, committing to agile development over Waterfall, and taking time to figure out the right blend of offline and online experiences.
With Cyberpunk, CD Projekt Red tried to deliver a traditional $60 single player offline game with a dynamic scope of a live service.
Simultaneously, they were building a live service with microtransactions on top of an an unstable single player game without any SaaS expertise or experience.
CD Projekt Red's Rise and Fall is a demonstration of how volatile the traditional video game business can be.
All it takes is one game to take you to the moon and one game to crash you back down.
When you only launch one game every 5 years or so like CD Projekt Red, it intensifies the risk on an already risky coin flip.
The longer you spend in development, the more pressure and greater the stakes become.
As a gamer, I find it admirable how much CD Projekt Red believes in tradition.
But if you're only shipping two games every 10 years, you have to get at least one of them right to sustain the company.
If you get both of them wrong, bankruptcy can be just right around the corner.

There are other companies similar to CD Projekt Red who have enjoyed historical success in the traditional video game business but have fully pivoted to live services and microtransactions in recent years to keep up with the industry.
But just building a SaaS product doesn't guarantee success, and this is the story of Square Enix.
Square Enix is a Japanese publisher who owns iconic franchises like Final Fantasy, Kingdom Hearts, Dragon Quest, Tomb Raider, Deus Ex, Hitman, and Just Cause.
With IPs like these, it can be argued that Square Enix's expertise with the traditional video game business and single-player RPG roots runs a lot deeper than CD Projekt Red.
In 2013, Square Enix had a disastrous year with a $100 million loss.
They had launched three major titles that year with Sleeping Dogs, Hitman Absolution, and Tomb Raider.
Even though all three games were received favorably and had been developed as console-first titles, each significantly underperformed in sales.
Square Enix ended up having to eat its own margins and incentivize retailers with rebates, discounts, and price protection in order to improve their sales.
Square Enix's longtime CEO resigned and new leadership took over as part of a massive management reform.
Square Enix's new leadership offered a thoughtful reflection to investors when the year came to a close.
To quote their annual report, the financial results in this fiscal year reflect an intrinsic problem within the game business model.
Under the model of selling packaged games, the timing by which we may offer a game to customers is limited to the release of the product.
Profit opportunities are nonexistent during the game's development.
Although we are making efforts to streamline our development process, game development requires increasingly long periods of time as the performance of game consoles improves.
I believe the problem is not a one-time event.
