We face the structural issues of an inflexible earnings model and long-term, large-scale development resulting in a low rate of investment turnover.
It is extremely important for us to enable a transition from a disc-based earnings model to a more flexible one.
This will define the future of how we pursue game development at Square Enix.
To give credit to the company's leadership, they recognized the risks of continuing to operate in this traditional business and saw the need to evolve.

In 2014, Square Enix's top line in video game sales had mostly recovered thanks to continued MMO growth and better-than-expected sales of a remastered Final Fantasy X, Thief, and a full-price re-release of Tomb Raider.
In 2015, Square Enix had a quiet year and intentionally kept a low profile.
The company was hard at work preparing what it believed to be an unbeatable lineup of AAA sequels that would make 2016 the most successful year in company history.
Square Enix hit the market with all its best IPs in 2016.
The blockbuster lineup featured Rise of the Tomb Raider, Just Cause 3, Deus Ex Mankind Divided, Hitman, Final Fantasy XV, and Dragon Quest Builders.
The company's revenue grew by 30% and video game sales skyrocketed by 42%, going from $860 million in 2015 to $1.2 billion in 2016.
With the exception of Just Cause 3, all titles were critically acclaimed with solid commercial debuts.
Square Enix's net income doubled from $75 million in 2015 to $153 million in 2016.
Square Enix's revenue continued to grow in 2017 based on the sustained sales from its blockbuster lineup.
Total revenue grew 20% from $1.6 billion in 2016 to $1.9 billion in 2017 which was largely driven by its 25% growth in video game sales.
Even though all the numbers were going up, behind closed doors, the blockbuster lineup was actually underperforming and Square Enix was not happy.
Nearly all the games in the blockbuster lineup had some form of SaaS and microtransactions built in.
Hitman was actually released as a live service, meaning consumers paid full price for the game, but there were really only a few levels to play at launch.
The studio explained that additional levels would be featured as DLC over time, and episodes, so that developers could take player feedback and refine future levels under agile development.
This explanation landed pretty poorly with customers, and ultimately Hitman failed to sell.
In 2017, one year after its launch, Square Enix gave up on Hitman entirely.
They sold off the studio and franchise rights and wrote down a $43 million loss.
While no official numbers have ever been given, the studio came out in 2021 to say that Hitman needed another 4 years of sales at its current pace just to break even.
So all in all, 4 years of development and 9 years of sales for an ROI of zero.
Deus Ex Mankind Divided launched as a full-priced single-player game alongside Breach, which was a separate free-to-play live service in the same game universe.
Both games were filled with microtransactions.
Mankind Divided's single-player campaign was widely criticized for selling in-game upgrades and virtual currency.
Breach as a live service incurred even greater criticism, selling pay-to-win items and in-game cosmetics for a game where players couldn't even see each other.
Later, it was revealed that Square Enix had forced the company to implement microtransactions and SaaS into the game with little notice and support.
Despite being critically acclaimed, Mankind Divided failed to sell while Breach died at launch as a live service without a player base.
Mankind Divided had been in development for 5.5 years and cost $55 million to make.
Square Enix internally estimated that it needed to sell about 3 million copies to break even.
As of today, Mankind Divided has reportedly only sold 2 million copies.
So 5.5 years of development, 6 years of sales, and Mankind Divided is still operating at a loss.
Just Cause 3 and Rise of the Tomb Raider were the only games out of the entire lineup to live up to its sales expectations.
So Square Enix dropped Hitman, paused Deus Ex, and gave Tomb Raider and Just Cause the green light to proceed with its sequels.
To Square Enix's leadership, the commercial failure of this lineup validated everything they had been saying since 2013.
The company could no longer keep launching these expensive flops, nor could it continue taking half measures implementing microtransactions and live services into its games portfolio.
If Square Enix was to succeed, the company believed it had to go all-in on Software as a Service.
In 2017, around the peak of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Square Enix signed a massive license agreement with Marvel.
The company gave its most trusted development studios, Eidos Montreal and Crystal Dynamics, three years and a massive blank check to build the next big live service game based on the Avengers.
In the interim, Square Enix launched Just Cause 4 and Shadow of the Tomb Raider, sequels from the remaining few franchises that the company could trust to sell.
Unfortunately for Square Enix, what it thought were safe investments turned out to be flops.
In 2018, Square Enix's overall revenue declined 3% and video game sales dropped 4% despite the launch of both games.
Leadership called out Just Cause 4's disappointing sales as the main reason for the company's struggles.
On the other hand, Shadow of the Tomb Raider was one of the most expensive games ever produced with a budget of $135 million over 3 years of development.
Yet the game received a lukewarm reception and is widely regarded as the weakest installment in the reboot trilogy both in terms of quality and sales.
Square Enix continued to commercially stagnate from 2017 to 2020.

In 2021, Marvel's Avengers was finally released as the full-priced live service game that Square Enix hoped would be the money printing sass that would make up for all the single player flops of the past 5 years.
Unfortunately, the game was a dud.
Marvel's Avengers at launch was hammered by players and critics alike for being repetitive, buggy, unfinished, and boring.
Square Enix released free DLC every quarter, adding new characters and missions as part of the SaaS playbook to try to keep users engaged.
But players weren't sticking around.
Two months after its launch, the Steam player count for the game had declined by 96% to 1,000 players, even dropping as low as 500 players on certain days.
Square Enix's revenue in 2021 grew 28% and its video game sales spiked by 40% thanks to the strong initial sales from Marvel's Avengers.

But once the dust had settled and word spread, consumers were ultimately unwilling to spend $60 on another unfinished live service game, and existing players had no interest buying $20 skins for a dying game.
Marvel's Avengers cost an estimated $180 million across three years of development.
With only 3 million copies sold to date, Square Enix's leadership admitted that once again, another big game had underperformed.
In its latest earnings, Square Enix wrote down $105 million in losses directly associated with Marvel's Avengers.
Even if you go all in on software as a service, it's just not a silver bullet.

While EA and Activision are infamous for their microtransactions and ruthless monetization, there is one company that has consistently and quietly outperformed both of these giants when it comes to software as a service.
That company is Take-Two Interactive, who owns Rockstar Games and 2K.
Take-Two's portfolio features AAA franchises like Bioshock, Borderlands, NBA 2K, Max Payne, XCOM, Red Dead, and Grand Theft Auto.
Rockstar Games is a renowned studio who follows the traditional less-is-more development philosophy.
Like CD Projekt Red, Rockstar Rockstar only launches a handful of games every decade.
The studio took 8 years to release a sequel to Red Dead Redemption and 5 years between GTA 4 and GTA 5.
But the main difference between Rockstar and CD Projekt Red is that Rockstar consistently hits home runs.
GTA 5 on launch broke industry records in 2013.
To this day, the game maintains its record as the fastest selling entertainment product in history, earning $1 billion in its first three days.
With a development budget of $265 million, GTA V achieved profit and a 280% ROI in just 72 hours.
By 2018, Grand Theft Auto V had made $6 billion.
And as of 2022, 160 million copies of the game had been sold worldwide.
Five years later in 2018, the studio hit another home run.
The launch of Red Dead Redemption 2 set records, making the game the second fastest selling entertainment product in history, earning $725 million in its first three days.
The game reportedly cost $400 to $500 million to make over eight years of development.
Even with this massive price tag, Red Dead Redemption 2 made profit in just 72 hours.

When we look at Take-Two's business performance, what's wild is that the company is actually hitting new heights every year in revenue and income four years after Red Dead Redemption 2 and 8 years after GTA 5.
Instead of the natural drop off in sales that you would expect after a game's launch, Take-Two actually makes more money every year.

While EA and Activision's revenue also increases every year, it's important to keep in mind that to keep up their growth, those two giants invest significantly more in R &D and release more games annually than Take-Two.
In 2013, Take-Two's revenue grew over 100% with the launch of GTA 5.
But the company kept its foot on the gas pedal and used its middle class franchises like Max Payne, XCOM, NBA 2K, and Borderlands to experiment with microtransactions and SaaS.
Borderlands 2 offered a season pass at launch and released 16 different types of DLC over two years.
NBA 2K13 was the first game in franchise history to offer virtual currency.
Despite the lukewarm reception, the company quickly noted the value of transactions as high margin revenue.
By the end of the year, every Take-Two game, including Bioshock Infinite, launched with a season pass.
In 2014, Take-Two came up with an official term called Recurrent Consumer Spending, in which they put microtransaction and DLC sales into one bucket and full game sales into another.
By 2016, every Take-Two game launched with not only a season pass but at minimum a one-year roadmap of DLC.
Recurrent consumer spending grew on average 60% every year from 2014 to 2017.
In four years, microtransactions and DLC sales went from being a tiny piece of the pie at 11% to almost half of Take-Two's overall revenue.
Longtail monetization became the focus.
Make $60 upfront and then try to make another $60 post-launch through DLC.

But what's unique is that Take-Two actively encouraged its studios to meaningfully tailor DLC and microtransactions to the game and not simply copy and paste proven industry tactics like loot boxes or card packs.
Take a listen to this professionally thoughtful commentary from Take2's CEO on DLCs and microtransactions.
And remember, when we talk about monetization, our goal is always to deliver a phenomenal entertainment experience first and foremost.
And we figure that if we do that, monetization takes care of itself.
We take it is axiomatic that the nature of an experience is the intersection of the quality of the experience and whether you feel you receive value for that experience.
If you go to a phenomenal restaurant and have an incredible meal, but the bill it should have cost, you're not going back.
Even if you can afford it, even if you're priced inelastic, you're not going back.
It just doesn't feel good.
So we need to make sure that we always deliver more than what we charge.
And that's the goal of our company and that's the goal of all of our labels.
In 2019, the company's revenue exploded once again by 50% with the launch of Red Dead Redemption 2.
Red Dead Online and GTA Online, live services that were widely criticized at their launch for being buggy, repetitive, and half-baked, were now picking up steam.
The consistent flow of free Pre-annual updates, co-op missions, and game modes to both Red Dead Online and GTA Online were paying off and players were returning in massive numbers.
By 2020, Take-Two had surpassed the $3 billion mark in annual revenue for the first time in company history, fueled by record concurrent consumer spending in NBA 2K, GTA Online, and Red Dead Online.
In 2021, microtransaction and DLC sales grew 50% from $1.3 billion to $2.1 billion in a single year.
This was the first time in company history where concurrent consumer spending surpassed full game sales, making up 62% of the company's total revenue.
That same year, Grand Theft Auto Online hit a record number of active players and microtransaction sales, along with better-than-expected performance from Red Dead Online.
Critics might say that it's not SaaS, but microtransactions that have transformed Take-Two.
But I think that abstraction downplays what the company has accomplished over the past few years.
What Take-Two has done is they've modernized their legacy single player titles like GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption into thriving live services with high engagement.
They then monetized that engagement with transactions.
For the other games in its portfolio like Borderland, XCOM, and Bioshock, Take-Two didn't rush to those and say hey, let's turn them all into live services then.
What they did was they said hey, it's possible that a lot of these games just don't work as live services so let's just commit to season passes and DLC, but let's not shoehorn those in.
Let's integrate it as thoughtfully and meaningfully as possible.
If all you need to make money is to introduce microtransactions or make the game a live service, then Square Enix and CD Projekt Red would be in much better places today.
Take-Two's lessons for the industry are powerful.
Microtransactions are how you can monetize software as a service, but it's not something you can mindlessly throw in and just expect results.
At the same time, just like not every product should be a SaaS, not every game works as a live service.
Software as a service is a format that has to be strategically applied and a muscle that requires continuous dedication year after year after year.

title: Tree to Box: The Billion Dollar Cardboard Business

sections: Types of cardboard and how it's made
Name of the game is volume
lines: The world runs on cardboard.
Produce, snacks, electronics, beverages, merchandise, household goods, just about everything these days is shipped in cardboard.
As a material, cardboard is exceptional.
It's simple, durable, collapsible, light, cheap to produce, easy to dispose of, and recyclable.
Cardboard can be made into different properties, strengths, and shapes.

Everything from heavy-duty bins that can hold a mountain of watermelons or merchandise, ice, ventilated trays for fresh produce, food safe boxes for greasy pizzas, candy boxes that can double as in-store displays, to Amazon boxes that are tough enough to survive the back of a FedEx truck.
As consumers, when it comes to cardboard, we pay attention to really only a few things.
We make sure our boxes haven't been stolen and we check that the stuff inside hasn't been damaged.
Usually, we just open our box, we get our order, we collapse the box, and we toss it into the recycle bin.
Despite how little we as consumers might think about it, cardboard is actually a global billion-dollar industry with strong momentum dominated by two big companies.
International Paper and Westrock are the two biggest players who have taken a lion's share of the American cardboard market in the past decade.
The next time you come across a cardboard box, take a second to flip it over and look for a logo at the bottom, and you'll likely find that it came from one of these two companies.

International Paper and West Rock are massive business empires that are basically hidden in plain sight, whose products not only shape American commerce, but also extend into the political landscape and shape the development of certain foreign countries.
In this episode, we'll cover the business of cardboard, how it's made, and the contrasting strategies of these two cardboard giants.

The rise of cardboard has been driven by the popularity of e-commerce, the decline of retail, the war against plastic, and paper maintaining its winning reputation as the most sustainable, environmentally friendly, and ocean safe material.
For outsiders like us, we typically think of cardboard as those brown Amazon boxes.
But go inside the industry and you'll find nuances.
Cardboard actually comes in two types.
The first type of cardboard is called paperboard.
Think of greeting cards, cereal boxes, toilet paper rolls, toothpaste boxes, those pink donut boxes, bakery boxes, paper towel rolls, soap boxes, Twinkie boxes, and bandaid boxes.
Paperboard is a single layer cardboard that's thicker than printing paper, but still thin and easy to bend, fold, and tear.
The second type of cardboard is corrugated fiberboard, which is those Amazon boxes.
Corrugated fiberboard is made up of three layers of cardboard, an inside layer, an outside layer, and a fluted medium in between.
Corrugated fiberboard gets the strength from not just having more layers, but also from that middle layer of rounded triangles.
From a structural engineering standpoint, triangles are one of the strongest geometric shapes.
They're able to balance weight evenly through their small, fixed angles.
Triangles are used to support everything from bridges to roofs, and that same principle applies at a micro level in cardboard boxes.

Since shipping is priced by volumetric weight, whether through ocean or air freight, the fact that corrugated fiberboard is light yet strong makes the material a clear winner over wood and metal when it comes to packaging.
Corrugated fiberboard itself comes in many different flavors.
Depending on what it is that you're shipping, you can make cardboard boxes to be single-face, single-wall, double-wall, triple-wall.
Ultimately, the more layers you add, the thicker the box becomes, and the more protection that the items stored inside obtain.
You can customize the size of the triangles in the middle from A to F, where smaller triangles enable for finer printing, and bigger triangles enables stronger cushioning.
Over 95% of physical goods in the world are packed, transported, and stored in corrugated cardboard boxes.
To understand the business of cardboard, we have to first understand how it's made.
In order to make corrugated cardboard boxes, you first need container board.
To make container board, you take wood fiber and you process it at a mill to create container board.
The main raw material is wood fiber.
You can use recycled wood fiber or virgin wood fiber from fresh cut trees to make container board.
Then you take that container board, convert it into corrugated fiber board, which then becomes your Amazon, pizza, and produce boxes.
When we recycle our cardboard boxes and paper, it all gets brought to a recycling plant where it's boiled and mashed into recycled wood fiber.
A common misconception is that paper can be recycled an infinite amount of times, but in reality, paper can only be recycled on average 4-6 times.
Every time paper or cardboard is recycled, its fibers degrade and become shorter and weaker.
As a result, you always need to introduce some virgin fiber to maintain the strength and quality of the cardboard you're producing.
The point here is that manufacturing cardboard is not an all-or-nothing proposition of picking the cheapest fiber available, but a delicate balance of cost, supply, quality, and availability.
Wood fiber is a commodity, and the market price for recycled and virgin fiber fluctuates every day.

As a rule of thumb, it's cheaper and easier to source recycled fiber over virgin fiber, but paper products that are made with recycled fiber objectively turn out weaker than those made with virgin fiber.
Forests in the United States are regulated natural resources that must achieve specific sustainable standards and certifications.
It's no longer like the old days where corporations aggressively mowed down acres of trees without any thought to get their virgin fiber.
When it monitored to make sure that it never exceeds growth.
At the same time, rotation is mandatory, meaning that only one area is harvested at a time, and young trees are tended and protected until they mature.
Forests are relevant because in order to make cardboard or paper in general, you need virgin fiber which comes from trees.
And to produce quality cardboard, you can't just use recycled fiber indefinitely.
The big reason why the cardboard industry thrives in the United States is because of the natural resources available in North America.
The United States has 8% of the world's forests, which puts the country in the top 5 countries in the world with the most forests.
More forests means more trees, which means more virgin fiber available locally.
Despite the antiquated rail network of the US, shipping wood via train is still much faster and cheaper than if you had to import wood into the country via ocean freight.
Canada ranks ahead of the US in third place with 9% of the world's forests.
To round out the top 5 list, Brazil is in second place with 12% of the world's forests within its borders, and Russia leads the way with 20% of the world's forests.
So wood fiber is the single most important raw material to producing cardboard.
If we put ourselves in the shoes of a cardboard company, you buy your virgin fiber from the forests and your recycled fiber from recycling plants.
As an alternative, you can also choose to lease or buy forests with harvesting rights so you can harvest the virgin fiber yourself.
You bring those fibers into a container board mill to turn it into container board.
You put that container board on a train and ship it to a converting facility.
At a converting facility, you use the container board to produce corrugated fiberboard, the inside layers, the outside layers, and the fluted mediums.
You hire salesmen and account managers to sell your corrugated cardboard boxes.
You also have graphic designers on staff who can provide creative services for customers who are looking for branded boxes.
As soon as you finish producing the cardboard boxes that were ordered, you deliver them right away to your customers via truck.
As a cardboard company, you produce corrugated boxes upon orders and based on customer specifications.
If you do have extra container board left over, you can save that material for future production, or you can choose to export it to countries with few forests like Turkey.
Even countries with a lot of forests can struggle to produce quality container board and cardboard.

While China has 5% of the world's forests, which still puts it in the top 5, the country has historically relied on importing recycled fiber from the United States and sourcing virgin fiber from Russia to produce cardboard.
Just because you have the natural resources, it doesn't mean much if you don't have the infrastructure to capitalize on it.
China's domestic recycling operations are too young and the consumer recycling habits there are too weak to produce the necessary volumes of recycled fiber.
As outsiders, it's tempting to think about the cardboard business at scale.

Being the cardboard supplier for companies like Amazon, Pizza Hut, Anheuser-Busch, and Walmart, international companies that ship massive amounts of goods to hundreds of locations regularly, that's the golden standard.
But the reality is that a majority of the cardboard business is done locally.
At converting facilities, the same place where container board is converted into corrugated boxes is where cardboard companies do most of their business.
They sell corrugated products to any business within a 150 mile radius of each converting facility and they compete with every other cardboard company that has a facility in that same local market.
These converting Focusing facilities are not only valuable in the supply chain for producing cardboard boxes, but also serve go-to-market purposes as distribution centers and storefronts.
If you're a farmer looking for cardboard for your produce, you want a packaging partner that has a local plan.
If you're a CPG company, you have the same criteria for your cardboard supplier.
Local, local, local as much as possible.
Keep in mind that as a customer, you not only have to pay for the cardboard boxes that you order, you also have to pay for the shipping cost to get it delivered to your farm or factory.
There's no prime free 2-day shipping in the world of B2B.
So having a local plant who can produce the cardboard you need, they can put it on a truck, and deliver it to you within 2-4 hours is critical not just for your logistics, but also for your costs.
In order to optimize production and maximize profits, cardboard companies have deep vertical integration from tree to box.
To recap the supply chain for a cardboard company, you buy fiber on the market or you harvest the fiber from forests that you own or lease.
You transport that fiber to your container board mill.
At your mill, you put in fiber and container board comes out.
You transport that container board to your converting facility.
At your converting facility, you convert the container board into cardboard boxes.
When production completes, you deliver the cardboard box via truck to your customers.
If you have extra container board left over, you can either save it for a future run or export the material to an overseas country.
It's easy to dismiss cardboard companies as basic, old-school, linear A-to-B businesses with raw inputs and finished outputs, but there's actually a lot of details below the surface.
Each handoff in the supply chain can be optimized.

The speed and price at which you source fiber, the speed at which you can move the fiber to container board mills, the efficiency of your mills to convert fiber into container board, how fast you can move that container board to your converting facility, the speed at which you convert container board to cardboard boxes, and the turnaround time it takes to deliver those boxes to your customers.
Within each step of this supply chain, there's also opportunity for further optimization.
What percentage of recycled fiber and virgin fiber do you use for your cardboard?
Do you go for the cheapest or highest quality available?
Do you predict that prices for virgin or recycled fibers will increase or decrease?
How can you protect against market fluctuations in fiber prices?
What kinds of trees do you want to source from?
Hardwood trees like oak or softwood trees like pine?
Should you intentionally overproduce cardboard in Q1 and Q2 when energy and transportation is cheap, or should you just produce exactly to what your customers order?
How can you mitigate seasonal bottlenecks and costs in Q3 when freight becomes congested and utilities become much more expensive in the winter?
Each go-to-market step in the same supply chain can also be optimized.
How much should you export?
At what market price for container board does it become more profitable to simply export your container board rather than keep it to produce cardboard boxes?
What incentives should you offer in distribution to beat out your competitors?
How do you ensure that the trucking companies will prioritize your shipments over others?
The opportunities for optimization and data-driven decision making are endless even in such a traditional business.
The name of the game is volume.
If you own the most trees, you can harvest the most virgin fiber.
If you own the most recycling plants, you can source the most recycled fiber.
If If you have the right connections, your export business can be a steady cash flow with very little work needed.
There's economies of scale.
If you own the most mills, your consumption of raw materials grants you greater purchasing power and the more money you can save buying fiber at below market prices.
The more converting facilities you have, the more local markets you can compete in, the more cardboard volume you can move, and the more you can undercut competitors on your pricing.

The more volume you have, the better your relationship becomes with your truck and retail partners, and the more likely they'll prioritize delivering your company's shipment over your competitors so your stuff is always arriving on time or ahead of schedule, and so on.
Under this abstraction, whichever company owns the most forests, recycling plants, container board mills, and converting facilities should win.
The current market leader is International Paper, which is a company that has enjoyed the top spot for decades.
Up until 2006, International Paper was actually the second largest landowner in the United States.
Back then, only the federal government owned more real estate than International Paper.
The company was once a sprawling business with over 16 business lines, selling plastic and paper alongside lumber and natural gas.
By 2006, leadership said enough.
The company was doing too much.
International Paper had become slow, bloated, and ineffective.
The company was hemorrhaging massive amounts of debt every year for a paltry ROI of 3%.
Since then, International Paper has aggressively streamlined its operations, selling off its consumer packaging division, its lumber division, and its forests for $11 billion.
The company today is laser-focused on two business lines.
Industrial packaging, which is those corrugated cardboard boxes, and cellulose fibers, which is the paper material used in absorbent hygiene products like diapers and tampons.
These two decades of streamlining turned international paper into a powerhouse when it comes to cardboard boxes.
Two out of every three Amazon boxes is reportedly made by International Paper.
International Paper's supply chain is robust.
The company owns 20 container board mills globally, with 17 in the United States, one in Mexico, one in Morocco, and one in Spain.
After the container board is produced, it's transported to one of 163 converting facilities in the United States.
There, it's converted into cardboard boxes and sold.
That's 163 markets that International Paper competes in the US alone.
The company also owns 41 converting facilities in Latin America, France, Italy, and Canada.
To source recycled fiber, International Paper owns 18 recycling plants with 16 of them in the United States.

While we all have to pay every month for the garbage company to come pick up our trash and recycling, what's fascinating is that these recycling plants don't make any money for International Paper or any other cardboard company that has them.
Having a consistent and source of recycled fiber is so important to their supply chain that recycling plants aren't treated as income generating assets, they're basically run at cost.
The paper and cardboard that you throw away every week is actually worth far more to the company than the fee that you pay every month for their service.
International Paper uses a blend of 65% virgin fiber and 35% recycled fiber.
When the company sold its forests in 2006 for $6 billion, the company didn't just pocket the cash and walk away.
The deal requires that the new owners supply virgin fiber exclusively from these forests to international paper at market price for the next 20-50 years.
So while international paper is still subject to market fluctuations in fiber prices like everyone else, they're still sourcing from an exclusive supply of trees.
The forest sale in 2006 not only allowed international paper to remove itself from the forestry trade, but also win political points.
The company had been getting heat from environmentalists and politicians for years for its aggressive harvesting and monopolistic ownership of America's forests.
The sale removed that scrutiny entirely.
International paper today doesn't own any forests in the United States, but the company does own 300,000 million acres of forests in Brazil.
As we mentioned earlier, Brazil has the second largest amount of the world's forests.
While the country's infrastructure is still developing, cutting trees and harvesting virgin fiber from Brazil will be significantly cheaper than in the United States.
Brazil is a developing country with light regulation and is more likely to overlook the environment in exchange for foreign investment.
International Paper's foreign investment also extends to Russia, the country with the most amount of the world's forests.
Through a 50-50 joint venture, International Paper has exclusive harvesting rights on 20 million acres of Russian forests where it makes money exporting those virgin fibers to China.

Despite being a direct beneficiary of e-commerce, winning Amazon as a key customer, customer, having a strong international presence, and operating a massive supply chain, International Paper's revenue is fairly stagnant.
Despite significant investment, its diaper and tampon division contributes less than 20% of the company's overall revenue.
Cardboard boxes remain the company's best-selling item.
Net income is also fairly pedestrian, sitting on average at 6%.
There's clearly still a lot of fat, and that's not lost on leadership.
leadership.
Lowering costs, reducing complexity, and accelerating profits are the focus these days.
Recent actions support that direction.
International Paper exited the Brazilian cardboard business in late 2020 where it sold off all its container board mills and converting facilities but kept its forests.
The company doesn't see much value competing in South America or selling to local Latin American companies, but the trees and forests are worth keeping.

While International Paper has also come under heat for continuing to do business in Russia despite the war in Ukraine, the company has tried to reduce that pressure by publicly stating that they're exploring all options when it comes to their Russian forests.
But looking at their performance, I honestly have a hard time seeing them give that up.
Russia and Brazil are long-term investments and it takes time for trees to grow.
Your cardboard box business is already at its peak since you're the main supplier for Amazon.
And while trimming fat is a worthy short-term endeavor, acquiring a substantially cheaper supply of virgin fiber will provide the biggest boost to the company's profits in the long term.
Next up is Westrock, who is the second largest cardboard company in the United States with customers like Domino's, Coca-Cola, and Modelo.
Westrock has a very different strategy from international paper.
The company has 19 cardboard mills, 17 of which are in the United States, one in Brazil, and one in India, along with 161 converting facilities to make cardboard boxes.
While it has less facilities than international paper, Westrock achieves supply chain differentiation as the largest paper recycler in the United States with 22 recycling plants across the nation.
Bigger recycling operations means a greater and cheaper source of recycled fibers, an advantage that Westrock fully capitalizes on during production.
The company uses 60% virgin fiber and 40% recycled fiber to produce its cardboard.
Westrock has two business lines, consumer cardboard packaging and corrugated cardboard boxes.
Westrock is a leading manufacturer in cardboard packaging for food, paper, beverages, dairy products, big tobacco, snacks, candies, health and beauty, and other household items.
Every time you tear open a box of Coca-Cola, Corona, Modelo, Budweiser, that's Westrock.
Anytime you pass the behind-the-counter displays of Marlboro, Camel, and Newport, those cigarettes are all packed in Westrock cartons.
Open up a box of chocolates from Seas or Dove, and that's Westrock.
Use a FedEx or UPS overnight mailer, and that's Westrock too.
Consumer cardboard packaging is a sizable contributor to Westrock's top line, making up on average 36% of the company's overall revenue.
Cardboard boxes bring in the remainder.
Just like international paper, the company produces cardboard boxes for e-commerce, produce, and merchandise.
But Westrock takes it a step further than its key rival, holding a winning position as the largest manufacturer and producer of pizza boxes, which are also made out of corrugated cardboard.
Anytime you order from Domino's, Pizza Hut, Papa John's, or even your local pizzeria, that pizza is coming in a Westrock box.
Westrock's strategy for its cardboard business is innovation.
The company actively monitors the market and regularly launches new products.
During the pandemic, Westrock launched Biopack Protect, a one-piece cardboard food container made just for delivery.

This new container retains heat but ventilates steam, offers a window so workers could verify the order is correct at a glance without opening the box, and is secured by a tamper-evident seal so that drivers can't mess with the food.
The company's forward-thinking mentality also shines through in its e-commerce solutions.
Rather than just selling an endless supply of pre-made cardboard boxes, Westrock offers its award-winning BoxSizer machines.
You feed the BoxSizer all the items you need packed into a single box.

The BoxSizer uses lasers to calculate the box measurements that would fit all those items, the machine then cuts, folds, and seals all those items into a perfectly sized cardboard box, so you don't have any more wasted box space.
Westrock's cross-sell and innovation strategy is clearly working.
Over one-third of Westrock customers today buy both their cardboard boxes and their consumer packaging from the company.
Since sourcing recycled fibers is so efficient, Westrock's attention these days lies more on sourcing virgin fiber.
paper.
WestRock buys its virgin fiber at market prices, but also owns 135,000 acres of forests in Brazil.
Similar to International Paper, WestRock is optimistic that once their Brazil operations mature, they'll be able to source virgin fiber at cheaper prices over time.

While International Paper plays a major role in cardboard exports, WestRock participates sparingly in that market with the belief that its local and domestic customer-first focus and innovation mindset will net better results in the long run.
When we look at Westrock's business performance, it's easy to see those results.
While International Paper's overall revenue has stagnated over the past few years, Westrock has slowly closed the gap, growing on average 9% every year.
As the company that's historically always been in second place, Westrock has just about caught up to International Paper in overall revenue.
With performance like this, it's no surprise that the tone from Westrock leadership on conference calls is one of enthusiasm and optimism.
Even though the company lacks the massive international presence, the political connections, and substantial export business, Westrack might be right in that they just don't need any of that.
If we evaluate purely the cardboard box business of both companies, we see that International Paper is still ahead overall in net sales thanks to its Amazon deal.
Even if we compare their businesses by annual volume, by how many million tons of cardboard boxes they sell every year, International Paper is still ahead by a healthy margin.

But to me, it feels like International The cardboard industry, as ordinary, plain, and boring as might seem, is dominated by these two billion dollar corporations, business empires hidden in plain sight.

title: How Adidas Caught Up to Nike
note: Business case study built around one CEO's strategy cycles (five-year plans) with a long fall, then a 2015 comeback and a successor section; no sponsor read.
lines: The year is 2014, and Adidas is struggling.
The once-dominant sportswear company is now lost and directionless, having suffered through declining revenue and profits for three years in a row.

Outside of football, consumers don't seem to care for the brand, retailers are giving up their most valuable shelf space to Nike, Adidas' new products are flopping, and activists are threatening a hostile takeover if the CEO isn't replaced within the year.

In this episode, we'll cover Adidas, the fatal mistakes that its former CEO made, which toppled the German brand to a distant third behind Nike and Under Armour, sparked an investor battle, and ultimately cost him his job.
We'll also cover the winning strategy that revolutionized Adidas and the new CEO's moves which have since then taken the company to new heights.
While the average CEO tenure is five years, Adidas has only had two CEOs in its modern history, Herbert Heiner and Casper Rorstedt.
Our story starts in 2005, the early Herbert Heiner era.
Heiner was a company man who rose up the sales ranks at Adidas for 15 years before being appointed CEO in 2001.
After four quiet years at the helm, Heiner made his first big move, acquiring Reebok for $3.8 billion in 2005.
Adidas had made its name in Europe as the leading sports performance brand.
European football is a true global sport, and Adidas was the leader for all things soccer.
For decades, Adidas had been the official partner of FIFA and UEFA.
In 2005, Adidas was a sponsor for renowned national football teams like Germany, France, Spain, Argentina, Japan, and prestigious clubs like Liverpool, Chelsea, and Real Madrid.
The company was also the sponsor for world-class players like David Beckham and Lionel Messi.
Everything from the ball to the kits to the boots had been made by Adidas for over 50 years.
For players and fans, Adidas and football were synonymous.
While soccer is the main sport in Europe, Africa, and Latin America, it's never enjoyed the same dominant popularity in America and Asia.
As a result, Adidas had strong market share in Europe, but small presence in the US and China.
Heiner believed that Adidas had reached its limit as a European brand and couldn't be stretched beyond its football roots.
By acquiring Reebok, Heiner believed that he had finally found the missing piece for Adidas to become a global company.
company.
As an American brand, Reebok would complement Adidas's European dominance by bringing in the high-value Chinese and American markets that had eluded the company for decades.
Heiner was so bullish on Reebok that he paid a 34% premium, an additional $1.3 billion on top of Reebok's market cap, to acquire the American brand.
Adidas's market cap at the time was only $7 billion.
When companies talk about M &A, they're usually referring to small additions or equal mergers.
For Adidas to buy Reebok for over half of its own market cap at $3.8 billion is extraordinary.
With so much capital spent in one move, Heiner presented a five-year multi-brand strategy to investors in 2005.
His pitch was that sure, buying Reebok cost them a lot of money, but this bold multi-brand strategy would turn Adidas from a humble German business into a global powerhouse.
Heiner believed that the company's future success would be less about making clothes and shoes, and managing brands.
Adidas and Reebok were just two brands in what, over time, could become a sprawling portfolio.
In his mind, each brand had its own market and demographic.
Let Adidas swim in its own lane, let Reebok focus on its own strengths, and over time, you could have something for everyone.
With this five-year multi-brand strategy, Heiner promised investors high single-digit growth and double-digit operating margins by 2010.
He broke down his strategy into three strategic priorities for the company to execute towards.
The first priority was to leverage Reebok's strong presence and existing partnerships in American sports to grow sales in North America.
At the time, Reebok was the exclusive uniform and apparel supplier for the NFL, the NBA, the MLB, and NHL.
Keeping to his multi-brand strategy, Heiner kept Reebok as the brand for American football, baseball, and hockey.
Yet he opted for an aggressive approach with basketball, immediately tearing up Reebok's existing contract and signing a new exclusive 11-year NBA deal for Adidas for $400 million.
While Heiner left American football, baseball, and hockey to Reebok, he entrusted basketball to Adidas.
Basketball was the most popular support in Asia, and star players like Yao Ming had captured the attention of over 80 million Chinese fans in the 2000s.
To Heiner, basketball was critical to winning Asia, and Reebok's former leaders had failed to tap into the sport's true commercial potential.
If Adidas could become the leading basketball brand and leading soccer brand in the world, it would have a moat that Nike could never cross.
Heiner trusted Adidas over Reebok to handle basketball, and Adidas already had proven distribution networks in China.
Through Reebok, Adidas had gained four direct channels into the American and Chinese market.
Heiner's second priority was to maintain the company's core strengths.
Adidas needed to keep its lead in European football.
The 2006 World Cup, which took place in their home court Germany, further reinforced Adidas as a leader in all things soccer.
Adidas had been the dominant brand for the entire tournament.
Nearly every player was wearing Adidas boots, kicking an Adidas ball, and the runner-up France and infamous Zidane headbutt moment were all flashing Adidas kits.
While sponsorships and publicity helped generate consumer desirability, the reality was that professional athletes genuinely loved wearing Adidas.
The company had to maintain its claim to fame by building the best gear for professional players in nearly every sport.
Those product sales made up 70% of the company's revenue every year.
There wasn't much more that Adidas had to do but to keep the foot on the gas pedal.
Heiner's third priority in his five-year multi-brand strategy was to win the emerging markets.
Beyond European football, he believed running to be the next global sport.
Heiner Heiner wanted Adidas to become the leading running brand for runners of all levels.
The key elements for this strategy had been in place for a while as the company was already the sponsor for the London, Berlin, and Boston Marathon.
From a sales standpoint, Heiner designated Russia and Italy as the two strategic emerging markets to win.
He was committed to strengthening Adidas's European market share to keep Nike out.
While wholesale made up 85% and retail accounted for 15% of Adidas's sales in 2006, Heiner wanted retail to be a bigger piece of the pie.
The company was reliant on third-party retailers like Footlocker to move their product.
Heiner's belief was that opening more stores and selling directly to customers would generate higher margins and stronger brand desirability with better in-store experiences.
Before the Reebok acquisition in 2005, Adidas's revenue hovered at around the 6 billion euro mark for several years.
In 2006, the first year of Heiner's multi-brand strategy, Adidas broke the 10 billion euro mark in overall revenue thanks to Reebok's contribution.
But beyond the expected top-line boost, the company didn't have much to report and investors didn't have too many questions.
They understood that integrating Reebok into Adidas and aligning internal teams to this new strategy would take time.
The multi-brand strategy started to take shape in its second year, but the ride was bumpy.
Instead of the high single-digit growth that Heiner had promised, the company's overall net sales only grew 2% in 2007.
On a per-brand basis, Adidas sales were up 7%, while Reebok sales were down 5%.
Heiner highlighted the positives to investors and showed that combining both brands had netted the company an unrivaled network of league partnerships and sponsored athletes around the world.
But Heiner couldn't hide from the elephant in the room.
Despite the NFL, MLB, and NHL partnerships, Reebok's products just weren't selling.
If anything, the brand seemed to be getting less desirable.
Heiner's explanation was that Reebok had lacked focus long before the acquisition and cleaning up the brand had taken longer than expected.
To capture just how much of a mess Reebok had been in, he showed off a diagram detailing the before and after makeover that the brand had been going through for the past two years.
Reebok's appeal in business had been declining for years to the point that retailers were regularly relying on heavy discounts to sell Reebok products.

As a result, Reebok cultivated this long-running reputation amongst retailers as an aging brand that sold best when positioned as a value purchase at outlet malls rather than a full-priced premium purchase.
Discount shoes and clothes are not Adidas's forte, nor was it what Heiner had in mind when he purchased Reebok.

Under Reebok's prior leadership, the company had never prioritized selling branded merchandise to hockey, football, and baseball fans beyond the usual athlete jerseys, which left billions of dollars on the table.
But most damning of all was that Reebok today had no understanding of who its customer was.
Was it a lifestyle brand for outlet moms or NFL fans?
Reebok's leaders had no answers for themselves or for Adidas.
The entire situation is curious.
If Heiner knew Reebok was such an unfocused, mismanaged brand who had lost sight of its target customer, why did he buy the business at such a premium?
How were these problems not uncovered during due diligence?
But Heiner could never publicly say such things.
If he did, he would only be revealing his own incompetence.
The deal was done and there was no going back.
But as any self-preserving CEO would, Heiner cast a positive spin.
Reebok needed to be reinvented, he told investors.
Reebok could tap into Adidas' proven resources to accelerate its repositioning and rebuild its credibility quickly.
Reebok would get a new logo and return to its roots as an everyday fitness This was a very different Reebok than what Heiner had presented in his grand 5-year multi-brand strategy just a year ago.
But if anyone could turn around Reebok, Heiner stressed, it would be Adidas.
Impossible is nothing.
In 2008, the following year, it appeared Adidas had truly lived up to its iconic slogan.
Overall net sales grew 5%, closer to the high single-digit growth that Heiner had promised.
Operating margin improved to 10%, and net income increased by 16%.
This success was primarily driven by the successful Beijing Olympics and the Euro 2008 for which Adidas was the main sponsor.
Backed by solid results, Heiner's message to shareholders was simple, stick to the game plan.
Then in 2009, the recession hit, tanking the global economy and blowing up Adidas' momentum.
Sales dropped 4% and operating margin plummeted to 5% as the company found itself saddled with too much inventory and debt.
To generate cash flow, Adidas aggressively chewed into its profits, issuing generous discounts and subsidies to retailers in order to clear their stock.
To make matters worse, Heiner's five-year bet on winning the Russian market also backfired.
The Russian ruble depreciated significantly relative to other currencies during the recession, reducing Adidas's profits that year by over 200 million euros.
Despite the economic conditions, there were some wins for Heiner's multi-brand strategy that year.
When Ballon d'Or winner and Barcelona legend Messi scored in the Champions League final, he took off his Adidas F50 boot and kissed it in front of millions of fans.
When MVP receiver San Antonio Holmes caught the game-winning touchdown in Super Bowl XLIII, he wore Reebok Kryptonite gloves.
When Korean golfer Yongun Yang upset Tiger Woods in the PGA Championship, he was using Adidas tailor-made irons.
But beyond these moments, Reebok's struggles continued.
Heiner revealed to investors the true scope of what they had accomplished to reinvent Reebok over the years.
In 2007, they had fired the entire leadership team, overhauled the brand's supply chain, and stopped supplying products to retailers.
In 2008, they had updated Reebok's logos, slogans, marketing, and messaging to be a fitness brand that quote-unquote fits everyone.

Now, in 2009, Reebok was finally launching products that reinforced their new positioning like the Smooth Fit Select Ride, a running shoe that could turn into a training shoe with the push of a button, zigzag shoes with zigzag soles that propelled the wearer further with each step, and easy-tone technology to help women tone their legs and butts.
Heiner had more to show investors in 2009 beyond new products and timelines.
He was so committed to Reebok's success that he put the Adidas company through a massive reorg to consolidate both brands under one single operating model.
The idea here was to maximize synergies and efficiency, so Reebok would sell and distribute into Adidas's international channels, and Adidas would do the same with Reebok's US channels.
Under this single model, everything would be shared.
To facilitate this, Heiner created a new company structure, a global sales organization dedicated to selling, and a global brands organization dedicated to marketing.
All departments across Reebok and Adidas would roll up into one of these two organizations.
This reorg was one of the more controversial moves of the Heiner era.
Historically, Reebok and Adidas had operated independently and for good reason.

While a single operating model enables efficiency, eliminates miscommunication, and reduces duplication, it also reduces autonomy and speed as employees now have to consider both brands in their day-to-day work.
The other issue is the apples-to-apples oversimplification as this operating model assumes that what works for one brand will work for the other.
Beyond Reebok and the reorganization, Heiner made what may have been his biggest mistake as CEO in 2009 when he opted to double down on retail.
Contrary to Nike, Heiner believed future profits to be in retail and not e-commerce.
There were 2200 Adidas and Reebok stores around the world at the time and Heiner wanted more, better, and faster.

His vision was for Adidas to become a leader in retail where anyone could walk into an Adidas or Reebok store, request a product, and get it delivered to the store within a few days if it wasn't in stock.
In order to achieve this speed at scale, operation teams were now told to streamline and harmonize retail operations and supply chains.
Heiner also created a new department dedicated exclusively to retail.

He pitched that the consolidated single operating model combined with stronger retail presence would be the missing ingredient to achieving the net income and operating margin that he promised four years ago.
Heiner could not have picked a worse time to double down on retail.
2009 was the inflection point in which e-commerce surpassed department store sales.

Heiner's decision to go even more all-in on retail that year would not only cost Adidas hundreds and millions of euros, but also leave e-commerce open for Nike to take over, a decision that Adidas would regret to this day to the tune of billions of euros every year.
In a normal year, there likely would have been more scrutiny of Heiner's performance in 2009, but ultimately investors were too preoccupied with the global recession to make a fuss about Adidas.
The next year, in 2010, Adidas' revenue surged 15% thanks to the World Cup.
But the company had still failed to achieve the top line or bottom line that Heiner had promised five years ago.
Operating margin and net income sat at 7%, below the double digits that were committed to shareholders.
Between 2005 and 2010, revenue grew on average at 4.7%, well below the double digits that were promised.
On a per-brand basis, Reebok's annual sales had plummeted 22% from 2.4 billion euros in 2006 to 1.9 billion euros in 2010.
In the same time frame, Adidas sales had grown 32% from 6.6 billion euros to 9 billion euros.
But most worrying of all was that North American sales across both brands had dropped 15% from 3 billion euros to 2.7 billion euros in the same time frame.
Adidas was going backwards in its most crucial market.
To his credit, Heiner nailed basketball in the international segments of his strategy.
Sales in Asia grew 42% from 2006 to 2010 from 2 to 3 billion euros.
Sales in Europe grew 20%, while Latin America's sales skyrocketed 165% in those four years.
Shareholders were disappointed with the failure of Heiner's five-year strategy, but they weren't actively calling for his head.
Perhaps it was the international success or the recession serving as a timely distraction, but Heiner continued onwards.
He rolled out a new long-term strategy that he called Route 2015, a five-year roadmap with the goals of reaching 17 billion euros in annual sales and 11% operating margin by 2015.
In his Route 2015 presentation, Heiner proclaimed that Reebok's reinvention was finally complete.
Adidas would now dedicate itself in the next five years to pushing Reebok to market and establishing its new positioning as a fitness brand.
Heiner stuck to his multi-brand portfolio approach, but this time he visualized it on a spectrum.
He separated the Adidas brand into two.
On one end, there was Adidas Sports as the performance brand for competitive athletes.
On the other end, he had Adidas Originals as a lifestyle fashion brand for everyday consumers.
winners.
Heiner placed Reebok in the center of this spectrum as the casual fitness medium between both extremes.
Under Route 2015, Adidas would specifically attack three markets—North America, China, and Russia.
Heiner designated these three markets as must-win battlegrounds for Adidas in the next five years.
Winning these three markets, he believed, would unlock 50% growth.
For North America, Heiner felt that besides basketball, there wasn't much value in professional in the US.
Reebok's existing deals with the NFL, MLB, and NHL didn't match its new positioning as a casual fitness brand.
In 2010, Reebok signaled that they wouldn't be renewing their NFL and MLB deals and routed those cost savings to sign a deal with CrossFit which had hit mainstream popularity.
Heiner was convinced that running, fitness, and basketball would be enough to win the American market.
His decision to give up on the NFL and MLB in exchange for CrossFit would be a major mistake that Nike happily capitalized on.
Nike was popular in college football thanks to its bold pro-combat uniforms and flashy team sponsorships.
Applying that playbook and built up goodwill to the NFL was a cakewalk billion dollar move for Nike.
To solve for Adidas and Reebok both failing to sell in North America, Heiner switched the target audience.
Under Route 2015, the company would prioritize marketing to American high schoolers rather than adults for the next five years.
Heiner felt that Nike was too entrenched in adults and high schoolers were more viable as the next generation of shoppers.
But to go from sponsoring the Super Bowl to back to school campaigns and lockers is certainly one of the bigger head-scratching decisions of the Heiner era.
Meanwhile, Adidas was doing well in China but starting to see increasing competition.
In Russia, Adidas enjoyed 60% market share, but Heiner wanted more.
more.
He wanted complete market penetration, ordering further investment in Russia for the next five years.
Heiner strangely seemed to have forgotten about being burned by the Russian ruble depreciation just a year ago.
And once again, retail was at the core of Heiner's new strategy.
In his presentation, he preached the importance of winning the customer at the physical point of sale, believing that retail would continue growing double digits every year.
More stores, higher productivity, better store experiences, greater presence at malls and faster shipping to stores.
In Heiner's 35 slides of Route 2015, there was not a single mention of e-commerce.
In its first year, Route 2015 was a success.
In 2011, net sales in North America grew 12%, Russia was up 26%, and Asia grew 15%.
Heiner's bet on retail was validated as comparable store sales grew 14%.
Both brands grew at record levels in North America, with Adidas sales up 21%, The market seemed to react positively to Reebok's new fitness positioning and products.
Vindicated by these early returns, Heiner used this momentum to expand Adidas' ambitions.
Seeing the success of North Face and Patagonia, Heiner bought the emerging brand 510 for $25 million to enter the outdoor performance market.
The following year, 2012, was another strong year for Adidas.
Thanks to the London Olympics, the company grossed a record 14.9 billion euros with 11% growth.
Operating margin improved from 7% to 8% year over year.
This would have been a perfect year had it not been for Reebok.
Just when the company thought they were home free, they found the final skeleton in Reebok's closet.
During a routine audit, Adidas discovered irregularities in Reebok's India business.
business.
Upon investigation, they uncovered a criminal operation where Reebok management had colluded with local partners to inflate the region's sales and profits.
It was more than just overstating revenue.
Management intentionally didn't record customer returns, skimmed money from accounts receivable, and operated four hidden warehouses of stolen product.
This had been going on for years, meaning nearly all of Reebok's numbers had been misreported.
Seven years after the acquisition, Adidas was still paying the price for Reebok's mismanagement.
As embarrassing as the scandal was, Reebok's business was far more alarming.
The brand's success in 2011 turned out to be nothing more than a flash in a pan or a one-year wonder.
Reebok's sales declined 17% in 2012 after being up 20% the year before.
Heiner's spin to investors was to look on the bright side that the brand was now stabilizing, but it was clear that nothing was working.
The marketing wasn't sticking, CrossFit wasn't increasing desirability, the brand was unreliable, and the sales were simply too inconsistent.
2012 would be the beginning of the end for Heiner.
In 2013, investors were eager to see how Adidas would perform in a year with no major sporting events, no Olympics, and no international soccer tournaments to boost their sales.
Heiner put the company through another reorg that year, merging the retail, wholesale, and e-commerce teams within the global sales organization.
Historically, these teams had been operating as independent silos, but Heiner now wanted an integrated omni-channel approach.
On the R &D side, Adidas continued to make progress on running technologies with the launch of the Boost shoe.
Reebok continued to flatline despite the company's best efforts.

Adidas came up with a new target customer for Reebok that they called quote-unquote the fit generation, which it defined as consumers young in age or spirit, who enjoyed getting fit and staying fit with friends.
Needless to say, this generic persona failed to land in the market.

Reebok also expanded its sponsorship to the trendy Spartan race, but the company seemed to have misinterpreted that for most participants, the Spartan race was more about the social media photo op than about the running itself.
Overall revenue declined 3% that year to €14 billion, sales in North America fell 1%, while Asia and Europe dropped 5%.
Reebok sales continued to freefall, decreasing 4% year over year.
As a company, Adidas was getting further away and not closer to its 5-year goals.
Investors were losing patience.
Feeling the heat, Heiner even began to publicly question his own strategy, acknowledging that perhaps he had been overly ambitious when he set those goals back in 2010.
Behind closed doors, Heiner acknowledged to Adidas' biggest investors that the company was not where they needed to be or thought they would be three years into Route 2015.
While he admitted that Adidas had made quote-unquote a few mistakes, he pointed the finger at world events that happened beyond the company's control.

Raw material costs, unfavorable currency movements, the Boston Marathon bombing, Tyson Gay's suspension, Derrick Rose's season-ending injury, and RG3's career-ending injury were all specifically brought up by Heiner as unlucky incidents that hurt Adidas' sales.
When the meeting came to a close, Heiner tried to restore confidence in investors.
But what he intended to be an inspiring closing instead came off as an unhinged rant.
Who else in the industry could do what Adidas is trying to do, he challenged investors.
Quote, Who in our industry has the insight and know-how to unleash game-changing multi-billion long-term platforms like Boost, Klima, and MeCoach?
Who in our industry has the imagination and creativity to open up the wardrobe of the sports consumer, building not just one, but three highly diverse, authentic, inclusive brands.
Who in our industry has had the foresight to embrace the world of fitness?
It was likely this moment in which investors lost what little remaining confidence they had in Heiner.
At the time, Nike had Jordans, Air Forces, Air Maxes, Converse, Jack Purcell, and Nike Plus.
For Heiner to pound his chest and declare that no one else in the industry had anything close to what Adidas had in brands, products, and expertise is a delusional thing to say.
In 2014, Adidas' struggles continued.
Despite the Brazil World Cup and sponsoring Pharrell fresh off his happy single, the company surprisingly regressed in revenue and profits.
Revenue grew at less than 1%.
Operating profit fell from 9% to 7% year-over-year.
Adidas was not only entirely off track from its 5-year goals, it had also missed its own sales guidance for the year.
Heiner's five-year commitment to reaching complete market penetration in Russia significantly increased the company's exposure in that market, and now those chickens had come home to roost.
In 2014, the price of oil fell and took with it the Russian ruble.
The currency cratered, triggering a global sell-off of Russian assets, which was worsened by the international sanctions that had been placed on the country for Putin's annexation of Crimea.
While the 2009 ruble depreciation had cost Adidas 200 million euros, the 2014 Russian financial crisis burned the company over double that amount, wiping out 550 million euros in net sales.
Heiner had lost faith in Reebok's leaders and replaced the entire executive team once more in 2014.
This time, he picked a man by the name of Mark King to revive the American brand.
Mark King lasted four years at Reebok before becoming the current CEO of Taco Bell.

Mark King at Taco Bell has been widely criticized and deeply unpopular with consumers for discontinuing menu favorites like potatoes, Mexican pizzas, triple-layer nachos, and the seven-layer burrito in the name of cost-cutting.
That should tell you everything you need to know about Mark King as an executive, Heiner as the CEO who appointed him, and the dysfunctional state of Adidas and Reebok at the time.
Investors were furious and wanted Heiner out.
There were no words that could restore their faith in the CEO after 2014's disastrous results.
Heiner had failed to execute, grow revenue, or optimize the bottom line in the 13 years he had been in charge.
In the past decade, he had bounced from one failing five-year strategy to another.
Adidas had lost ground to Nike and at this point was even losing to Under Armour in the United States.
As much as investors wanted to blame all the shortcomings on Reebok for dragging the company down, the reality was that both brands were underperforming.
Incredibly, Adidas' board renewed Heiner's contract for two more years.
Investors were outraged as to why an underperforming, directionless 13-year CEO should be rewarded with higher pay, longer tenure, and greater job security for progressively worse results.
Investors went on the offensive, publicly questioning Heiner's leadership, calling out the mismanagement of Adidas, and threatening a hostile takeover if a new CEO was not appointed.
In early 2015, Heiner invited investors to Germany to a two-day event at headquarters, complete with five-star hotels, drinks, and private transportation.
To an audience of his harshest critics, he revealed his new five-year strategy called Create the New in a final attempt to keep his job.
With Create the New, Heiner promised high single-digit sales growth every year until 2020, 15% increase in net income every year, and a 30-50% dividend payout.
Heiner admitted that under his watch, Adidas had lost touch with consumers.
The decision to consolidate Reebok and Adidas under one single operating model back in 2009 had hurt the company's ability to be agile.
Products took too long to reach the market, while design and production were too slow and inflexible to adjust to emerging consumer trends.
This new 5-year strategy was based on three pillars, cities, speed, and open source.
Instead of prioritizing growth of individual countries like Russia or China in the past, Adidas would laser focus on six key cities, Los Angeles, New York, London, Paris, Shanghai, and Tokyo.
These cities were chosen as high-profile international destinations that are trendsetters in fashion.
Consumers in neighboring areas, countries, and regions often take inspiration from the celebrities and influencers who live in these six cities to determine what outfits or shoes to buy and wear.
Global brands, Heiner believed, were created in global cities.
As an example, if Adidas could win running in New York and Los Angeles, then the company would win running in the US as a whole.
Adidas would now over-proportionately invest in marketing and influencers in these six cities every year for the next five years to restore its relevance and consumer appeal.

To support this new localized focus, Heiner reversed the company's single operating model where everyone was forced to standardize behind one global message every year and move back to the original, decentralized, siloed approach where each group ran its own marketing.
Each division from running shoes to Adidas Originals would now have the creative freedom, messaging, campaigns, and budget.
This was another case of where Heiner's push to consolidate and centralize everything in 2009 had backfired.
The next pillar was speed.
Heiner targeted e-commerce as the next highest priority with goal of achieving 2 billion euros by 2020.
To put into perspective just how behind Adidas was in the world of ecommerce, Nike had already achieved Adidas' 5-year sales goal at the time of Heiner's presentation.
Nike had surpassed 2 billion euros in online sales in 2016, four years ahead of Adidas.
Nike's own 5-year goal was to surpass 12 billion euros by 2020.
That's how under-invested e-commerce had been under the Heiner era.

In addition, Heiner demanded an evolution of Adidas's design and manufacturing processes in order to reduce production times, improve the time to market, enable customization, and launch more in-season products.
The last pillar was open source.

To Heiner, Adidas's traditional in-house meticulous product design worked well for its performance products, where professional athletes obsessed over every single detail and only rotated their wear once a year.
But in the world of consumer footwear, this old-school approach was too slow to keep up with consumers and the in-house designers lacked the creativity and star powers to become trendsetters.

To win consumers, particularly those in the big cities, Heiner mandated collaboration with influencers like Kanye West and Stella McCartney to bring a fresh, unconventional look to the overly traditional German brand.
While Heiner's three pillars were solid, his five-year strategy for winning back North America was uninspiring and puzzling.
The new goal would be for Adidas to increase its visibility on the field through heavy grassroots marketing in American football, lacrosse, baseball, and volleyball.
High school locker rooms were the battlegrounds the company wanted to win in.
This was yet another case of Heiner going in circles attempting to fix mistakes four years too late.
If the goal was visibility, then he shouldn't have given up the NFL and MLB to his biggest competitors.
In potentially one of the best examples of modern sunk cost fallacy, Heiner continued to maintain his loyalty to Reebok.
To quote, Reebok is one of our three main brands.
We have been hammered for seven years about it, but we have turned the brand around.
We would be stupid to sell it now.
While there was merit and evidence that Heiner had learned from his past mistakes in this new five-year strategy, investors were not convinced that he was still the right leader.
Their offensive continued, and the public attacks kept coming.
To quote, Adidas responds to market conditions, but it seems to have forgotten how to set trends itself.
Where are the product innovations with which you want to take market share from Nike and Under Armour?
A new strategy would only be believable with new leadership.
Adidas is panting behind the competition.
It's lost the race, at least in 2014.
Nike is pulling ahead, and against this background, it's incomprehensible why the board extended Heiner's contract by two additional years.
It wasn't just shareholders who were souring on Adidas, it was also the wholesalers and retailers who had noticed the company's declining appeal.
Under Heiner, Adidas had lost ground to its biggest rival and even newcomers.
Retailers would now rather stalk Nike, New Balance, Lululemon, and even Under Armour over Adidas and Reebok, all of which was having a material negative impact on the business.
Even in areas of strength like football, Nike was also catching up with its sponsorship of Barcelona, Neymar, and an exclusive Cristiano Ronaldo boot collection.
The public criticism of Heiner from hedge funds and large investors was simply too overwhelming to ignore.
While Adidas initially hired investors and advisors preparing for a bitter fight, the board quickly backed down and gave in to investor demands.
Shortly after Heiner's new strategy presentation, Adidas kicked off a CEO search and settled with Heiner to take an early retirement once the new leader was appointed.
2015 turned out to be the most successful and pivotal year in Adidas' history, but for Heiner, it was too little too late.
As a CEO, Heiner had his flaws.

He was too reactionary, too stubborn about sunk costs, too loose with M &A, stifled creativity in favor of efficiency, underinvested in e-commerce, and made too many bets that backfired like Russia, retail, and Reebok.
But there was a lot of good that Heiner did in his last year that would revolutionize Adidas forever.
Heiner's 9-year strategic focus on running finally bore fruit in the launch of Adidas' best product ever, albeit not exactly in the way he had intended.
In 2015, Adidas launched Ultraboost, and the shoe became a global fashion phenomenon, widely praised and sought after for its unique blend of high performance running, comfort, and fashion.

The iconic silhouette of the Ultraboost, the prime knit upper, the separated lace cage, and the boost cushioning technology had culminated from the 9 years of continuous R &D that Heiner had initiated back in 2006.
In 2015, Adidas also launched NMD as a new lifestyle sneaker with performance elements of Ultraboost.
Yet the biggest launch in 2015 was neither Ultraboost or NMD, instead it was Kanye West with the highly anticipated release of the Yeezy Boost 350s and the Yeezy Boost 750s.
Sneakerheads and Kanye fans waited hours in line from London to Chicago for these $200 sneakers which were sold out online and in stores within the first hour.
Fueled by the Ultraboost, NMD, and Yeezy 350s, Adidas skyrocketed to the top in 2015 with 16% growth in overall revenue, going from 14 billion euros to nearly 17 billion euros in the span of a year.

Consumers fell in love with Adidas, making it the most popular brand on Instagram that year, and retailers took note of the company's new appeal, opening up significant shelf space and purchasing record-level quantities of Adidas products for their stores.
Adidas' 2015 performance was a picture-perfect example of a successful comeback in sports.

It's easy to say that Kanye West single-handedly saved Adidas with Yeezy, but it was an intentional decision by Heiner as CEO to give the musician the creative freedom, autonomy, and resources to create whatever it is that he wanted.
That level of partnership and collaboration was something that not even Nike had been willing to do.
Looking back, if we imagine a world where Heiner had made the right decisions as CEO, Adidas' already extraordinary 2015 could truly have been historic.

If the If the company had kept its NFL and MLB deals, invested in their e-commerce business to just be on par with Nike, and had launched Ultraboost, NMD, and Yeezy, Adidas might have truly eclipsed Nike that year.
As poor as Heiner was as CEO, there's no denying that he was handing off Adidas to the next CEO in its best possible shape.
A company that was struggling one year ago to be cool and relevant now had three new best-selling mainstream franchises and incredible momentum.
Casper Rorsted was appointed as the new CEO of Adidas in 2016.

Rorsted was a proven CEO who was best known for his tight control over costs, his ruthless focus, and restoring profits at his prior company Henkel, a Germany-based multinational consumer goods company.
In 2016, the first year of the Rorsted era, Adidas achieved a record revenue of 19 billion euros, growing 14%.
Rorsted, true to his reputation, aggressively sold off what he deemed to be wasteful businesses in the TaylorMade Golf brand and the Canadian CCM Hockey brand.
In contrast, Heiner had kept those underperforming brands around for years in the name of diversification.
There was also a strategic shift in marketing with the new CEO.
In Heiner's last year, Adidas had outbid Nike and its competitors to become the exclusive kit sponsor of Manchester United in a landmark deal.
Under the agreement, Adidas would pay the English Football Club £75 million every year for the next 10 years for the right to produce jerseys.
While Heiner saw this as a necessary expense to maintain relevance, Rorsted saw these tit-for-tat deals like this to be wasteful and bring little strategic value.

Rorsted recognized that grassroots marketing and social media were making a greater influence on the modern consumer than these high-profile, expensive sponsorships and cold outbound media advertisements.
Adidas decreased its sponsorship budget, gave up the NBA deal, and routed those cost savings into funding limited-time collaborations with creators and inventing new shoe franchises.
Rorset was brutally upfront about where Reebok stood in his eyes.
The brand had zero growth in North America, its home market, for several years and its margins were significantly below the company average.
Growth was a lost cause, and tweaking messaging and positioning at this point would be pointless.
The best Reebok could now aim for was just to restore its profitability.
Rorset rolled out a cost-cutting plan for the American brand that he titled Muscle Up, which included shuttering 50% Reebok stores across three years.
Meanwhile, the momentum continued for NMD, Yeezy, and Ultraboost with new colorways and models that continued to dazzle consumers and sneakerheads around the world.
Adidas continued to reach new heights in 2017, growing 7% in overall revenue from 19 billion euros to 21 billion euros.

New UltraBoost, NMD, and Yeezy shoes accounted for 77% of Adidas brand sales, yet Roarsid noticed that the longer the models lasted on the market, the faster the price dropped and the lower their margins became.
