To counter this, the company proactively expanded its creator network, launching limited collections with people like Alexander Wang.
Roarsid saw these one-time collaborations as invaluable to maintaining both profits and relevance.

By launching new models, collections, and also limiting the quantity available every season, Adidas could maintain its gross margins and extend the lifespan of UltraBoost, NMD, and Yeezy franchises through scarcity.
Having a large pipeline of new in-season products, especially when it came to shoes, became critical to Adidas' success.

Rorsted adjusted R &D to support this new luxury approach, replacing the traditional development of products in advance of high seasons with in-season production and rapid replenishment manufacturing.
By 2017, the majority of Ultra Boost and NMD shoes had been manufactured with a lead time of 60 days or less.
With greater desirability, luxury positioning, and intentional scarcity comes greater pricing power.
Adidas began shifting its business towards its full-price premium products and started issuing fewer discounts to retailers who had no choice but to accept the terms.
Meanwhile, North America was surging.
The company's sales in the region were growing 25% every year for the past three years, going from €2 billion in 2014 to €4 billion in 2017.
From 2018 to 2019, Adidas enjoyed stellar years, achieving for the first time in company history 9% growth and double-digit operating margins back-to-back.
Investors were delighted as Rorsted delivered the top line and bottom line that Heiner could not.
Yeezy became a forcing function and driver for Adidas's e-commerce business as the company began doing digital drops of its most coveted products like the Yeezy Boost 350 V2 Triple Whites.

Ultra Boost continued to flourish, releasing the widely praised Ultra Boost 4.0 which many consider to this day to be the franchise's best model alongside a limited edition Game of Thrones collection during the show's peak.
Adidas formally entered the high-end outdoor market with its MyShelter line to compete with Patagonia, Arcteryx, and North Face.
To this day, Adidas' success continues, but there are signs of staleness.
By a function of age, Ultra Boost and NMD have lost some of their shine among sneakerheads and consumers.
While Reebok continued to make progress on its margins, Rorsted had seen it enough and eventually sold off the brand at a loss for $2.5 billion in 2021 to a fashion brand conglomerate.
Having finally shed Heiner's 15-year mistake, take, Roarshead's new company vision is a single brand focused on Adidas, with a greater emphasis on e-commerce and international growth.
They've added six more key cities to win in Mexico City, Berlin, Moscow, Dubai, Beijing, and Seoul.

title: DoorDash & The Myth of Profitable Food Delivery
note: Personal-anecdote opener from a failed founder, then unit-economics analysis of DoorDash and global rivals, returning to the thesis that delivery cannot be profitable.
sections: The narrator's startup of food trucks
Shutting down: no way to make money
Uber Eats, Delivery Hero, Just Eat
lines: Food delivery is a simple business.
While the market today is dominated by DoorDash, Uber Eats, Delivery Hero, and a few others, back in 2014, food delivery and the gig economy were just emerging in Silicon Valley.
Back then, the barriers to entry were so low that anyone could open up their own food delivery business in a matter of weeks with just a few thousand dollars and a website.

Food delivery seemed like such a simple and obvious million dollar idea that as a starry-eyed 20-year-old at the time, I left college to start a food delivery company, joining many others in the gold rush.
The market in 2014 was wide open for the taking.
DoorDash had not yet become a household name, Uber Eats was just spinning up, and Grubhub was primarily used for looking at restaurant menus online.
Food delivery is a marketplace business.
On the supply side are the restaurants.
What dishes and cuisines do you offer?
Are they fast food?
Chains?
Mom and Pops?
Bakeries?
dessert shops, cafes, or fine dining.
The more diverse, the greater, the more reputable, and the more exclusive your restaurants are, the stronger the supply of your marketplace.
Back in 2014, not many restaurant owners were thrilled with the idea of entrusting food delivery to a pair of 20-year-olds.
We quickly realized that to deliver for big players like McDonald's or the Cheesecake Factory, you needed the capital and the connections, neither of which we have.
But most of all, you need order volume.
Consumers are the demand side of your marketplace.
The number, amount, and frequency in which they order determine your overall order volume.
There are three ways to win consumers in the world of food delivery.
One, you can compete on speed.

In order to be the fastest to deliver food, you need lots of drivers on the road and you're making a bet that you can assign pickups, route deliveries, and pay out higher earnings to drivers more efficiently than your competition.
You're also betting that consumers are willing to pay the highest premium for guaranteed convenience.
You can compete on price.

By undercutting the competition as the cheapest delivery in town, or maybe it's free delivery, you're betting that the greater order volume over time will make up for all the loss that you're swallowing on every order.
You can compete on supply.

If you can become the exclusive delivery partner for McDonald's and other big restaurants, then customers will have no other choice but to order from your marketplace no matter how expensive or slow your actual delivery service might be.
Today's giants like DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Delivery Hero all have the economical, technical, and operational means to balance between speed, price, and supply.
But the barriers for entry continue to remain low, with new food delivery startups seemingly popping up every year.
But these new startups simply can't afford to compete on speed or price.
No investor or board member would approve the significant operational risk and cash burn involved with going head to head with Uber or Dardash.
As a result, these startups tend to specialize on supply.
They try to monopolize delivery for a specific restaurant type like Chinese or fine dining, but these niches are generally too narrow to sustain over time.
If you don't have enough customers, you won't have sufficient order volume.
If you don't have sufficient order volume, then restaurants won't partner with you for delivery.
If you don't have restaurants on your marketplace, then you won't have customers.
This balancing act between supply and demand is the fundamental chicken or the egg dilemma that all food delivery businesses grapple with.
For each additional restaurant you bring onto your marketplace, you improve supply and demand with greater diversity and consumer choice.
But there are downsides.
The more restaurants that you bring on, the greater variance in orders, and the more diluted the average restaurant sales and returns become.
There are also diminishing returns with scale.
When consumers are given too many options to choose from, then browsing and ordering delivery can become overwhelming and exhausting.

When your marketplace on the supply side scales to hundreds of restaurants, then discovery becomes a challenge as it's impossible for the restaurants that are buried at the bottom of the list to stand out to customers.

And if those restaurant owners feel like their returns aren't good enough, they may choose to leave your marketplace and sign on with a different delivery competitor who can offer them better order volume, reach, and terms.
Here's how we approached this problem back in 2014 as two naive 20 year olds.
VC backed players like DoorDash and Uber were opening up their war chests to recruit as many drivers as possible through relentless job postings and sign on bonuses that we could never match.
For our startup, competing on speed was out of the question.
Without restaurants, we couldn't pull in customers.
Since we didn't have customers, we couldn't pull in restaurants.
For the few restaurants that were interested in working with us, it was meaningless to bring them on since they were already offering delivery on Postmates, DoorDash, and Uber Eats.

Our strategy was to specialize in supply by exclusively targeting food trucks, street vendors, and food stands, mobile food businesses who generally had more unique foods and had been neglected by the existing delivery apps for not having dedicated brick and mortar locations.
Since mobile food vendors are transient businesses with very weak online presence beyond Instagram, we really focused on centralizing the experience.
The goal was to provide consumers with one curated menu of multiple cuisines that were made up of the best dishes from credible vendors that we had vetted as a delivery company.
This meant that customers could combine dishes from multiple vendors into one order.
They weren't locked into ordering delivery from one vendor at a time.
Before any vendor could sell in our marketplace, we would take the time to painstakingly work with the owners to figure out what specific dishes they had were worth selling.
To ensure quality and prevent menu bloat, no vendor was allowed to sell every item on their menu.

For these mobile food vendors, e-commerce, enabling customers to place orders online, paying with a credit card, having a website, offering delivery were all new ways to expand their business that they never had done before.

They were really excited to work with us as a delivery company who would take professional photos of their food, handle their website and e-commerce, do the credit card processing, do all the online marketing, and then handle the last mile delivery for free.
In exchange, we would take 30% and they would keep 70% of net sales.

Since many of these mobile food businesses had no reputation and needed to build up their credibility, we leveraged prices to pull in customers by offering free delivery and satisfaction guarantees on all orders.
This heavy-handed strict curation approach that we took was really labor-intensive.
It would take us anywhere from 10 to 15 hours to onboard a single vendor onto our marketplace, but we stubbornly believed that our relentless focus on quality would pay off long-term.
But after operating for a year, we ultimately concluded that there was really no way to make money from delivery.
In seven months, we had delivered over 3,400 orders and grossed over $35,000 off an initial bootstrap budget of $2,500.
For two 20-year-olds, this was great, but in reality the margins were never sufficient enough for us to pay ourselves or hire a single person.
We were doing everything by ourselves, from taking photos of the food, to handing out flyers and giving out samples, to packing orders at 4 in the morning and delivering to customers in our own cars.
During the day we would do marketing to try to build up demand, and into the night we would work on supply, push website updates, and process orders.
On the supply side, retention was difficult with inconsistent order volume.
Our vendors would unleash their frustrations on us whenever they felt like they weren't making enough sales and threatened to quit.
And some actually would, they would make all the hours we had spent curating their food and taking photos a total waste.
The other issue was that there were only so many mobile food businesses in our area.
At one point we had onboarded every single possible supplier to our marketplace within 75 miles of each direction.
And whenever our menu became stale and we didn't have new vendors or dishes to offer, However, consumers would get bored and stop ordering.
Caught in between the supply and demand of our marketplace to the point where our own friendship had completely deteriorated, it was a no-brainer for us to shut down our startup.
With food delivery, it's really easy to get cash flow and momentum and get started, but it's impossible to make money and profit.
To sustain, you need a ridiculously high burn rate that pulls in customers and generates enough order volumes to keep your suppliers and drivers happy.
Fundraising from investors would just be robbing Peter to pay Paul.
Having millions of dollars in a bank doesn't change the reality that you only make a couple cents on every order.
Six years after our startup, it's been interesting to see the continued hype of food delivery companies around the world even though everyone seems to know that the unit economics just don't work.
When you have to rely on tips to pay a livable wage to drivers, it's obvious that there's something fundamentally broken with the business model.

If none of them could make money during this once in a lifetime global pandemic, how could any of them turn a profit in this new environment where gas is going up, inflation is rising, and a recession is materializing?
In this episode, we're going to look at the four biggest food delivery companies around the world.
DoorDash, Uber Eats, Delivery Hero, and Just Eat.
What are the strategies that these companies believe will lead them to profitability?
And are these just fantasies that they spin for investors?
And which companies have made the most progress?
The current industry leader is DoorDash, who holds the highest valuation and the largest share of the food delivery market in the United States.

The company's vision is that if they can build logistics and delivery to deliver ice cream before it melts, or pizza before it gets cold, or groceries within an hour, then DoorDash can become the on-demand delivery provider for everything including clothes and medicine.

This same ambition is rooted in the design of DashPass, which is DoorDash's membership program where customers can pay a flat monthly fee of $9.99 for unlimited free deliveries and lower service fees from eligible restaurants.

Over time, DoorDash's leaders are hopeful that they can turn DashPass into a quote-unquote wallet for the physical world, where consumers can get delivery and special perks from not just restaurants but all the other local businesses in their community, whether they're shopping in the store or lying on their couch at home.
DoorDash's rise to the top has been fueled by its strategy of winning suburban markets and small metropolitan areas.
While food delivery is the most visible in large dense cities like Manhattan, Chicago, and Los Angeles, DoorDash always focused on the smaller markets that had been traditionally underserved.
Suburban and small metropolitan consumers have fewer options when it comes to delivery, which meant that DoorDash could win meaningful customers at manageable acquisition costs.

As annoying as it is for people in New York City to suffer on packed subway cars during rush hour, the reality is that the distance that big city dwellers travel is still significantly shorter than the many miles that suburban residents have to drive in their cars to buy a single thing.
In addition, suburban consumers tend to be more families and less individuals, which results in larger order sizes and higher spend.

The lighter traffic and easier parking in suburbs and small metro areas also benefits drivers who can do pickup and delivery more efficiently than in the cities where they have to do double parking in bike lanes and fire lanes.
When it comes to driver earnings, DoorDash makes no attempt to hide that the tip is the most significant element to making its economics work.
The current pay model for DoorDash drivers is made up of three elements.
The first is the base pay, which is calculated based on the estimated time, distance, and desirability of the order.
The second is the tip from consumers, which drivers get to keep 100% of.
The third is promotions, where if drivers meet certain goals and conditions, then they can get a bonus payout for completing that order.
But these promotions are generally too non-transparent and too inconsistent to be considered part of a driver's regular earnings.

Not every driver is offered promotions, and the conditions to achieve such bonuses can vary for each driver depending on when they started using DoorDash, what sign-up codes they may have used, and what region they're in.
If we look at the pay model for DoorDash drivers, the base pay is really the only stable element that DoorDash pays out.
The tip is entirely funded and contributed and set by the customer.
Let's look at DoorDash's own breakdown of an example delivery and see how much is given to the restaurant, how much is kept by DoorDash as the middleman, and how much is given to the driver.
For a sample $33 order of which food costs $22, service fees make up $6, taxes $2, and the customer adds a $3 tip.
The driver earns $8, the restaurant gets $20, and the DoorDash pockets $5.
In DoorDash's own example, the customer tip makes up almost 50% of the driver's earnings.

Tipping is so central to DoorDash's economics that the company itself calls out the risks that if customers consistently provide low tips or simply just don't tip at all, then there would be material harm in the company's ability to provide delivery and retain drivers.

Earning on base pay alone is inadequate, but rather than directly educating or requiring customers to tip, DoorDash opts for this hands-off approach and they let drivers and consumers socialize amongst themselves on how to be successful in its marketplace.
This dog-eat-dog mentality is most visible in the DoorDash communities where seasoned dashers shame no-tip customers and fellow drivers who take no-tip orders.
New DoorDash customers who assume that tipping is optional or don't understand how significant the tip is, end up learning the hard way why their food never gets delivered.
To put into perspective just how favorable COVID has been for food delivery, DoorDash's annual revenue grew at an astounding 1,580% in the past 3 years.
In 2018, DoorDash was grossing $290 million in overall revenue with 83 million orders placed.
Fast forward to 2019, DoorDash had grown 200% to $890 million on 263 million orders and 18 million monthly active users.
At the height of the pandemic in 2020, DoorDash grew another 200% to a record $2.8 billion in revenue on 816 million orders and 20 million monthly active users.
In 2021, DoorDash's top line increased by another $2 billion to hit $4.8 billion on 1.3 billion orders and 25 million monthly active users.
Despite this historic growth, DoorDash continues to post a loss of $500 million every year with an average negative operating margin of minus 42%.

While DoorDash can't escape the losses under traditional business accounting, the company Pending pushes a set of operational metrics that it believes more accurately capture how profitability for them is just right around the corner.
The first operational metric they have is called Marketplace Gross Order Value, or Marketplace GOV, which is simply the total amount that users pay on DoorDash.
It combines the cost of food, taxes, tips, service fees, membership fees, Dash Pass fees of all the DoorDash orders that were placed that year.
Marketplace gross order value is the closest public metric to order volume.
DoorDash's revenue itself is just a slice of the Marketplace GOV.
It's made up of the 15-30% commission that it charges restaurants and the service fee that it charges customers.
The rest of the Marketplace GOV pie is paid out to restaurants and drivers.
In 2018, Marketplace GOV was $2.8 billion, with $290 million of that pie being DoorDash revenue.
In 2019, Marketplace GOV had grown 4 times to $8 billion, with $890 million of that being revenue.
In 2020, GOV had grown to $24 billion, with $2.8 billion of that pie being DoorDash revenue.
And finally, in 2021, GOV hit $42 billion, with $4.8 billion of that pie being DoorDash's revenue.
DoorDash's second operational metric is called Net Revenue Margin, or Take Rate, which is the percentage of gross order value the company can pocket as its own revenue.

The question that this metric asks is that, as the total amount of money that people spend on DoorDash's marketplace increases, as this overall GOV pie grows every year, is DoorDash able to take a bigger slice for themselves?
There's several reasons why this metric is so significant.
One is that it determines DoorDash's elasticity as a middleman.
Delivery itself is a commoditized service.
There's nothing particularly special about how DoorDash delivers or charges its customers or restaurants.
If DoorDash increased its restaurant commissions and decreased the amount it pays out to restaurants to pocket more of this pie for itself, how many restaurants would leave its marketplace?
If DoorDash increased the service fees that it charges customers, how many of these customers would leave in favor of a cheaper competitor?

If DoorDash decreased the amount it pays out to drivers, if it removed promotions, or started taking a portion of the tips, or they reduced base pay even more, how many drivers would still stay on with DoorDash?

An increasing net revenue margin or take rate would suggest that DoorDash is building the loyalty, leverage, and strength with its restaurants, drivers, and consumers to demand a bigger slice of the pie for itself.
But the results indicate that it's not really there.
In 2018, DoorDash took 10.35% of the pie for itself.
In 2019, 2019, the company slowly increased its take rate to 11% in 2020 to 11.7% and then in 2021 slightly back down to 11.65%.

There's something clearly very fragile about DoorDash even during this rocket ship growth, but the company continues to be extremely cautious about upsetting the balance on its marketplace between the price sensitive customers, the commission sensitive restaurants, and the earnings sensitive drivers.

If you know you're not getting another pandemic with guaranteed growth where customers are compelled to use your service, yet you still aren't comfortable demanding a bigger slice as a middleman, at what time could you actually do so?
The last operational metric that DoorDash pushes is contribution margin.

Contribution margin is simply the money left when you deduct all the direct expenses, all the direct sales, marketing, delivery, payment processing, insurance, customer support, platform operations, all the direct expenses involved in generating and fulfilling orders on DoorDash.
To play through DoorDash's logic, the company's contribution margin had been negative 20% in 2018 and 2019.
That means that for every $10 order that was placed on DoorDash, the company was losing $2 at least gross on every order for those years.
In 2020 onwards, contribution margin turned green, meaning DoorDash had finally achieved positive unit economics.
That means now, for every $10 order, DoorDash grosses $2.22.
cents.
But contribution margin doesn't include R &D or G &A, which are critical expenses and strategic investments that can't be ignored.
DoorDash calls itself a tech company and prides itself on building proprietary technology to enable operational efficiency above its competitors.
If we include R &D and G &A expenses, which combined make up over a billion dollars worth of expenses every year, then we arrive at DoorDash's net losses of half a billion dollars.
Could DoorDash's technology really reach a point of maturity where drivers and deliveries are so optimized that a high enough contribution margin could offset these billion-dollar investments?
Or maybe try this angle.

If you have to spend half a billion dollars on software and R &D every year just to squeeze out a higher gross margin of literally $1 to $3 more in every delivery order, is that investment really worth it?

Even if contribution margin one day reaches 50%, how many more orders and customers do you need to turn a profit when you're already at 25 million monthly active users and 1.3 billion orders in the US?
DoorDash's leaders have been consistent in that they want to get the unit economics right in America before scaling and expanding internationally.

When it comes to the labor pool, the company seems to favor having a large, replaceable, flexible pool of on-demand drivers that jump in whenever they want rather than a growing, committed, dedicated, reliable group of drivers.
DoorDash executives proudly highlighted that in 2021, even though there were 6 billion dashers that year, all these drivers worked on average less than 4 active hours per week.
Of course, there's some nuance here in that active hours is actually the time spent from when a driver accepts to completes an order.
The time that a DoorDash driver spends waiting for orders to come in can actually be much longer.
DoorDash believes that acquiring drivers isn't difficult, and they believe that dashers are an entirely different type of gig workers than Uber drivers, Instacart shoppers, or Lyft drivers.

With DoorDash, you can deliver orders on scooter, bike, or car, and the company believes that this quote-unquote safer working experience allows them to bring on a unique audience of drivers and bikers who aren't contested or interested in using other gig economy apps.

Despite the positive contribution margins of the past two years, DoorDash leadership pushes that the path to profitability is not really in growing margins point by point, but actually in generating higher order frequency.

While the company acknowledges that there's still lots of areas to optimize for its drivers, like they can give better predictions on when the kitchen will finish cooking, so that reduces the time that a dasher has to spend waiting at a restaurant for the food to be ready, I still think DoorDash realizes that these remaining inefficiencies are generally speaking too complex and expensive to rabbit hole into the pursuit of saving a couple cents.
I sense DoorDash also recognizes that there's also little that they can do to influence order sizes at this point of maturity, but there's still a lot that they can do to influence frequency.
Driving adoption and penetration of DashPass amongst DoorDash users is the company's biggest current focus.
With DashPass, the company is making the tradeoff to accept lower unit margins in exchange for higher order frequency.
So while DoorDash makes less money on DashPass orders, But if DashPass can unlock a higher order frequency and eventually greater cumulative spend from its customers, then that's profitability.
DashPass reminds me of Costco, where membership fees only make up 2% of the company's overall revenue.

But those membership fees does wonders in encouraging customers to spend large orders at a regular frequency, which then drives up Costco's overall order volume and top line, despite having very minimal markup on each item.
Newer DoorDash initiatives like Dash Mart further reinforce the company's goal of achieving high order frequency to reach profitability.

Dash Mart is a relatively new rollout which brings an inventory of grocery and convenience store essentials into geographies where such stores didn't physically exist or have 24-7 hours of operations.
However, the latest economic conditions continue to expose the underlying fragile nature of all food delivery marketplaces when it comes to price elasticity.
To offset the rise of gas prices, DoorDash recently rolled out two programs for driver retention.
One was a 10% cashback on fuel expenses and the other paid out a bonus that the driver drove over a certain distance.
For both of these programs, DoorDash chose to absorb these programs entirely rather than pass on these costs to the consumers in order to preserve order volume and growth.

To quote, if we keep the consumer prices unchanged and if we ensure Dasher earnings are preserved, That enables us to maximize growth because having adequate supply ensures that the customer quality is preserved which then drives the growth flywheel.
But with inflation, higher gas prices, and a recession coming, it's impossible to keep consumer prices unchanged.
Even if DoorDash doesn't increase its service fees, the restaurants will inevitably increase the prices on their platform to offset their higher ingredient and labor costs.
And if DoorDash increases its cut of the pie, the restaurant will more likely than not just past those costs on to the customer.
When we look at other food delivery companies around the world like Uber Eats, Delivery Hero, and Just Eat, we see the same story but with slight differences.
Despite all of them enjoying rocket ship growth during the pandemic, none of these companies have come close to turning a profit.
Uber Eats is probably the most amusing one.
Buried deep in their financials, you'll find this horrifying line.
Quote, cumulative payments to drivers for Uber Eats deliveries historically have exceeded the cumulative delivery fees paid by customers."
This is Uber admitting that the service and delivery fees that they charge customers for Uber Eats orders has never been enough to offset the costs of delivery.
Uber Eats from 2018 to 2021 grew from $1.4 billion to $8.3 billion in revenue, which is much higher than that of DoorDash and that's largely thanks to Uber's greater international presence.
As a result, Uber Eats Marketplace GOV is much higher than that of DoorDash with $51.6 billion for the most recent year.

Despite burning money on every Eats delivery with a negative 2% contribution margin, Uber offsets the per-order loss by demanding a much greater slice of the pie from its restaurants with a 16% take rate.
That's 5% more than DoorDash.

Delivery Hero also enjoyed spectacular growth during the pandemic in Europe, going from 687 million euros in 2018 to 5.8 billion euros in 2021, but still ended up netting annual losses of 1 billion euros.
Thankfully, in Europe and Asia, tipping is not the same cultural or business requirement like it is in the United States.
With stricter labor laws, Delivery Hero employs its own drivers and hires additional drivers through agencies.
However, despite the company's impressive international presence and scale, Delivery Hero is doing the worst of all when it comes to margins.
Even with 20% of the pie, Delivery Hero is still losing 14-20% gross on every order with no light at the end of the tunnel.
Its fellow European competitor, the Netherlands-based Just Eat, seems to be in the same boat.

When Just Eat grew from 2.7 billion euros to 5.3 billion euros from 2018 to 2021, largely thanks to its acquisition of Grubhub, the company has still continued to post annual losses of 200-300 million euros.
The only time the company has been able to not lose money on every order was when they hiked their take rate during the pandemic, taking a record 30% slice of the pie from its restaurants.

Now that the pandemic is ending, Just Eat has been forced to lower its take rate to a more tolerable 19% of the pie, but the company has then swiftly returned to negative contribution margins and is now losing 7% gross on every order.

It's no surprise that its investors are now revolting, they're calling for Just Eat's CFO and board to be fired in an open letter for quote-unquote torpedoing the company's future amidst a 75% drop in market valuation.

When I see the payouts for the CEOs of some of these unprofitable food delivery companies, I can't help but wonder what could have been in a different universe had we stuck to our startup and joined the parade.

But ultimately, if a company has to spend hundreds of millions every year just to squeeze one more dollar profit out of a $10 transaction, or rely on consumer tips to pay drivers a livable wage, I think there's a good case to be made that perhaps that business just isn't worth it.
Profitable food delivery is a myth, and value creation is meaningless without sufficient value capture.

title: Real Estate Tech: A Crumbling House of Cards
note: Hype-to-reality takedown of a celebrated startup: explains the model, exposes fees and fragile financing, then contrasts Zillow's failure and Offerpad.
sections: The problem of selling a home
The catch: fees and niche appeal
House of cards and VC backing
lines: In 2014, there was one Silicon Valley startup that was widely applauded for its ambition to revolutionize a massive, high-stakes industry that was as old and antiquated as the Middle Ages.

In an era where tech startups and venture capitalists were criticized for thinking small, not solving real problems, and constantly bringing Instagram clones, Airbnb copies, and other petty mobile apps to the market, this company was considered a breath of fresh air and celebrated for its risk-taking.
The media portrayed this startup as a rare embodiment of the type of big problems that Silicon Valley should be solving and that all other startups should aspire to their level.
That company was called Opendoor, and their idea was to make it possible to buy or sell a home in just a few clicks.

Opendoor was heralded as the next big startup behind Uber and Airbnb given the scope of the problem they were going after, the size of the real estate industry, and the company's proposed value creation.
Opendoor was the perfect mix of all the hottest Silicon Valley trends from the 2010s.
online to offline businesses, data science, machine learning, algorithms, artificial intelligence, and automation all applied to the old-fashioned world of real estate.

In Silicon Valley, where academia is greatly devalued, Opendoor's differentiation was that by recruiting the best Stanford PhDs, data scientists, mathematicians, software engineers, and quants, they could build proprietary algorithms that could accurately price the exact current market value of any given home and then predict the resale value of that same home over time.

With these proprietary algorithms that could price in every aspect about a home and its neighborhood, Opendoor's value proposition was that they could value homes with more precision, rigor, speed, and accuracy than a traditional real estate agent.

The company could then use these algorithms to buy homes at scale, quantify their value, repair and renovate them with as little capital as possible and then resell that home at a higher price within 3-4 months.
Basically flipping homes at scale with algorithms and automation.
Through the years, Opendoor was treated as Silicon Valley elite.
It was a startup that was so bold and so disruptive that it was considered untouchable.
Opendoor was not flipping homes, instead in their own words, they were a quote, once in a lifetime market maker that could transform the American residential real estate industry.

In its early years, Opendoor and its founders collected award after award, teased publicly the progress and scale of their technology, and raised massive amounts of funding from every reputable investor in Silicon Valley.

Since the company's numbers and technology were selectively shown under NDA to only a trusted few behind closed doors, there was no way for the public or the greater industry to know whether or not Opendoor's business model was viable or the company's true business performance.
As a result, Opendoor was able to quickly build up hype in its private years, and entrenched industry giants like Zillow and Redfin began to worry that they were missing out on something big.

This ushered in the instant buying phenomenon, or iBuying for short, where Zillow, Redfin, and Opendoor burnt hundreds of millions of dollars every year, flipping thousands of homes across the country based on algorithms.
Fast forward several years to 2020, where iBuying has revealed itself to be a short-lived fad.

Zillow, the company with the biggest market share, presence and pockets, terminated its iBuying business in a high-profile failure, laying off thousands of employees after losing over half a billion dollars.
Opendoor settled for an IPO via SPAC at $6 billion valuation, yet the company today is a shell of its former self.
Even during the low interest rates of the pandemic and the hot real estate market of the past 4-plus years, Opendoor has never once lived up to its billing as a market maker.
with a current stock price of less than $5 a share and a public valuation below $3 billion, lower than its valuation four years ago in 2019.

In this episode, we'll explore Opendoor, the iBuying business model, its business performance, and the long-running misconception that computers, machine learning, and algorithms make better decisions than humans.
Let's start with the problem.
Opendoor's goal is to be an online marketplace that pulls in people looking to sell their homes and people looking to buy homes.

Because Zillow and Redfin already dominate real estate as the main informational and networking platforms that connect buyers, sellers, and agents online to handle transactions offline, Opendoor needed to go further by bringing the entire transaction online to create and capture sufficient value for itself.

But in order to entice home buyers and home sellers to transact online on Opendoor, the company needed to offer homeowners a significantly A home by design is the most significant financial transaction that most Americans make.
Buying a home enables the accumulation of wealth through stable appreciation and leverage, the reduction of tax liability, and an increase in net worth, whereas selling a home nets a sizable payout.

Because of how much is at stake when it comes to buying or selling a home, the real estate industry has always thrived in these offline, manual, face-to-face, high-touch, relationship-based one-to-one engagements that are guided by agents.
Selling a home on average takes about three months and it can be a stressful, time-consuming, and complex experience.
To ease the process, roughly 90% of sellers in America use a real estate agent.
A real estate agent relies on their experience, the home's condition, local sales comparables, to come up with the listing price.

And this is all subjective, so each agent will have their own take on how much a home can sell for and may suggest that owners make these simple repairs or make major upgrades to increase their sale price.
Homeowners generally look for a credible local agent with a proven track record, but this is similar to finding a good doctor which is a hit or miss.

A good agent knows the market, prices the home competitively so it reaches its highest value, maximize the returns for the seller, they set up the right staging to attract buyers during open houses, and they close quickly.

A bad agent will overestimate or underestimate the market, suggest unnecessary repairs or renovations that end up costing the sellers more money than it adds, negotiate poor terms, or price the home so low that they leave money on the table or too high that the listing languishes and becomes unattractive.
75% of homeowners only ever consider one agent when they're selling their home, which can make all the difference in returns.
Homeowners spend on average $6,200 on cleaning, storage, repairs, renovations, and staging to prepare their home for a sale.

When a buyer makes an offer on a home, they generally conduct an inspection to uncover hidden problems that can result in additional demands or further negotiation, both of which can cut into the seller's return and prolong the deal cycle.
Once the offer is accepted and the terms are agreed to and the contract is signed, it can take another 35 days on average to close.
The seller has to wait for the buyer to coordinate their agent, their mortgage broker, the escrow, and their bank.
Roughly 20% of offers end up falling through due to the buyer being unable to secure financing or getting cold feet.
When this happens, sellers have to relist their home on the market, they have to wait for a new buyer and offer to come in, and then go through this entire three-month ordeal all over again.
Most sellers are also buyers themselves, but they can't afford to buy a new house before selling their current one.

This means that when sellers submit purchase offers for homes they want to move to, but they have contingencies that they have to sell their current home first, it can put these sellers at a disadvantage when they're competing with other buyers who are bidding for the same house.
While a good agent lightens this overhead, the reality is that these complexities and timelines under traditional real estate buy and sell transaction are fundamentally unavoidable.
Opendoor's bet was to reinvent this experience online by eliminating the open market along with all the third parties involved like the buyers, banks, brokers, and agents.
Sellers could avoid all this stress and complexity by selling their home directly to Opendoor.
Any homeowner can go to Opendoor's website, put in their address, answer questions about their home, and immediately receive a preliminary cash offer.
After an in-person assessment to verify the home's condition, Opendoor then presents a final all-cash offer to purchase the home.
With Opendoor, the homeowner also gets the freedom to choose their date of closing so that they can sell the home, move out, and buy a new home all on their own schedule.
Opendoor's business model centers around this value proposition of convenience and liquidity for sellers.
The company takes a flat 5% service fee, which is subtracted from the all-cash offer, and it's a cut that the company argues is cheaper than using a traditional real estate agent.
Agents typically charge a 5-6% commission, which doesn't include the repair, renovation, storage, move out, and staging costs if one was to list their home under the traditional open market.
Depending on the home's condition, Open Door also charges another percentage for repairs and renovations.

When you sell your home to Open Door, the company takes ownership immediately as the buyer, and you as the seller get to walk away with cash in hand without ever having to repair, touch up, or even clean your home.
This streamlining in exchange for convenience and liquidity is fundamentally the same as those places where you trade in your old phones, cars, and electronics for cash.
The twist is that Opendoor is doing this at scale with a lot of homes, a lot of money, and algorithms.
When sellers go to Opendoor's website to get an estimate of how much the company would pay for their home, these numbers are automatically generated by algorithms.
When the company conducts its home assessment, that data is collected into the underlying pricing algorithms which then generate the final cash offer.
There are also other algorithms that identify the repair and renovation opportunities for that specific home that would generate the most returns on paper.

When the repairs and renovations are complete, Opendoor lists that home again back on the open market at a higher price with the goal of flipping that property within 3-4 months and that resale price is also set by an algorithm.
Opendoor's differentiation lies in its proprietary algorithms and data science.
With each free home assessment, even if the owner ultimately chooses not to sell to Opendoor, the company says it's collecting data on the home and its surroundings.

Then through its machine learning and artificial intelligence, Opendoor claims that it's able to process these inputs to drive accurate home prices that dynamically adjust in real-time with all these other algorithms that can forecast local demand, detect risks, identify outliers, and predict future housing inventory in the exact area.

Since its founding, Opendoor has claimed that its algorithms are more rigorous and accurate than the tedious, static, small-sample size, napkin math, weighted average pricing that traditional real estate agents do to come up with home prices.
While agents only look at a few comparables and some big-ticket items like bathrooms, bedrooms, square footage, and lot size.

Opendoor boasts that its algorithms can quantify hundreds of variables in any given home, like floor types, stainless steel appliances, pool sizes, granite countertops, even to surrounding factors like proximity to transit and schools, and even abstract variables like road noise.

Opendoor also claims that their algorithms adjust for appreciation, so local sales and regional trends are all continuously priced into a home's value and updated, so they occur when they happen, whereas an agent's valuation becomes outdated quickly as a one-time fixed calculation.
And these algorithms with machine learning and artificial intelligence keep improving with more data and iterations, whereas an agent's approach rarely ever changes.
Opendoor's business is all about economies of scale.
The cost it takes their algorithms to price one home is the same as pricing five homes or a thousand homes.
The company argues that its economies of scale apply all the way through when they resell that same home later for a profit.
Operationally, Opendoor reuses local contractors and they buy materials in bulk so that when it does repairs and renovations, it's cheaper and faster with volume discounts.
But like everything in life, there's a catch when you sell to Opendoor.
When you sell to Open Door, you're giving up on your upside and returns.
In exchange for convenience, flexibility, and instant cash, Open Door offers are generally priced below market value.
Open Door's all-cash offers generally come in at 0.2% to 2% lower than a home's fair market value.
When you add on Open Door's 5% service fee, that means then sellers are generally leaving at least 5% to 7% of their home's fair market value on the table.
Ultimately, Opendoor has to buy homes below their fair market value in order to resell them later within 3-4 months for a profit.
This is a huge contrast to the traditional open market approach where agents typically list properties at or above market value in order to get as much money as possible.
Opendoor's instant liquidity and convenience really appeals to only a subset of homeowners.
The average length of homeownership in America is 8 years, and states like California and cities like Austin have been red-hot sellers' markets for a long time.

Most people, when they're selling their home, are looking to get as much money as possible, and find that the traditional approach and the headaches that come with that are a small price to pay for maximizing their appreciation.

When we wave away all the flashy tech buzzwords, data science, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, we can actually see how Opendoor's business is fundamentally a lot more niche than the company would like to admit.
The lack of mainstream appeal is reflected in the real seller conversion, which is one of Opendoor's key operational metrics.

Real seller conversion is the percentage of homeowners who accepted the below market cash offer from Opendoor and sold their home to the company out of all the homeowners that got a free estimate on the company's website.
Real seller conversion for Opendoor has hovered at 35% for the past three years, meaning that roughly 4 out of every 10 engaged sellers who get an offer choose to continue to sell to Opendoor.
The company operates only in 44 markets today, so that 35% real seller conversion is significantly lower when you put it in the perspective of the entire nationwide market.
From a qualitative standpoint, the success stories that Opendoor highlights seem to reinforce how niche the company's appeal really is.
In one recent example, a family relocated from Syracuse to a small Arizona suburb during the pandemic.
This unhappy family urgently wanted to move to Phoenix, but they couldn't afford to do so.
So they used Opendoor, where the family was happy to take a loss in their home value in exchange for the cash and flexibility.

In a single year, this family had sold two homes and moved to two new places, which is really unorthodox, especially when you consider that there are significant tax penalties incurred for selling a home before two years of ownership.
These tax penalties are how the American government discourages flipping and incentivizes long-term ownership at the individual level.
The other success stories that Opendoor shares are similar.
One family spent an entire year RVing across the country for fun before deciding to sell their home.

Since the parents worked remotely and their children were homeschooled, they didn't want to go through the disruption of listing on the open market and having strangers come in their home for open houses.

They sold their home to Opendoor for less than fair market value in exchange for convenience, but their lifestyle suggests that they were already financially comfortable and didn't need to maximize the sale of their home.
Other families were inexperienced, nervous first-time sellers who deemed it was worth giving up 5% of their home's fair market value to avoid the stress of the open market.
The other catch if you dig deep enough into Open Door's financials is that you'll find flipping homes in itself is actually not where the company's margins come from.
Quote, our business model is designed to generate margins from our service charge to sellers and not from the spread between acquisition price and resale price.
So while While Opendoor charges a flat 5% service fee to sellers, the reality is that the total cut that Opendoor takes at the end is actually higher than that 5%.
After the in-person assessment, that offer price will typically get lower as Opendoor identifies problems in the home that need to be repaired.
Depending on the scope and severity, Opendoor's repair fee ranges from 0.5% to another 5%.
Whether or not these repairs are needed or if the percentage taken is fair are not things that sellers can negotiate with Opendoor.

By charging an additional percentage of home value for repairs, rather than simply crediting the cost of repairs, which is what would happen in a traditional transaction, Opendoor gets to pay even less of the home's fair market value and pocket those savings to increase its own profit margin.

So while the company gives initial cash offers that are close to a home's fair market value, a seller still walks away with roughly 5-10% less after the service fee and non-negotiable fees like the repairs are tacked on.

And Opendoor now has a home in its inventory that they've bought for 5-10% below market value, which then increases its profits and lowers its risks when it flips that same home back onto the open market.

It's worth noting that under the repair case, after Opendoor acquires the home, the company actually has no obligation to actually do the repairs or even provide proof that it's completed the repairs.
In one recent example, Opendoor deducted an additional $20,000 from a seller saying that this cost was needed to replace the HVAC, replace the flooring, and repair the foundation.
The company ended up relisting the home on the open market in 10 days with just a fresh coat of paint and without any of these major repairs that it charged for.
In this example, that $20,000 became Opendoor's additional profit.
This is pricing power in action.

Opendoor's strategy is that even if its business overall is pretty niche, the sellers that it does attract and the sellers that it does appeal to are in these life situations where they have no choice but to eat these heavy, non-negotiable premiums to achieve the cash, convenience and speed.
Open Door is like a house of cards that's only as stable as the housing market.
It's a risky, capital-intensive business where if your algorithms are wrong, then your valuations are wrong and the whole business goes belly up.
When you're buying homes based on algorithms, you're amassing this huge multi-million dollar inventory of vacant homes across many states with non-trivial carrying costs.
If you do get your valuations right, the housing and economy could shift in the wrong direction for factors that are mostly beyond your control.

Your algorithms also have to be able to forecast future demand and the highest realistic value that each home can get on the open market after repairs within 3-4 months and then hope to actually sell it at that predicted price to successfully complete the flip.
Opendoor, for better or worse, is a modern example of Silicon Valley's incestuous system between its VCs, its founders, and its startups.
To pull off such a business, a ton of capital is required not just to buy the homes, but also to build the technology.
Only a handful of people in the world can fundraise $320 million for the idea to flip homes at scale using algorithms in the name of disruption, machine learning, and artificial intelligence.
Open Door was hatched by Keith Raboi, a Silicon Valley icon best known as a member of the PayPal mafia, an early executive at LinkedIn, and the COO of Square before a sex scandal forced him out.

Keith put together an all-star team of angel investors made up of his friends who were also tech royalty like the CEO of Y Combinator and the founders of PayPal, Affirm, Yelp, YouTube, Reddit, Box, and Lyft.
The collective star power of this angel investment team brought immediate credibility for the idea and company by association.
Opendoor got to work in 2014 with a $10 million Series A buying up $200,000 homes in Phoenix as a testing ground for its algorithms.
By 2016, Opendoor stated that it was responsible for 2% of all home purchases in Phoenix.
Opendoor continued to raise funding at then-historic levels with very little scrutiny, public criticism, or skepticism.

More and more VCs joined in, with an $80 million Series C led by NEA and Coastal Ventures, a $210 million Series D, a $325 million Series E from Andreessen Horowitz and from the second largest home construction company in the United States, and eventually $400 million from SoftBank.
But what was more important than the money was the institutional reputation and connections of these venture capitalists.
Backed by such a large roster of reputable equity institutions, their collective credibility made it easier for Opendoor to raise billions more dollars through debt.
Opendoor burns money at an astronomical level higher than any typical tech startup.
There's a significant upfront R &D cost needed to build, maintain, and tune these algorithms.

There is equally high operational costs in having contractors who inspect the homes, repair and renovate them after acquisition, along with local boots-on-the-ground operations team who help manage the inventory, validate trends, and verify the algorithm results in person.

Finally, there's also high sales, marketing, and administrative overhead needed to successfully flip these homes within three to four months in advertising them online and manually engaging interested buyers, even if all the numbers are automated by the algorithms.
The cash that Opendoor raises from its equity sales is only ever enough to fund the company's operations but not enough to fund also buying homes in cash.
Opendoor's business model is all about scale.
If it doesn't flip enough homes, it'll never be able to offset its operational overhead.
Opendoor leans on debt from traditional lenders to fund its home purchases and this part is a fascinating exercise in corporate finance.
The way that debt financing works is that Opendoor has a set of non-recourse senior debt debt facilities and mezzanine debt facilities, all of which are backed by the homes it purchases.
So Opendoor can borrow 80-90% of the cost of a home from its senior debt facilities.
As soon as Opendoor sells a home, the company is required to repay what it has borrowed immediately back to these senior debt facilities.
If the home is sold at a loss, then Opendoor has to come up with the cash elsewhere to pay off what was borrowed.
If Opendoor is unable to pay off what was borrowed, then that home will be foreclosed.
These senior debt facilities charge a variable interest rate based on LIBOR and other global benchmarks, which these days is only getting higher.
Under its senior debt facilities, Opendoor can borrow a total of $7.8 billion.
The company can also borrow an additional $3 billion through its mezzanine debt facilities, which will fund 100% of the cost basis for any given home.
But this generosity comes at a price.
The interest rate for borrowing any money from its mezzanine debt facilities is a flat 10%.
Through 2019-2021, Opendoor has purchased more homes, and so its outstanding debt balance has ballooned from $271 million to $6.1 billion.
Based on their most recent year-end balance, if the interest rate goes up a single percent, Opendoor needs to find cash to pay $40 million more in interest expense.
One can quickly extrapolate just how much financial 3HS is needed to keep the company alive on a day-to-day basis.
Opendoor makes these big $100,000 bets regularly.
They burn cash daily to keep the lights on, and that's just because of how much labor is required in flipping homes.
and they have to hope that they hit a certain scale where they've resold enough homes to be profitable, and maintain enough cash on hand to pay off the debt and interest whenever a home is sold.
and they need to hope that the homes in its nationwide inventory don't tank in value before they're flipped.
and they have to keep their equity valuable in order to keep their funds going.
Opendoor is truly a modern-day house of cards.
The company's revenue grew from $1.8 billion in 2018 to over $8 billion in 2021.
To grow, they scaled, going from 18 markets to 44 markets in the US in those four years.
The company went from flipping 7,000 homes a year back in 2018 to now flipping 21,000 homes most recently in 2021.

It could be Opendoor's growing confidence in its algorithms or investor pressure to keep up equity value in a market downturn or potentially both as the company's inventory and deal sizes have grown significantly.
In 2019, Opendoor had 5,500 homes in their inventory worth a total value of $1.3 billion with an average home value of $233,000.
By 2021, the company had tripled that number in 17,000 homes in its inventory worth a total of $6 billion and an average home value of $358,000.
Opendoor is clearly now targeting higher-value homes in markets to generate profits after proving accuracy on lower-value properties.
Opendoor's gross margins aren't high, but like we said, they don't have to be when you're taking a percentage of a $300,000 transaction.
Despite a flat 5% service fee, the company's gross margin has increased year-over-year from 6% to 9%.
This reinforces that shift in Opendoor's monetization strategy that we covered earlier.
In order to improve their top of funnel and to pull more sellers through the door, Opendoor likely had to lower their service fee to 5%.
It used to be as high as 12%.
Once these sellers get hooked on the cash offer, Opendoor then takes a bigger cut through its repair fees.

But even repair fees have a sane limit, and so it's safer for the company to spread additional fees and disguise its additional margins through various ancillary services like the title, escrow, and mortgage, and not just repair alone.
Despite Opendoor's top-line growth, the company has incurred loss after loss after loss, each bigger than the last.
Even in a strong rebound year in 2021 where the company sold a record number of homes, Opendoor incurred a record loss of over $600 million.

But what's most worrying is that while revenue grew by 3.5 times from 2020 to 2021, its operating expenses also increased by 3.2 times to achieve those numbers, indicating that there's a much more linear business here than what one would expect from a tech company.
The one metric that Opendoor constantly champions to its investors is contribution profit after interest.

And contribution profit after interest takes the final home sale price minus the purchase price, the direct repair costs, holding costs, selling costs, and the interest that's repaid to those senior debt facilities.
Total contribution profit after interest of all the homes sold in a single year grew from $27 million in 2019 to $482 million in 2021.
If we divide this metric by the number of homes sold every year, then we find the unit economics.
In 2019, Opendoor made $5,800 gross profit for every home that was sold.
For every home that was sold in 2021, Opendoor made slightly over $22,000.
If we take Opendoor's total operating expenses in 2021, we add up their advertising, marketing, sales, engineering, legal, and administrative costs and salaries, we get $1.3 billion.
How many homes does Opendoor have to flip at its current unit economics of $22,000 of gross profit for every home sold to offset these operating expenses?
The answer is that Opendoor would need to sell roughly 60,000 homes a year just to break even with how much it costs the company to exist in its current burn rate.
Every time the interest rate goes up a single point, Opendoor needs to sell an additional 2,000 homes in order to offset that additional $40 million in interest expense.

Opendoor's leaders love to pound their chest about how amazing their contribution profit after interest is to investors, but the rub here is that no one's questioning whether there's money to be made in flipping homes.
People have been flipping homes all over the world for decades.
People still flip homes today.

What people are questioning with Opendoor and all these other iBuying companies is that whether or not there's enough money to justify trying to do it at scale with these algorithms, technology, and automation.
The hype that Opendoor generated during its private years ended up attracting competitors and copycats who all wanted a slice of the next big thing in real estate.
Zillow jumped headfirst into the iBuying trend, with the launch of Zillow offers in 2018, proudly predicting that the business could achieve a run rate of $20 billion by 2024.
Redfin followed shortly after with its own home flipping business called Redfin Now.

Zillow had actually invented computer home valuation 15 years ago with Zestimate and the company believed that while they weren't the first mover, they still had the advantage and expertise since they were the pioneers of these algorithms in the first place.
For three years, Zillow spent hundreds of millions of dollars in pure cash buying up homes in Phoenix and Dallas based on its algorithms before things crashed during the pandemic.
The housing market initially froze during the lockdown, then exploded as interest rates were lowered and the economy resumed, but then since have cooled down.

Zillow's algorithm mistakenly continued to assume the market was still hot and overestimated prices, leaving it with a sprawling inventory of homes that they had grossly overpaid for but could only sell at significantly increasing losses.
In a single quarter in 2021, Zillow had lost more than $400 million.

The CEO shut down Zillow offers and terminated its entire home-flipping business division, made a public apology, and laid off 25% of the company's workforce, leaving over 6,000 people without jobs in a looming recession.

To the glee of Keith Raboi, Opendoor, and the Silicon Valley elite, the demise of Zilla offers was validation that these algorithms, machine learnings, and artificial intelligence, the technology was the moat.
And Opendoor's technology was best in class, and the quality of technology can be a competitive advantage in itself.
In the case of Zillow offers, it seems like the folks there just turned on the computer and blindly followed whatever it told them to do.
In the case of Opendoor, they do invest in having local field teams with boots on the ground to regularly validate their algorithms and buy decisions to ensure accuracy before committing the cash.
But while this proves that Opendoor's algorithms are objectively better than Zillow's algorithms, it still doesn't validate if the business model even works at scale.
In the words of Zillow's CEO, the entire instant buying business, quote, looks far more like a leveraged housing trader than a market maker.
What's interesting is that when you look at Offerpad, who is an exact copycat of Opendoor and its biggest remaining direct competitor, their financials are eerily similar.
It's really eerie how identical Opendoor and Offerpad are when you look at their materials, their wording, their content, their value proposition, their pitches, and their presentations.
The only difference is in branding.
One of them is blue and one of them is orange.
While Offerpad also flips homes at scale using its algorithms, the company takes an intentionally slow and picky approach.
Offerpad only buys homes that it has confidence that it can flip in and the company really optimizes for profitability over growth and volume.
When we compare Opendoor and Offerpad unit economics by lining up their contribution profit after interest side by side, both of them are identical at roughly $22,000 per home sold.

While Offerpad sells significantly fewer homes than Opendoor year over year, Offerpad has tightly controlled its cost to achieve a net profit of $6 million in 2021 for a measly 0.31% net profit margin.
While it's encouraging that at least one iBuying company is profitable, it still fails to answer whether or not this entire business model is lucrative enough to justify its own existence.

title: The Dreadful Business of Balding & Hair Loss
note: First-person journey through the hair loss industry, testing each treatment tier (prosthesis, drugs, surgery) with business facts and a personal transplant in Korea.
sections: Three options: nothing, shave, fight back
lines: Balding is a deeply personal and emotional process that 85% of men around the world will experience at some point in their lives.
70% of men will have experienced hair loss by the age of 35.
Male pattern baldness accounts for 95% of cases worldwide and is the most common form of hair loss.
The stages of male pattern baldness are noticeable and predictable.
It starts with hair loss at the temples and thinning hairs at the crown.
Over time, these two areas form a receding M-shaped hairline.
An O-shaped bald spot at the back of the head will then follow and together, both areas will combine into a U-shaped horseshoe balding pattern.
Like Thanos, male pattern baldness is inevitable.
It's a genetic condition that's passed down and typically emerges between the ages of 25 and 35.
For some men, male pattern baldness starts as early as their late teens.
For me, I started balding in my early 20s, and it sucked.

It felt bad to see my hairline recede every day in the mirror, to shed every time I washed my hair, to feel the hair at the crown of my head become thinner and fewer, to fight against the wind from exposing my temples around coworkers, and to hide my progressively large forehead in social outings.
In my early 20s, I'd visit barber after barber before realizing that it wasn't their lack of skill, but instead the fact that I was balding that made it so difficult to style.
I could only ever pull off one type of haircut, a taper comb-over that pulled hair from the sides to cover my temples and receding hairline.
But no matter how hard I tried to downplay or hide my hair loss, I always felt and looked much older than I really was.
The Hamilton-Norwood scale is a measurement system used by doctors to classify the stages of male pattern baldness.
In my early 20s, I was at a stage 2.
After college, I did no favors to my hairline as a new grad, working late nights and weekends at the office to climb up the corporate ladder.
By my mid-20s, I had reached stage 3.
Now in my late 20s and approaching stage 4, I was confronted with three options.
One, I could do nothing.
I could see balding as a way of life and learn to live with hair loss.
Two, I could actively embrace the inevitable, proactively shave my head, and go bald by choice.

Or three, I could fight back and restore my hair loss through prosthesis, medication, and or surgery just like Elon Musk, Gordon Ramsay, Zalzi, Wayne Rooney, Tom Hanks, Nicolas Cage, Van Affleck, Drew Brees, and Antonio Conti.

With so many possible treatments with different degrees of effectiveness and cost, HairLoss is a global billion-dollar market with ties not just into big pharmaceuticals, but also the medical tourism of developed countries like Turkey and South Korea.
While we typically take a sideline analyst perspective on this channel, the reality is that there's only so much one can learn through financials and headlines.

The best way to truly understand a business is to experience it yourself, and as someone who started balding in their early 20s, there's no better candidate to be a test subject, patient and consumer of the hair loss industry than me.

In this episode, we'll navigate the business of balding, the different treatments available, and the companies behind those solutions all through my own personal experience and transformation from medication to hair transplant at a prestigious clinic in South Korea.
When it comes to balding, the easiest treatment is prosthesis.
Wigs and hairpieces are non-invasive, low-risk solutions.
Toupees are the most popular choice of prosthesis for male pattern baldness.
While wigs cover the entirety of one's head, toupees are customized hairpieces that cover only the specific areas of hair loss.
With wigs, you can buy and wear one off the shelf, but toupees by design must be fitted properly to match your scalp, forehead, and hair.
A toupee can costs from $20 to thousands of dollars.
And the more convincing and natural a toupee looks, the more expensive it will be.
The global hair prosthesis industry is a low-value $6 billion market.
China is the world's largest producer, supplying 70% of the world's wigs, hair pieces, hair extensions, and toupees.
Henan Rebecca is the largest producer of wigs and toupees in the world and was the first ever hair prosthesis company to go public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2003.
Henan Rebecca is a timely demonstration of the unsustainable expansion and radical diversification that is so popular with today's Chinese companies.

In less than two decades, the company has gone from manufacturing wigs and toupees to also somehow managing four-star hotels, developing high-rises, buying an entire mountain and converting it into a tourist destination, operating luxury resorts, managing private high schools, mining gold in Africa, running amusement parks, supplying water to municipalities, processing sewage, and providing public transportation.
With so many different businesses wrapped into one company, Hun and Rebecca's finances don't provide a clean look into the business of hair prosthesis.
Common sense would indicate that such a massive business expansion could not have been funded from just selling wigs and hair pieces in the first place.
A cleaner example would be the Hong Kong-based Evergreen products, which is the fifth largest producer of hair prosthesis in the world.
The company has three business lines, wigs and toupees, hair extensions, and Halloween costumes.
If you ever wondered where those crappy costumes at Spirit with the outdated branding and models come from, it likely came from Evergreen.
The US alone accounts for 90% of Evergreen's annual revenue, while wigs and toupees contribute 85% of the company's overall top line.
While Evergreen's wig business has grown over the years with decent 20% gross margins, toupees make up an insignificantly small slice of the pie.
Evergreen's go-to-market strategy has remained consistent in the past decade in targeting women, particularly African-American women, through wholesale to retailers and salons.
In the past five years, male consumers and toupees have never once been mentioned in any company strategy, presentation, or report.
While social acceptance has improved, toupees remain unpopular and niche for balding men.
While production is concentrated in a few overseas suppliers like Evergreen, the actual salons and retailers who fit and sell toupees to end users are mostly local small businesses.
These independent stylists and mom and pops are the ones who bear the cost of marketing, customizing, bidding, educating, and evangelizing toupees to male customers.
customers.
Toupees are a difficult product where procurement requires personalization and trust.
Sellers have to build trust, address the psychological barriers and cost concerns, and customize toupees with customers one at a time in order to close a sale.
While I could order a $20 toupee from Amazon or even a $5 toupee from AliExpress, it's obvious how unrealistic these cheap hairpieces are.
The higher-end toupees in the $200 to to $800 range stand up better to the eye test, but the effort needed to size, fit, glue, style, and maintain just seemed troublesome and illogical.
Toupees have to be regularly maintained as the glue sticking to your scalp will wear off over time.
At least once a month, you have to shave your scalp, apply new glue, spray special products to reduce odors, and reapply the entire toupee to keep hygiene and maintain the illusion.
While there are salons who can do this for you for the price of a high-end haircut, these maintenance costs add up quickly.
Conceptually, a toupee is only valuable if it's convincing to others.
It's a temporary solution and half measure that disguises your baldness to the people around you, but it doesn't actually change the reality that you're balding.
And at some point, whether it's once a night or once a month, I still have to take the toupee off.
Ultimately, I would rather be balding out in the open than to constantly worry about maintaining a perfect illusion or being caught wearing fake hair.
My goal was to find a permanent and sustainable solution to my baldness, not illusions.
The next treatment I explored was medication.
There are only two proven drugs for hair loss, finasteride and minoxidil.
Finasteride is a tablet that you take every day to slow down hair loss.
In its simplest abstraction, there is an enzyme in your body that converts testosterone into DHT.
DHT is the hormone that directly causes hair loss.
Finasteride blocks the actions of that enzyme, which then lowers your body's production of DHT and then significantly slows down the rate at which you lose hair.
Fundamentally, finasteride is a preventative measure.
It slows baldness, but it doesn't stop it entirely.
It also doesn't restore hair that's already been lost.
Finasteride was invented by the American pharmaceutical giant Merck in 1993 and to this day is the most clinically effective drug against male pattern baldness.
Finasteride is just one of many blockbuster drugs in Merck's portfolio.
In 2020, Merck boasted six drugs that each surpassed over $1 billion in annual sales.
The top four being Keytruda, a cancer treatment with sales of $14.3 billion.
The second was Genuvia, a medicine for type 2 diabetes with $5.3 billion.
The third was an HPV vaccine with $3.9 billion.
And the fourth was a chickenpox vaccine with $1.9 billion in sales.
These days, Finasteride is a widely available generic prescription as Merck's patent on the drug expired back in 2013.
But in the 20 years from 1994 to 2013 when Merck's patent was valid, the company held a complete monopoly over hair loss medication.
While Merck didn't break out product sales by medication until 2006, we can see that Finasteride's sales were healthy, contributing nearly $500 million every year.
Keep in mind that you have to take finasteride every day for as long as you don't want to go bald.
While you can always lower the dosage or frequency, people on finasteride are generally on it for life.
It's remarkable that this single drug, with almost half a billion dollars in annual sales, accounted for no more than 2% of Merck's annual revenue over its 20 years of exclusivity.
It's a demonstration of how dominant Merck's pharmaceutical portfolio is in that not even finasteride, at the height of its monopoly, was ever one of the company's top 5 best-selling drugs.
One theory I have as to why Finasteride didn't sell as much for Merck has to do with the US healthcare system.
American health insurance companies like Aetna, Cigna, and Anthem don't consider alopecia, hair loss, or male pattern baldness as a medical condition.
As a result, consumers have to bear the entire cost of any medication or treatment for balding themselves.
During Merck's monopoly in the mid-2000s, a 30-day supply of finasteride cost at least $90.
Nowadays, a 90-day supply of finasteride costs me less than $30.
The second reason for finasteride's commercial underperformance, again relative to other drugs in Merck's portfolio, has to do with its troubling side effects and dark history.
With lower testosterone in your body, finasteride introduces potential side effects like decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, impotence, and male infertility.

While Merck insists that finasteride is totally safe and that these side effects only ever appeared in less than 4% of patients, the reality is that even 1% chance of decreased libido and impotence is still 1% too high for many men.
This potential gamble on your masculinity for the sake of appearance is why finasteride remains so controversial.
There's no shortage of horror stories from men who experienced the side effects and had difficulty shaking them off even after stopping the medication.
There's also many success stories from men on finasteride who downplayed the side effects and insist that the bad experiences are exaggerations, fear-mongering, or placebo.
In 2016, hundreds of men who took finasteride filed lawsuits against Merck, alleging that the pharmaceutical giant knowingly hid these side effects to keep sales up.
They accused Merck of bringing an unsafe drug to market and manipulating the trial data to downplay the risks.

Merck ended up settling most of these lawsuits out of court with hush money payments of $5,000 to $10,000 while successfully sealing away all the clinical data, dispositions, and confidential information away from public records.

This was a win for Merck and another timeless demonstration of the immoral behavior, shady cover-ups, and the pay-your-way-out-of-trouble corporate capitalism that big pharmaceutical companies thrive in.
These days, there are less than 25 lawsuits still pending against Merck.

The individuals and families behind these lawsuits have organized themselves into the Post Finasteride Syndrome Foundation, a non-profit dedicated to exposing all the internal secrets that Merck has buried over the years about the drug.

Given that Merck spends at least $10 million every year on lobbying, which by the way is only the amount we can find in public records, and the American healthcare system doesn't recognize balding as a real medical condition, it's no surprise that these lawsuits have been stuck in limbo for years and remain low on the list of FDA priorities.
When I pressed my dermatologist on the risks of finasteride, she unsurprisingly downplayed the side effects, claiming that none of her patients had ever experienced any.
In the same breath, she tried to sell me non-FDA approved natural herbal supplements that she claimed were just as effective as finasteride.
Putting aside my dermatologist's shilling, her questionable morals, and Merck's unethical behavior, I eventually took the plunge on finasteride after being on the fence for weeks.
Elon Musk, Gordon Ramsay, and the many other celebrities who went from bald domes to full heads of hair are all on finasteride.
