If these billionaires couldn't figure out a better, safer, anti-balding medication for themselves, then at least I can take some comfort knowing that this is the best boat available today and that we're all riding in it together.
My experience four months in on finasteride has been a net positive.
My hair loss has significantly slowed.
Before Finasteride, any time I ran my fingers through my hair, my palms would be covered with clumps of hair falling out.
On Finasteride, this same motion only removes a few individual strands of my hair at most.
As for side effects, there's no change in my libido, nor have I experienced anything close to impotence.
But it does take more conscious effort for me to get in the mood in the bedroom.
As an unexpected positive, I actually no longer wake up with the same aggressive energy or raging masculine temper that I used to have in my mid-20s.
Perhaps this is placebo, but I'm tempted to chalk it up to the lower testosterone in my system.
While the first few days on finasteride were a little nerve-wracking, I've gotten more comfortable with it over time.
Like many others, I've experimented with reducing doses to find the right balance for myself between hair loss prevention and lower testosterone.
The other anti-balding drug is minoxidil, or more commonly known as Rogaine.
It's a medication that you apply to your scalp every day through foam and ointment in order to stimulate hair growth.
However, Minoxidil's effectiveness is modest at best.
Since Minoxidil is a local treatment for your scalp, it doesn't target the hormones in your body that directly cause hair loss the same way Finasteride does.
While some men opt for both Finasteride and Minoxidil as a comprehensive solution to hair loss, I personally have only stuck to Finasteride.
My perspective is that it's easier to maintain hair than it is to regrow it.

Finasteride is a guaranteed preventative measure, while Minoxidil is an inconclusive reactive measure where hair regrowth itself is not guaranteed, it takes months to see results, and is yet another drug where as soon as you stop taking it, everything goes away.
Having already signed onto one lifelong drug with finasteride, I've been hesitant to add another to the list.
Surgery is a last treatment option and is widely considered to be the most effective, long-lasting, yet invasive and expensive solution for male pattern baldness.
Hair transplants are by definition invasive surgeries, meaning there's a puncturing of skin, open wounds, and a recovery period involved.
With finasteride and minoxidil, progress is noticeable only after months of continuous use and it comes with its aforementioned risks.
In comparison, a one-time 4-10 hour hair transplant in exchange for a clearly defined, visible, immediate, and improved end state is a great ROI compared to prosthesis or medication.
As someone in their late 20s, I wanted to tackle my male pattern baldness as early as possible and had plenty of healthy hairs at the back of my head to donate for a transplant.
Hair transplants are simple procedures.
A surgeon relocates healthy hair from the areas of your head where you have lots of it, typically the back or the sides of your head, to the areas where you don't have hair.
It takes 9-12 months for the newly planted hair follicles to grow fully and not every hair that's transplanted over will survive the journey.
A hair transplant in its simplest form is a permanent rearrangement of the hair on your head.
There are two types of hair transplants.
The only difference between these two is how the hair is extracted and harvested from the donor area.
FUT stands for Follicular Unit Transportation.
The surgeon cuts out an entire piece of your scalp, closes the incision with stitches, and then separates that piece of scalp into smaller pieces called grafts.
Grafts contain 1-4 hairs, their follicles, along with the surrounding skin tissue that provides the nourishments for those hairs to grow.
The surgeon will then make small holes in your bald recipient areas and insert the grafts one at a time.
FUT is the most traditional form of hair transplant and can take 10-20 hours depending on the number of grafts.
A single hair transplant can involve anywhere from 600 to 5000 grafts depending on the health of the donor area, the severity of the hair loss, and the size of the recipient areas.
FUT results in slightly higher yield but is overall more invasive, requires a longer recovery period and leaves permanent scarring.
FUE, the other type of hair transplant, stands for follicular unit extraction.
Instead of cutting out and transporting a piece of your scalp, a surgeon meticulously extracts hair follicles one at a time from your donor area.
The harvested grafts are then planted one by one into the recipient areas.
FUE is the more popular form of hair transplant as it's easier, less invasive, faster, and more affordable.
FUE surgeries can be completed in 4-8 hours with no scars or stitches involved.
While I personally never wanted to take finasteride, the drug is required for successful long-lasting hair transplants.
A hair transplant restores hair in bald areas, but it doesn't do anything for your existing hair.
If you got a hair transplant, but you didn't slow down your hair loss through finasteride, you would end up with a tail of two heads.
In the front, you would have healthy hair growing out, but in the back you would be balding, shedding, and losing hair, so you would see Moses parting the seas on your scalp.
Getting a hair transplant in the West is expensive.
Reputable clinics in the United States and Canada can cost anywhere from $10,000 to $25,000 for a single hair transplant.
While one has the freedom to stop and start medication whenever they want, hair transplants are generally one-and-done surgeries.
There's a finite amount of hairs that can be harvested and the hairs that are extracted from the donor areas will never grow back.
While the surgical methods and tools are consistent around the world, hair transplants are more art than science.
It takes skill and experience to transplant hairs in a natural manner and construct new hairlines that align with one's forehead, facial features, and face shape.
How the new hairs are specifically arranged is critical to the final result.
A bad hair transplant can lead to infections, inconsistent growth, and unconvincing appearances.
As a less invasive and more cost efficient procedure, I settled on FUE for my hair transplant and began looking overseas.
Shelling out $10,000 to $25,000 up front for a hair transplant in the United States was out of my budget.
Because of how cost prohibitive these hair transplants are in the West, I had a lot of open concerns on how much these doctors really had when they only perform a handful of surgeries every month.
Turkey, Mexico, and Spain came up as a popular medical tourism destination for hair transplants that cost only $2,000 to $5,000.

Many clinics in these countries advertise their all-in-one packages where they take care of not only the surgery, but also the hotel, itinerary, transportation, translation, and even drop you off back to your flight to the US 24 hours after the surgery.

While these package deals are convenient, what I was really after was a highly skilled surgeon with a great track record and whose customers were local and not Americans and foreigners looking to save a quick buck.
South Korea is the cosmetic surgery capital of the world.
In this land of K-pop, K-dramas, and parasite, cosmetic surgery is a way of life.

The country performs over 1 million cosmetic surgeries every year and has the highest per capita rate of cosmetic surgery in the world, with 14 out of every 1,000 Koreans going under the knife every year.
The beauty ideals and standards in Korea are so high that it's normal for celebrities, celebrities, singers, and other public icons to undergo multiple surgeries as early as their teenage years.
A friend of mine who grew up in Korea offered me the name of several clinics that many locals considered to be the best in the country.
One of them was Dr.
Kim Kyung-bok of Moment Clinic, a celebrated surgeon who rose to local prominence after having performed a successful hair transplant for celebrities.
Dr.
Kim was so popular that there was a waiting list for his new clinic in Gangnam.
Gangnam is the wealthiest neighborhood in South Korea and known as the Beverly Hills of the country with the highest concentration of cosmetic surgery clinics in its 15-mile borders.
Dr.
Kim and his Moment clinic are so oriented for local Koreans that they don't actually have any English-speaking staff on hand.
For every conversation I had with his clinic over KowKowTalk, which is Korea's equivalent of Facebook Messenger, I had to use Google Translate.
While I went through multiple virtual consultations with different clinics and doctors in Korea, it was Dr.
Kim's professionalism, detail, his local popularity, and his body of work that sealed the deal for me.
I flew out to Korea in mid-July for my hair transplant with Dr.
Kim.
As a first-time visitor to South Korea, I was blown away with the maturity and government sponsorship behind the country's medical tourism.
When you land at Incheon Airport and walk towards Arrivals, the largest booth at the center of the lobby is not a generic information desk, but rather a huge medical tourism support center.
There's staff on hand who can speak English, Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese, French, French, German, and they're all hired by the Korean government to facilitate medical tourists like me.
Walking through the streets of Gangnam to Moment Clinic on the day of my surgery was equally eye-opening.

In just four blocks from the subway station, I had passed nearly 20 different plastic surgery clinics, doctor offices, and pharmacies, each with signs in Korean promoting their services and success stories to locals.
Located on the sixth floor, Moment Clinic was a clean, modern, new, and sophisticated office.
And as I had expected, Dr.
Kim was a gracious, soft-spoken, and kind man.

While he spoke very little English, he made every effort to communicate his approach, detail, and vision, using a pen to draw out my new proposed hairline and the exact areas he felt would be most effective.
Looking back, as a very nervous American in a foreign country, I'm most grateful for Dr.
Kim's empathy as he would regularly pause to listen and hear my feedback through the translator.
At one point, he even redrew the lines during consultation after I shared some suggestions and perspective.
Surgery started right after the consultation.
As they put in the IV, I was a pretty anxious mess, shaking on the operating table.
I'd never done any surgery like this before, and hair transplants rely on local anesthesia, so I was awake and conscious the entire time.
The surgery was an exercise of patience, lying down without moving for roughly 6 hours while he and his staff of 5 nurses operated on me.
Even though Dr.
Kim didn't see many foreigners, he made a lot of small gestures like intentionally playing an American radio station during the surgery so I would feel comfortable.
What amazes me to this day was the staff discipline during my six hours of surgery.
Beyond one or two words here or there, there was no chatter or gossip, just six hours of silent concentration, music, and surgical noises.
The whole time my face was covered with an eye mask and bandages, so at no point did I see or feel anything.
Extraction of my hairs took about 3.5 hours, and then planting the hairs took another 2.5 hours.
For around 4,300 grafts, my total cost for this hair transplant with Dr.
Kim came to $5,500, which was payable with Visa.

title: Buy Now, Pay Later: Echoes of the 2008 Recession
note: Explainer essay with a personal first-person test-loan segment; thesis plus a mid-film reveal that the sector loses money, closing on the subprime parallel and regulation. Transcript cuts off near the end.
sections: What BNPL is and its scale
History of debt and payment plans
How Affirm, Klarna and Afterpay compare, with the host's test loans
They all lose money: scale and revenue streams
How the loans are financed via partner banks
Regulation and human nature, West vs China
lines: Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay In just five years, these three companies have popularized a new form of consumer spending called Buy Now, Pay Later.

Buy Now, Pay Later is a type of short-term, unsecured personal loan where instead of paying the full price upfront at checkout, you can defer the cost of any item by splitting the payment into smaller installments over time.
If you want to spread out payments over a longer period of time to make the installments even smaller, you'll have to pay interest.
And if you miss a payment using buy now, pay later, there are penalties with late fees, collections, and lowered credit score.
The concept of debt and payment plans have been around for centuries.
America itself was founded on buy now, pay later.
In the 1600s, the pilgrims borrowed money from lenders in London to pay for their voyage to the New World.
The pilgrims agreed to a long-term loan with a payment plan of four annual installments.
While the pilgrims didn't have to put up any collateral, most ended up dying upon reaching America, so you could say they repaid with their lives.
Examples of long-term consumer loans these days are mortgages and car loans.
If you miss enough payments, the lender will repossess your vehicle or home through foreclosure.
In the 1800s, during the Second Industrial Revolution, short-term personal loans became popular with Americans.
Furniture, farming equipment, and sewing machines were investments that were only affordable when paid in installments.
These days, short-term consumer loans are typically offered only by select businesses for large, infrequent one-time essentials like furniture or appliances.
These loans are generally unsecured and based on your trustworthiness as a borrower, which is measured by your credit score.
If you miss enough payments, the lender will penalize you with interest, fees, and collections.
What Klarna, Affirm, and Afterpay have done is they've broadened the purpose of short-term unsecured personal loans from large, one-time essentials into everyday impulse and splurge purchases.

They've made it easy for anyone to borrow money, simplifying a historically opaque, time-consuming process of applications and manual underwriting into a scalable user experience that provides instant credit in just a few taps.
apps.
With Buy Now Pay Later, you can afford just about everything you desire by splitting costs into as many tiny payments as you want.
Most of all, there's instant gratification.
When using Affirm, Parna, or Afterpay, you can get your order delivered right away on or before your first payment.
In 2020, Buy Now Pay Later accounted for $97 billion, or 2% of the $4.6 trillion that was spent on e-commerce around the world.
In 2021, Affirm, Farm, Klarna, and Afterpay together boasted over 173 million global active customers.
These days, 4 in every 5 Americans use Buy Now Pay Later on everything from clothing and groceries to gifts and cleaning supplies.
Even though the valuations of Affirm and Klarna have been pummeled in recent months, Buy Now Pay Later seems here to stay even if it doesn't make much business sense.
While no one knows if Buy Now Pay Later is even profitable, companies don't want to miss out.
Fintech has a terrible track record when it comes to both idea and execution, like blockchain, peer-to-peer lending, and equity crowdfunding.
Yet companies are always eager to jump on fintech bandwagons before the wheels are even placed.
Scared of losing their duopoly, Visa and Mastercard have jumped headfirst into buy now pay later.
PayPal and Stripe have launched their own products, Chase and Citibank have thrown their hats in, and even Apple and Samsung have joined the party.
Putting aside fundamentals, Buy Now Pay Later itself is controversial.
To critics and regulators around the world, it promotes irresponsible spending and enables overconsumption.
In this episode, we'll explore the business model of Buy Now Pay Later, its eerie similarities to the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, and why that matters now more than ever in the coming recession.
First, we have to understand the three core trends that have led to the emergence and rapid growth of Buy Now Pay Later.
These three trends are connected to one another.
The growth of e-commerce, the decline of credit cards, and high customer acquisition costs.
E-commerce boasts an exceptional runway as only 14% of global retail sales today take place online, while the remaining 86% still occurs offline in old-fashioned stores.
But with the death of shopping malls, brands see the writing on the wall for retail.
While boomers continue to dominate consumer spending, millennials have surpassed boomers as the largest living adult generation.
Millennials are now coming of age, having children, and will soon hold the reins to the economy.
Retailers know that if they are to thrive, they have to nail this handoff and adapt to the consumption preferences of each generation before they peak.
Millennials and Zoomers are ecommerce power users, with over 70% preferring the convenience, flexibility, and selection of online shopping.
In response, retailers continue to optimize every pixel of their ecommerce strategy, from storefront redesigns and load times to order fulfillment and checkout experiences.
While e-commerce is the feature venue where consumers will go to buy things, how consumers spend is also changing with the generations.
Traditional banks like Wells Fargo, Citi, and Chase are seen by millennials and Zoomers as untrustworthy and incompetent.
And there's good reason for this.
Look up any major bank today and you'll find fraud, laundering, manipulation, bribery, and corruption charges spanning decades that have been shrugged off with slap-on-the-wrist fines.
Combined with a poor consumer experience, it's no surprise that younger generations would rather take their chances banking with fintech startups over entrenched banks.

This lack of trust in traditional banking institutions has driven consumer interest and adoption of fintech, from online banking in SoFi and Chime, to buy now pay later in Affirm, Varna, and Afterpay.
It's not just the immoral behavior of banks, but also the legacy system in which these institutions operate that turn off younger generations.
Accessing and building credit is difficult.

When we started our food delivery business as 20-year-olds back in 2014, there was only one bank in town that allowed us to open a business account without fees and gave us a useless credit line of $200.
We rotated buying gas every other week just to make that credit card work.
When I graduated with Stable Employment, it took 2 months just to get approved for the Chase Sapphire Reserve card.
While my income has grown and my credit score is just below 800, my credit lines have barely increased, despite never missing a payment or carrying a balance.
If I request an increase, Chase will do a hard inquiry, and my credit score will go down, so I have no option but to wait and hope my credit rises in the future.
If I ever carry over purchases on my card, I'll get slammed with 19% interest.
This interest is compounded daily, so every day the balance carries over, I pay interest on both the owed balance and the accrued interest.
And if I ever miss a payment, there's a $40 late fee.
Credit card penalties are punishing by design to get people to repay as soon as possible.
Banks make billions of dollars annually from credit card interest.
The more credit card holders borrow beyond their means, the higher balance they carry over every month, the more compound interest they have to pay, and the greater the profits are for these banks.
In 2019, consumers paid out $121 billion in credit card interest, and as of August 2022, Americans owe nearly a trillion dollars in credit card debt.
Length of credit history also makes it difficult for young people to acquire and grow credit.
How long you've had your credit plays a significant role in determining your trustworthiness.
If you haven't had your credit cards for 8-plus years, the system automatically penalizes you for not having long enough history as a borrower.
Yet because credit history is a function of time, there's little that millennials and zoomers can do except to wait.
The only other alternative is debit cards, which are inflexible as your buying power is limited to how much you have in the bank, which for most people starting out is not a lot.

Because of the restrictive nature of the legacy credit system, how difficult it is to access and grow credit, the unforgiving penalties of delinquency and constrained buying power, younger generations are turning away from cards and looking for better purchasing tools when it comes to spending and fulfilling consumption desires.
As more and more consumer brands flock to e-commerce, the costs to acquire and convert customers are rising.
With greater noise and limited ad space in both digital and physical channels, it's increasingly expensive for retailers to attract, convert, and retain customers in websites and stores.
As a result, more retailers are forced to use discounts or promotions to drive traffic, improve conversions, reduce abandoned carts, and make their products more affordable.
But discounts have a finite runway and hurt brand positioning, and at the end of the day, retailers just want to sell and move as much product as possible off their shelves.
For simplicity and peace of mind, they only deal with customers who can pay for their products.

For customers at the edge who don't want or can't pay the full price upfront, the overhead of financing, underwriting, managing payment plans, and collecting installments is beyond the means and capacity of most retailers.

It's the shift away from cards, the appetite for better tools that enable greater purchasing power, the acceptance of fintech startups over traditional financial institutions, combined with the e-commerce gold rush, increasing customer acquisition costs, and the pressure to grow sales without discounts that have made Buy Now Pay Later so popular with both consumers and retailers around the world in such a short period of time.
Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay are the three big Buy Now Pay Later players who see themselves as modern, consumer-friendly successors to traditional credit cards and their predatory legacy system.
When we compare these three companies, it's uncanny how similar they are to each other in messaging and products.
They all position themselves as honest lenders committed to responsible spending.
They downplay the money they make from interest or late fees.
They talk up their retailers and user growth.
They boast about their proprietary machine learning algorithms that can underwrite, assess risk, protect against fraud, and grant credit instantaneously to individuals of all backgrounds.
All three companies point to their low default rates, how buy now pay later loans are smaller and less risky than credit cards, and their healthy customer mix of prime and subprime borrowers.
The products and user experience between Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay are identical.
They all actively funnel their users to a mobile app for maximum engagement and retention through push notifications.
Their apps serve as centralized shopping portals that aggregate retailers, overlay over website checkouts, and manage loan payments.
Rather than using your email or Facebook account, these companies tie your identity and loans into something far more personal and static, your cell phone number.
And they all offer savings accounts where you can deposit cash and earn interest at higher rates than in traditional bank accounts.
Creating an account was easy and took me two to three minutes at most.
Affirm was the strictest and asked for my social security number and photo, while Klarna and Afterpay only needed my name, phone number, address, and birth date.

With a credit score slightly below 800, Affirm gave me an opening limit of $500, dollars, teasing that it could quickly go up to $5,000 if I proved myself first on smaller purchases and on-time payments.
Afterpay and Klarna were more generous, granting me the ability to borrow up to $1,000 immediately upon account creation.

If I could contextualize just how easy it was to create an account and suddenly be able to borrow thousands of dollars within minutes, it really takes far more steps, effort, and time to do an online wire transfer or schedule an appointment at the DMV.
Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay offer the same core product that they call Pay-in-4.
With this type of loan, you can flexibly split the cost of any purchase into four equal interest-free payments due every two weeks.
If you want even smaller installments for a longer period of time, up to 36 months, that's when you'll have to pay interest.
The interest rate varies and reflects how trustworthy the company deems you to be as a borrower.
The consumer advantage that these companies advertise is their transparency in charging simple interest on their loans and not the punishing compound interest of credit cards.
Pay-in-for is Buy Now Pay Later's claim to fame and most popular loan type amongst consumers.
As long as you pay off each installment in full, on time, every two weeks, you've won flexibility at no added cost.

With Pay-in-for, consumers have paid the exact same price that they would have had they charged the entire thing to their credit card, the only difference being the cost is spread across six weeks versus one day.
Since consumers can sign up, borrow, and combine as many loans as possible from Affirm, Afterpay, and Klarna for maximum spending power, the differentiation between all three lies in their retailers.
Exclusivity is the name of the game.
Retailers tend to partner with only one buy now pay later company at a time.
As a result, Affirm, Afterpay, and Klarna are in an arms race to sign as many reputable retailers as possible.
While Affirm has Amazon, Peloton, and Walmart, Parna has Lululemon, H &M, Nike, Saks Fifth Avenue, Wayfair, Sephora, and Afterpay has Nordstrom, Adidas, Gap, Tory Burch, and Bed Bath & Beyond.
Their pitches to retailers are identical.

Let us be your exclusive buy now pay later option, and you'll grow your customer base, accelerate revenue, revenue, increase order sizes, and open up your business to high LTV customers who will literally borrow money just to buy your products.
In the simplest abstraction, buy now pay later companies are loan brokers building their own marketplace of consumers and retailers.
Without high profile retailers, there would be no desirable products.
Without desirability, there would be no demand and then no consumer appetite to borrow money to buy products.

Every time someone buys something with buy now pay later, regardless of whether it's split into four zero-interest installments or 12-month installments with interest, whether or not the consumer has repaid their loan or runs off halfway through, the retailer still immediately recognizes the sale at full price upon checkout.
To the retailer, a sale with buy now pay later is the exact same gross transaction as if that person had paid with card or cash.
Since retailers are paid in full immediately after each sale, they are never exposed to the loan risk or details.
Affirm, Parna, and Afterpay are left to collect and carry the bag in the event of a default.
To demonstrate the arms race and the psychology of buy now pay later, I took out loans to buy two luxury products I had always liked but always felt were overpriced.
The first was a Dyson Airwrap.
Awesome company, innovative engineering, but a $600 hairdryer is nowhere on my list of needs.
The second was a pair of common projects.
Classic, minimalist, white leather low tops.
But $400 for a pair of sneakers is just wasteful.
Dyson has exclusively partnered with Affirm, meaning the only way to buy now, pay later any Dyson product would be through Affirm.
While my loan limit was only $500 to start, Affirm re-ran my profile and instantly allowed me to borrow up to $5,000 just for Dyson products.
I got to choose between three payment plans, Pay-in-3, Pay-in-6, or Pay-in-12, with the first two being zero interest options.
A firm clearly didn't trust me, so they limited my payment options to debit with no credit card allowed.
Eager to pay off this loan as soon as possible, I chose Pay-in-3.
And even though I paid nothing at checkout and my first payment wasn't due until 30 days later, there was instant gratification.
Dyson shipped me my $650 order the very next day, giving me immediate ownership and basically an entire month to use the product for free.
Common Projects was interesting as many retailers carry their shoes, so there is no retailer level exclusivity.
I first went with Farfetch, who had partnered with Klarna.
Even though Klarna tells me that I'm approved to borrow up to $1000, they continually declined to approve my $400 order with no explanation.
Since Klarna and Farfetch were dead ends, I looked for another retailer with a different Buy Now Pay Later option.
Nordstrom had partnered with Afterpay, and I could feel the psychology of Buy Now Pay Later creeping in just by looking at the Pay In For plan.
$400 for a pair of white sneakers to me is too much, but with Buy Now Pay Later, it's not $400, it's $90 every two weeks.
I can afford to burn $90 every two weeks.
That's like two runs to the grocery store.
What a cheap shoe.
Even nicer was that Afterpay let me pay with my credit card.
That means every installment is posted to my credit card every two weeks, but I only really pay every four weeks when my credit card statement arrives.
In less than 10 minutes, I had borrowed $1,000 to buy two luxury products that I didn't need.

The ease of getting these loans and the small installments had diluted my brain, warping my personal budgeting and spending habits into a deceivingly liberating, seductive adventure where buying luxury goods suddenly felt more affordable than a meal at Five Guys or Shake Shack.
It's a test of self-control to not buy now pay later more frequently, especially when there's a strong incentive to continue this kind of spending.
The more I pay back, the more loans I can take out, and the more money I can borrow for future purchases, and then the more expensive items I can quote-unquote afford.
Luxury purchases are the last thing I should be buying these days with the coming recession.
Unlike a $400 pair of common projects, a $650 Dyson hairdryer, and everything else I could buy now pay later, what I really should be doing is investing.
While the moat is supply-side exclusivity, Klarna, Affirm, and Afterpay are all fundamentally the same business, from messaging and marketing down to the products and roadmap.
While they operate at different scales, these three companies share one last defining key characteristic.
They all lose money.
What money is there to make in being a broker of short-term unsecured personal loans?

When the most popular buy now pay later option is an interest-free loan where consumers are just splitting the exact same retail cost of the product into four installments, what profit is there for Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay?
How much of their business is centered around the late fees and interest that they claim to not profit from?
And what is the end game for buy now pay later companies.
In recent months, the big three, Klarna, Affirm, and Afterpay, have gone from a high-flying oligopoly to a shell of their former selves.
Afterpay was acquired by Square in late 2021 at the peak of the buy now pay later hype for $29 billion.
Klarna, who was preparing to IPO at $50 billion, was forced to scrap those plans since the market crash.
Klarna ended up raising a massive downrun at $7 billion, a massive 80% drop from its $45 billion valuation just one year ago.
Affirm remains as the only standalone public buy now pay later company.
When it comes to scale, Klarna is the largest.
In 2021, consumers took out loans with Klarna to buy over $80 billion worth of products.
In comparison, Afterpay users bought out over $22 billion worth of merchandise, and Affirm users transacted a little over $8 billion.
Klarna has the largest global presence, available in 45 countries today, while Afterpay is in nine, and Affirm operates only in the US and Canada.
In 2021, Klarna had 145 million active customers, defined as someone who has taken out at least one loan that year.
Afterpay had 16 million customers, and Affirm was the smallest, at 7 million customers.
Even with their most recent report of 14 million customers in 2022, Affirm is still the smallest of the big three when it comes to the user base.
Klarna leads the arms race, with over 400,000 retailers signed to their platform.
Affirm is second with 235,000, and Afterpay is last with 98,000.
Like Diplomacy, where these companies started out has had a major influence on their expansion.

While the Sweden-based Klarna has the largest presence in Europe, and the Australia-based Afterpay has the most customers in Asia-Pacific, the golden goose that all buy-now-pay-later companies chase is North America.
Americans consume more than anyone else, and the United States is the world's largest retail market, accounting for 25% of global retail sales.
So while Affirm operates only in the US and Canada, their top line has quickly grown thanks to their backyard advantage.
In the past three years, Affirm has grown at insane rates to surpass Afterpay and catch up to Klarna.
While Klarna has not yet reported their 2022 results, it's likely that they will continue to lead with the highest total revenue, but Affirm is certainly closing in.
Since Affirm is the only standalone public company, its financials and disclosures provide us with the cleanest look into the business model of buy now, pay later.
Affirm today has five main revenue streams—interest income, merchant fees, virtual card fees, loan sales, and servicing income.
Late fees don't exist in their top line, as Affirm is the only company out of the big three with the policy of never charging late fees if consumers miss a payment.
When we plot these revenue streams over the past four years, we can see the maturity and evolution of Affirm's business model.
Let's start with merchant fees and interest income.
Affirm takes a cut from the retailer, for each sale made on its platform, just like a commission.
While Affirm reportedly takes 2-5% of each sale, each retailer ultimately negotiates their own arrangement.
The nuance here is that the merchant fees are generally not flat rate commissions.
The percentage taken of each sale also depends on the type of loan that the customer chooses.
Affirm generally takes a greater cut with zero interest loans.
Let's take my $650 Dyson loan.

If we assume that Affirm agreed to a baseline commission at 2% in exchange for Dyson's exclusivity, since I opted for a zero interest loan, it's possible that a firm earned a higher commission for my order at 3%.

Since retailers already pay 1-3% of their sales to a credit card processor for any regular in-store or online sale, giving up a few more points may feel like a fair exchange for closing a sale that would not have otherwise occurred without Buy Now, Pay Later.
Interest income is the money that users pay for all the simple interest loans they take out.
This is the flywheel that Buy Now, Pay Later businesses aim for.

The more retailers on their platform, the more desirable the products, the greater the intent to borrow, the more users that will come, the more loans that are issued, and the greater subset of users who will opt for interest-bearing loans, and the more interest and commission the company then makes.
And if they charge late fees like Afterpay and Klarna, then late fees can be a whole other revenue stream.
volume.

With growing user base, purchasing power, and transaction volume, the endgame for buy-now-pay-later companies is to gain leverage, demand higher commission, and grab a bigger slice of the pie for themselves.
Merchant fees and interest income are the two largest revenue streams for a firm, together contributing on average 85% of the company's annual revenue.
Over the past four years, interest income has quintupled for a firm, going from $120 million in 2019 to $530 million in 2022.
Merchant fees have quadrupled from $132 million to over $450 million.
This 4-5x growth in interest income and merchant fees is backed by the linear growth in a firm's users and merchandise volume, which both have increased 7x in the same period.
When we look at the top line for Afterpay and Klarna, we can see this same flywheel in effect.
For Klarna, interest income and merchant fees are also their largest revenue streams, accounting for on average 98% of annual revenue for the past three years.
Interest income has grown 30%, from $232 million in 2019 to $303 million in 2021.
Klarna has more than doubled its earnings from merchant fees, going from $438 million to $973 million.
Afterpay is unique in that they exclusively offer only interest-free loans.
So Afterpay makes up for this lost interest income by charging retailers higher commission in the 4-6% range and fining customers heavier late fees.

Merchant fees alone are Afterpay's primary income stream, accounting for nearly 82% of the company's annual revenue for the past three years, and then in 2021, contributing nearly 90% of the company's revenue.

Afterpay's merchant fees have quadrupled from $200 million to $800 million in a direct, linear relationship with merchandise value and customers, both of which have also quadrupled in the past three years.
Late fees play a bigger role and represent 13% of revenue, doubling from $46 million in 2019 to $90 million in 2021.
The expensive, never-ending zero-sum arms race for retailers appears to be coming to an end.
Affirm and Klarna have both launched digital debit cards where consumers are no longer limited to the retailers on the platform and can now buy now pay later just about anywhere.
Consumers generate these one-time virtual cards for each purchase, load on a loan amount just like a prepaid balance on a gift card, and can pay at any online or physical store that accepts Visa.
Any purchase charged on a virtual card is automatically converted into a loan and split into multiple installments, even if the retailer doesn't support buy now pay later.
In these cases, a firm earns a portion of the credit card processing fee that the retailer normally pays out to be able to accept cards in the first place.
Virtual card revenue has become a steady top-line contributor for a firm, growing from $7 million to $100 million in four years, representing 7% of overall revenue in 2022.
While the Big Three's business performance validates both the concept and network effects of the buy-now-pay-later flywheel, the reality is that the economics are simply not sustainable.
Merchant fees, simple interest, and late fees combined are just not enough for buy-now-pay-later companies to sustain themselves.
A firm has lost over a billion dollars in the past four years, snowballing from $127 million in 2019 to nearly $900 million of losses in 2022.
too.
Klarna is not far behind with an operating loss of $600 million, while Afterpay is $200 million in the red based on their combined 2021 results.
There's an argument to be made here that if a firm and Klarna both charge daily compound interest instead of simple interest, their paths to profitability would be significantly easier.

It's easy for buy-now-pay-later companies to romanticize themselves as disruptors of a predatory system, but ultimately your business has to last and be sustainable in order to truly disrupt something.
While simple interest is consumer-friendly, it doesn't keep the lights on.
To demonstrate, we can revisit my two loans.
A firm offered me a 12-month simple interest loan at 24% APR for my $400 common projects.
The company would have made over $50 in interest income.
Under daily compound interest, a firm would have earned over $100 or double in interest income.
For my $650 Dyson loan, a firm would have made around $90 in interest from a 12-month loan at 24% APR.
They would have earned twice as much with daily compound interest.

Under this abstraction, if any of these buy now pay later companies earned double their interest income by charging daily compound interest over simple interest, these companies would all be profitable today or very close to it.
At the same time, Affirm and Klarna would certainly not have so many customers if their loans had daily compound interest, so this is more of a thought experiment than a foregone conclusion.
The reason why merchant fees, simple interest, and late fees are not enough has to do with how buy now pay later loans are financed.
Whenever you place an item in a cart, select buy now pay later for payment, and click checkout, you always wait a minute or so before the next page loads.
While you might think that the loading is just the retailer processing your order on their backend, what's really happening is that your order is also serving as a loan application.
Every time you try to buy something with Buy Now Pay Later, you're effectively applying for a loan of that amount with Affirm, Klarna, or Afterpay.
Each loan application is reviewed and underwritten by each company's algorithms, which then spit out an automated decision.
These algorithms can reject your application for any reason, just like when Klarna declined to approve my purchase on Farfetch.
When they do approve your loan, you choose your preferred terms, and then you end up with your loan.
But that loan is funded and issued not by the Buy Now Pay Later company, but instead from a traditional bank that they partnered with.
In the case of my Dyson purchase with Affirm, that $650 loan was funded and issued by Cross River Bank.
Nearly 80% of Affirm's loans in 2022 were funded and issued by this Jersey-based community bank.
Afterpay loans are funded and issued by New Zealand, Citibank, and National Australia Bank.
Parnas loans in the US come from the Utah-based web bank.
Buy now pay later companies basically borrow money from the bank so that you can borrow money from them to buy the things that you want.
This transfer of debt, or robbing Peter to pay Paul, is not a new practice in the world of finance, but it's the details that are so spicy.
In the case of my Dyson purchase, a firm's algorithms performed the underwriting and approved my loan application.
Cross River Bank doesn't perform any underwriting of its own, they fully trust the decision that's made by Affirm, and then they fund my $650 loan from its own cash.
Assuming in our example that Affirm's cut is 3%, CrossRiver Bank distributes $630 to Dyson as the sale amount net of merchant fees and then sends the remaining $20 to Affirm as commission.
CrossRiver Bank now has a $650 loan in its records.
As a customer, however, I owe $650 to Affirm and not CrossRiver Bank.
This is because Affirm is contractually bound to purchase and take ownership of this loan from the bank within days of its creation.
The bank didn't perform the underwriting or have any exposure to me as a borrower, so they don't want to hold on to my loan any longer than necessary.

But since Cross River Bank is the one who makes this entire transaction possible, they naturally want to be compensated for fronting the cash, funding the loan, and distributing payments to all parties.
So after a few days, a firm takes over the $650 loan by purchasing the loan at face value and and paying an origination fee to the bank for their troubles.
The installments that I pay as a customer then go directly to Affirm so that they can make whole.
If I don't pay, then Affirm comes chasing after me so they can get their money back from this loan.

These are the behind-the-scenes transactions that take place between traditional banks and buy now pay later companies that made my $400 sneaker loan possible and supports every single purchase that's made every day and every hour by customers using Klarna, Affirm, or Afterpay.
The reality is that with these funding arrangements, Affirm and Buy Now Pay Later companies actually lose money on zero interest loans.

With no interest to collect and inclusive of the origination fee, the purchase price that Affirm, Klarna and Afterpay pay banks for zero interest loans exceeds the actual fair market value of the loans themselves.
This is an unavoidable cost of business for Buy Now Pay Later companies to the extent that Affirm has an entire category dedicated to this expense called loss on loan purchase commitment.
A firm's annual losses on zero-interest loans have grown from $73 million to $200 million as customers have grown and more loans have been issued in the past four years.
Loss on loan purchase commitments represent on average nearly 20% of a firm's annual operating expenses.

So if a firm and other buy now pay later companies lose money on pay in four and other zero-interest loans, which also happen to be the most popular amongst consumers, then why do they keep offering this option?
The answer is in Vintage.
In banking, Vintage is a measurement of the quality of credit and returns in a loan portfolio based on historical losses and default rates.
Based on Vintage, one can forecast future risk and extrapolate the quality of borrowers in a loan portfolio.
Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay are essentially building and managing these annual billion-dollar portfolios filled with millions of short-term unsecured consumer loans every year.

If their portfolios were mostly filled with high-interest 12-month loans, then on paper, these portfolios would have good returns, but they would also bear significantly higher risk and suggest that a majority population are subprime borrowers.
Subprime borrowers pay the highest interest on loans in general.
If payments are made in full and on time, then subprime interest-bearing loans naturally become the most lucrative assets for Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay.
But lending to too many subprime borrowers is the equivalent of building on quicksand.
If the bubble bursts, and the majority of buy now pay later loans were issued to subprime borrowers who have no means to pay, then these billion dollar loan portfolios will become worthless.
To prevent such a disaster, buy now pay later companies must cultivate a healthy population of prime loans to balance the subprime loans.
Prime borrowers are individuals with good credit history and considered the safest and most likely to repay their loans in full and on time.
But prime borrowers are not the target of buy now pay later services as they generally already have adequate access to credit or possess the means to pay for such purchases in full.

So to attract prime borrowers and to balance out the subprime loans in their portfolio, which must be many, a firm and other buy now pay later companies continue to offer zero-interest loans at a loss to maintain stability.
This is why savings accounts have become such a big priority for Buy Now Pay Later companies.
A firm and Klarna actively push consumers to deposit funds into their high-yield savings accounts with no fees or minimums.
If customers deposit their cash with a firm or Klarna, then these Buy Now Pay Later companies can use these deposits to fund loans instead of relying on Cross River or other banks to do it for them.
By becoming the lender and not just the broker, Affirm and Klarna can avoid losses on zero interest loans, eliminate origination fees, and improve their transactional economics.
Ironically, using balance sheet deposits as funds to advance loans to customers is a page straight out of the traditional banking playbook.

In 2022, Affirm funded 20% of all loans through customer deposits rather than through Cross River Bank, which consequently reduced their loss on loan purchase commitment by $40 million year-over-year.
It would be of no surprise if a firm's long-term goal is to increase the percentage of self-originated loans to as high as possible in the coming years.
Since simple interest and merchant fees are not enough to sustain the business model, a firm has two final revenue streams that it's aggressively investing towards in the pursuit of profitability.
The two are loan sales and servicing income.
Every year, a firm packages a portion of the loans in its portfolios and sells them as securities to investors.
A firm remains as a loan servicer responsible for administration, customer service, and collections so in their words they can control the user experience end-to-end.
A firm charges the investors that buy its loans a regular servicing fee.
So, loan sales and servicing fees go hand-in-hand together, and both revenue streams have grown from $5 million in 2019 to over $250 million.
Loan sales and servicing fees accounted for 15% of a firm's total revenue in 2022.
While lucrative, the securitization and sale of subprime loans brings eerie parallels back to the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis.
The 2008 housing collapse and subprime mortgage crisis was due to many of the same core elements that are present in Buy Now, Pay Later.
Access to cheap credit, excessive spending, overextension of subprime borrowers, and unregulated lending standards.
While there is a difference between a loan for a $400 shoe versus a mortgage on a $400,000 property, Buy Now, Pay Later companies continue to move in a worrying direction that feels all too familiar.

Packaging and selling subprime consumer loans as securities to Wall Street is a slippery slope, especially in a time where the market has tightened, • Cost of capital has increased • Buy now pay later.
companies are desperate to turn a profit.
A firm admits that if the economy does take a greater turn for the worse, borrowers would first default on these short-term unsecured personal loans.
In a crisis, borrowers will naturally prioritize the other loans, like their mortgages and credit cards, over buy now pay later purchases.
While the next recession is never the same as the last, the core ingredients and dominoes that lead to an economic contraction are always consistent.
– artificially inflated spending, consumption beyond means, excessive debt, unsustainable growth, and asset bubbles.
Yet in the face of inflation, layoffs, reduced production, and increasing interest rates around the world, consumers continued to spend at record rates rather than cut back on consumption.

While the billions of dollars in merchandise purchased every year with Affirm, Harna, and Afterpay is not at the same trillion-dollar scale that subprime mortgages were at in 2008, the reality is that the underlying consumer behavior that Buy Now Pay Later promotes is still very much part of the problem.
What's equally scary is to see the continued expansion of Buy Now Pay Later into other categories such as rent, groceries, healthcare, B2B, and even car repair.
Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay all argue that they communicate everything up front and they shouldn't be penalized for providing tools when every action is ultimately still made by the consumer.
Regulators counter that transparency and calling out the risks have never been enough to protect consumers from themselves.
So buy now pay later raises deeper philosophical questions around human nature.
Do people know what's good for them?
And if humans don't know how, or can't be trusted to be responsible, then who should be the one to put in safeguards to prevent these natural impulses of greed and overconsumption?
When we look at the stance that different governments have taken with buy now pay Later, it's fascinating to see the contrast between Western individualism and Eastern collectivism.
On one end, you have China, who says that humans and corporations can never be trusted to make responsible decisions.

Chinese regulators have ruthlessly cracked down on Ant Financial, the biggest buy-now-pay-later company in China, and have turned its unsecured personal loan business into a state-owned venture where lending decisions and user data are regularly shared with their central bank.
On the other hand, you have the United States, who has long favored corporations over consumers and predictably opted for a wait-until-it-falls-over approach with buy now, pay later.

title: Fried Chicken Wars: The Fall of KFC in America
note: Business-case essay with an early thesis, a chapter on category economics, a strong-numbers-then-reveal turn, and a closing lesson about legacy brands.
sections: Fried chicken love and KFC's decline
Why fried chicken is a lean, booming category
Yum Brands, pure franchisor model, strong numbers
Signs of trouble: overseas reliance, rock bottom 2015
One-year wonder, Zinger flop, US deprioritised
lines: Fried Chicken To some, it's a comfort food that evokes precious childhood memories, and to others, it's a timeless representation of American culture.
As I've gotten older, I've given up many junk foods, but fried chicken is one guilty pleasure I just can't let go.

There's something magical about it, the contrasting textures, the combination of juicy chicken with crispy breading, along with its spice, salt, and fat that make for such a satisfying meal any time of the year.
Fried chicken is loved around the world and these days there are more varieties than ever before.
There's classic southern bone-in buttermilk fried chicken, pub-style buffalo wings that are slathered in hot sauce, diner chicken and waffles drenched in maple syrup.
boneless Japanese karage coated in potato starch.
citrus marinated fried chicken from Latin America, Nashville hot chicken that's served with pickles.
Taiwanese popcorn chicken doused and five spice.
and my personal favorite, the sticky, sweet, ultra-crunchy Korean fried chicken.
Beyond flavors and textures, fried chicken comes in many forms like tenders, nuggets, bone-in, wings, wraps, and sandwiches.
Kentucky Fried Chicken was once widely considered to be the golden standard, the best fried chicken one could get.
While I grew up on KFC and its family buckets and biscuits, KFC these days is far from the golden standard that it once was.
it's nothing like the KFC from my childhood.

The mashed potatoes taste like glue, the chicken is greasy, it's dry, it's expensive, and even when it's served at its best, KFC doesn't come close to the quality of other establishments like Popeyes, Chick-fil-A, Jollibee, Raisin Canes, and more.
There are a variety of places nowadays to get your fried chicken fix, and Kentucky Fried Chicken is an afterthought.
As fried chicken has evolved, consumer tastes have also changed.
Nowadays, I prefer to pay more for less, for a product that's fresher, smaller in quantity but higher in quality, and more unique like soy garlic or honey glazed Korean fried chicken.
KFC has dominated fried chicken around the world with legacy and scale, but its relevance and popularity in America has been declining for years.
As the kernel has weakened, long-time rivals in Popeyes and Chick-fil-A have all laid claims to the chicken throne.

Even the world's second-largest investment bank, Goldman Sachs, sees this rare opportunity to upset the established order and take a piece of a booming multi-billion dollar food category that's growing faster than burgers and fries.
In 2020, Goldman Sachs acquired Zaxby's for $2 billion with the ambitions of taking the southern chain nationwide and soon international.
On the other side of the world, the eastern siege has begun.
Jollibee and Kyocan, who have both dominated East Asia for decades, have now shifted their focus to the West, eager to carve out a slice of the kernel's market share for themselves.

The popular narrative amongst Americans is that KFC's drop in quality over the years is the result of ruthless cost-cutting measures from out-of-touch executives looking to juice earnings per share and who wouldn't know good fried chicken if it hit them in the face.
When you look at KFC in America, it's outdated, run-down, cheap, and uncreative with a really boring menu.
But when you look at KFC around the world, in South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East, KFC is a star brand that's known for its quality chicken, great service, and unique offerings.
So how is it that the same company can be so great internationally and so poor in its home market?

In this episode, we'll cover the fried chicken wars, the strategy and missteps that have brought KFC in America to where it is today, and how legacy and brand power can be just as much as a curse as it is a blessing in the world of business.
Chicken is the world's most popular protein.
As chicken consumption per capita continues to break records and coming fresh off the chicken sandwich mania, companies and investors believe that there's still room for growth.
Two decades ago, people would have told you that a quarter pounder and a Whopper would be the best burger that you could get.

Fast forward today and you have Five Guys and Shake Shack who have both elevated the lowly burger from a cheap bite into a high-end premium with each of these new brands grossing nearly a billion dollars in sales every year.

While Shake Shack and Five Guys are not at the scale of the golden arches, having two thriving billion-dollar businesses is still a significant milestone in a mature market that many historically believed had no room for competition.

The evolution of burgers and the success of new entrants is a parallel that feeds the ambitions of restaurateurs and fast food companies who both believe that the same developments will play out with fried chicken.
Restaurants are a notoriously hard business.
In a typical full-service restaurant, food costs are roughly 30-35% of sales, labor costs are 30-40%, and overhead, which is rent and advertising and utilities, clocks in at about 20-30%.
With such heavy cost structures, it's no surprise that the average restaurant profit margin hovers at 3-5%.
Like all restaurants, fried chicken shops face the universal challenges of saturation and acquisition.
But modern fried chicken shops have some natural operational advantages compared to most restaurants with lower labor costs, food costs, and overhead.

Fried chicken is a takeout business, so consumers are looking to grab and go with no expectations As a result, fried chicken shops have gotten smaller and more bare bones over the years, with floor plans that have little to no dine-in areas for consumers.
In contrast, dining space is critical for almost every other type of restaurant, as their business is a function of how many customers they can seat and how fast they can turn over tables.
Modern fried chicken shops can get away with a few tables or sometimes nothing at all, just a counter for people to order, pick up, and leave.

As a place for people to stop at but not stay at, fried chicken businesses can save on overhead, fit into smaller spaces for cheaper rent, and are less dependent on location and foot traffic for business.
Food costs are a function of ingredients and menu diversity.
The bigger the menu, the greater the variety of dishes to choose from, the wider range of price points a restaurant can offer, and the better chance a customer will find something that they like.
But on the flip side, the more items on a menu, the more ingredients that must be sourced, and the higher the food costs.
Fried chicken shops in comparison generally have very simple, concise, easy to understand, and predictable one-page menus.
Beyond the chicken itself, fried chicken shops will typically offer low-cost, high-margin fried sides like french fries or pre-made sides like mac and cheese to round out their menu.
They'll sometimes have a few salad or dessert options for balance.
Modern fried chicken shops lean on their sauces and marinades for differentiation.
And the core ingredients that make up 90% of the menu for fried chicken shops all around the world are all cheap, widely available, and stable in supply.

While fried chicken shops can use just about every part of a chicken with little waste, restaurants who serve beef or pork generally can only use ground forms or premium cuts like ribs, chops, or ribeye.
Since the customer interaction is so limited, fried chicken shops don't need a proper front of house and waitstaff and servers.
Some shops these days are so operationally lean that the person frying the chicken can be the same person who takes the order from the customer.
For the back of the house, most shops fry in batches in advance of customer orders.
And since nearly everything on the menu is fried, cooks just need to be trained on how to fry something.
When it comes to cooking, fried chicken shops just need fryers, ovens, and warmers.
In contrast, restaurants need ranges, flat tops, fryers, ovens, warmers, microwaves, steamers, salamanders, boilers, along with a space to operate such equipment.
While the modern fried chicken shop has evolved to become smaller and leaner while offering better quality over the years, KFC has struggled to adapt.
To set the stage, KFC is owned by Yum Brands, who also owns Pizza Hut, Taco Bell, and the Habit Burger Grill in its portfolio.
In portfolio companies, investment is never evenly distributed across all brands.

Just like in a family with multiple kids, in every portfolio there's always a golden child, a brand that executives have the most hope for and consequently gets the most attention, prioritization, and investment.
On the flip side, there are neglected brands who chug along with really minimal investment and attention.
KFC for decades has been that golden child.
In the past 10 years, KFC has made over double the amount of sales of Taco Bell and Pizza Hut combined.
KFC made over $30 billion in 2021 and single-handedly contributes over 50% of Yum!
Brand's annual revenue.
In calls and presentations, KFC is always featured or mentioned first.
Knowing this, it would be unfair to attribute KFC's regression in America over the years as a result of underinvestment or a lack of care.
On paper, KFC looks like a solid business.
When we look at all the traditional metrics that a fast food chain would be evaluated by, KFC by that definition is successful.
System sales, which are the dollar value of food and beverages sold at all KFCs in the United States and around the world with the exception of China, has increased year over year.
KFC global system sales has grown 36% in 9 years, from $23 billion in 2013 to $31 billion in 2022.
Just like McDonald's and other fast food corporations, KFC has moved away from being an operator and franchisor to becoming just a pure franchisor.
By operating fewer stores, KFC gives up any sales upside in exchange for franchise fees, which are a lower but more stable form of recurring revenue.

Franchise fees are made up of two components, the first being one-time, fixed, upfront payments that franchisees must pay upfront for the right to operate a store and whenever they renew or transfer those rights to someone else.
These one-time fees range from thousands to tens of thousands of dollars.
The second and more lucrative fee for KFC is the royalty.
Every month, franchisees have to pay up 4-6% of their gross sales or a fixed minimum, whichever is greater.
Under this pure franchisor strategy, KFC reduces its own overhead and places all the operating risk on its franchisees.
In 2013, 9 out of every 10 KFC stores were franchised.
As of 2022, 99% of all KFC stores around the world have been franchised.
When nearly 10 out of every 10 customers are being served by a local operator, that means the customer experience and food quality of the KFC brand is almost entirely in the hands of its franchisees.

If we put ourselves in the colonel's shoes as the franchisor, while we can sit back and count our cash safely every month in our ivory tower, we have to maintain our relationships with our franchisees and maintain consumer demand so we can keep the royalties flowing in.
The more stores we open, the more franchisees we get, and the more fees we can collect.

The franchisor strategy is a volume play that works at scale, and it certainly helps that KFC is the second largest restaurant chain in the world and the global fried chicken leader, with over 25,000 restaurants in 145 countries.

While KFC provides guidelines, sets the menu, runs the advertisements, and supplies everything from equipment, food and packaging, down to the furniture, cleaning supplies, utensils and napkins, it's ultimately up to the franchisee on how they want to operate and execute.
Franchisees can set their own prices, staff as many people or as few as they want, and establish their own hours of operation for each location.
The relationship between a franchisor and its franchisees is always a testy one of power and control.
Both sides need trust and support from each other in order to thrive.
But when they don't get along, things can get nasty.
And when 99% of stores are franchised like they are with KFC, the power dynamics naturally shift away from corporate and towards the favor of the franchisees.
When we break down KFC's revenue over the years, we can see the powerful results from its franchisor strategy.
Back in 2013, franchise fees accounted for 28% of revenue, while sales from locations that KFC directly operated accounted for 72% of revenue.
By 2022, these two revenue streams have flipped, with franchise fees representing 56% of revenue and self-operated store sales accounting for 21%.

This same inflection point can be seen when graphed by dollar value, where KFC franchise fees have grown from $800 million to $1.5 billion, and self-operated sales have decreased from $2 billion down to $600 million over the same timeframe.
In the same period, KFC's annual operating margin with less overhead has improved significantly, almost doubling from 23% to 42%.
As KFC has opened and franchised more stores worldwide, food and beverage at franchised locations have also grown over the years.
System sales at franchised KFCs have grown from $20 billion in 2013 to $30 billion in 2022.
At the same time, KFC has successfully demanded a higher cut over the years from its franchisees.
In 2013, a KFC franchise paid out on average 4% royalty.
Fast forward 9 years and the average KFC franchise now pays out a little over 5%, which is a sign of brand and franchisor strength.
Along the way, KFC has doubled its stores worldwide, going from 13,000 locations in 2013 to over 26,000 locations in 2022.
too.
Same-store sales, which is a measure of if and how many customers are coming back to the restaurants every year, has also remained steady, averaging at 2% every year both before and during COVID.
Cannibalization, saturation, and retention don't seem to be issues for the world's largest fried chicken shop.

Yet the fundamental issue with most business analysis is that it's always historical, meaning only after something has obviously happen, do all the numbers, graphs, rationale, commentary, and case studies get made.
Despite KFC's aforementioned success, there are signs that if we dig deep enough, that this is a company that is playing its last cards.
Instead of addressing the declining consumer popularity, loyalty, and sentiment in America, KFC these days looks overseas to replace the churn at home.
The company focuses on international expansion while doing just the bare minimum domestically to stay relevant.

The only viable strategy that KFC has is to leverage its brand equity in the areas of the world where it's still worth something, and those places are overseas markets that its competitors haven't reached and where the kernel's legacy remains intact.

While KFC is happy to invest in localization, build beautiful international stores that have massive, comfortable dining areas that are designed to encourage consumers to stay as long as possible, and compete on quality by constantly releasing new and creative menu items, the company makes no effort to do the same in the United States.
KFC stores in America are old, rundown buildings with inferior dine-in spaces that look cheap and feel uncomfortable, the menu is just as stale as ever before, and the food quality is getting worse.
KFC is a tale of two businesses, a star chain with great food and service around the world, and yet is an inconsistent, unpopular, dying brand in America.

While KFC languishes in America but thrives overseas, its executives don't seem to realize the reality that success from first-mover advantage, legacy, and capital is always short-lived, especially in a high-growth food category like fried chicken, where it's no longer the brand that dictates quality.
In the years leading up to 2015, KFC in America had hit rock bottom.
Fried foods had become public enemy number two behind soda.
The company had just resolved a high-profile dispute with its franchisees over the brand's failed healthy repositioning and grilled chicken offerings.

Customers became confused, grilled chicken failed to sell, and sales plummeted, and franchisees all rallied together to stop what they saw as an act of self-sabotage and to raise the heat on the executive team.
Like many other fast food brands in the early and mid-2010s, KFC was caught in an external identity crisis and internal strife, attempting to keep the peace at home with its franchisees.
As a result, revenue, system sales, and operating profit all stagnated between 2013 and 2015.
While the future looked uncertain at home, KFC continually told its investors that the company had two main strategies.
One was to transition to franchise-led growth, and two was to become the fried chicken leader in emerging international markets.
Between 2013 to 2015, KFC and the U.S.
launched dud after dud, like the Colonel's original sandwich, which was just a boneless tender place on a Hawaiian roll.
the original recipe and hot shot bites, which was just a cross between a nugget and a tender.
KFC Go Cups to make it easier for people to eat in their cars.
Bucket Kids Meal, which was just a repackaging of the kids meal into bucket form, and the loaded potato bowl, which just added a different sauce and green onions on existing core menu item.
Unsurprisingly, these items failed to inspire sales, and KFC had no highlights to celebrate about its domestic operations during this three-year stretch.

Instead, executives focused on KFC's international success for three straight years, talking up its overseas achievements like 40% sales growth year-over-year in Russia and double-digit growth in Africa and Thailand.
The thing is, though, by 2015, 92% of KFCs in the world were already franchised, and and Americans only accounted for 24% of KFC's sales.
70% of all KFC stores at this time were already located outside of the United States.
So international expansion and franchise-led growth were not some new goals for KFC.
These were initiatives that the company had already been doing for decades.
To continuously restate the potential of overseas growth and the importance of international sales year-over-year just shows how little was going right for KFC in America.
In 2016, KFC unveiled a grand turnaround plan that it called the re-kernelization to win back customers at home in the United States.
The company unveiled this plan at a major media event in New York City as a part of a, quote, public recommitment to the standards set forth by founder Colonel Harlan Sanders.

Coming off a string of viral, embarrassing incidents that had the American public openly questioning the sanitation and standards of KFC, like mutant chickens and deep-fried rats, the company had decided that enough was enough.
In the eyes of KFC, its American franchisees had failed to live up to their end of the bargain with years of neglect and sloppiness.
Perhaps it was corporate complacency, too much focus on international expansion over the domestic business, or laziness from franchisees, or potentially all of the above.
Whatever the case was, it was obvious to everyone that KFC in America was and had been operating at below acceptable standards for years, and that had to change.

KFC wanted to get back to competing on quality as a way to make up for all the ground that it had lost to its national rivals in Chick-fil-A, Popeyes, Raisin Canes, and even to regional challengers like Bojangles, Zaxby's, and Churches.
KFC cracked the whip on its franchisees, using this public event as a way to restore food quality, operator discipline, and consumer confidence.

KFC temporarily shut down all their stores nationwide, created a mandatory chicken mastery certification program for its franchisees, and retrained all 20,000 of its operators on how to cook, quote, the way the kernel intended, showing just how far and how wide the standards had fallen in America.

These were highly publicized and aggressive steps that placed the blame of KFC's downfall on its operators, but KFC was just as much to blame for letting franchisees operate so poorly for so long in America.
Yet KFC had its hands tied.
There was only so much they could push before the franchisees would revolt like they did back in 2011.
So to enforce this new focus on quality, KFC looked to the public to hold franchisees accountable with the new kernel quality taste guarantee.
This new worldwide policy stated that anytime a customer was unsatisfied with their meal, that KFC store and by extension, that franchisee would have to remake that portion out of their own pocket.
as part of the plan kfc also committed to renovating its stores in the us into american showrooms sleek modern eye-catching bright red and white striped exteriors with vintage interiors.

when it came to marketing the company went back to its tried and trusted roots relying once again on legacy and nostalgia bringing back the kernel as the mascot along with the always original and finger lickin good campaigns.
the reintroduction of the five $5 fill-up boxes and $20 family buckets were commercial successes, reinforcing value in the mind of consumers.
KFC is not better than Chick-fil-A or Popeyes, but it's a lot cheaper and more bang for your buck.
The wins continued for KFC throughout 2016 with the launch of Nashville Hot and Georgia Gold.
These new menu items were not only significant in breathing new life into the brand, but also in their design and symbolism.
These new flavors and dishes were a major departure from the iconic 11 herbs and spices that KFC had conservatively clung onto throughout its existence.
This newfound momentum in the United States and the continued international success in emerging markets propelled KFC to new records in 2016.
Same-store sales grew to 3% in 2016, and the KFC U.S.
business surged back to $5.5 billion in gross sales.
But this would turn out to be no more than a one-year wonder.
Hidden behind these top-line successes is that in the United States, KFC had been closing over 100 stores every year for nearly a decade.
While the new offerings and stronger marketing had improved the overall brand, there was just never enough demand to go around.
KFC stores were shuttering, and the local demand for fried chicken in America was continually and swiftly replaced with Chick-fil-A, Popeyes, and other independent shops.
Yet in 2017, KFC had reason to be optimistic about its U.S.
business based on 2016.
The company believed that it had finally cleaned up its act and could now compete on quality with its rivals as a trendsetter.
With high hopes, KFC launched their original hand-breaded Zinger sandwich with the ambition of conquering the chicken sandwich category.
KFC spared no expense in marketing the Zinger, literally launching the sandwich into space and auctioning off a 400-year-old meteorite for virality.
While the Zinger was an international hit, it failed to catch on with Americans.

Company executives were probably crushed two years later when Popeyes came out with its own chicken sandwich in 2019, and that turned into the mainstream hit that KFC had so desperately hoped the zinger would be.
At the same time, KFC's international business continued to overperform in emerging markets like Brazil, where KFC grew an astounding 18% in same-store sales.
In Russia, where KFC opened 1,000 new stores in a single year, they experienced 33% sales growth year over year.
And at this point in 2017, KFC's international business already accounted for nearly 90% of the company's profits, and the U.S.
business was already well on its way to becoming an afterthought.
The United States, which historically contributed the most and nearly a quarter of KFC's overall sales up to 2016, had actually devalued over time, dropping as low as 16% by 2019.
Sales from KFCs in the U.S.
have steadily declined from $5.6 billion in 2014 to as low as $4.4 billion by 2018, long before COVID.
The problems of KFC's U.S.

business are continually masked and overshadowed by KFC's international success, which skews not only the company's top line, but also the bottom line and the traditional metrics that we covered earlier.
Yet KFC's leaders to this day proudly proclaim mission accomplished and that the KFC turnaround in the United States is a complete success.
Predictably, the executives who came up with the re-kernelization plan in 2016 have used its success to leapfrog up the corporate ladder.
One is now the CEO of Chili's, and the other became the CEO of Carl's Jr.
before moving into tech.
Sometime between 2017 and 2019, KFC executives must have gone over these same numbers and arrived at an obvious decision to cut losses and quietly deprioritize the U.S.
business.

While KFC continued to try its hand at menu innovation for Americans with the pickle fried chicken, the crispy kernel sandwich, Smoky Mountain barbecue, chicken and waffles, mac and cheese bowls, and Cinnabon biscuits.

this tactic feels similar to Taco Bell's playbook, who regularly releases limited-time offerings with very small quantities as a way to build up hype but more importantly to juice demand and energize sales for stores on a regular basis.
In contrast, the products that KFC introduces for its international customers are regularly celebrated for their commercial success and become a core part of the menu.
In Japan, it's the Peri Peri Chicken, in Australia, it's the Popcorn Chicken Slab, or the Crunch Double Down and Wrap Star Lunchbox in Africa.
When KFC executives talk about the US business these days, quality is not mentioned anywhere, and there's only one strategy, value.
Add more options into the $5 fill-up and $20 family meals.
Introduce an a la carte menu where consumers can now mix and match two sides for $6.
Throw in an add-on where Americans can get 12 tenders for just $10 more on a $20 family meal.
Blasting advertisements constantly on social media, reminding people how cheap KFC is.
Releasing gimmicky marketing stunts, each more outlandish and crazy than the last for virality and clicks, but have nothing to do with the product or brand.
The goal for KFC in the United States nowadays is to offer consumers, in the words of the CEO, quote, a truly incredible value with enough food to feed a family for multiple meals.
KFC is a powerful demonstration of how legacy and brand power is a double-edged sword that is as much a curse as it is a blessing in the world of business.
