It's KFC's legacy that has fueled the company's international success and appeal in emerging markets where the kernel is the first taste of American fried chicken that those people get.

With its first-mover advantage and war chests, KFC is able to reach customers and markets today that its competitors simply can't, and to win those customers through first impression, even if KFC's rivals have a much better product.

What KFC is betting on these days is that when Popeyes or Chick-fil-A eventually scale to those markets one day, that hopefully by then, consumers will have become too accustomed for KFCs to prefer anyone else's fried chicken.

KFC knows that its legacy and brand power in America is on its last legs, and any attempt to wrestle back domestic market share from its rivals would be futile, especially when customers know that KFC cannot compete on quality.

The pure franchisor play that has fueled so much of KFC's expansion domestically and internationally, has also fueled their profits and dominance in prior decades, is now a hindrance to the Kernel's evolution.

Rather than downsizing the stores to become more efficient like modern fried chicken shops, KFC is stuck with its franchisees and can only remodel its existing properties in place to make them grander but not leaner.
Its new modern concepts only apply to new constructions and not existing stores.

Rather than experimenting with sauces, marinades, and batters to match the changing consumer tastes, KFC is forced to constrain its creativity and preserve its legacy by keeping to the iconic 11 herbs and spices as its core flavor, which Americans these days have simply become tired of.

And there's a case to be made that those international emerging markets where people love KFC, that over the decades, they will begin to also tune their own tastes and potentially prefer other brands.
In business, one expects companies to dominate their backyard first, viciously defend it from new competitors and entrants, and then chip away at international markets over time.
It's rare to find a company like KFC who relies so heavily on international expansion to replenish a shrinking domestic market share.

There is great irony that the United States, which has the greatest fried chicken consumption and serves as the birthplace of Kentucky Fried Chicken, is now KFC's weakest market with the most competition and lowest ceiling.
As an American who grew up pigging out on buckets of KFC, it's sad to see the kernel regress to a discount volume brand.
Businesses like humans must adapt or die.
For KFC in America, adaptation came too little, too late.

title: A Tale of Greed: How 4 CEOs and $5B Failed Twitter
note: Chronological boardroom saga organised by CEO, driven by Jack's scheming; film opens with Elon's takeover and closes by returning to it.
sections: Elon takes over; Twitter's failed decade
Founding, Noah Glass fired, Jack as first CEO
Ev Williams ousts Jack and builds Twitter
Jack rewrites history and plots Ev's removal
Dick Costolo takes over in a coup
Dick's strategy, API shutdown, IPO and stall
Board and allies push Dick out; Jack returns
Jack's second reign, Parag Agrawal, Elon
lines: Twitter has a new owner, and true to his word, his presence is sinking in.
Under Elon, the company has undergone rapid and radical changes to accelerate a turnaround.

As soon as the acquisition closed, Elon fired Twitter's board of directors, nine individuals who presided over the company's rudderless execution, and forced out four different CEOs in the past 10 years.
A week later, Elon laid off 50% of employees and told the remaining staff that long hours and high intensity would be necessary in the months ahead to get the company back on track.

While the world is watching closely to see what the future holds, regardless of whether or not you believe Elon Musk can save Twitter, the harsh reality is that Twitter as a private company under Elon can't get any worse than the Twitter that has existed publicly for the past 9 years.
While Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, and Reddit have all built walled gardens to drive engagement, albeit to the point of becoming echo chambers, Twitter has gone in the opposite direction.
Twitter remains a wild west where conversations are one-sided broadcasts that are constantly weighed down with low-effort remarks and flame wars.
Tweets fly out at such high volume and yet are so short-lived that it's not quality but instead controversy that's required for virality.
Finding quality content on Twitter is like finding a needle in a haystack, and users must proactively and continuously self-moderate their feeds.
Wall Street had lost faith in Twitter long before Elon appeared.
Twitter has visibly struggled over the years with declining users, weak engagement, executive turnover, lack of innovation, infighting, massive net losses, and non-existent vision.
Twitter burned through four different CEOs and $5 billion in 10 years with little to show for its efforts, regressing further and further away from being a viable business or an attractive product.
The longer Twitter struggled as an independent company, the more apparent it became to everyone that there was no easy solution.
The board regularly put up Twitter for sale, and yet once interested buyers like Google, Facebook, Disney, and Salesforce all chose to walk away over concerns that ran deeper than price.
For Elon Musk to buy Twitter shows just how pessimistic the company was on its own future to accept an outside bid from a private individual.
twitter is not just a case study of business mismanagement and poor strategy but also a story of betrayal ego and greed where good friends backstabbed each other in order to become the ceo.
since its founding the company has been like game of thrones plagued by politics hidden agendas plots and schemes.
at the center of twitter's story.
beyond the revolving door of ceos and executives there are two constants.
The first was the board, who frequently engineered regime changes and created a culture of chaos.

The second was the founder, whose desire to be seen as a spiritual, futuristic, philosophical, genius CEO, more eccentric than Steve Jobs, was so important to him that he would do everything he could to achieve this recognition, even if it meant backstabbing friends and undermining his own company to do so.

In this episode, we'll cover the death of Twitter, how the once promising social media platform deteriorated to the point of an Elon Musk takeover, the schemes that brought each CEO to power, and an evaluation of their strategies, successes, and failures that have led Twitter to where it is today.
Twitter was founded in 2006 by four friends, Noah Glass, Biz Stone, Ev Williams, and Jack Dorsey.
The power struggle started early.
Noah, who came up with the name and idea, was so passionate about Twitter that he threw himself into work to get away from problems at home.
As his marriage fell apart, Noah became emotionally unstable, ranting at co-workers and gatekeeping code.
After a few months, Noah was fired for being difficult to work with.

So while Biz, Ev, and Jack have all gone on to become billionaires and widely recognized as the founders of Twitter, Noah has been written out of the company's history and has never once been acknowledged or credited for his role and contributions to Twitter.

With Noah's departure, Jack Dorsey, an NYU dropout with a nose ring and a taste for punk rock, became the lead engineer and CEO as Twitter moved from a promising prototype to a venture-backed, fast-growth startup.

But Jack was immature and inexperienced as both a leader and an employee, having flip-flopped through careers in his 20s as first a licensed masseuse, then a part-time programmer, and eventually an illustrator.

As CEO, Jack was distracted and and regularly left the office early to pursue his personal interests like drawing classes, hot yoga, and fashion design, leaving his co-founders annoyed and employees questioning his commitment.

Jack, who by all accounts was an unaccomplished introvert, was suddenly thrust into the spotlight with Twitter as venture capitalists wind and dine him with exclusive parties and luxury tickets to baseball games in an attempt to get on the cap table.
Jack's product decisions as CEO lost him just as much credibility as his personal decisions.
Twitter in 2006 was nothing more than a website where people could go and post a public message in 140 characters or less.
There was enough about Twitter that intrigued people, but no one, not even the four founders, was sure about where it would go or what it would become.
Jack uniquely believed that Twitter would replace text messages as a place where people would post statuses on whatever they were doing in the moment.
He pushed employees to dogfood Twitter over SMS, incurring a massive monthly six-figure bill.
Under Jack, R &D was a mess where Twitter ran its prototype build in production and regularly suffered outages with no backups.
And at one point, Jack had tracked and miscalculated the entire company's expenses on his personal laptop.
Ev Williams, one of the three remaining founders, could not stand by and passively watch disaster unfold from the sidelines.
Ev was the most experienced founder and a proven tech visionary who had pioneered online blogging in 1999 with Blogger.
Ev didn't see value in Twitter as a digital pit where people could publicly post every little thing they were doing every day, even if that was how users were using the product at the time.

Ev and Noah both believed in Twitter's future as an informative service where people could share and react to what was happening around them rather than an egotistical service of endless status updates.
But beyond Vision, what Ev disagreed with Jack the most was about his lack of care for the company.
While the two friends met weekly over dinner to discuss Twitter, their relationship began to unravel as the conversations turned blunt.
You can either be a dressmaker or the CEO of Twitter.
You can't be both.
Ev wasn't the only one who noticed Jack's lack of commitment and lack of results as CEO.
From 2006 to 2008, under Jack, expenses continued to increase, Twitter remained unstable, and the product's future remained as hazy as ever.
Behind the scenes, Ev had enough and through back-channeling, secured the blessing of the board to overthrow Jack.
Over a seemingly harmless invitation to breakfast, Jack was ambushed with the news that he was being replaced by Ev as CEO, given severance, stock, and stripped of all his voting rights and power.
To maintain optics, Jack would be given a meaningless silent chairman role on the board.
He was free to talk, but no one on Twitter was obligated to pay any attention to what he was saying.
Jack was effectively shut out.
Whether due to risk or wanting to protect his power, Ev shut down Jack's Twitter email, a petty move that only deepened the rift between these two one-time friends.
Ev took power in 2008 and enacted swift changes as CEO, providing clarity in direction and pushing for improvements.
With Jack relegated to the sidelines, Ev focused on what he was best at in product development.
To put into perspective just how new and weird Twitter was in 2008, the iPhone had been just released a year ago in 2007.
Twitter existed as a bare-bones website and not as the mobile app that many of us know today.
In his first year, Ev focused on user enablement, stability, and communication, teaching early adopters how replies worked and reporting outages whenever they occurred.
In 2009, Ev's second year at the helm was an R &D success.
Twitter shipped a slew of improvements and features that have remained years later a core part of the platform.
Under Ev, Twitter didn't force innovation.

Rather, they observed the creative ways in which power users would add depth to their 140 character messages, they would monitor which ideas had momentum, and they would convert those hacks into official features.
For example, hashtags were how early users took it upon themselves to tag and organize tweets under one specific topic.

While Jack refused to support hashtags, believing that the practice was too complicated for the average person, under Ev, Twitter embraced hashtags, adding hyperlinks so users could click in and easily see all tweets organized under that hashtag.
That same year, Twitter rolled out retweet to cut down on the redundancy and copy-paste that occurred every time people wanted to reshare someone else's message.
To help with discovery, Twitter launched lists to help users discover who to follow, location awareness so that people could mark this neighborhood or city.
they were tweeting from, notifications whenever users were mentioned with the at symbol.
hyperlinked profile pages for better account visibility, verification checkmarks for public figures, and a redesigned homepage to better communicate the value of Twitter.
These features were well received, and Twitter's audience grew from 2.9 million unique visitors under Jack in 2008 to 45 million unique visitors under Ev in 2009.
55% of those 45 million unique visitors came from outside the United States, making Twitter the 52nd largest website in the world, bigger than even ESPN, in just three years.
With user adoption taken care of, Ev began exploring ways for Twitter to make money.

Twitter had signed search deals with Bing and Google where the two search engines would pay millions of dollars to include tweets in their results, but that income would not be enough to sustain the cash-hungry startup.

Ev toyed around with the idea of a special version of Twitter made just for business owners that had premium features like contributors where multiple users could manage a single brand account from their personal account.
While people tend to associate Twitter with American politics and Donald Trump, the reality is that politics in general has always driven the platform, dating as far back as the Arab Spring.
In 2009, protesters in Iran used Twitter to organize rallies, spread awareness, and document the government crackdown.
Later that same year, Obama used Twitter to connect with younger voters, cementing Twitter's credibility and role in future American political campaigns to come.
For every political event that has happened ever since around the world, Twitter has been a beneficiary with ever-increasing traffic, engagement, and media attention.
In 2010, Ed kept his foot on the gas pedal in his second year at the helm.
As the iPhone and smartphone adoption in general began to take off, the company released the first-ever official iOS app.

At a launch event hosted at headquarters, Ev announced the new Twitter.com, a redesigned two-pane browsing experience where tweets would now include photos and videos that would expand to full resolution upon clicking in.
Before this, media was only viewable on Twitter as external links which would pull people out of the website entirely.
There were also improvements to infrastructure, a new logo for the company, and various design tweaks.
But the most notable highlight was that there was a clearer and stronger understanding of Twitter's product market fit.
Ev talked about the future of Twitter as a balance between discovery, consumption, and production.
Not every user needs a tweet to get value out of the platform, rather they could achieve sufficient value just by discovering and consuming tweets posted by others.
Eventually, with enough exposure and experience, users over time would graduate their comfort and competency levels to be able to tweet themselves.
Twitter's main channel was its website, twitter.com, but through a free public API, third-party developers were able to build their own desktop and mobile clients for Twitter.
While most people consume tweets directly on twitter.com, 20-30% of users still use Twitter through third-party clients like TweetDeck, LauncherPro, and Seismic.

While having a thriving developer ecosystem is a real asset for any tech company, Twitter Twitter no longer liked this arrangement because each third-party client had its own user experience, unique features, and enabled deeper customization.

These third-party clients had been invaluable for Twitter in driving user adoption in years past by giving power users alternatives and richer browser experience when the product was stagnating under Jack.
But now under Ev, Twitter.com was rapidly improving and official apps were now available for iOS and Android.
Ev wanted to funnel all users into the official first-party clients where the experience was consistent and unified.

He didn't want a fragmented experience with third-party clients living out in the wild, some of which were well-supported, others were not well-maintained, and a few even charged users a few dollars to use, which took money out of Twitter's pocket.
Twitter's relationship with its developers and API access would only get more contentious over the years and eventually become one of the company's biggest mistakes.
Twitter's improvements under Ev put the company on an astronomical growth trajectory.
In 2008, under Jack, Twitter had 500,000 users.
In 2009, under Ev, that number grew to 58 million, and now in 2010, Twitter boasted 175 million registered users, with roughly 370,000 people signing up for the service every day.
Under Jack in 2008, people were tweeting 5,000 times a day.
Two years later, under Ev, users were sending 35 million tweets a day.
People were gaining a clearer understanding of what Twitter had to offer, at least enough to sign up for an account, and were sticking around to consume content that they couldn't get from Facebook.
As a product-minded founder, Ev opted for a methodical approach to monetization.
He was unwilling to jeopardize adoption for revenue, and he regularly resisted calls to display banner ads on Twitter.com.
Ev opted for native advertising solutions.
Twitter rolled out three ad products that year in promoted tweets, promoted trends, and promoted accounts.
Promoted accounts was woven into Twitter's discovery, so brands could pay to be suggested to relevant users.
Promoted trends offered another way for brands to insert themselves into trending topics, and promoted tweets elevated specific messages into user timelines.
With so many eyeballs on Twitter every day, advertisers weren't sure what they were getting into, but they all wanted to get in on the ride.
So it ultimately may not have mattered what exactly Twitter launched in terms of ad products when every brand wanted and was willing to pay for presence on this fast-growing platform.
As Twitter moved forward under Ev, Jack made sure that the world never forgot about him.
Jack saw his ouster from Twitter as his own John Scully Steve Jobs moment.
In defiance, Jack went rogue, feeding tales to the public who were captivated by Twitter and hungry to worship more tech founders.
Jack went to the media to rewrite history and to paint himself as the genius behind Twitter.
During interviews and at flashy red carpet events, Jack labeled himself as the quote-unquote inventor of Twitter and spun a creation story that excluded not just Noah but also Ev and Biz.
While the two remaining founders and employees were hard at work, Jack went on a PR spree spitting stories that Twitter had been his life's work.

He even went as far to assert that he single-handedly came up with not only the idea, but also the name for Twitter, which had always been Noah's work that no other founder ever dared to publicly claim credit for.
As the media accepted these tales and hyped up Jack as the next Steve Jobs, Jack became more comfortable manipulating the truth.
His narratives turned more grandiose and shameless.
He told Vanity Fair in a feature that the idea of Twitter came to him when he was just 8 years old.
Jack would tell CBS later in a 60 Minutes episode that he founded Twitter because he was fascinated by trains and maps.
Even later, Jack would tell the Los Angeles Times that he had presented the idea of Twitter in its entirety to childhood classmates at the school playground in 1984.
In every interview and public appearance, Jack would represent himself acting on behalf of Twitter and in charge of the product, despite having no involvement in the company.
In the years that Ev was CEO, Jack was working on his own startup Square, yet he made himself the public face of Twitter.
Jack would monitor every newspaper article about Twitter, and any story that failed to mention him received an immediate request for correction to include Jack Dorsey as the founder of Twitter.

As naive as Jack may have been in the past, he knew exactly what he was doing now, planting seeds and positioning himself for an eventual return to Twitter, but this time not just as the founder, but also as its savior.
Ev was furious.
Instead of staying quiet during exile, Jack had become a talking nightmare.
At one point, Ev was so frustrated that he confronted Jack about his statements.
Quote, no, you didn't invent Twitter, Jack.
I didn't invent Twitter either.
Neither did Biz.
People don't invent things on the internet.
They simply expand on an idea that already exists.
Ev was a decorated founder who had done enough startups to know personally what he wanted most was to run an impactful and successful business.
He didn't need the marginal fame.
But Ev's biggest flaw was that he was too product minded and lacked the political awareness, decisiveness, and ruthlessness required for self-preservation in the corporate world.
Ev chose not to punish Jack out of fear of risking Twitter's trajectory.

If he was to remove Jack entirely, Ev worried about the irreparable damage to the company's growth from the ensuing public relations nightmare and Jack's potential to make things even uglier beyond public misrepresentation and narcissistic manipulation.
For the sake of Twitter, Ev swallowed his pride and downplayed his grievances with Jack as private interpersonal affairs that were below the product and company.
But this would be a fatal mistake that would open Ev up to be backstabbed and cut his promising reign as CEO to just two years and make 2010 his last year at Twitter.
What Ev didn't know was that behind the scenes, Jack was curing favor with the board and gathering allies to orchestrate Ev's removal as CEO.
In private conversations, Jack had positioned himself as a visionary who had been unjustly removed from his role, who had been unfairly treated, and who knew what was best for Twitter.
While Twitter grew exponentially under Ev thanks to his sharp product sense, Ev had plenty of flaws as CEO.
His weaknesses were only further amplified by his poor political awareness and diplomatic ability.
Like many technically gifted and product-minded leaders, Ev's strength was not in operations.
Twitter was rapidly growing and had to scale.
The company needed a CTO, COO, CFO, and other leaders to drive structure and productivity.
It was here that Ev was at his weakest, slow, indecisive, untrusting, and in the end would always fall back on his personal network to hire trusted friends for key positions.

Ev opened himself up to murmurs of cronyism and nepotism when he hired his sister to run the employee cafeteria, his wife to design the office spaces when she had no experience or qualification as an interior designer, and various friends from his Google days.

All of this is common in Silicon Valley startups, but for a first-time CEO who came to power through force and who was in charge of a visible company with such high stakes, you would think he would exercise a little more caution before making moves like these.
Ev ended up hiring his friend Dick Costolo to be COO in 2009.
Dick was a former comedian, business consultant, and Google veteran who enjoyed using humor to break ice.
In his very first tweet after being hired, Dick joked, first full day as Twitter COO tomorrow.
Task number one, undermine CEO, consolidate power.
While Dick didn't know it at the time, he would do exactly that one year later, betraying Ev and taking his spot as CEO with the help of Jack Dorsey.
Jack soon graduated from narcissism to sabotage.
Through two years of calculated effort, he had successfully manipulated the public narrative.
More people knew about Jack than Ev, Biz, or Noah combined.
In the eyes of the media, users, employees, and even investors, Jack Dorsey was the face and founder of Twitter.

Whenever employees were frustrated with Ev, Jack was in their ears like Littlefinger, posing as a well-intentioned confidant and letting them vent discreetly to him at coffee shops, Square's offices, or even in his mansion.
Jack's goal was to fan the flames.
If he could get enough executives and leaders and senior staff to complain about Ev directly to the board, then Jack could paint a narrative of how employees were losing faith in Ev as CEO.
Tech is like any other industry.
People complain all the time.
Middle management complains about executives, executives complain about the CEO, the CEO complains about the board, and the board complains about shareholders.
But to weaponize employee frustrations and to start a proxy war with the goal of forcing Evout is a radical step that goes beyond typical workplace gossip.
But Jack was smart and patient.
Getting Evout would be enough payback for now.
If Jack had demanded that he be instilled as CEO to replace Ev, it would have only revealed his true agenda.
So posing as a selfless founder thinking of nothing but the good of the company, Jack spun a seductive narrative to the board that who Twitter needed now more than ever as CEO was a mature operator.
Based on the employee complaints, Jack argued that Twitter no longer benefited from having Ev or any technically gifted product-minded coding nerd from Silicon Valley at the helm.

Twitter needed a grown-up like Eric Schmidt had done for Google, an operator with proven business acumen that could bring stability, scale the organization, inspire employees, and bring the company to IPO while looking and acting the part for Wall Street.
The one person that fit this bill was Dick Costolo, Ev's friend and the current COO of Twitter.
Dick was a personable executive who reportedly knew almost every employee by name.
He also enjoyed a strong reputation with the board as the leader responsible for closing the search deals with Microsoft and Google in the years before.
Jack recruited Dick to his scheme, proposing an arrangement between both men where Dick would focus on operations and Jack, the gifted visionary and genius founder, would lead and advise product.
Under this arrangement, everybody won.
The company would suffer no loss with Ev's departure, Jack would return to Twitter with his power and title restored and Dick would get to be CEO.

This turned out to be an easy sell to the board and early investors, all of whom had believed every word of Jack's tales over the years and had been pushing the company to go public as quickly as possible to get a return on their investment.
On a random afternoon in 2010, Ev was ambushed with the news that he was no longer the CEO of Twitter.
Dick had replaced him effective immediately.
Shocked and hurt, Ev called his friend and members of the board to make sense of what had happened, but it was already too late.
Dick tried to downplay his own involvement and pleaded with the board to give Ev a graceful exit.
Yet when the scheme reached fruition and Dick was formally offered the position of CEO, we have to remember he had every opportunity to say no.

Dick was fully aware that this was a coup and that accepting the job would be a direct betrayal of Ev, the very friend who had brought him into Twitter in the first place and had entrusted deeply over the years.
Yet Dick, who was caught between loyalty to his friend and his own personal ambitions, chose himself.
The board messaged their latest regime change as Ev's own decision to step down.
When it was simultaneously announced that Jack Dorsey would also be returning to Twitter as executive chairman, it became clear who had been pulling the strings the entire time.
This is where Ev's story comes to an end.
He never got over being betrayed by his friends, and chose to leave Twitter entirely.
It was reported that it was only years later that he was able to get back on speaking terms with Jack.
In the years following his exit, Ev would play a passive role at Twitter, feeding a few canned lines of the press whenever the company asked him to.
There is enough data that Ev was a promising CEO, and that if given the right guidance, support, and feedback from the board and the executives around him, he could have grown to be great.
Ev's flaws are not unique and certainly not severe enough to justify such an extreme action by the board.
Of all the CEOs in the company's history, Ev really did the most for Twitter as a product and possessed a natural humility that his successors lacked.
But on the flip side, there's also data that suggests that as technically gifted and product-minded as Ev was, he was not cut out to be the CEO for a company that needed to make money fast.

After leaving Twitter, Ev found refuge in his roots by returning to online blogging, a frontier that he had pioneered and where he could start another company and be CEO without the politics and pressure.

Yet after 10 years of being the CEO of Medium, Ev chose to step down in 2022 as the company struggled to make money and come up with a viable business model, the very same issue he was dinged for at Twitter a decade ago.
Dick Costolo took over in 2010 as Twitter's third CEO in its four years of existence.
Under Dick, Twitter shipped many features and explored many directions, but the releases lacked the ruthless focus on users that Ev had.
In 2011, Dick's first year as CEO, Twitter rolled out its own photo service where users could snap and upload photos directly into their tweets to compete with Instagram.
The company even rolled out galleries to see how far it could get into the photo sharing and album storage business.
As a business-minded CEO, Dick was more reactionary than prescriptive.
In 2012, when Instagram was taking off, Dick positioned Twitter as a direct competitor by adding filters and blocking Instagram posts on tweets.
When Facebook purchased Instagram for a billion dollars months later, Twitter bought Vine in direct response before the app had even launched.
Dick didn't want to lose what he saw was a critical war with Mark Zuckerberg over photo sharing and video hosting.
He wanted Twitter to own media and not just distribute it.
Under Dick, Twitter invested significantly in infrastructure, eradicating outages, and revamping Twitter.com to be usable on as many mobile devices and browsers as possible.
If there was one major thing that Dick got right, it was mobile, not desktop, that was the future.
But that wasn't a hard bet to make at the time with the way the iPhone and Android phones were trending.
In his first two years, Dick was constantly on the lookout for ways to make big bucks.
Promoted tweets, accounts, and trends were fine, but he wanted to unlock more spend from advertisers.
He set his eyes on television, where tens of billions of dollars are spent every year by brands.
Twitter was lighting up every week with thousands of tweets about the latest American Idol and Game of Thrones episode.
While Dick wasn't foolish enough to think that Twitter would replace TV, his bet was that brands could be enticed to spend money on integrated ad purchases between Twitter and television.
Dick pursued this new frontier by wooing Hollywood producers to create exclusive content for Twitter.
Twitter, he pitched, could turn television into an interactive medium by letting users share feedback with showrunners or vote out contestants on reality shows.
Twitter partnered with Nielsen to create the Nielsen Twitter rating, an official metric for measuring the amount of social conversation generated by a TV show.
Dick hoped that this partnership would provide institutional credibility and inspire brands to route spend to the social media platform.
Yet social TV, which is what Dick called this idea, never panned out the way he thought it would.
The reality was that cable television was dying.
Viewership for the Emmys, Grammys, Oscars, Golden Globes, sitcoms, and other live events had been declining for years.
More and more people were cutting the cord and opting for Netflix and YouTube.
Cable television went out of fashion, and Nielsen consequently lost much of its influence in the industry.
The Nielsen Twitter rating in particular hasn't been mentioned anywhere publicly since its initial announcement back in 2012.
Social television was an expensive flop, but not Dick's greatest mistake as CEO.
Instead, it was his decision to shut down the API, which destroyed Twitter's ecosystem and eroded relationships with developers that takes the cake.
Dick had a simple charter as CEO, to scale Twitter, and to monetize relentlessly so that the company could IPO as soon as possible.
To maximize traffic, user growth, and ad revenue, that meant that Twitter could no longer tolerate having third-party clients in the wild competing for its users.
In the race to go public and under the scrutiny of Wall Street, every single user needed to be accounted for.
Ad revenue is a function of impressions.
So to count every view and to earn every dollar, users needed to be on either twitter.com or the official mobile apps.
They could not be anywhere else, and this meant consolidation by force.
Twitter came down hard on developers, telling them that anyone using the API to create third-party clients would be banned, and that existing third-party clients would also be shut down.
While 90% of Twitter users at this time were already on the official website and the official mobile apps, this decision permanently destroyed the relationship between Twitter and developers.
Developers had played an important role in Twitter's early success, providing power users the functionality they needed and injecting credibility when the product lacked innovation.
Yet now these developers were being cast aside and shut out in the name of business.
The loss of the developer community only increased expectations and pressure on Dick and Twitter to drive innovation since no one else was now allowed to touch the product.
It would be The ironic that just three years later, Dick would lose his job for failing to deliver product innovation.
In 2013, his third year as CEO, Dick fulfilled his promise to the board by taking Twitter public.
He had been talking up the company as the next billion dollar social media platform and had been sharing cherry-picked data with journalists to build up hype.
Dick had certainly lived up to his reputation as a company builder.
Under his watch, Twitter scaled dramatically.
In 2010 under Ev, there were only 200 employees.
By 2013 under Dick, Twitter had nearly 3,000 employees.
He had also made credible progress since taking over, growing revenue from $30 million in 2010 to $664 million in the span of three years.
Twitter was unprofitable, but people back then were used to that from Silicon Valley startups.
At the time of IPO, both retail and institutional investors were all eager to get a piece of Twitter in their portfolios.
It's difficult even now to explain what Twitter is, but Dick tried his best, calling Twitter a simultaneously public, real-time, conversational, and widely distributed platform.
He couldn't resist taking a shot at Facebook along the way, asserting that no other social media website could combine these elements at scale.
In a wave of optimism, Twitter stocks surged from $40 at opening to nearly $70 a share.
Wall Street believed that with Twitter's arrival, Mark Zuckerberg now had something to worry about.
But when Twitter reported its full year results for 2013, any hype that the company had as a challenger to Facebook quickly faded away.
People had expected losses, but not to the extent that Twitter was incurring them.
In order to make as much money as possible, as fast as possible, Dick had spared no expense staffing up sales and engineering.
Twitter was spending over half a billion dollars a year on R &D and a quarter of a billion dollars on selling to brands with a net loss of nearly $700 million.
This burn rate would have been easier to swallow if Twitter had the revenue or user growth to justify these expenses.
Twitter had grossed a little over $600 million and was still short of Dick's pre-IPO projections of the company being a billion-dollar business.
In the same year, Facebook had spent twice as much on R &D and four times as much on sales and marketing, but had made profit on $8 billion of revenue.
Dick defended these expenses as critical investments that were part of a long-term strategy.
He pushed back against comparisons between Facebook and Twitter.
While you have to log into Facebook to access content, Twitter is in this weird conundrum where you don't need an account to get value out of the platform.
Over 500 million people were coming to Twitter every month but not logging in.
But only after do people log in does Twitter make money.
Without an account, Twitter doesn't know enough about the users to show them personalized ads.
In contrast, Facebook requires your real name, your birthday, gender, school, work, and location upon signup.
So even if you aren't active, Facebook still knows enough about you to issue targeted ads.
Dick told investors that the best way to scale revenue would be to grow users.
The more engaging the Twitter experience was for those people that logged in, the more likely these visitors would sign up for accounts.
The more visitors signing up, the more active users there would be to monetize and the more ad inventory Twitter could sell and charge brands for.
Twitter needed to grow users in order to grow revenue.
There was no shortage of awareness or engaging content on Twitter.
The problem was converting visitors to users.
Twitter had grown from 54 million monthly active users under Ev in 2010 to 240 million monthly active users in 2013 under Dick.
Dick pointed to multiple R &D initiatives designed to drive signups, like connecting friends through mobile accounts and threaded conversations to encourage conversations.
And unsurprisingly, he kept pounding the drum about the potential of Twitter and television to Wall Street.
While Dick was fundamentally right about the connection between user and revenue growth, there was still plenty of data in 2013 to suggest that simply growing users would not be enough.
For advertisers, the quality of the user matters just as much as the quantity.
Facebook had grossed $8 billion off 1 billion monthly active users in 2013.
One way of looking at it is that a single Facebook user is worth $8.
Twitter grossed $664 million off 240 million monthly active users, making each Twitter user worth $2.75.
The reality is that advertisers themselves, even back then, the very customers who keep social media companies alive did not perceive Facebook users and Twitter users to be at the same quality.
Investors weren't giving up on Twitter, but the illusion of the company going toe-to-toe with Mark Zuckerberg was quickly fading away.
In 2014, Twitter delivered what Dick had promised, grossing over a billion dollars in revenue.
But despite this achievement, the company was under pressure.
Investors weren't reacting positively to the top-line successes Dick had hoped.
Twitter's stock plummeted below its IPO price as investors began to pick apart the results.
No matter how hard Dick tried to sidestep the incoming questions, even he couldn't deny the numbers.
User growth was weak, existing user engagement was declining, and the company had no answers for how to turn it around.
Twitter had 288 million monthly active users in 2014, just 20% more than the 241 million active users it had in 2013.
The growth flywheel and compounding payoff was nowhere to be found while operational costs continued to skyrocket.
To break the billion dollar mark in revenue, Dick had simply thrown more bodies at the problem.
Sales and marketing expenses doubled year over year, going from $300 million in 2013 to over $600 million in 2014.
R &D grew from $593 million in 2013 to nearly $700 million in 2014, but throwing more engineers and designers at the product wasn't improving signups.
The numbers seemed to indicate what critics had been saying.
The quality of users on Twitter is just simply not high enough, nor is the core experience compelling enough to get people to stay after the virality passes and the trend fades away.
Advertisers were slowly catching on to these realities.
While beating revenue targets is always a win, Wall Street was rightfully concerned that engagement and user growth was slowing down so dramatically and had only been one year after IPO.
Under the heat, Dick started changing up his talking points and throwing out new ideas quarter after quarter to calm investors and to rally employees.
But he just couldn't find a solution or strategy that would stick.
Things became even worse when an executive at NBC came out to say that Twitter was overstating its influence on television and social media in general had very little impact on viewership.
Quote, a lot of people want to show that they are on the cutting edge.
One of those things that is on the cutting edge is social media.
Why wouldn't I, as an NBC executive, want to say that we as a cable network have a potent new way in which we can drive ratings?
But what Twitter is saying just isn't true.
I am saying the emperor wears no clothes.
It is what it is.
These are the numbers.
What was even more damning was that this executive had concrete data to back up his assertion with the 2014 Winter Olympics.
NBC had broadcasted 1,500 hours on television to 21 million primetime viewers.
On Twitter, there were 10.6 million tweets related to the Olympics from 3 million users.

While the executive agreed that those tweets may have reached many more millions of people, his conclusion was that it was still the quality of the show that drives activity on social media and not the other way around.
These comments single-handedly killed social TV as a credible strategy for Twitter.
As Twitter stagnated through 2014, Dick's struggles became more apparent.
But it might be unfair to pin everything on Dick when Twitter as a product has inherent issues that simply make it difficult to monetize.
Since the vast majority of traffic to Twitter is not logged in, Twitter can't match the deep personalization and targeting of Facebook or Google.
As a result of this lowered effectiveness, brands are just not willing to pay the same premium to run ads on Twitter.
And it's not just an issue of spend.
Because of how open Twitter is and how most of the traffic coming to the website is simply unidentifiable, brand marketing is really the main type of ad that performs well on Twitter.
If a brand wants awareness, Twitter is a great place for it.
But if a brand wants to run direct response campaigns to get people to download an app or buy a product, Twitter would be a waste of money compared to Instagram, YouTube, AdWords, or Facebook.
Beyond monetization, Twitter as a product has inherent issues that make growing users difficult.
Information on Twitter is transient and the lifespan of a tweet is short.

Since there's no meaningful conversation and because anyone can access tweets without an account, there's no need to be logged in when you can just catch the tweet like a one-time highlight after it goes viral.
Your only cost is timing.
Without an account, you might not be the first to know about it and will probably hear about it from somewhere else later.
At the same time, Twitter can't reg wallet's content because that would significantly reduce the platform's reach, which would in turn stifle virality.
And without virality, people wouldn't be incentivized to tweet in the first place.
But Dick was the CEO of Twitter.
This was the job he wanted and betrayed his friend for.
Investors began to hold Dick to his words, exposing his constant flip-flopping in strategies and vision.
Back in 2013, Dick had proclaimed that the Twitter core experience didn't need to change, it just needed to be easier to use.
A year later in 2014, Dick was on a whole new talk track.
He was now downplaying the importance of logged-in users and stating that Twitter would optimize for three different audiences.

One was the minority of logged-in users, the other was the majority of users who came to Twitter regularly but don't log in, and the last third was the remaining millions on the web who get exposed to Twitter through embedded tweets.
Wall Street wanted to hear about product innovation, and yet Dick was still talking about how Twitter complements television.
Employees wanted alignment and clarity, and yet Dick would flip-flop from one idea to the next.
Like most professional CEOs, Dick was at his best as a go-to-market tactician and a company builder.
But with declining user growth and engagement, Dick's biggest weakness was now exposed.
People wanted innovation and vision, but Dick wasn't a visionary.
He just wasn't good at these things.
Ironically enough, vision and innovation is what the previous CEO of Twitter and his former friend Ev was best at.
But Ev wasn't coming back and certainly not to save the friend who had betrayed him.
As Dick ran out of answers, he looked to his executives.
And when they couldn't give him solutions, he fired them.
This happened so frequently that even the media began to pick up on the excessive executive turnover that was happening at Twitter.

In 2014, Dick fired the COO, the CFO, the head of product, the VP of engineering, the creative director, the SVP of engineering, the VP of media, the head of North American media, and the head of news.
He then handpicked their replacements, who all exited as fast as they came in.
One executive poached from Google last six months as the VP of product before resigning.
It was now not just Wall Street, but also the media and employees that were losing faith in Dick.
In 2015, Twitter hit rock bottom.
Shares fell to just above $20.
In the first quarter, Twitter missed its revenue targets and had to reduce guidance both in earnings and in user growth for the remainder of the year.
While Instagram and WhatsApp had solidified themselves as mainstream services, Twitter was becoming more niche.
There were some positives.
Periscope, Twitter's newly launched live streaming service, brought in over a million users in its first 10 days.
Vine was exploding with over 1.5 billion loops a day, but there was no clear path to monetization, nor was there any connection to Twitter.
And based on the executive turnover and the employee leaks, the company looked more and more like a circus.
Twitter doubled its revenue in 2015, going from a billion-dollar business to now a two-billion-dollar business.
But one quick look revealed the realities of the situation.
Dick had once again thrown more people at the problem, blowing up operating expenses to untenable levels.
The company was burning nearly $2 billion every year on engineering, sales, and marketing alone.
Despite no improvement in user growth and no real product innovation, engineering costs were over $800 million a year.
sales and marketing expenses were now approaching 900 million dollars.
from a cost structure standpoint twitter was looking more like an enterprise software company than it was a social media platform.
mau slowed even further growing just 11 from 288 million in 2014 to 320 million monthly active users in 2015.
losses continued to mount as twitter posted another half a billion dollar net loss for the year.
The writing was on the wall for Dick.
Wall Street wasn't listening to what he had to say, and he sounded progressively jaded in interviews.
While Dick vented to close friends that he was unsure of how much longer he wanted to remain CEO, Dick was still a prideful captain who remained stubbornly loyal to his ship.
While the board repeatedly assured Dick that they believed in him to turn things around, behind the scenes they were already plotting to push him out of Twitter.
The board was not about to gamble on wishful thinking, nor were they going to wait for Dick to come to a decision about his own future.
As they had done twice before, once with Jack, once with Ev, and now with Dick, they would opt for a quick ambush and a clean removal.
But the board didn't want an ugly mess on its hand by firing Dick.
The company was now public, and it would be much easier for everyone if he just stepped down.

After the plot was sent into motion, weeks later, a prominent venture capitalist by the name of Chris Saka published a scathing 8,500 word analysis on just how poor Twitter had become and what it needed to do to improve.
In his analysis, Chris called for deeper thinking and more creativity, experimentation, innovation, and risk-taking, the exact same things that Dick was on the hot seat for.
Chris implied in his essay that this responsibility should not squarely be on a few engineers and product managers, but instead should be shouldered by top-down leadership.

Quote, While Chris clarified publicly that his intention was not to criticize anyone at Twitter, the timing and the content of his essay is simply too pointed and too perfect to be anything other than a hit piece.
Chris is a seasoned venture capitalist who knows how the game is played, but most importantly, remains one of Jack Dorsey's biggest allies.
Sure enough, Chris's essay goes viral.
Wall Street cranks the heat up on Dick to intolerable levels, pushing him into a corner where he had no choice but to commit professional seppuku.
Dick announced that he would be stepping down effective immediately, and that Twitter would begin a search for a successor.
This was the moment that Jack Dorsey had been waiting for for over seven years.
Twitter needed a visionary CEO, someone who believed in the mission, had a track record of innovation and execution, and could inspire employees and investors.
With Ev out of the running, there was only one person left in the entire world who fulfilled this impossible criteria.
That was Jack Dorsey.
Jack's stock in 2015 was at an all-time high as he had struck gold twice, leading Square to a successful IPO the same year that Dick stepped down from Twitter.
Bringing one company from idea to IPO is hard enough.
To do it twice in a row is exceptional.
Even his harshest critics couldn't deny that Jack had the Midas touch.
Combined with deep relationships with the board and his carefully perfected reputation, everyone at Twitter welcomed Jack's return as CEO with cheers and open arms.
The prodigal son had returned.
Fairy tales aren't meant to come true, but they certainly did for Jack Dorsey.
His latest arc perfectly mirrored that of Steve Jobs, who Jack had idolized for decades.
Steve Eve had been forced out of Apple, then founded Next, and then the success of Next brought him back to Apple where he saved the company from ruin.
Jack was now at Act 3.
He had been forced out of Twitter, then founded Square, and his success there now brought him back to Twitter.
All that was left to do was to save the company.
With Eve and Dick permanently out of the picture, there was no one left that would even dream of questioning or challenging Jack at Twitter.
His word was gold, his position was invincible, and his actions were irreproachable.
There would be no more boardroom coups or mutinies or takeovers, as the real architect and schemer behind all those regime changes to date had achieved his ultimate goal.
Jack was now sitting comfortably back on his rightful throne as CEO of Twitter, but this time he wielded more power than Ev and Dick combined.
Yet even with five years of protection, a blank check, and the freedom to do whatever he deemed necessary, not even Jack Dorsey could fix Twitter.
In 2015, his first year back, he used honesty to appease investors.
He publicly admitted the ugly truth that yes, the majority of people in the world still don't understand how or why they should use Twitter.
Jack promised change but emphasized that improvements would not come as quickly as he had to first clean up the quote-unquote unacceptable mess left by his predecessor Dick.
You should expect Twitter to be as easy as looking out of your window.
You should expect Twitter to show you what's most meaningful in the world to live it first before anyone else.

If we meet these expectations, and we will, Twitter will become the first thing everyone in the world checks to start their day, and the first thing that people turn to when they want to share ideas, commentary, or simply what's happening.
While any other CEO would have been hammered for such flowery language, Jack had the aura to get away with it.
Under Jack, Twitter moved away from reverse chronological ordering and into an algorithmic timeline where the most popular tweets would be at the top of users' feeds rather than the most recent.
Twitter also introduced Moments as a way to surface the best content on Twitter to build up mainstream appeal.
Through human editors and algorithms, Twitter would highlight tweets, videos, images, and gifs of a trending event into digestible, bite-sized pieces.
With Moments, users wouldn't even have to scroll through their timeline to find quality content.
Both Both of these features represented a shift in product philosophy to prioritize relevance over recency.

While Twitter had always prided itself on the speed and volume of its content, these improvements were a clear admission that finding quality content on the platform was like finding a needle in a haystack.
Having a human or an algorithm pick out the most useful content in theory could drive engagement as users could achieve value without having to work for it.
In 2016, Twitter went all in on live streaming.
Video was the hottest format on Twitter, both in terms of engagement and advertiser demand.
Encouraged by Periscope's momentum, Jack believed real-time video to be the next frontier.

Since written communication was already occurring at such high volumes and frequency on Twitter, Jack had this new vision that Twitter could be a live-streaming leader and create, quote, the planet's largest daily connected audience, where people could talk and watch together in real-time.
The company struck a deal with the NFL, shelling out $10 million for the streaming rights for Thursday Night Football.
Soon after, the Wimbledon, Republic National Convention, and the Democratic National Convention were all livestream events on Twitter.
Periscope and Twitter became tightly integrated so that users could go live on Periscope from Twitter in one click or join an ongoing Periscope stream from an embedded tweet.
It would be remiss to talk about Twitter without mentioning the 2016 American presidential election and Donald Trump.

While politicians in the past used Twitter to broadcast carefully prepared and polished statements, Trump's tweets were unconventionally raw, unfiltered, and confrontational, each sparking millions of reactions and conversations on the platform.
Journalists, opponents, supporters, and everyday people would actively monitor Trump's Twitter account that year to catch his latest remark or to watch the latest controversy unfold.
For Twitter, a company that had been long struggling with user growth and engagement was happy to take whatever it could get.
But monetization continued to be a problem.
While video ads were in high demand, advertisers were thumbing their nose against Twitter's direct response offerings.
Perhaps brands and agencies had collected enough data over the years to confidently determine what they had suspected.
Twitter is only strong for brand marketing purposes.
If you want to sell a product, a service, or an app, you're still better off with Facebook and Instagram.
Even Jack began to openly question if Twitter could ever be competitive in direct response advertising.
Despite the live streaming deals and the product advancements, Twitter continued to struggle.
Jack showed a little more restraint than Dick, reducing R &D expenses from $800 million in 2015 down to $700 million in 2016.
But he still followed his predecessor in throwing more bodies at the revenue problem.
Sales and marketing expenditures in 2016 increased from $870 million to nearly a billion dollars, but revenue grew at just 14% year-over-year the lowest it had been in the company's 10-year history.
And while it seemed that every day in 2016, everyone around the world was hearing about Donald Trump's latest tweet, all that attention strangely had no material impact on user growth.
MAU went down from 320 million monthly active users in 2015 to 319 million monthly active users in 2016.
Worst of all, it looked like Twitter's revenue had finally reached the end of its runway.
With user growth now officially flatlined, revenue was now following suit, and Twitter was still operating at a net loss of nearly half a billion dollars.
Jack's Midas touch was nowhere to be found.
2017 was another weak year as user growth remained non-existent and revenue dropped 3% to $2.4 billion.
Product improvements were equally lackluster as other companies jumped into live streaming, making real-time video a commodity rather than a unique offering.
Following a successful debut, Twitter was eagerly looking forward to renewing its deal with the NFL, only to find out that they were outbid by Amazon for Thursday Night Football.
And unsurprisingly, Amazon used Thursday Night Football to promote its own streaming service in Prime Video.
The only notable product highlight that year was expanding the character limit from 140 to 280 characters.
With nothing working, Jack pivoted.
He switched his focus from growing users to optimizing for profitability.
Having thrown in the towel on growth, the company no longer needed an army of engineers and salesmen to ship features and to push deals.

Through a series of aggressive cost-cutting measures, which included shutting down Vine, Twitter shaved off $400 million across R &D and go-to-market expenditures, reducing its net loss by $300 million.
MAU improved marginally by 3% year-over-year from 319 million to 330 million monthly active users, but expectations were so low that this change barely registered with investors.
Suddenly in 2018, Twitter turned itself around.
Revenue grew 25% to break $3 billion even as the user base declined.
User growth was in such a rough spot that Twitter stopped reporting MAU entirely.
Yet Twitter's business performance was propelled upwards based on the tailwinds of two major trends.
The first was in cord cutting.
Cable subscriptions were dropping, and thanks to Netflix's dominance, streaming looked every bit like the future.
Brands and agencies in response began shifting money away from television and into online video.
The second was the saturation of Facebook and Instagram.
Facebook and Instagram only had so much ad inventory, and the cost to advertise on Mark Zuckerberg's digital properties was only getting more expensive by the day.
When advertisers were picky and digital budgets were small, Twitter was unattractive.

But from 2018 onwards, Twitter became attractive simply by existence as digital budgets were bigger than ever before, money that was historically allocated towards television was now flowing over to social media, those ad dollars had to be spent, and Twitter as a platform had enough inventory to go around.
In comparison to Facebook and Instagram, Twitter's video ads are priced cheaper due to their lowered effectiveness, but they still offer adequate reach and engagement.
Video ads alone now accounted for more than half of Twitter's revenue, and advertisers were putting more of their money into social media than ever before.
For the first time in company history, Twitter was profitable.
The company ended the year with a net income of $1.2 billion, with R &D, sales, and marketing expenses remaining consistent year over year, the magic of being in the right place at the right time.
This trend continued onwards in 2019 as Twitter marched towards its second year of profitability.
Revenue grew 14% to $3.5 billion and net income clocked in at $1.4 billion.
Twitter demonstrated that it could grow revenue without having to grow users, but questions still remained.
From a product standpoint, Jack was now focused on combating misinformation and hate speech as social media was now in the crosshairs of politicians on both sides of the aisle.
User growth was no longer a priority as Twitter, in Jack's words, was now more of a quote, interest network than a social network.
Twitter had historically been marketed as a place where people go to discover what's happening.
The expectations there were that people would want to sign up to be at the center of this information so that they would be the first to see something unfold.

Now the company was moving away from this decade-long positioning to assert that people were not coming to Twitter to discover things, rather they already knew about something but they just wanted to get a more live, raw, and direct exposure to it.
Under this new positioning, MAUs and signups were just no longer as relevant as before.
A visit by someone who's logged in versus someone who's not logged in should be weighed the exact same.
This was another fundamental shift in philosophy for a product that was nearly 14 years old.
In 2020, Jack found himself in the crosshairs of Elliott Management, one of Wall Street's most ruthless activist investors.
Elliott Management demanded that Jack be a full-time CEO or to step down and give the role to someone who would be.
Since his return back to Twitter in 2015, Jack had been working part-time, splitting time between Twitter and Square as CEO of both companies.
While the board could safeguard Jack from any internal threats, there was little they could do about an external threat as big as Elliott Management.
Elliott in years prior had successfully forced change at eBay, AT &T, SoftBank, and even in world governments.
Despite Twitter's 2018 and 2019 top-line wins and bottom-line achievements, investors were still not convinced of the company's future.
The stock was volatile and even on earnings beats remained low as Wall Street attributed Twitter success to macro-level trends rather than in-house innovation and product engagement.
In 2021, Jack stepped down as CEO of Twitter, citing that at a certain scale, companies no longer benefit from being founder-led and that Twitter should be no different.
He swiftly departed but not before naming Parag Agrawal as the next CEO of Twitter.
Parag was a company veteran who had climbed up the ranks at Twitter over the past decade from a simple engineer to the chief technology officer.
But Parag was still a curious choice.
He was a soft-spoken executive that was so under the radar at Twitter that it's even hard now to find more than one video of him on the internet.
A critical take is that Parag was chosen as CEO as someone who could be easily controlled, who would do what the board asked him to, and would keep the wheels turning until a buyer materialized.
Twitter's stock surged 10% on the news of Jack Dorsey's departure, but its business was still as volatile as ever before.
Twitter grossed $5 billion in 2021, growing its revenue by 37%, but still posted a net loss of $220 million.
The revenue growth may have been more convincing if the company hadn't once again thrown more bodies at the problem.
Sales and marketing grew 30% to $1.1 billion and R &D grew 43% to $1.2 billion even as Twitter's product regressed to its most uninspiring state.

With no articulate vision, the company had launched dud after dud, like Fleets, which were tweets that expired after 24 hours, just like Instagram stories, Spaces, which were live audio chat rooms meant to mimic Clubhouse, and Twitter Blue, a subscription service where you could now undo your tweets and read ad-free articles for $3 a month.
While some projected that Parag would be for Twitter like what Satya Nadella was for Microsoft, Elon Musk ultimately arrived before Parag could affect any meaningful change.
It's curious how strangely quiet Jack was during Elon's takeover.
Going through Twitter's history, pivots, and the politics that have plagued the company for the past 16 plus years gives a clear understanding of what Elon can bring to the table.

It feels more likely that as a private company, without being constantly compared to Facebook, without the need to pose as a billion-dollar platform with unlimited growth, without Jack Dorsey, and especially without the board, the company can truly focus on becoming a sustainable business.
Twitter is as much a business lesson as it is a timeless tale about friendship, ego, betrayal, power, and greed.
Elon's takeover and the subsequent layoffs are painful, but perhaps they are necessary measures for the company to truly move on from its troubled past.
Creation myths need villains as much as they need heroes, and Elon Musk is the rare public figure who can play both the hero and the villain for Twitter to succeed.

title: Why Football Is Bad Business
note: Three-club case study structured around the same flaw: revenue flywheel eaten by wages; includes a first-person Barcelona match day vignette.
sections: Premier League and Manchester United's flywheel
Barcelona on the edge of collapse
lines: Football is a beautiful sport that brings in billions of dollars every year as the world's most popular sport.
There's been no shortage of controversy with the World Cup underway in Qatar.
The tournament has renewed attention on the governing bodies behind football that have dodged corruption and bribery charges for decades.
But the average fan isn't directly exposed to FIFA or UEFA.

Instead, most people learn and follow football at the player and team level through European clubs like Liverpool and Manchester City in England, Juventus and AC Milan in Italy, or Barcelona and Real Madrid in Spain.
It's these private clubs that make the spectacle of football possible.
On the outside, the biggest football clubs seem wildly successful.
They win trophies, they pay high salaries, they play on the biggest stages, and they sign the best talent possible every transfer window.

That success appears to carry over commercially, where these leading football clubs are international brands with loyal fan bases who religiously spend thousands every year on merchandise, tickets, and jerseys that aren't even designed to be reworn after a single game.
And it's not just bodies at the stadium.
These clubs make millions more through sponsorships, television rights, and competition prize money.

As these clubs achieve success on the field, their brands off the field get stronger, which grows their overall fan base and then fuels their monetization and revenue through tickets, membership, and merchandise.
The business of football clubs seems simple enough, and with so many famous elite clubs all over Europe, this flywheel must work.
But in reality, football clubs are businesses that are barely cash flow positive, unprofitable, and they continuously bankrupt themselves in order to sustain their on-the-field success.
They all cling to the hope that if they keep winning, money will materialize in the future to offset their costs today.
Or these clubs intentionally operate at losses year over year with the goal of one day flipping the team for billions in appreciation.
The reality is that whether they're run by corporations or Saudi sheiks, a successful football club, simply put, is an unprofitable one.

In this episode, we'll look at the problematic business of football clubs through the financials of Manchester United, Juventus, and Barcelona, and how it's only a matter of time before every successful football club is run by a rich oligarch looking for their latest passion project.
England is the most developed and lucrative football market today.
The English Premier League, considered to be the most competitive and the highest level of professional football, is the most watched sports league around the world.
The Premier League is broadcasted to over 200 countries and watched by over 3 billion people every year, which puts it at the same mark as the World Cup.
The difference is that the World Cup is an international tournament played once every four years, whereas the Premier League occurs every year in England.
In comparison, the Super Bowl, the biggest, most visible global event in American sports, pulls in 100 million viewers.

The high viewership of the Premier League not only drives brand interest, but also attracts talented players who naturally want to play on the biggest stages and be paid top salaries as direct beneficiaries from all that ad spend.

Within the Premier League are many successful clubs who all have their own history, stadiums, and famous players like Arsenal, Chelsea, and Liverpool, but there is no English club more iconic than Manchester United.
In the past 13 years, Manchester United has aggressively seized every opportunity to generate as much money as possible, even at the expense of its team.

Investors, not fans, are the priority for Manchester United, and the club has rewarded its owners and investors with tens of millions of dividends every year, even as the team has underperformed and struggled on the pitch.
As long as money keeps flowing in, the ownership and management don't seem to mind how poor the team is playing.

Fans, critics, and former coaches have called out Manchester United as a commercial club rather than a football club, and for this very reason, Manchester United provides a fascinating look into the ceiling or best-case scenario of how far football clubs can go with their business model.
Manchester United is one the most valuable football clubs in the world and IPO'd on the New York Stock Exchange in 2012.
To this day, it is one of the few football clubs that remains publicly listed, available for both fans and the general public to invest in.
Manchester United has nailed the flywheel, tripling the club's revenue from £280 million in 2009 to almost £600 million in 2022.
For football clubs, there are three core income streams.
The first is match day revenue, which is money that comes from the tickets, food, and drinks sold at home games.
Match day revenue for any club is a function of the number of games played at home, the number of seats that are filled, along with the price of tickets and concessions.
The better the team plays, the more people willing to attend games, and the higher the ticket prices get.
Historically, football clubs have been reliant on home games, gate receipts, and concession sales in order to generate cash flow.
Through the 2000s, clubs were always looking for ways to either upgrade their stadium experience to justify price increases or increase seating capacity to bring in more fans and more money.
But as we can see through Manchester United's financials, matchday revenue has become less significant over time.
In 2009 and 2010, matchday sales made up 41% and 37% of Manchester United's revenue.
Fast forward to the early 2020s, and matchday revenue contributes less than 20% of revenue.
While the other two income streams have grown, matchday revenue has understandably stagnated, never going over £114 million or below £90 million in a single season.
But that's not for lack of trying.
Manchester United has actually the second largest stadium in England, with a seating capacity for 70,000 people.
Broadcast revenue, on the other hand, has grown consistently as streaming and television have made things only more lucrative over time for the clubs in the Premier League.

As television viewership has grown, advertiser bids have also intensified, and broadcast revenue overall has doubled going from £100 million in 2009 to bringing in £250 million by 2022 for Manchester United.
It's the league administration who negotiates the broadcast revenue on behalf of all the clubs that play in the Premier League.
TV networks bid every year for the rights to broadcast Premier League games, and the league naturally defaults to the highest bidder.
Sky, one of England's largest networks, paid £2.3 billion in 2013 for the rights to broadcast 116 Premier League games in a single season.
Eight years later in 2021, Sky is now paying £3.75 billion to broadcast 128 Premier League games.
While there's nuance in how the broadcast revenue is split amongst all the teams within the Premier League, it mostly comes down to just staying in the league.

As long as the club and team isn't losing so many games that it's relegated to a lower division, every club in the Premier League, including Manchester United, is guaranteed a slice of the broadcast pie.
Broadcast revenue alone has accounted for 34% of Manchester United's revenue since the late 2000s.
Commercial revenue is where Manchester United has executed heads and shoulders above any other club in the world.
Commercial revenue is revenue that's generated from limited time agreements that Manchester United as a club enters in privately with a separate company.
In exchange for cash, Manchester United will allow this brand to associate itself with the club even if their industries aren't related.
So whether it's promoting an airline, a beverage, a car, or a watch, Manchester United will do it for a price.
And brands are also willing to pay the club with the belief that this increased visibility and association will elevate their own image and sales.
Commercial revenue has been Manchester United's fastest growing revenue, quadrupling from £65 million in 2009 to £260 million by 2022.
Commercial revenue used to account for only 24% of revenue 13 years ago and now accounts for 44% of the club's revenue.
The most visible spot is the jersey.
From 2000 to 2006, Vodafone paid out £8 million every year to Manchester United to sponsor the team's jerseys.
AIG then paid out £14 million a year for the next three years.
Once that deal expired, Aon shelled out £90 million across four years to be the latest sponsor for Manchester United.

General Motors then signed on to be the next jersey sponsor in 2014, paying out $70 million in their first year to Manchester United, and then increasing their payments by 2.1% every year to the club for the next eight years.

Manchester United has ruthlessly monetized every bit of real estate where not just the training jersey and the game jersey have their own sponsors, but also the sleeve of the jerseys, a practice that the club popularized back in 2009.
Manchester United signed blockbuster commercial deals with not only jersey sponsors, but they've also done so with suppliers.

When Arsenal announced an eye-popping five-year, 150 million pound deal with Puma for Puma to be the exclusive producers of their jerseys back in 2014, Manchester United blew that record out the water months later with a historic deal where Adidas would pay the club 750 million pounds over 10 years.

In football, any space that can fit a logo is available at a price, but it's credit to Manchester United how the club has been able to consistently stir up bidding wars and close landmark deals, every time walking away multiple times richer than before.

The second layer here is that sponsors can be geographically segmented, which allows the same Atom or Pixel to be monetized multiple times, once at the global level and then once again at the regions.
In 2009, you wouldn't find Saudi Telecom, Smirnoff, Honda, or Telecom Asia associated with Manchester United in the West, but in the East, you would have seen those sponsorships in those markets.
In 2009, Manchester United had 12 major global sponsors and half a dozen regional sponsors.
Fast forward to 2022, Manchester United today boasts over 20 global sponsors and dozens of regional sponsors in industries as diverse as wine, bathroom fixtures, and crackers.
In the late 2000s, there was some rationale as to why brands would be so eager to throw so much money at this particular football club.

At the time, Manchester United was unrivaled as the most successful English club of all time, having won the Premier League a record 12 times and having never finished lower than third place in a single season.

Manchester United's popularity over the decades wasn't just because of its winning results under coach Sir Alex Ferguson, but also due to the world-class talent it harbored like David Beckham, Ryan Giggs, Cristiano Ronaldo, and Wayne Rooney.
Many of these famous players started out as unproven homegrown teenagers who were nurtured and developed into superstars at Manchester United.

This strengthens the club's allure, which then in turn drives brands to commit boatloads of money under the belief that the club will continue to dominate on and off the field for generations to come.
The reason why Manchester United and football clubs in general love commercial revenue so much is because these deals are huge, predictable, guaranteed payouts that are locked in for multiple years.
Compared to match day revenue or broadcast revenue, Manchester United incurs no variable costs or overhead to collect commercial revenue.
Once the deal is signed and agreed, beyond that upfront legal cost, the money just comes flowing in at high margins, regardless of how the team actually performs on the field.
Over the years, Manchester United's on the field product has actually gotten worse and worse with the team finishing outside of the top 4 in the Premier League 5 times out of the past 10 years.
If we mark the years where Manchester United was at its least competitive and the team netted its worst results, there was no loss to commercial revenue as the payouts still continued to flow in.
In 2013, Manchester United finished 7th place in the Premier League, its worst ever domestic placement and was criticized for playing uninspiring football.
Yet in the same year, the club's commercial revenue skyrocketed from £120m to £152m.

In 2015 and 2016, even when fans lashed out at the poor play and the club finished 5th and 6th place in back-to-back years, commercial revenue still grew, growing from £195m to £268m thanks to its blockbuster deal with Adidas.
TeamViewer is now Manchester United's latest jersey sponsor after signing a five-year £235 million agreement in 2021.

But even as TeamViewer's stock has crashed and its company executives have revolted and spoken out against the sponsorship deal as an unnecessary expense, the German software company is actually stuck.

They're unable to pull out of the sponsorship deal from Manchester United, who's a football club that has every intention to collect, no matter how poorly the team might be playing or how bad the finances are for its sponsor.

Despite the growth in broadcast and commercial revenue, even if we add up all the sponsorship deals, the 10 years at 750 million pounds, the five years at 235 million pounds, along with all the sales, web jerseys, tickets, merchandise, all of those combined are still not enough to pay for player salaries.
The biggest operating expense for every football club is player salaries.
While commercial revenue has grown 12% year-over-year, player salaries have actually grown inline and at a higher basis over the same time frame.
Even with Adidas, TeamViewer, and a £24m a year training jersey sponsor, commercial revenue alone is not enough to offset the cost of player salaries.
