Starbucks has been a mainstay in business school literature and management training as a role model for innovation, branding, vertical integration, and corporate social responsibility.
The impact of Starbucks is well known.

They reposition coffee from a cheap, simple, bitter medicine that the working class forced down before work into a fashionable, mainstream, branded drink that people consume these days for taste and aesthetics as much as function.
Starbucks made their stores into a casual third space between home and work, where people could come in, relax in comfortable chairs, hang out, and surf the web while sipping coffee.
Neighborhood baristas provided essential frontline evangelism and preparation for first-time coffee drinkers.

The uniquely experiential nature of the stores, their widespread presence, and the emphasis on service and product helped Starbucks not only introduce coffee to the masses, but also charge unprecedented high prices at $3 to $5 a cup.

Thanks to efforts from its famous CEO, Howard Schultz, Starbucks has carefully crafted a uniquely respected and celebrated image in academia, business, political and investment circles over the past decades.

See, Starbucks is not some basic coffee chain, but instead of forward thinking, fast growing, innovative, socially responsible company that always does the right thing for its customers, employees, investors, farmers and the environment.

So the love and humanity is also about creating a value system in which the company stands for something in addition to making money, doing great things for the people that it employs and the communities it serves.
And I think as a result of that, and this is not a U.S.
phenomenon, businesses are going to have to do more and they're going to be called on to do more.
I also believe that those businesses that do the right thing in the right way will make more profit as a result of doing the right thing.

Over the last 40 plus years, as Starbucks has grown from one store in the Pike Place market to over 19,000 around the world, I think the one thing that has stayed consistent has been our commitment to providing health care to all of our employees, all of our partners, who work more than 20 hours a week.
We saw firsthand that we were the only company in America, only retail company, providing this benefit to our people.
No one company has come into New Orleans and done a block of volunteerism that anywhere approaches what we're doing.
Over 50,000 hours of volunteer hours.
And I got to see very up close and personal the values that Starbucks ascribes to.
It's fundamental commitment to changing people's lives.
investing in schools, investing in jobs, making neighborhoods better.
That's the kind of company that I want to be a part of.
Over 4,000 African lives are lost every day to preventable, treatable disease.
Dying for lack of drugs you can buy in any drug store.
12 million AIDS orphans in Africa, 18 million by the end of the decade.
A whole generation of active adults wiped out.
Children bringing up children.
It's not a cause.
It's an emergency.
We're going to do something about it at Starbucks.

This makes it all especially ironic that Starbucks, the poster child of corporate social responsibility and model employer, is now waging such a high-profile, visible, ugly war with its baristas across the United States, using every trick in and outside of the book to crush unions and squash any conversation of labor progression before it can form.
While union efforts by retail workers are also happening at Apple stores, REI, Walmart, Target, and Amazon, none of these corporations have followed the scorched-earth approach of Starbucks.
While these companies intentionally keep themselves away from controversy through jargon and bureaucracy, Starbucks has opted to be as subtle as napalm.
For a company that makes billions every year selling cups of syrup and sugar alongside glorified microwavables, surely the profits must be high.
Can Starbucks really not afford to pay a few more bucks to its retail workers?

In this episode, we'll dive into the business of Starbucks, strip away the corporate embellishment, and uncover why the company's image as a dominant, fast-growing business depends on successfully crushing unions in America.
The coffee industry breaks down its evolution into three waves.
The first wave was the 50-cent dark, bitter black coffee found in gas stations, diners, and dehydrated instant mixes in the 80s and earlier.
Consumers then had little regard towards the taste of coffee, they valued convenience, and they pursued coffee as a cheap vehicle for caffeine.

What Starbucks accomplished in the 90s was to usher in the second wave of coffee, elevating the drink into a social pastime, emphasizing bean varieties and origins, turning shops into destinations, hiring baristas as stewards, and broadening appeal of coffee through lighter, sweeter flavored forms like lattes, cappuccinos, espressos, macchiatos, mochas, and frappuccinos.
Coffee continued to evolve with the third wave in the 2000s.

Consumers started seeking greater sophistication like artisanal roasting, single-origin sourcing, latte art, manual brewing, and diverse flavor notes, things that only independent shops could provide and big corporations like Starbucks, Dunkin' and Pete's cannot offer.
The third wave of coffee is best represented by the smaller chains like Blue Bottle, Fills, and Four Barrel.
Despite the trend towards third wave coffee, Starbucks has maintained success as an acceptable baseline.
Its products still sell even if most of the menu and orders these days are much closer to dessert than coffee.
Its stores remain packed across America, Europe, and Asia.
In the world of food service, shops that sell beverages like tea and coffee generally enjoy higher margins than that of restaurants.
Beverage shops deal with significantly fewer ingredients and far simpler preparation methods – water, milk, syrup, juices, fruits, tea leaves, and coffee beans.
All of these ingredients come stable, ready to use, and can last for weeks with very low risk of spoilage.
In contrast, restaurants must deal with a wider variety of time-sensitive ingredients that must be replenished weekly, require processing, and are far more perishable.
While skilled labor is necessary to turn raw ingredients into palatable meals, making beverages have significantly lower labor requirements.
Drinks are simplified for workers behind the scenes into easy-to-memorize recipe cards and choreographed movements that anyone can quickly pick up.
The opportunity to make money is high when you're in the business of selling a consumable for $5 that only cost you $1 to make and can be assembled in seconds by a cheap minimum wage worker.

The low barriers to entry and the massive paper profits is what drove Starbucks and continues to attract new entrants into the beverage industry in the form of artisanal coffee shops, bubble tea shops, smoothie shops, and juice shops.
Beverage shops win on margin per transaction, but with smaller transaction sizes, they need volume to achieve profits.
volume is what Howard Schultz optimized for in Starbucks rise in the 80s and 90s.
It's impossible to cover Starbucks without mentioning Howard Schultz.

Howard Schultz is a celebrity CEO who was not only integral to the company's past success, but also now the same exact person spearheading the company's public scorched earth approach to crushing its unions.

In today's progressive political climate, where brands are just as likely to be canceled as individuals, waging a public war against your own workers would be a one-way ticket determination for any CEO.
While Tim Cook and Jeff Bezos opt for neutrality, Howard is in a league of its own on how outspoken he is on any form of labor progression or labor movements that do not come from the company.
Could you ever see doing that and embracing the union as part of it?
No.
Why not?
The primary reason is we are in business to exceed the expectations of our customers.
A hundred million people come into Starbucks.
The customer experience will be significantly challenged and less than if a third party is integrated into our business.
Because they're not acting in good faith?
Because we have a different view.
And I don't want to spend the entire time in the union.
Come on.

It is Howard's invincible larger-than-life persona as the man who single-handedly built Starbucks, alongside his high levels of social and political capital, built through the decades as the champion of corporate social responsibility that has protected him from being vilified by the media, targeted by politicians, questioned by the board, challenged by his own employees, or pressured by investors.
As a result, it's useful to first understand what Howard Schultz did in the past that grants him this present-day credibility and autonomy to crush unions.

When Howard first stepped down from Starbucks in 2000, he handed the reins over to a series of executives who followed the classic MBA playbooks of operational consolidation, product simplification, cost-cutting, and relentless expansion.
In order to hit the growth targets promised to Wall Street, these CEOs focused on opening a certain number of stores in every state and across the country.
In the mid-2000s, Starbucks opened stores anywhere it could, sometimes even within a mile of each other, to impress investors and without the usual meticulous due diligence in site selection.
As the stores scaled rapidly, the workforce was spread thin, so the company naturally focused on improving worker productivity to do more with less.
Instead of using the conventional fresh coffee beans, Starbucks pivoted to more modern solutions like prepackaged ground coffee, powdered mixes, and automated machines.

The overexpansion led to predictable sales cannibalization and declining retention as customers naturally questioned why they were paying $4 for a cup of coffee made from a bag at Starbucks when they could get the same for a dollar from McDonald's.
These same CEOs also focused on growing ticket sizes by introducing food offerings, but predictably, they chose the cheapest vendors to maximize their margins.
Howard Schultz was called back with a hero's welcome to save Starbucks in 2008.
He moved to restore the authentic customer experience that he had formerly built the brand on, kicking out the inedible sandwiches.
mandating coffee aromas in store, requiring coffee to be freshly ground.
installing shorter machines so customers could see their drinks being made.
shutting down hundreds of underperforming stores.
introducing a new medium Pike Place roast and a light blonde roast.
requiring coffee to be brewed every 30 minutes in smaller batches.
and retraining baristas nationwide.

Starbucks had lost its soul and Howard returned it through public self-criticism and personable acknowledgement, a rarity for corporations back then, and a playbook that Domino's Pizza would copy just one year later to its own success.
There were other wins credited to Howard during his second tenure as CEO from 2008 to 2017.
He believed that CPGs, or consumer packaged goods, would be an important complement that would net higher profits than the core retail business.
Coffee shops had been facing pressure from these new single-serve machines where consumers could make their own espressos and cappuccinos at home with a single pod and no mess.
Starbucks had a partnership with Kraft in the mid-2000s to exclusively create coffee pods for Kraft's machines.

When the computing Keurig system and K-Cups began taking off as a far more popular option, Starbucks broke off with Kraft and launched Via, its own platform-agnostic soluble coffee mix and K-Cups to build up its CPG business.
Under Howard, the company also rolled out Starbucks Rewards, which to this day remains one of the most successful customer loyalty programs.

They started selling gift cards at big box retailers like Costco, which have contributed to the $1.3 billion of gift card balance sitting on the balance sheet today, and made Wi-Fi free at all stores.
Over a decade later, Starbucks is still the only place in the United States where you can consistently walk in and get free Wi-Fi, with no questions asked and no purchase necessary.
Pike Place Roast and Blonde Roast are now bestsellers, with Pike Place being the most popular in-store brew and the top-selling whole bean in instant and single-serve markets.
Howard seized every opportunity to grow Starbucks beyond just a coffee chain in image, product, and fundamentals.
He applied the same quality-first approach to food, opting for vertical integration in order to satisfy his exacting demands.

Unsatisfied with the food options from external vendors, Howard bought out Le Boulanger Bakery for $100 million for the sole purpose of creating food products that he believed would be worthy of Starbucks.

In 2011, Starbucks entered the fast-growing billion-dollar cold-press premium juice market through an acquisition of Evolution Fresh for $30 million to expand its core business beyond coffee and beyond a single brand.
Diversification continued with entry into the $90 billion global tea market with the $620 million acquisition of Teavana.
Howard championed corporate social responsibility at every opportunity through the 2010s.

The company labeled its retail workers as, quote, partners, built agricultural centers overseas to teach locals sustainable farming, enforced ethical sourcing, and reduced employee attrition through proactive raises.

The rationale that Howard presented was that all of these investments would build a stronger long-term business and that taking less profits in the short term to do the right thing would have compounding payoffs in the future.
Howard's desire for control and exacting standards had also been applied to the company's approach to expansion.

Rather than relying on the traditional B2C franchising model where individuals can apply to operate their own store, Starbucks relies on a stricter form of franchising where they partner with only established companies in a B2B arrangement.
These companies are usually grocery stores, colleges, bookstores, hospitals, hotels, airports, and resorts.
venues looking to generate more money from their existing land and with exclusive space to offer.
The compensation is identical to that of franchising.
Starbucks sells equipment, packaging, supplies, coffees, teas, and food at wholesale quantities to licensed stores who then resell those products to customers at higher retail prices.
This is why some Starbucks stores won't accept your gift cards, they'll have different prices, and they won't participate in rewards.
If you've ever seen a Starbucks that's inside a Target, a Safeway, an airport, or a train station, that's a licensed store.
Partnering with other businesses helps in not just getting Starbucks into exclusive, desirable venues that are not publicly available, but also to maintain control.

In the various fast food companies we've covered in past seasons, like Burger King, McDonald's, and KFC, individuals who are running franchises are much more liable to subvert standards, rules, and regulations to make the most out of their primary investment.

Starbucks has greater confidence and lower risk in these B2B arrangements as established companies have little incentive to cut corners or jeopardize their brand, especially as Starbucks to them is just safe supplemental income and not their primary business.

The physical areas that licensed Starbucks stores occupy in airport terminals, big supermarkets, train stations, and college campuses are by nature isolated venues, which reduces competition with the corporate stores for customers and eliminates cannibalization.
Under a renewed emphasis on customer experience and product quality from 2008 to 2017, Starbucks roared back to success, with revenue skyrocketing from $10.3 billion to $22.3 billion.

The CPG business, made up of the Via instant coffee mixes K-Cups and ready-to-drink bottled frappuccinos, Evolution Fresh juices, and Tivana, grew from $674 million in 2010 to a $2 billion business by 2017.
The CPG business enjoyed 40-plus percent operating margins over multiple years.
Despite a near 200% increase in sales over seven years, the CPG business accounted for at most just 11% of Starbucks total revenue in a single year.
Revenue to Starbucks from licensed stores in the form of royalties, fees, and wholesale sales was even smaller, accounting for on average just 9% of revenue.
The biggest revenue stream by far has been the direct food and beverage sales from company-operated stores, which stood for 80% of revenue on average from 2008 to 2017.
Upon reestablishing Starbucks' leadership in coffee, Howard resumed expansion.
In the eight years between 2009 to 2017, Starbucks stores worldwide grew 50% from 16,000 to 27,000 locations.
Company-operated locations scaled by 40% from 8,800 to 13,000 locations, whereas licensed Starbucks stores grew by 60% from 7,800 to over 14,000 stores in the same period.
Licensed stores were more important for cost-efficient international expansion and less needed for domestic growth.
Starbucks in North America would scale at a much slower pace from 11,000 to 16,000 locations as the majority of the domestic fleet would remain company-owned and operated.
Overseas, Starbucks grew from 5,500 stores to over 10,000 stores across Europe and Asia, with licensed stores making up the majority.
Starbucks retail business, on the other hand, is split by geography and not store type, meaning that all stores in Europe, Asia, and America are reported as three separate segments.
In America, the majority of stores are corporate-owned and operated and contribute over 60% of Starbucks' annual revenue.
The operating margins across both licensed and corporate-operated Starbucks in America hovers in the low 20% range.
Wages paid to retail workers were the second highest expense behind rent and raw ingredients by $200- $300 million every year.
In comparison, the European business for Starbucks has been disastrous.
In 2011, net revenue from Starbucks stores in Europe was $1.04 billion, and six years later, net revenue had dropped below $1 billion.

Despite investing more into licensed stores and scaling from 1,800 locations in 2012 to nearly 3,000 locations in 2017, the Europe business had not improved by any meaningful measure in Howard's tenure.
Operating margins for Starbucks in Europe were equally low, hovering at just 9.8% and would drop even lower in the coming years after Howard's exit.
The success of Starbucks in Asia, specifically in China and Japan, has continually masked the underperformance of Europe.
In 2016, Starbucks was operating over 2,000 stores in 100-plus cities across China, with over 500 in Shanghai alone.

Winning China was a long-term strategy that Howard had put into motion back in 2000 before he initially stepped down as he saw the Chinese to be the single largest market for coffee outside of Americans.
China's fast-rising and fast-growing middle class enthusiastically embraced Starbucks over the year, making the country an and valuable profit engine for the coffee chain.
The number of Starbucks stores in Asia exploded from 3,000 to over 7,000 in just five years, with the vast majority of those openings being in China.
The Asia business overall grew from $400 million in 2011 to a $3.2 billion business by 2017.
Starbucks Asia business, which at this point was overrepresented by China, enjoyed operating margins comparable to that of the United States in the low to mid 20% range.
Wages paid to workers in Asia were still the second highest expense behind rent and raw ingredients, but the gap between the two was sizable at $400- $500 million difference every year.
Howard stepped down in 2017, believing Starbucks to be in a good spot to hand off.

It had a strong business in China, a positively trending business in the United States, a foot in emerging markets like juices and tea, an encouraging CPG business, new promising products like the upscale Starbucks Reserve and Nitro Cold Brew, and most of all, a compelling image of a forward-thinking, innovative, fast-growing, socially responsible company that was far more than just a coffee chain.
He handed the reins to his COO Kevin Johnson.

In his four years at the helm and through the pandemic, Kevin prioritized growth in China, sold off Tiavana to Unilever at a loss, and signed away the global rights to market, sell, and distribute any and all Starbucks CPGs like K-Cups and Instant Coffee to Nestle.
Starbucks walked away with a $7 billion check from Nestle and with a profit-sharing stake from future sales, but effectively gave up on its own CPG business.

This was counter to Howard's vision, as the CPG business was one he had built up to improve the company's margin, appearance, and future prospects, all of which had been continually dragged down before by the fundamentals of its retail business.

Starbucks' operating margins over the years had been trending upwards from the low teens in the mid-2000s to the high teens by the late 2010s thanks to the strength of its China business and greater contribution from its CPG business.
Yet following a failed presidential campaign, Howard Schultz could not keep away from his life's work and forced his way back in as CEO in 2022.
This time, the Starbucks that Howard inherited was completely different from the one he had stepped down from four years ago.
In the United States, coffee is no longer the draw for Starbucks.
These days, millennials and Zoomers make up 51% of the customer base.
Over 76% of beverages sold at Starbucks in the United States today are cold drinks, and over 60% of all drinks sold are customized.

This change can be seen on social media, where influencers and customers show off their frighteningly colorful concoctions and stomach-churning creations with record levels of cream, milk, sugar, and artificial flavors.
Quote, cold beverages have surprised us all at Starbucks, but our ability to customize beverages is a significant competitive advantage.

There is no other coffee company anywhere in the world that has our ability to respond instantaneously to a customer's request about customization, nor is there a coffee company that has our ability behind the counter in terms of flavors, syrups, modifiers, foams, etc.
to provide the customer what they want.
It is a weird world that we live in when the largest coffee chain in the world boasts its competitive advantage as having the biggest collection of Tehrani syrups.
When we look at the demands of the Starbucks worker union, their requests are relatively straightforward.
They want protection against no notice terminations, guaranteed hours, and of course, higher base pay starting at $20 per hour for all workers in all states.

Using the company's financials, we can calculate what would happen if these unions were to succeed and if Starbucks was forced to raise the salaries of workers in the United States from $15 an hour today to $20.
From a pure cash perspective, given that Starbucks takes home $3 billion every year in net income, paying $5 more per hour per worker is clearly possible.
The question is more of what is the cost to Starbucks margins and by extension their image.
We start with what we know.
We know that a Starbucks worker in the United States on average earned $15 an hour in 2022.
We also know that Starbucks employed 248,000 retail workers and its company-operated stores in the United States.
There are a total of 35,000 Starbucks stores worldwide today, with 18,000 of those being corporate-owned and operated locations, And 10,000 of those 18,000 are stores in America.
10,000 company-owned and operated stores divided by 35,000 total stores tells us that company-owned and operated locations in the United States represent 56% of all Starbucks stores in the world.
Starbucks states that it paid out $8.1 billion in 2022 in wages for retail workers.

Given the representation of corporate-operated stores in North America, we can assume that 56% of worker wages, or $4.5 billion, was paid out amongst the 248,000 retail workers that Starbucks employed in the United States.
The remaining $3.6 billion in wages went to paying the retail workers in Europe and Asia, which at a quick glance seems logical.
Retail workers in Europe on average have higher than U.S.
compensation while workers in Asia earn compensation that's significantly lower than the West.
Plus, we know that Starbucks' European in business is much smaller than that of Starbucks Asia business, both in scale and revenue contribution.
Next, we assume that the average Starbucks worker in the United States worked 25 hours a week and worked 48 weeks in a single year for a total of 1,200 billable work hours.

We divide our $4.5 billion in US retail worker wages by the number of workers in the United States and then by the number of total billable work hours every year to get the hourly compensation per worker.
Our final output of $15.40 matches what we know, which is that the average worker compensation at Starbucks in the United States that year was roughly $15 an hour.

If we repeat the same exercise but this time we set the hourly pay to the union's demand of $20 an hour and work in reverse, holding everything consistent, we see that the total wages in 2022 would have been 16% higher at $9.5 billion if the unions had taken over.

If we apply this difference of $1.38 billion more in operating expenses, we can see how Starbucks' operating margin in 2022 would have dropped from 14% to 10%, which is an operating margin that's comparable with full-service restaurants and lower than even Chipotle.

Even if we say that our calculations are off and that an increase to $20 per hour only results in a 6-9% bump in annual total wages and not 16%, the operating margin still goes down by 1-2% and moves closer towards single digits.

When we strip away all the top-line growth and corporate marketing, Starbucks can't hide the reality that at its core, its economics are fundamentally the same as a restaurant, with ingredient costs at 30%, labor and rent at 50%, and the remaining chewed up by administrative overhead, leaving a company with respectable cash flow, stable income, but perpetually low margins.
When China went into a multi-year lockdown during and after the pandemic, the Starbucks Asia business went down with it.
This put greater pressure on the American Starbucks business to perform and to compensate for both the underperforming European business and the slow openings across Asia.
Without its CPG segment, Starbucks is now exclusively reliant on its core retail business for both income and a growth story.

The pressure to maintain profits in Starbucks' American business is further exacerbated with the uncertainty of China, who has clearly demonstrated that it's the government who runs the show there, and companies will operate as they deem fit, which is liable to change any time.
The threat of unions, even if it seems distant and small at the moment, is one too great for Starbucks to ignore, especially in the company's most reliable and highest-grossing geography.
fee.
Unions would not only increase labor costs significantly, but also make them fix costs and drop Starbucks margins overnight into single digits.

And the longer that Starbucks operating margins hover in the low teens or worse drops into the single digits, the more the company's fundamentals will look like any run-of-the-mill food and beverage business.

And the harder it will become for Starbucks to maintain its image as a socially responsible, forward-thinking, fast-growing company with great future potential deserving of praise, recognition, and high P.E.
ratios.

Business is as much optics as it is product, and if crushing unions and suppressing worker wages is the difference between being seen as a high-flying, high-potential, innovative industry leader versus a top-heavy, conventionally fragile, maturing, legacy food service business, Starbucks, like any big corporation, will do so without hesitation.

title: How Cruises Make More Profits Than Airlines
note: Business explainer, not a character story: setup of a counterintuitive industry, a tour through three company strategies with numbers, then costs and a closing race framing.
sections: Why cruises sell spectacle and who rides them
Two revenue streams: tickets and onboard spend
Royal Caribbean: thrills and Coco Cay
lines: Speed and efficiency rule every aspect of modern life.
With so much information online, anyone can plan a vacation and fly to any destination with an itinerary that matches their interests, schedule, and budget.
With the commoditization of air travel, the destination matters far more than the journey.
People in first class share the same sentiment as the people in the economy.
Everyone wants to get off the plane as fast as possible to maximize their time at the destination and to minimize the time spent getting there.
The travel industry has adjusted to this change as resorts, tour guides, agencies, hotels, and airlines now all compete on how fast they can get you to where you want to go.
Yet there remains one business who continues to insist that the journey is just as important as the destination.
That is the cruise ship.
Maritime travel is a difficult sell in the 21st century.
A flight from New York to Barcelona takes 8 hours, whereas the same route by ship would be 8 to 10 days.
The advantages of air travel in efficiency and speed are so significant that cruises know they can't just rely on nice ocean views to get customers.
As a result, cruises are more than just floating hotels that serve food and move slowly on the sea.
To reduce conflict with airlines, cruises strategically specialize in routes to remote tropical destinations that fit the fantasy of sea travel like the Caribbean, the Bahamas, and Ibiza.
They also offer just about every recreational activity on planet Earth to not just help pass the time, but to make the journey so excessively stimulating that passengers have no excuse to be bored.

Cruise ships these days boast restaurants, bars, bowling alleys, water parks, Broadway musicals, basketball courts, mini golf, comedy shows, swimming pools, rock climbing, ice skating, casinos, movie theaters, go-karts, nightclubs, laser tags, and even arcades.

Throw in unlimited booze where adults can get hammered every morning and bottomless french fries and endless pizza that kids can gorge on every night in a transient low-stakes environment, it makes sense why cruises would lean on spectacle and excess for mainstream appeal.
Beyond the onboard consumption and extravaganza, cruises are traditionally most popular with older travelers.
Over 50% of cruise passengers every year are between the ages of 50 to 70 plus.
Elderly retirees not only have the time and money, but also value the low stress and convenience that cruises uniquely provide.
On a cruise, you get to visit many destinations and countries in a single trip.
You don't need to deal with repacking luggage, checking into different hotels, and commuting to and from different airports.
You get a private room to call home for the entire trip, and the boat serves as a one-stop shop for everything that you would need.
Dining, exercising, lounging, shopping, and entertaining.
When you get to your destination, you get some time to explore the land on your own, but everything offshore and off the boat can and will be arranged if you don't want to plan anything.
Thanks to James Cameron, people all around the world are familiar with cruises and have a solid baseline for what the experience would be like, short of crashing into an iceberg.
Yet despite the high awareness and nearly three decades after the release of the Titanic, cruises remain a niche market with low penetration.
In 2019, the airline industry carried 4.5 billion passengers on 42 million flights around the world.
In comparison, there were 29 million cruise passengers, which was a record high for the industry.
Over 50% of passengers who ride cruises every year are Americans.
Even if we add up all the passengers that come from Asia, Europe, South America, and the Middle East, the rest of the world combined doesn't match the volume of cruise passengers from North America.
By these numbers, cruises are very much an American phenomenon, but even then, it's reported that only a third of Americans have ever gone on a cruise.
Industry insiders promote these statistics every year, stating that cruises are a uniquely fast-developing, under-penetrated leisure market with significant growth potential.

The collective belief is that continued investment in onboard innovation, in the form of food, rooms, and entertainment, that no one would think possible to be on a ship like roller coasters, ice skating rinks, go-karts, water parks, and 4D movie theaters will help move the needle, bring in more passengers, and strengthen the value prop of cruises for travelers of all ages, not just the elderly.
The cruise industry is an oligopoly run by three players, Royal Caribbean, Carnival, and Norwegian Cruise Line.
In this episode, we'll cover the business of cruises and dive into these three companies who each have their own strategy and go after travelers at very different price points.
Out of the three major players, Carnival is the most commercially successful.
Before the pandemic, Carnival grossed $20.8 billion in 2019, which was over twice the amount of revenue of Royal Caribbean and over three times as much money as Norwegian cruise lines.
Throughout the pandemic, Carnival has maintained its lead with $12 billion in sales versus Royal Caribbean's $8 billion and Norwegian's $4 billion.
dollars.
Carnival is the largest cruise company in the world, but its success is not just a case of having more ships at sea than its competition.
Historically, cruises were positioned like the Titanic as luxury voyages for sophisticated travelers.
Carnival was the first company to throw that script out of the window, to undercut its competition, to optimize her volume, and to design for simple affordable fun over high-end excess.
Rather than appealing to the elderly traveler, Carnival targets younger demographics.

The company has wielded hip marketing for decades in order to reshape the perception of cruises from formal, serious, posh multi-week commitments into simple, casual, rowdy, affordable fun for just a few days.
With taglines like fun for all, Carnival's message is to not take cruises so seriously.
The company will happily bundle food and entertainment into your ticket, so you walk away with the best deal, and Carnival's reputation holds as the party boat with the lowest prices in the industry.

Carnival's volume and value approach has clearly been successful as the company carries the most passengers with over 12 million passengers every year compared to Royal Caribbean's 6 million and Norwegian's 2 million.
Cruises make money in two ways.
The first and primary revenue stream is through ticket sales.

Cruise tickets aren't charged by entry, rather they're priced and presented like hotels where passengers pay for a nightly rate for a specific room on the ship that lasts for the entirety of their trip.

The rate depends on room type, if it's a suite, if it has a balcony, how big the room is, if it's on the upper deck, and what section of the boat it's on, with the middle being the most desirable, along with the usual variables like the number of guests, the length of the trip, and the destination.
The ticket is what locks down your room, grants access to amenities, and is the biggest cost in any cruise trip.
The second main income stream for cruise companies is the sale of onboard goods and services.
Cruise ships operate like airports, stadiums, concerts, nightclubs, and movie theaters, as venues where customers have no choice but to pay high markups for basic goods.

The same way that flightgoers, ravers, and moviegoers are stuck paying $4 to $6 for soda or $8 to $10 for popcorn, cruise ships do the same with a significantly broader range of products over a longer period of time and on customers with deeper pockets and a greater appetite to spend.

While tickets include access to amenities and entertainment, cruise Cruise ships separately sell beverages, essentials, internet, spas, merchandise, photo shoots, laundry services, casino credits, arcade tokens, spirits, candy, beauty products, watches, shore excursions, jewelry, and art.

While theaters, concerts, airports, stadiums, and nightclubs can only monetize for the few hours in which their guests are at their venues, cruise passengers are stuck on the boat for days or weeks at a time.
This enables cruises to continuously monetize its passengers around the clock for anything and everything.
Once you're on board, the goal is to get you to keep spending.
If you don't like the price for a drink, for Wi-Fi, for sunscreen, or for a pair of sunglasses, well too bad.
What's on the ship is your only option until the boat arrives at its destination.
It's an interesting extreme compared to airports, which generally maintains some facade of competition with multiple vendors.
If you don't like what's being sold at one place, you can always try a different store or terminal.
In comparison, cruise companies own and operate nearly every single store on their ships.
Not just the ones selling the drinks and souvenirs, but also the same casinos, gift shops, candy stores, laundromats, spas, jewelry stores, restaurants, and even those shore excursions.
This way, the cruise directly captures every dollar on every onboard sale in full for themselves with no competition.
The few shops on cruise ships that are operated by third-party external vendors must pay up a percentage of their gross sales so the cruise company still nets in every transaction.
The house always wins and that is very much true in the world of cruises with high markups, broad cross-sell opportunities, and onboard monopolies.
Carnival's value strategy means that they include most of the food and amenities into their tickets.

carnival passengers can feast on unlimited tacos, burritos, chicken sandwiches, noodles, stir-fry, barbecue, soft-serve, pasta, pizza, fries, and burgers, even ones from the mayor of Flavortown all day every day on the boat for no added cost.

There are some a la carte options, but for the vast majority of budget-conscious travelers, the free inclusion of copious and endless amounts of comfort food in an already cheap ticket makes carnival an irresistible deal.
While food is Included beverages aren't so.
if you want soda beer juices cocktail or wine by the glass you'll have to pay separately or buy packages.
Unlimited soda and juice starts at $10 a day or unlimited alcohol at $60 a day.
You don't get to choose which days that you want unlimited drinks.
despite being presented as daily rates These packages are all-or-nothing expenses.

They're charged in one lump sum based on the total number of days in your trip Now that we've covered the two ways in which cruises make money, tickets and the sales of goods and services on board, we can understand how Carnival's strategy drives its commercial performance.
Carnival's revenue has exceeded over $10 billion every year from 2010 to 2019.
Passenger tickets are the largest income stream and make up a majority of Carnival's revenue, accounting for nearly 75% of the company's revenue every year since 2010.
Because of the company's orientation towards value and their generous bundling, there's naturally less passenger demand for onboard goods and services.

Sales of onboard goods and services are still a respectable income stream, having grossed nearly $5 billion every year from 2010 to 2019 and representing on average 33% of the company's annual revenue.
Between 2010 and 2019, the average Carnival passenger spent a total of $1,529 per trip, so that's the ticket and onboard purchases combined.
The total spend of Carnival passengers has remained consistent year-over-year in the past 13 years, even during the pandemic.
We can see just how much Carnival values volume over margin.
The average cost of a Carnival trip in 2022 was $1,580, which is only a dollar or so less than the cost of a trip back in 2010.
For context, a dollar in 2010 was worth a dollar and 34 cents in 2022.
So despite a 34% decrease in dollar value, Carnival is charging the same prices today as it was 12 years ago.
The interesting story here is that the average passenger spend on Carnival was going down even before the pandemic.
In the period between 2010 and 2017, where passenger spend dropped from $1,581 to $1,443, Carnival carried more than 3 million new customers.
The number of passengers on Carnival cruises grew from 9.1 million in 2010 to 12.4 million by 2017.
The average ticket price steadily decreased from $1,211 in 2010 to $1,096 by 2019.
Onboard spend remained consistent for nearly 8 years, hovering at $350 per passenger.
Every $1 that a passenger spent on their Carnival ticket translated to an additional $0.30 of spend on board.
If lowering ticket prices while bundling in more food means a better chance of bringing in new passengers and getting existing ones to come back, Carnival will happily do so.
Cruise ships are built from scratch and are customized for every company.

If you want ice skating rinks over there, basketball courts over here, then putting rooms here, restaurants over there, and then an infinity pool over there, these are all things that have to be built during the construction of the ship and can't be tacked on after.
A new cruise ship costs roughly a billion dollars, over twice the cost of a new Boeing 747.
And while a Boeing 747 can be built in two months, a cruise ship can take anywhere from three to five years from order to completion.
Cruises are simultaneously so niche and so expensive that Carnival's current-day fleet of 26 ships makes it the industry leader at scale.
Carnival also offers the most home ports in the United States, which reinforces appeal with budget-conscious Americans.
Carnival passengers can drive to a point of departure nearby rather than shelling out extra for a separate plane ticket just to get on the boat.
Despite significantly lower passenger volumes and costly assets, cruise companies surprisingly enjoy great bottom lines.
Carnival's annual operating margin, which one might predict to be in the single digits as the value play in a niche market hovers in the mid-teens at 15%.
A 15% annual operating margin is higher than that of American Airlines, nearly double that of United Airlines, and on par with the most valuable airline in the world in Delta.
If Carnival is simple, affordable fun, then Norwegian Cruise Lines is the opposite in elegance and sophistication at a premium.
NCL believes that it's marketing, not cost, that should drive demand.
The company's philosophy is that if customers want a good deal, then they should book their cruises early, but prices should always go up, not down.
NCL ships are designed with a modern and reserved aesthetic that contrasts from the rowdy backyard pool party vibe of Carnival.
Norwegian cruises are more general purpose with a broader range of dining and entertainment options to appease all generations.
For the young, NCL provides go-karts, teen lounges, dance parties, laser tags, and water slides.
For the older crowd, they offer musicals, spas, casinos, live music, acrobatic shows, and long outdoor promenades that stretch up to a quarter of a mile to enjoy the ocean view from.
Despite leaning upscale, NCL makes every effort to message that they're not pretentious or uptight.
The average cruise ship carries between 2,000 to 4,000 passengers and crew alone is another 500 to 1,000 bodies.
If all 3,000 passengers were to eat dinner or to attend the same show at the exact same time, the traffic and crowds would be catastrophic.
Cruise companies avoid this very problem by controlling passenger flow through time slots and seat assignments.
Norwegian throws this convention out the window with its quote-unquote freestyle cruising, where their passengers can dine whenever and wherever they want with no dress code.
While Carnival centers on basic comfort foods, Norwegian puts greater emphasis on dining innovation to drive margin and onboard spend over volume and value.
NCL ships feature a diverse range of specialty foods and restaurants that passengers would not be able to easily find on other cruises.
Foods like grilled ribeye, truffle fries, sea bass, veal shank, risotto, Brazilian barbecue, sushi, lobster, tapas, teppanyaki, and gelato.
These specialty restaurants are not bundled into tickets and are not the standard grab-and-go or endless buffets.
Instead, each dish is made and charged to order in a fancy sit-down experience, and Norwegian offers no packages for unlimited dining.
The dining package that passengers can purchase for their trip on Norwegian cruises is a set of limited credits that values each meal at $30 to $50 per person, not including tip.
When it comes to accommodations, NCL's rooms are not as spacious as carnivals, but Norwegian makes up for its smaller room sizes with greater diversity.
A single NCL ship has over 35 different types of rooms.

By offering so many room types, the company can sell tickets at a wide range of price points without relying on discounts and flash sales, from a bare-bones 135-square-foot interior cabin that has no windows for the budget solo traveler to the multi-room grand suite for the family that wants to splurge.
To emphasize comfort and elegance, Norwegian also sells exclusivity and privacy at a price.
The Haven is an exclusive area on NCL ships which have rooms and amenities that are sectioned off from the rest of the passengers.
There are only a few rooms available at the Haven and they're a lot more expensive.
But travelers who choose to live at the Haven get to enjoy private pools, courtyards, lounges, bars and restaurants, along with hot tubs and a personal butler.
You get to stay away from the crowds, the loud noises, and the long lines with this smaller cruise within a cruise experience as regular passengers can't enter the Haven.
While NCL's strategy is to lead with quality, the company knows it cannot cater exclusively to an upscale audience without offering some value, especially as cruises are still a niche activity.
Norwegian runs a promotion called Free at Sea.

Free at Sea enables the company to maintain its higher ticket prices, to deliberately complicate the shopping experience so travelers don't immediately just settle on the cheapest option, and it lets customers still feel like they're getting a deal when they go with Norwegian.
Anytime you book an NCL cruise, you get a lineup of free perks in free Wi-Fi, free shore excursions, free specialty dining, and free unlimited open bar.
If we take a closer look at the fine print, the bundling is not as generous as the headline would suggest.
Free specialty dining doesn't mean you get to eat veal and lobster for free every night.
Rather, it just means you get two free meals for the duration of your trip.
Once you've spent those credits, the only way to enjoy more would be to buy more meals or to pay the bill.
The free wifi only lasts for 150 minutes, and the free shore excursion is just a one-time $50 coupon.
The only perk that actually seems to live up to its billing is the free unlimited open bar, but even then it has its limits.
If you order any drink over $15 during your trip, the difference is charged to your account.
NCL has 17 ships in its fleet, making it the smallest player by capacity.
With higher ticket prices and an upscale target market, Norwegian carries the fewest travelers out of the big three and has seen the slowest growth in terms of volume.
In the nine years in which Carnival grew over 3 million passengers, NCL grew by just 1.3 million.

While Carnival pushes prices down to drive volume, Norwegian has been pushing prices and spend up in order to compensate for lower volume, and these two differing strategies clearly work in their own ways.
The average total spend of a Norwegian passenger in a single trip grew by nearly 70%, from $1,433 in 2010 to almost $2,400 by 2019.
While the price of a Carnival ticket went down by $100, the price of a Norwegian ticket increased by over $600 per passenger.
Norwegian follows the same high markups of onboard goods and services that Carnival does but to even greater levels.
A standard Wi-Fi package that supports audio and video streaming costs $20 a day on Carnival.
On NCL, the exact same plan and service costs $40 a day.
Unlimited alcohol on Carnival starts at $60 per day, while the same package on NCL is charged at over $100 a day.
Even Norwegian's go-karts are charged at $15 per ride per passenger.

Since most things on Norwegian ships are not actually free, they're not bundled into the ticket, they have higher markups, and they're charged per use, it's no surprise that NCL boasts the highest onboard spend per passenger in the entire industry.
The average Norwegian passenger spent $427 on onboard purchases in 2010 and was spending over $700 per trip by 2019.
Every $1 that a passenger spent on their Norwegian ticket translated to on average $0.40 of additional revenue onboard.
Sales of onboard goods and services have contributed on average 30% of Norwegian's annual revenue and has grown from a $600 million business to a $2 billion revenue stream.
This continuous increase in prices and spend have fueled NCL's topline growth.
The company tripled its overall revenue from $2 billion in 2010 to over $6 billion by 2019.
The stronger margins also translate to better profits for Norwegian with an average annual operating margin of 17% that has reached as high as 20% on certain years.
In every niche, there is always room for someone to corner the high-end market.
In the case of Norwegian, there are clearly a chunk of customers out there who value the specialty restaurants, the onboard sophistication, and the exclusivity enough to pay this premium.
Royal Caribbean is the last mass-market cruise line and is the most well-known out of the big three.
From a positioning standpoint, Royal Caribbean occupies the middle ground between upscale modern elegance and rowdy cheap pool parties.
The company's priority has been on onboard innovation above all else and constantly pushing the envelope on entertainment.

Royal Caribbean boasts amenities like the largest and deepest swimming pool at sea with 30-foot diving platforms, the biggest water park with headfirst slides, an 82-foot tall dome, and even a 40-foot long surf simulator.

The fun continues indoors, where Royal Caribbean ships are decked out with bumper cars, escape rooms, skydiving simulators, carousels, bungee trampolines, and even a slide that drops you down 10 decks on top of all the conventional amenities.
The live shows offered are not just the standard Broadway musicals and comedians, but also feature divers, acrobats, aerialists, and synchronized swimmers.

Royal Caribbean's value prop is that while they don't have the fancy dining of Norwegian or the affordability of Carnival, they'll give you adventure, adrenaline, thrill, and excitement that no one else can.
This has helped Royal Caribbean establish a more vibrant atmosphere compared to other cruise lines as these amenities companies naturally attract thrill-seekers and more sociable travelers.
Beyond the ships, Royal Caribbean's greatest success has been the development and construction of its own private destination, Coco Cay.
The company has invested $250 million to turn an island in the Bahamas into its own private resort to take passenger monetization to record levels.

As we covered earlier, cruise ships continuously monetize passengers for anything and everything when they're on the boats, but when the ship docks, those same passengers are no longer physically available to be monetized once they disembark.
The shore excursions are decent money, but cruise lines really want to milk every single dollar possible from its passengers.
From a psychology standpoint, it makes sense that passengers are generally more frugal and more cost-aware when they're on the boat.
No one wants to blow all their money on stuff on board at sea, and everyone saves up in order to have enough so that they can really go all out when they reach their destination.
For Royal Caribbean, having their own private island and resort as the destination means that the company doesn't lose out on the greater spend that happens on land.
Coco Cay is where the adventure and monetization reaches even greater heights with water parks, zip lines, pools, balloon rides, clubs, restaurants, bungalows, and cabanas.
And of course, some of these are free, but most of them are not.
Because Royal Caribbean owns every part of the resort and the underlying land, including all the sand and trees, the company can once again sell and charge anything it wants.
While all cruise companies mark up the goods and services that they sell on board, those prices must remain in a reasonable range relative to its competition.
In the case of Cocoa Key, there's really no comparable.
When a Royal Caribbean cruise arrives at Cocoa Key, passengers are essentially walking from one monopoly on water into an even more aggressive monopoly on land.
For instance, Royal Caribbean charges between $1,500 to $4,000 just to rent a cabana for a day.
The rental cost of a cabana can be just as much if not more than the cost of the cruise itself.
This is why there is no public pricing available for Coco Cay.
Prices for island amenities are only revealed upon booking and they fluctuate daily.
Coco Cay serves over 10,000 guests every day who are all brought to the single destination from various Royal Caribbean ships around the world, which enables true economies of scale for the company.
Royal Caribbean's passenger volume sits in between Norwegian and Carnival, as the company has grown from 4.5 million passengers in 2010 to 6.5 million by 2019.
Spend on Royal Caribbean cruises is marginally higher than Carnival, as total spend per passenger grew from $1,472 in 2010 to $1,671 by 2019.
Ticket cost per passenger on Royal Caribbean average only at $100 more than Carnival.
Onboard spend is slightly higher on Royal Caribbean as the cruise line boasts a wider assortment of specialty restaurants like Johnny Rockets and fewer complimentary options.
With marginal differences in spend and pricing, Royal Caribbean's bottom line is in the same ballpark as Carnival with an average annual operating margin of 14%.
The final interesting part about cruise companies is how they keep their operating expenses low.

As we touched on earlier, each single cruise ship requires a crew of 500 to 1,000 workers to keep everything running smoothly, sailing the boat, entertaining guests, cooking food, cleaning up, and running the attractions.
To have a large workforce, tens of thousands of employees who must be fed, clothed, housed, and who are stuck on a boat away from home for months on an end, these workers must be well compensated.
And the reality is that they are, just not by Western standards.
Cruise payroll accounts for less than 25% of total operating expenses for all three companies.
In the various industries that we've covered over the past three seasons, labor costs are conventionally 35% or higher.
The simple answer here is offshoring.
Royal Caribbean doesn't have a single US-based employee working on their ships.
Instead, the vast majority of the shipboard workforce are people from the Philippines, Indonesia, and India.
These international workers, who make the artificial environment and manufactured magic of cruises come alive for passengers, are paid on average just $14,400 a year.
On Carnival, the annual wage for a shipboard employee is $25,000.
Norwegian, who has always emphasized its great premium service with smaller crew-to-passenger ratios, pays the highest at $26,000 per worker per year.
These labor costs are offset by the automatic 18-20% daily gratuities that each cruise company charges each passenger based on their room type as a prepaid line item during booking.
When passengers use an onboard service during their trip like ordering a drink, eating at a restaurant, or getting a massage, they're heavily encouraged to also tip then.

title: How Axon Became Wall Street's Hottest Stock
note: Company case study in three eras: blunders, learning via forced taser cam, then dominance via software and subscriptions; closes on a lesson about picking a space.
sections: Policing, body cams and picking the right space
Era one: Taser blunders of the 2000s
Slump, lawsuits, failed military and animal-control bets
Era two: Evidence.com and body cams
lines: Law enforcement takes different forms around the world.
If you go to the UK, Western Europe, and China, you'll see mass surveillance everywhere you go, which went on reach and scalability at the cost of privacy.
In the US, you'll find a modest amount of cameras, but a massive presence of conventional boots-on-the-ground policemen who are armed to the teeth.

In America, policing is a $100 billion annual business that has grown in power for decades in a country with high gun ownership, weak infrastructure, archaic legislation, mass incarceration, and a society rooted in individualism, classism, and racial tensions.
Yet these days, law enforcement agencies across the West are undergoing a shakeup from opaque, omnipotent, unchecked organizations into ones of transparency and accountability.
Policing these days can be seen in the endless stream of body cam footage that lands on the internet.
Whenever you watch those viral videos, look at the top right, and 10 times out of 10, it will say Axon, the one company that has made this revolution possible.
In business theory, some say that great companies are not about flawless execution and perfect prediction of the future, as in reality, no organization at any scale can do either.
Every company has dirty laundry, and no amount of capital can force the future, at least not a profitable one.
This school of thought suggests that the most important ingredient to success in business is picking the right space to be in.
You can tread water, develop expertise, and even make lots of mistakes along the way.
But once the market trends in your direction, you can quickly capitalize on those tailwinds, find your footing, and snowball that momentum into billions of dollars.
Axon is a modern embodiment of this theory.
The company's rise can be broken down into three eras.
In the 2000s, Axon was in its first era as a struggling, directionless single product startup that was under fire from the media, public, and politicians.

Then, in the 2010s, a series of high-profile killings by law enforcement in the United States ignited nationwide protests, surfaced long-buried issues of discrimination and police brutality, and placed police around the world under the spotlight.
American lawmakers, who were caught between the people that they serve and the police that they depend on, tried to seek neutrality in data.

With public pressure for accountability, the demand for full-color, high-resolution footage and modern recording solutions skyrocketed beyond static dashcams and the conventional grainy public surveillance.

This demand was further amplified as several killings like the shooting of Tamir Rice ended without judgment as the public, the lawyers, and even federal investigators could not make sense of the little low-quality footage that was available.

Incident recording went from a nice-to-have to a must-have, not just for police departments in the U.S., but also those abroad, as governments overseas faced similar scrutiny about their own agencies and the absence of such data to drive accountability.
These tailwinds propelled Axon, who had been building software and wearable technology into its second era of prosperity in the 2010s.

And as killings by law enforcement have persisted into the 2020s, political pressure has continued with global efforts to reform policing with greater emphasis on de-escalation, non-lethal force, and transparency over the traditional intimidation, oppression, and broken windows.

Axon has held onto this rocket ship to its present-day era as a powerhouse where every single interaction that happens every day with law enforcement is recorded with an Axon body cam and stored in Axon's cloud platform.

In this episode, we'll cover the three eras of Axon and how this one company in two decades transformed from a struggling, directionless, single-product startup into a critical hardware and software essential for revolutionizing law enforcement around the world.
In the 2000s, Axon was in its first era of blunders and had a different name.
The company was a small 200-person startup by the name of Taser International that manufactured and sold one product in tasers.

Making one product is not a problem, as early-stage companies can really only afford to focus on one thing at a time, but this singular focus can be devastating if everyone happens to be calling for your product to be banned.
While nowadays everyone enthusiastically endorses the use of tasers over guns and law enforcement to preserve life, this was not the case 20 years ago.
Back in the 2000s, tasers were controversial.
The idea of shocking a human through 50,000 volts of electricity was unacceptable to many.

After a string of high-profile incidents where suspects died soon after being tasered, activists and watchdogs pounced, asserting that these deaths were part of a concerning national pattern, that the electricity caused cardiac arrests in the healthy human heart, and that tasers were just as dangerous as firearms.
While the independent autopsies officially pinned the cause of death in many of these incidents to drug overdose, that didn't stop the media and public from pouring on their outrage and condemnation.
The taxpayer pressure quickly snowballed into political scrutiny, and in the mid-2000s, Axon found itself in a storm of negative publicity that threatened the company's very existence.

26 states were in active judicial debates and were considering legislation to ban tasers, The DOJ was closely monitoring the situation, and large cities like Chicago were suspending the use of tasers in their police forces, and the SEC had just opened an official investigation into Axon's product safety.
It wasn't just city councils and regulators, but also individuals coming out to take down Axon.

There were wrongful death lawsuits from surviving families that claimed that their loved ones would still be alive if they hadn't been tasered, and lawsuits from police officers who claimed that they suffered injuries after being tasered in training.

And since someone generally needed to volunteer to be tasered during training in order for the entire group to acquire the certification needed to carry tasers on the job, these lawsuits in particular flowed in at a high volume, attract greater negative publicity, and fanned the flames of controversy.
The premise of the taser had always been a straightforward sell as one of the few non-lethal options on the market for neutralizing a human being.
But its effectiveness in the field has always been inconsistent.
Tasers don't magically shoot electricity, rather they use compressed nitrogen to shoot out two metal darts.
These darts have tips like fish hooks that are designed to pierce clothing and to embed themselves in the skin of the target.
And they're connected to high voltage insulated wires which then transmit the electricity from the taser into the target.
The fundamental challenge is that both darts must penetrate and remain in the skin.

If the target is moving around, if they're wearing thick or baggy clothing, If their arms are flailing around, if a strong wind happens to blow by, then a dart can miss, a wire can become entangled, a dart can get dislodged, and the connection won't be enough to disable the target.
Tasers also have the flexibility to turn into a stun gun up close, but its main use case has always been about neutralizing threats at a distance.
While firearms run on bullets, tasers run on cartridges.
Each cartridge contains two darts, nitrogen, and wires and can only be fired once.
And just like the Taser itself, the cartridges are proprietary and sold separately.
Axon had been on a positive trajectory, growing from $24 million to $67 million in net sales from 2003 to 2004 before sinking in 2005 amidst controversy.
As a single product company, Axon's revenue could be easily broken down into its four SKUs, the Taser X26, the Advanced Taser, the Air Taser, and cartridges.
The Taser X-26 was the newest model that had been sold exclusively to law enforcement and corrections agencies for $799 and was designed for better dart penetration of clothing.
The older advanced Taser sold for $399.
And the Air Taser was a discontinued model that had been designed exclusively for consumers but had failed to make any meaningful traction.
Cartridges were sold at $16 apiece to law enforcement and $30 apiece to civilians.
Cartridges alone were the second highest grossing product in the 2000s, accounting for a quarter of Axon's revenue every year.
The negative press and political heat suddenly plunged Axon into a three-year slump where business was effectively put on hold.
Any tasers that were deployed in the field were put back on the shelf.

America, by nature, is litigious, and Axon fought fire with fire, diverting millions to assemble its own in-house legal and medical teams to save on outside counsel, to conduct its own scientific studies, and to send a message that there would be no easy settlements.

While Axon eventually won as the medical science held up, that the courts ruled that tasers didn't cause 90% of the injuries or deaths, and the investigations were closed without judgment, these legal battles were numerous and drawn out over many years.
In 2004, Axon had been named in 15 lawsuits.
By 2007, that number was 49 and it was only until 2014 did the number of lawsuits dwindle back down to 16 and at that point, over 100 lawsuits had been dismissed in favor of Axon.
Annual SG &A costs ballooned from $7 million a year in 2003 to well over $40 million by 2009, which was 8 to 15 times the company was spending on R &D.
As a lean hardware startup, litigation alone decimated their bottom line into the single digits.
This diversion was not only costly from the monetary sense, but also left the company confused in the direction that it should pursue.
As the heat gradually faded away in the years after 2007, Axon recovered, but revenue continued to fluctuate as the US entered a recession.

The consumer market had failed to show any meaningful progress, as later models in the 2000s designed for private use like the C2 showed even less momentum as civilians opted for simpler and cheaper tools for self-defense like pepper spray.
In the backdrop of the U.S.
invasion of Afghanistan and Iraq, Axon decided to target the military for its growth.
It was a market that was much bigger than law enforcement, that was not as complicated as a municipality, and was not as sensitive as the public.
While the American military certainly had the dollars and the appetite to do business during a recession, their demands were so exacting that it was impossible to satisfy.
The military required wireless tasers that could shoot up to 100 yards, engineering feats that are impossible even two decades later.
The best that Axon could come up with was a rail system where a soldier could attach an under-barrel taser to their rifle, similar to a bayonet or grenade launcher.

a non-lethal landmine that never saw the light of day, the world's first ever electrified shotgun shell, and the Shockwave, a portable crowd control system that would shoot 24 tasers at the push of a button.

The shock wave was quietly discontinued after years of poor sales, the X-Rep shotgun shell was simply too expensive for anyone to use at $180 per shell, and the X-26 remained the company's best-selling product throughout the 2000s.
Law enforcement remained the bread and butter, but Axon had hit a ceiling.
Taser was an established name brand, but growth was inconsistent as the weapon was perceived as viable but not essential for every officer, and Axon was just one vendor out of many.
The tightening of budgets across the public sector made it difficult for Axon to sell, and internal R &D mistakes only exacerbated these challenges.
Tasers had long been criticized for being unforgiving, where if the user missed their only shot or if the dart failed to penetrate past the clothing, the weapon was basically useless.
few officers could afford to reload their taser if the threat was still coming at them.
In response, Axon launched the X3, the first-ever model that allowed a user to fire multiple shots before needing to reload, but the X3 was too bulky and heavy to fit on standard duty belts.
The X3 ended up selling below expectations, the unsold inventory was discarded at a loss, and the older X26 model remained the far more popular option.
After posting operating losses for three consecutive years, Axon desperately sought new sources of revenue.
The military and civilian markets were clearly not sustainable.
The company proposed that there were decent markets that were adjacent to law enforcement where the taser could be lifted and shifted to capture sales with little overhead, like animal control.

Hilariously, the company stated that a wildlife-specific taser could become an essential purchase in places like Alaska or Africa, where governments have to deal with keeping large wild animals away from local populations.

Axon's founder went so far as to publicly suggest that a taser could incapacitate a bear or other large predators, seemingly ignorant of the reality that tasers today were already not consistent at incapacitating humans and that a charging bear is not something anyone should try to take down in the middle of winter with a single-shot, non-lethal, battery-operated weapon.
Thankfully, this idea and product was killed off as quickly as it was mentioned.

To relieve public fears and to protect against taxpayer complaints, governments soon began demanding Axon to build accountability into the taser itself in order to ensure appropriate use of the weapon.
Law enforcement leaders followed this mandate from their political superiors as it was ultimately these local lawmakers that approved their budgets.
To comply, Axon built the taser cam, a backwards compatible $400 accessory that would record video and audio even in low light.
But a live demonstration was not enough.
It became a hard requirement for several major agencies that every taser be outfitted with a taser cam before it could be deployed and used by any officer.
The same rigor existed overseas.
The highly desirable and strategic French National Police and Jean de Marie made it clear that no adoption of tasers would be considered without taser cam.
For a startup stretched in so many different directions and struggling to execute, the taser cam itself was a brilliant piece of engineering.
The accessory could record up to an hour of local video and audio, and most importantly, officers never had to hit a record button.

As soon as an officer switched off the safety on their taser, the taser cam would automatically start recording, capturing what was happening in the moments before, during, and after the taser was fired.
Negative publicity, lawsuits, political scrutiny, R &D mistakes, failed products, lack of growth, and now a regulatory pressure for a camera were all challenges that Axon endured in its first era.
Yet many of these problems had more to do with the immaturity and inexperience of the company rather than poor leadership and negligence.
Axon's blunders in the 2000s were painful lessons that would in hindsight plant the necessary seeds for the future and spur the company onto an era of prosperity in the 2010s.
Axon emerged from the 2000s with plenty of scar tissue and a better understanding of how to build products.
The company overhauled its product development processes and required continuous validation from real-world law enforcement during the design of every product and not after.
This reduced manufacturing risk and ensured a better reception of newer taser models on their launch like the DoubleShot X2 and the UltraSmall X26P, which both outsold the X3 by a significant margin.
And despite the regulatory mandate, taser cams were more of a compliance add-on than anything else and contributed less than 5% of the company's annual revenue in the 2010s.
Yet what TaserCams taught Axon was that video would be useful not just in the rare moments in which a Taser was deployed, but really in any law enforcement encounter.
The rush to stick cameras onto Taser's had introduced new unaddressed issues like data extraction and management.
The videos on each TaserCam had to be manually exported.

the data was piling up into mountains of gigabytes, and no one had really thought through where these digital files should be stored, how long these files should be kept, how to protect this data against manipulation, how to back up this data, and how to organize it all in a world still ruled by pen and paper.
These unaddressed problems were Axon's opportunities.
In 2010, Axon launched ATC and Evidence.com, the company's first ever wearable hardware and software product.
Police officers could wear ATC as a headcam that would capture audio and video on a 10-hour battery and even included a separate touchscreen display for real-time playback in the field.

Evidence.com was a turnkey service where agencies could upload and manage the footage from their taser cams and ATCs without having to worry about storage, security, and manipulation, with Axon providing the clear chain of custody for each file.
Evidence.com was not some innovative feat of engineering.
From a tech stack perspective, it was just a custom interface sitting in front of AWS S3.
But for many agencies, Evidence.com was their first ever exposure to cloud infrastructure.
As is the case with all first-generation hardware, the ergonomics of ATC left a lot to be desired.
The company went through multiple iterations in an attempt to find the right blend of comfort and convenience that would convince officers to put cameras on their heads in the early 2010s.
At the time, there was no political pressure for this kind of recording or accountability.
Law enforcement agencies weren't against the idea of wearing cameras, but they also didn't see the impetus or have the urgency to adopt.
Quote, the important point here is that the value prop that we've put forth has been very well received.
We're seeing a near universal acceptance that these types of systems are coming.
I cannot recall a customer that we have met that has disputed that this is the future.
They all recognize that video systems are coming and believe they will be standard issue for every officer in the future.
Obviously, however, there are some different viewpoints on how long that process will take.

There were some early adopters who saw the value of Axon's newest products in helping modernize evidence rooms, in reducing case prep time, and protecting officers against false complaints, but these progressive police chiefs were few and far between.
From a distance, there wasn't much data to suggest that this path would have a big payout.

Both of Axon's products launched with very little fanfare and generated less than a million dollars in sales in their first two years as the company found selling software to be a lot more complicated than selling tasers.
But at this point, Axon had built up enough expertise within the space to feel confident that they were onto something, even if they hadn't quite nailed the implementation yet.
Quote, our new products clearly have the potential to be comparable or frankly, significantly larger than our core taser business.
We continue to believe in these signs in the market and we believe that as we look back in a few years, this will have been an excellent opportunity for our business to have moved into.

It leverages our core business relationships in law enforcement, our core training capabilities, our hardware innovation, and our new software development capabilities that we have built for the last few years.
Yet not every police officer carried a taser, not every taser had a taser cam, and not every taser with a taser cam was fired.
Evidence.com improved quickly through the 2010s as Axon turned their product into a single pane of glass.
The company added tagging, geospatial mapping, customizable retention policies, better playback, multimedia search, and opened up the platform to ingest digital files from any and all sources.
Axon continued to make mistakes along the way, but because the company was building in a space that no one else was looking into, these mistakes were invaluable and helped them ship better products.
Axon realized that it made no sense for them to be building wearable computers and wearable cameras at the same time, so touchscreen displays were scrapped from future iterations of the ATC.

When headcams failed to catch on, Axon tried mounting the camera on glasses instead with Axon Flex, pushing that the resolution and POV captured at eye level would be superior to any conventional body cam or dash cam.
Axon Flex only generated $4-6 million a year in sales, but this was still progress.
After much experimentation and a lack of acceptance for any other form factor, Axon settled for building the best body cameras it could.
Demand suddenly skyrocketed in the mid-2010s as the killings of Michael Brown and others created urgency for such technology overnight.
At this point, Axon's body cameras were so far ahead of its competition.
They could be customized to automatically start recording when sirens were activated, when doors were opened, or when a gun was removed from a holster.
Axon's differentiation from its competition was that it was providing a connected hardware and a managed software solution as a single vendor, not just one or the other.
Axon's products were managed modular services and not the conventional, complicated, fragile, monolithic on-prem software of traditional vendors.
Even when Google Glass came out, the company didn't lose any sleep.
Quote, the progression towards cloud computing and wearable technology is actually faster than we had previously anticipated.
We strongly feel that the long-term play here is not with the cameras and the hardware, but rather with the cloud platform Evidence.com.

If an agency chooses to use Google Glass or any other hardware to collect evidence, they're still going to need a digital evidence management system, and Evidence.com is the most flexible and accommodating system to handle digital evidence from multiple sources.
To paraphrase Bill Clinton, it's not the camera, stupid.
It's the back-end, and that's where we're focused.
Axon's revenue soared from $90 million a year in 2011 to $530 million by 2019.
Evidence.com alone climbed from $30 million in 2010 to a $130 million cloud business by 2019 which was more money than the company made selling cartridges or any single taser model.
