Body cameras surged from a $4 million business in 2015 to a $44 million business by 2019 and at this point, the greater software and sensors market was making as much money as the overall taser business.
While product improvements and direction were integral, these strong results would not have been possible without an improved go-to-market strategy.
At this point, Axon had over a decade of experience selling to agencies to understand all the dynamics and variables needed to close a deal.
Profitability was strong in this second era of prosperity, with a healthy bottom line and a clear allocation towards future investment.
Now in present day, Axon is in its most dominant era as an essential for modern law enforcement around the world.
Scrutiny of police has only intensified to record levels in this decade, with the killings of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and many more.

Political pressure for police reform has followed, with municipalities, lawmakers, and police chiefs now all being held under the microscope to bring greater transparency and oversight through technology.
Sales of body cameras have doubled from $57 million in 2020 to over $124 million by 2022.
Evidence.com has doubled from a $176 million software business in 2020 to $371 million in 2022 with no advertising required.
Axon's moat has proven to be far more robust than just attaching cameras to police officers.
Data extraction, ingestion, and management has proven to be untenable for the few agencies still rolling their own DIY solution.
Any organization still manually exporting videos, clipping locally, and storing them in Google Drive or on local servers have found themselves running back to Axon.
Axon's transformation into a suite of hardware and software solutions has enabled diverse strategies to market penetration.
Law enforcement is not homogenous, as each agency has its own needs.

Small agencies that police small towns or rural areas are generally more interested in tasers, as their officers tend to be closer with their communities, and the risk of complaints is lower, and the opportunity cost of a lethal incident is higher.
On the flip side, large agencies responsible for major cities are more interested in body cams, as the greater transient populations naturally bring a higher probability of incidents and complaints.
Axon's overall revenue has grown from $680 million to $1.2 billion in just two years.
And despite a 20-30% growth year-over-year in the overall taser segment, models and cartridge sales have contributed less and less to the company's top line.
Tasers might seem like an afterthought, but The Weapon has remained a top-three bestseller in the 2020s.
Axon has continued to make the taser more effective with the goal of one day matching the stopping power of a standard-issue 9mm handgun.
While tasers are now widely accepted by the public, they're still not seen as essential by agencies.
The largest and most well-funded police department in the United States that costs over $10 billion every year doesn't see the need for every officer to carry a taser.
Instead, the NYPD, like many major police forces, has an allotment of tasers that it shares amongst a subset of officers.
This gives Axon the confidence that with the right innovation, there is ample room for growth in tasers on a unit basis.

The Taser 10 features better clothing penetration and allows a user to fire up to 10 individual shots on a single cartridge where only two of those shots are needed to land in order to incapacitate the target.
Software and sensors has become the majority contributor to Axon's revenue, doubling in three years from $314 million in 2020 to $658 million by 2022.
The fastest growing product within this segment is Axon Fleet, which is the company's first product built for state agencies like the CHP.
While state troopers in theory need tasers and body cams like everyone else, they have a greater need for in-car ALPRs.
ALPRs are automated license plate readers, which are essential for highway police to identify who's who in a sea of cars.

ALPRs have existed for many years, but they were historically dedicated systems that cost $20,000 to $30,000 up front, which was a luxury that only a few agencies could afford for just a handful of cars in their fleets.
Axon Fleet, in comparison, is sold at a fraction of that cost for $200 per month per vehicle, which is inclusive of the hardware and software.
Axon Fleet doubles as both a dashcam and ALPR, and all of the video footage recorded there naturally flows into evidence.com for storage, processing, and retrieval.
Having made a long-desired technology available at a drastically lower price point, Axon Fleet has grown from $3 million in sales at launch in 2017 to over $60 million by 2022.
Over 90% of Axon's customers today are on a subscription plan.

The Officer Safety Plan is the company's most popular bundle where agencies can get a taser, a body cam, a license for Evidence.com, unlimited storage, and full warranty coverage for $99 to $239 per month per officer.

While this high-end comprehensive plan fits the large agencies, the small agencies with tighter budgets have access to cheaper bundles that are body camera only, taser only, or have less tiers of storage.

Bundling enables Axon to monetize both ends of the market with easy-to-understand value-based pricing, to fly through procurement as a predictable and consistent expense, and to fit flexibly into any government's budget, things that the company learned through trial and error in its first era.

While Axon wins with a reoccurring revenue model that Wall Street loves, subscription customers also benefit by being on a hardware refresh cycle where all their tasers are upgraded every five years and body cameras every two and a half.
Cartridges, however, are not included in subscriptions.
Sales of Taser cartridges continue to account for 15-18% of Axon's overall revenue every year.
With progress in computer vision and machine learning, Axon believes that Evidence.com can become just more than a repository of video footage.
Axon envisions a future that all law enforcement would gladly welcome in which officers spend more time in the field and less time behind a desk.

All an officer would have to do is to wear their body camera to upload those videos onto Evidence.com and the software platform would soon be able to transcribe dialogue, to flag every key moment like swearing, yelling, fighting, weapon discharge, and then pre-populate a police report with all that data.

There's also another world where Evidence.com moves up the chain from just boots on the ground law enforcement and into the greater criminal justice system as a platform for state and federal prosecutors.
The evolution of Evidence.com is like a page straight out of the Silicon Valley playbook.
You start with a moat in hardware, you expand that moat to software, and then all the data that you own as an aggregator becomes a valuable and defensible platform with network effects.
Newer products like Axon Respond, where a police officer can live stream what's happening from their body cam back to dispatch, carry even greater promise of revolutionizing law enforcement.
In a recent school shooting, an officer's Axon body cam live-streamed the situation on the ground to a command center.
When the suspect was subdued, the command center was able to see the situation unfold and call off the SWAT teams in real time.
But in a traditional system where the only information available would be in lagging audio updates over radio, the SWAT teams would have likely rushed in and caused even more chaos at the scene.

The final interesting angle about Axon is that the company has embraced its tailwinds to craft a new identity for itself as a pacifist, as an advocate of both civil rights and law enforcement, as a leader in police reform, and a uniquely profitable tech company.

In a time where Silicon Valley companies are demanding workers to return to office, Axon is doing the opposite, pushing its fully remote job opportunities with the tagline work anywhere, save lives, to win engineering talent from a predominantly liberal workforce.
